lecture_title: Lecture 1: Introduction to RL (CS234, Winter 2019, Emma Brunskill; part 3 adapted from David Silver's intro slides)
one_paragraph_summary: This lecture establishes vocabulary rather than results. It defines reinforcement learning as learning to make good *sequences* of decisions under uncertainty, and isolates four axes — optimization, delayed consequences, exploration, generalization — that it then uses as a coordinate system to separate RL from AI planning (has a model, so no exploration), supervised learning (has labels, one decision, no exploration), unsupervised learning (no labels, no exploration/delay), and imitation learning (learns from others' experience, sidestepping exploration). The second half builds the sequential-decision formalism from the ground up: discrete-time agent/world loop emitting (a_t, o_t, r_t); history h_t as the full interaction record; agent state s_t = f(h_t) as distinct from the true world state; the Markov condition p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) = p(s_{t+1}|h_t,a_t) as the statement that s_t is a sufficient statistic of h_t; and the resulting taxonomy MDP (s_t = o_t) / POMDP (agent must build state from history, beliefs, or an RNN) / bandit (actions cannot influence the next observation). It then names the three components an RL agent may carry — transition-plus-reward model, policy (deterministic π(s)=a or stochastic π(a|s)), value function V^π(s) = E[r_t + γ r_{t+1} + γ² r_{t+2} + ... | s_t = s] — and instantiates all three on a 7-state Mars rover chain with reward +1 at s_1, +10 at s_7, an agent-side transition model that moves with probability 0.5, and V^π computed at γ = 0. The lecture closes on three framing distinctions the rest of the course elaborates: planning vs learning, exploration vs exploitation (including the honest observation that finite-horizon optimal policies are non-stationary and that exploration has zero value on the final decision), and evaluation vs control (with the note that evaluation can be done off-policy from data generated by a different policy, provided that policy was stochastic enough). Nothing is proved; the entire lecture is definitions, a taxonomy, one worked numerical example, and a set of promissory notes.
prerequisites: Probability and statistics: random variables, expectation, conditional distributions, and conditional independence (needed to read the Markov condition as a statement about equality of two conditional distributions)
Basic supervised/unsupervised ML framing: labelled datasets, classification, loss functions, gradient descent, generalization from finite samples
Multivariable calculus and linear algebra at the level of CS229/CS221
Python proficiency (for the assignments, not this lecture)
Enough familiarity with geometric series to know that an infinite discounted sum converges for gamma < 1 with bounded rewards — the lecture never mentions this but silently relies on it
Helpful but not required: having heard the term Markov decision process; a passing acquaintance with active learning / label complexity, for the machine-teaching aside
No prior RL knowledge is assumed

concepts.name: RL in one sentence
concepts.one_line: Reinforcement learning studies how an intelligent agent can learn to make a good sequence of decisions; the three load-bearing words are sequence (many coupled decisions, not one), good (there is a utility/optimality criterion), and learn (the agent does not know in advance how its actions affect the world or which actions pay off, and must acquire that from experience).

concepts.name: Brain-as-decision-organ motivation (Yael Niv's sea squirt)
concepts.one_line: A creature that swims with a primitive brain and one eye as a larva, then anchors to a rock and digests its own brain as an adult, is offered as suggestive evidence that the function of a brain is to guide decisions: once no decisions remain, the brain is dispensable.

concepts.name: The Atari / DQN paradigm shift
concepts.one_line: The DeepMind Atari results (workshop-presented around 2015, Nature 2015) mattered because the agent learned to play Breakout better than humans directly from raw pixel input, moving RL from artificial toy problems to large-scale tasks and marking the start of roughly five years of rapid scaling.

concepts.name: Application breadth
concepts.one_line: Beyond games and robotic grasping/cloth-folding, RL is applied to educational games (Refraction; Mandel, Liu, Brunskill, Popovic, AAMAS 2014), healthcare (seizure-excitability control, Pineau et al.; treatment policies from electronic medical records), and as a general-purpose optimizer inside NLP and vision pipelines where the objective is hard to optimize directly.

concepts.name: The four defining ingredients of RL
concepts.one_line: RL is characterized by the simultaneous presence of optimization (there is a best or at least a very good strategy to find), delayed consequences (an action's payoff may only be revealed much later), exploration (the agent must act to learn), and generalization (the policy must be learned rather than pre-programmed because the input space is astronomically large).

concepts.name: Temporal credit assignment
concepts.one_line: Because outcome feedback is not immediate, the agent faces the credit-assignment problem: determining the causal contribution of each past decision to a later high or low reward — a difficulty largely absent from standard supervised learning.

concepts.name: Censored data / counterfactual unavailability
concepts.one_line: Exploration data is censored in the statistical sense: you receive a reward only for the action you actually took, so the outcome of the untaken action is permanently unobserved (choosing Stanford means never observing the MIT trajectory), and the choices you make also determine what you can subsequently learn about.

concepts.name: Why a policy must be learned rather than programmed
concepts.one_line: A policy maps past experience to an action; writing it as an explicit if-then program over raw Atari-style images is intractable because the number of distinct images is on the order of 256^(100*200*3), which forces both learning from data and some high-level representation that generalizes to unseen configurations.

concepts.name: AI planning vs RL
concepts.one_line: Planning involves optimization, generalization and delayed consequences but not exploration: the dynamics and reward model are given (e.g. the rules of Go), and the entire difficulty is computing a good action sequence from that model with no interaction with the real environment.

concepts.name: Supervised and unsupervised learning vs RL
concepts.one_line: Supervised learning has optimization and generalization but typically neither exploration (the dataset is handed over) nor delayed consequences (one decision per input), and supplies the correct label; unsupervised learning is the same minus labels; RL sits in between, receiving a utility score for the action it chose rather than the true label.

concepts.name: Imitation learning vs RL
concepts.one_line: Imitation learning has optimization, generalization and often delayed consequences but avoids exploration by learning from demonstrations of others; it effectively reduces RL to supervised learning, inheriting supervised tooling but bounded by the demonstration data, and its failure mode is drifting off the demonstrated trajectory into states where no supervision exists (Abbeel/Coates/Ng expert-helicopter work is the canonical early success).

concepts.name: Goal of sequential decision making
concepts.one_line: The agent selects actions to maximize total expected future reward; the expectation matters because the world may be stochastic, this criterion may not always be the right one (motivating distributional and risk-sensitive RL), and achieving it may require strategic behaviour that sacrifices immediate reward for greater long-run reward.

concepts.name: Canonical worked examples of the loop
concepts.one_line: Web advertising (action = which ad, observation = dwell time, reward = click); robot unloading a dishwasher (action = joint movements, observation = kitchen camera image, reward = +1 when no dishes remain on the counter — an intentionally delayed and gameable reward); blood-pressure control (action = prescribe exercise or medication, observation = measured blood pressure, reward = +1 in healthy range, small negative for medication side-effects, 0 otherwise).

concepts.name: Artificial tutor reward-specification puzzle
concepts.one_line: A teaching agent chooses between addition (easier) and subtraction (harder) activities for a student who initially knows neither, and receives +1 when the student answers correctly and -1 when incorrect; the class is asked to predict the reward-maximizing behaviour.

concepts.name: Reward hacking
concepts.one_line: The reward-maximizing tutor learns to serve only easy addition problems, since once the student masters them there is no incentive to introduce difficulty — the agent does exactly what the specified reward says rather than what the designer intended; the reward function is chosen by the designer, is not intrinsic to the agent, and (per an early intelligent-tutoring paper around 2000 associated with Beverly Woolf's group) this failure is empirically real, yet RL practice devotes very little effort to reward design.

concepts.name: The environment may itself be a learner (machine teaching)
concepts.one_line: The course will mostly ignore that the world an agent interacts with may itself be an RL agent; the adversarial version of this is game theory, and the cooperative version is machine teaching, where both agents know the other is trying to help — for learning a threshold on a line this collapses the label requirement from about n samples (passive) to about log n (active learning) to one or two points (cooperative teaching).

concepts.name: Discrete-time agent/world interaction loop
concepts.one_line: At each time step t the agent takes action a_t; the world updates given a_t and emits observation o_t and reward r_t; the agent receives (o_t, r_t) and uses them to choose a_{t+1}. Time is treated as discrete throughout the course.

concepts.name: History
concepts.one_line: The history is the full interaction record h_t = (a_1, o_1, r_1, ..., a_t, o_t, r_t) — every action taken plus every observation and reward received — and in principle the agent chooses its action as a function of it.

concepts.name: World state vs agent state
concepts.one_line: The world state is the true state that actually determines how the environment generates the next observation and reward; it is usually hidden from the agent and may contain information the agent does not need. The agent state is the agent's own internal representation used to choose actions, generally a function of the history s_t = f(h_t), and it may also carry meta-information such as how much computation has been spent or how many decisions remain before the episode ends.

concepts.name: Markov assumption
concepts.one_line: State s_t is Markov if and only if p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) = p(s_{t+1} | h_t, a_t) — i.e. s_t is a sufficient statistic of the history, so that the future is conditionally independent of the past given the present, and predicting the next state requires nothing beyond the current state and action.

concepts.name: Perceptual aliasing in the corridor world
concepts.one_line: A robot in an L-shaped pair of corridors senses only whether a wall is adjacent on each of its four sides; many distinct locations in a long corridor produce identical observations, so the last observation alone is not a sufficient statistic while the full history is — a concrete counterexample showing that s_t = o_t can fail the Markov condition.

concepts.name: Markov check on the running examples
concepts.one_line: Taking state = current blood pressure with action = medicate-or-not is almost certainly not Markov (recent exercise, meals, ambient temperature, air travel all affect the next reading); taking state = currently viewed product with action = which product to recommend is likewise not Markov. The claim is about the chosen representation, not about the underlying world — another representation of the same system could be Markov, and one may knowingly run Markov algorithms on a non-Markov state while remaining aware of the violated assumption.

concepts.name: Why the Markov assumption is popular
concepts.one_line: It can always be satisfied by setting s_t = h_t, and in practice the most recent observation (or the last few) is often a workable sufficient statistic; the reason not to use the whole history is that it is unbounded and must be stored, and the size of the state representation has large implications for computational complexity, data requirements, and resulting performance — a state as rich as everything that ever happened to you yields exactly one data point per state and nothing to generalize across.

concepts.name: MDP as full observability
concepts.one_line: If the agent treats the most recent observation as its state, s_t = o_t, then the agent is modelling the world as a Markov decision process: it takes actions, receives observations and rewards, and identifies the environment state with the observation.

concepts.name: POMDP as partial observability
concepts.one_line: Under partial observability the agent state differs from the world state and must be constructed — from the history, from a belief distribution over world states, or from a recurrent network — as in poker (own cards visible, opponents' hidden, discards observable, so a belief over opponents' cards is maintained) or healthcare (unobserved physiological processes monitored only through proxies like blood pressure and temperature).

concepts.name: Bandits
concepts.one_line: A bandit is the special case in which the actions taken have no influence on the next observation, hence no delayed rewards — showing an ad to one website visitor does not change which visitor arrives next — and this setting has been studied for at least fifty years for clinical-trial allocation and web content selection.

concepts.name: MDPs/POMDPs as the coupled case
concepts.one_line: In MDPs and POMDPs the action does affect the state of the world and hence the next observation and reward, closing the loop (the product you recommend is meant to change the customer's disposition on the next step), which is precisely what makes credit assignment and strategic action necessary.

concepts.name: Deterministic vs stochastic dynamics
concepts.one_line: Deterministic: a state-action pair yields a single next observation and reward, the common assumption in robotics and control. Stochastic: a state-action pair yields a distribution over many outcomes, the common assumption for customers, patients, and hard-to-model domains. Lozano-Perez's remark that a coin flip is really deterministic and only modelled as stochastic because our model is inadequate frames stochasticity as an epistemic modelling choice rather than an ontological fact.

concepts.name: Mars rover MDP (running example)
concepts.one_line: A seven-state chain s_1..s_7 encoding rover location, actions Left and Right (labelled try-left/try-right to signal that motion can fail), with true rewards +1 in s_1, +10 in s_7, and 0 elsewhere; motivated by the communication latency that makes remote planetary rovers need autonomy.

concepts.name: Model
concepts.one_line: A model is the agent's representation of how the world responds to its actions: a transition/dynamics model p(s_{t+1} = s' | s_t = s, a_t = a) giving the distribution over next states, and a reward model r(s, a) = E[r_t | s_t = s, a_t = a] predicting the expected immediate reward.

concepts.name: A model may be wrong yet still useful
concepts.one_line: The rover's agent-side model is deliberately mis-specified: it believes reward is 0 everywhere (whereas the truth is +1 at s_1 and +10 at s_7) and that its motor control is poor, staying put with probability 0.5 and moving with probability 0.5, e.g. 0.5 = P(s_1|s_1,right) = P(s_2|s_1,right) and 0.5 = P(s_2|s_2,right) = P(s_3|s_2,right); this is a perfectly legitimate model for the agent to hold, it just happens to be incorrect, and wrong models are often still usable.

concepts.name: Policy
concepts.one_line: A policy pi determines action selection as a mapping from states to actions, pi: S -> A; deterministic policies assign exactly one action per state, pi(s) = a, while stochastic policies specify a distribution pi(a|s) = Pr(a_t = a | s_t = s) — e.g. flipping a coin each morning to choose between the back roads and the highway. Taking try-right in every rover state is a deterministic policy.

concepts.name: Value function
concepts.one_line: V^pi(s_t = s) = E[r_t + gamma*r_{t+1} + gamma^2*r_{t+2} + gamma^3*r_{t+3} + ... | s_t = s] is the expected discounted sum of future rewards under policy pi, with discount factor gamma in [0,1] weighting immediate against long-term reward; it quantifies how good or bad states are and lets policies be compared.

concepts.name: Mars rover value function at gamma = 0
concepts.one_line: Under the always-try-right policy with gamma = 0, the value function is V^pi(s_1) = +1, V^pi(s_7) = +10, and 0 in the five intermediate states: gamma = 0 makes the agent purely myopic, caring only about the reward attributed to the state it currently occupies.

concepts.name: Non-zero discount factor
concepts.one_line: In answer to a student question: with gamma > 0 the reward at distant states bleeds back into the values of nearby states, so the agent is no longer myopic and values increase toward high-reward regions — deferred to the following lecture.

concepts.name: Model-based vs model-free agents
concepts.one_line: Model-based agents explicitly represent a transition and reward model and may or may not also carry an explicit policy or value function (they must compute a policy somehow, but need not store one); model-free agents explicitly represent a value function and/or a policy and no model. Explicit here means retrievable without additional computation: hand it a state and it returns the value or the action immediately.

concepts.name: Where the reward is indexed: r(s), r(s,a), r(s,a,s')
concepts.one_line: In answer to a student's objection that s_6 should be worth 10 since try-right from s_6 reaches s_7: there are three conventions — reward attached to the current state, to the state-action pair, or to the transition (received only on arriving at s') — the slide example uses reward-in-state, and the course will default to r(s,a), meaning you are in a state, choose an action, receive a reward, then transition.

concepts.name: Agent taxonomy Venn diagram
concepts.one_line: Borrowing David Silver's figure, agents are classified by which of model, value function, and policy they represent explicitly: model-based (explicit model, implicit policy/value obtainable by planning), value-based (explicit value, policy derived from it), policy-based (explicit policy, no value function), and actor-critic (both policy and value explicit); many algorithms sit in the intersections and in practice maintaining several is often useful, since each has distinct strengths.

concepts.name: Planning as a challenge in its own right
concepts.one_line: Even with a correct model in hand, the agent must still compute what to act on: given transition and reward models one can compute the optimal action entirely offline, by dynamic programming or tree search, with no further environment interaction — solitaire with a known rule book, or Go, or chess.

concepts.name: RL as planning without a rule book
concepts.one_line: Reinforcement learning is solitaire without the rules: the agent acts, observes what happens, seeks higher reward, and may either build a model from experience and plan inside it or directly compute a policy or value function without ever forming a model.

concepts.name: Exploration vs exploitation
concepts.one_line: The agent only observes outcomes for actions it actually tries (the rover learns the consequence of try-left in s_2 only by trying it), which forces a dilemma: exploitation chooses actions expected to be good given past experience, exploration tries actions never tried or that looked bad but may have been unlucky, and reward may have to be sacrificed to learn about a potentially better policy.

concepts.name: Exploration/exploitation instances
concepts.one_line: Movies: rewatch a favourite (exploit) vs try a new film (explore). Advertising: show the highest click-through ad so far vs show a different ad. Driving: take the fastest known route vs try another. The five-dish restaurant in a new town illustrates why an agent with a long remaining stay should deliberately sample all dishes early.

concepts.name: Finite vs infinite horizon and policy stationarity
concepts.one_line: With an infinite horizon in a Markov setting the optimal policy is stationary — in the same state you act identically at step 3 and step 3000 — whereas with a finite horizon the optimal policy is in general non-stationary, depending on the time step as well as the state; correspondingly, exploration only pays for its effect on future decisions, so on the last step of a finite horizon it is always optimal to exploit, and in general finite-horizon decisions must weigh the value of information against the remaining horizon.

concepts.name: Indefinite horizon
concepts.one_line: When the horizon is finite but its length is unknown (common in games), the problem gets genuinely tricky; one way to fit it into the formalism is to treat it as infinite-horizon with absorbing/sink states that end the process, and then reason about the probability of reaching each termination state.

concepts.name: Interleaving exploration and exploitation
concepts.one_line: In answer to a student question: it is generally better to intermix exploration and exploitation, and exploration need not be uniformly random — one can demand some evidence that an untried action is plausible; in some decision processes doing all exploration up front is optimal or at least equivalent, but this depends on the process. Exploration matters most in high-stakes domains that affect real people (customers, patients, students), where learning must be fast.

concepts.name: Generalization across unvisited states
concepts.one_line: In answer to a student question about a never-before-seen state: rather than acting randomly, the agent can share information through state features (deep-learned or otherwise), so prior experience informs behaviour in a novel state — but sharing in the wrong direction over-generalizes and overfits prior experience, and can pick the wrong action where a genuinely better one exists.

concepts.name: Evaluation (prediction)
concepts.one_line: Evaluation is the problem of estimating the expected reward from following a *given* policy — someone hands you a policy and asks how good it is, possibly with no model available, so data may have to be gathered; you are not searching for a new policy, only scoring the current one.

concepts.name: Control (optimization)
concepts.one_line: Control is finding the best policy, and it typically contains evaluation as a sub-component because 'best' presupposes the ability to score candidates; a well-posed control question also has to specify what is being maximized — value from a particular start state, from all start states, or averaged over some start distribution.

concepts.name: Off-policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: A distinctive strength of RL is that evaluation can be done off-policy: data gathered under one policy can estimate the counterfactual value of a different policy, so one need not run every candidate policy in the world; the caveat raised in response to a student question is that the data-generating policy must have some stochasticity or generalization, because an action never taken in a state cannot be learned about.

concepts.name: Mars rover evaluation and control questions
concepts.one_line: Evaluation instance: given pi(s_1) = ... = pi(s_7) = right and gamma = 0, compute V^pi. Control instance: given gamma = 0 and no policy, return the policy maximizing the expected discounted sum of rewards.

concepts.name: Course roadmap
concepts.one_line: Sequence: MDPs and planning; model-free policy evaluation; model-free control; RL with function approximation and deep RL; policy search (singled out as currently the most influential family in practice, especially robotics); exploration; advanced topics. Administrative frame: prerequisites are an ML or AI class plus Python, probability, and multivariable calculus; three assignments, a midterm, an unusual two-stage individual-then-group scratch-off multiple-choice quiz, and an open-ended final project with a default-project alternative; Piazza for all communication; six free late days.

concepts.name: Other issues flagged but deferred
concepts.one_line: Where rewards come from and what happens when they are specified wrongly; robustness and risk sensitivity; multi-agent RL and game-theoretic aspects; and the recent Microsoft Research New York result suggesting a fundamental formal gap between model-based and model-free RL — all named as important and explicitly set aside.

theorems_stated: Markov criterion: s_t is Markov if and only if p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) = p(s_{t+1} | h_t, a_t), equivalently that the future is conditionally independent of the past given the present.
Any process can be made Markov by choice of state: setting s_t = h_t always yields a Markov state (slide: 'can always be satisfied').
In an infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision process, an optimal policy exists that is stationary — the action depends on the state alone, not on the time index.
In a finite-horizon problem the optimal policy is in general non-stationary: the optimal action depends on both the state and the current time step / remaining horizon.
Zero value of information at the horizon: on the final decision of a finite-horizon problem it is always optimal to exploit, because exploration has value only through its effect on later decisions.
The three reward conventions r(s), r(s,a), and r(s,a,s') are 'basically isomorphic' — any problem posed under one can be re-expressed under another.

Label-complexity hierarchy for learning a threshold on a line: passive learning needs on the order of n samples, active learning reduces this to roughly log n by choosing query points strategically, and cooperative machine teaching needs only one or two points (i.e. constant).

An indefinite-horizon problem (finite but unknown length) can be represented as an infinite-horizon problem with absorbing/terminal states, with analysis in terms of the probability of reaching each termination state.

There may be a fundamental separation between model-based and model-free RL (attributed to recent Microsoft Research New York work), in contrast to the murky empirical picture on the deep-learning side.
A bandit is the degenerate sequential decision process in which actions have no influence on the next observation, and consequently has no delayed rewards.
proofs_given: No formal proof is written on the board at any point in this lecture. Three arguments rise to the level of informal proof sketches and nothing more.

Proof by counterexample that the most recent observation need not be a Markov state: in the two-corridor navigation world with a four-sided wall sensor, many distinct rover locations along a corridor generate an identical observation, so o_t cannot determine the next-state distribution while h_t can. This is a correct and complete argument, delivered verbally at the whiteboard.

Constructive argument that cooperative teaching of a threshold on a line requires only one or two labelled points: a cooperative teacher would never label randomly, and instead places one positive and one negative point straddling the boundary, which pins the threshold down. This is essentially the constructive half of a teaching-dimension bound, given informally.

Informal argument that the +1/-1 correctness reward for the artificial tutor induces easy-item-only behaviour: easy addition items are learned quickly, after which they are answered correctly and yield +1 with near certainty, and no term in the objective rewards introducing harder material — so the reward-maximizing policy serves only easy items. Presented as an argument plus an empirical citation, not a proof.
proofs_skipped: That s_t = h_t always yields a Markov state. Asserted flatly on the slide and in the transcript. The notes should prove it (trivially, p(s_{t+1}|h_t,a_t) = p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) when s_t := h_t by construction), and then state what it costs: the state space grows without bound, one has exactly one visit per state, and generalization becomes impossible — Brunskill gestures at this ('one data point for every state') without formalizing any dependence of sample complexity on |S|.

That the Markov condition on transitions suffices. The stated condition constrains only p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t); the reward-side condition p(r_t | s_t, a_t) = p(r_t | h_t, a_t) is never stated, yet everything downstream (V^pi being well defined as a function of state, the reward model r(s,a) = E[r_t|s,a] existing at all) requires it. The notes must state the full information-state definition and show that both halves are needed.

That a belief distribution over world states is a sufficient statistic in a POMDP, i.e. the belief-state MDP reduction. Gestured at ('you can maintain a belief state over what the other cards are and use that to make decisions'). The notes must prove that the belief b_t is Markov, give the Bayes filter update b_{t+1}(s') proportional to p(o|s',a) sum_s p(s'|s,a) b_t(s), and note that this converts a discrete-state POMDP into a continuous-state MDP.

That the infinite discounted sum defining V^pi converges. Never mentioned. The notes must state that for gamma < 1 and rewards bounded by R_max, |V^pi(s)| <= R_max/(1-gamma), and flag that Brunskill's stated range gamma in [0,1] includes gamma = 1, where the infinite-horizon sum can diverge and additional assumptions (episodic termination, or average-reward criteria) are required.

That V^pi exists and is unique. The Bellman consistency equation V^pi = R^pi + gamma P^pi V^pi is never written down, let alone shown to have a unique fixed point via the contraction property of the Bellman operator. This is the single most important omission for the downstream notes, since every subsequent lecture rests on it.

That an optimal stationary deterministic policy exists in an infinite-horizon discounted MDP. Asserted in response to a student question. Requires the Bellman optimality operator's contraction property plus a measurable-selection/argmax argument; none of this is given.

That the finite-horizon optimal policy is non-stationary, and the accompanying backward-induction construction. Asserted ('very different', 'depends on the time step as well as the state'). The notes must give the finite-horizon Bellman recursion V_k*(s) = max_a [r(s,a) + gamma sum_{s'} p(s'|s,a) V_{k-1}*(s')] with V_0* = 0, exhibit a concrete MDP where the optimal action at a state genuinely changes with the remaining horizon, and prove optimality of the induction.

That exploration has zero value on the final decision of a finite horizon. Asserted as intuitively obvious ('there's no benefit from exploration for the future because you're not making any more decisions'). The notes should prove it properly: at k = 1 the Bayes-optimal action maximizes the posterior-expected immediate reward, so the value of information is exactly zero, and derive the general statement that the exploration bonus is a function of the remaining horizon.

That r(s), r(s,a), and r(s,a,s') are equivalent. Asserted explicitly with the word 'isomorphic' and then dropped. The notes must give the explicit reductions — r(s,a) = sum_{s'} p(s'|s,a) r(s,a,s') and r(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) r(s,a) for a fixed policy — show which directions are lossless and which are not (r(s) cannot in general express action-dependent cost, so the reduction from r(s,a) to r(s) requires augmenting the state), and reconcile the resulting index shift in V^pi.

That the Mars-rover value function under gamma = 0 and pi = always-right is (1,0,0,0,0,0,10). The numbers are simply displayed. The notes should derive them from the stated reward convention, and explicitly resolve the student's s_6 objection by showing that under reward-in-state with gamma = 0 the value equals the immediate reward of the occupied state, so the 0.5 transition probabilities are irrelevant at gamma = 0 but become load-bearing the moment gamma > 0.

That a wrong model can still be usefully acted upon, and how much value is lost. Asserted ('the model can be wrong... but often can still be used by the agent in useful ways'). The notes need the simulation lemma: if two models' transition and reward functions are close in total variation and sup-norm respectively, their optimal-policy values differ by O(epsilon/(1-gamma)^2), which is the quantitative content Brunskill leaves implicit.

That off-policy evaluation is possible, and under what conditions it is identifiable. Stated as a strength of RL with only a verbal caveat about needing stochasticity. The notes must state the coverage/overlap condition (pi(a|s) > 0 implies pi_behaviour(a|s) > 0 on the reachable support), prove the unbiasedness of the importance-sampling estimator under it, and show the variance blow-up as the behaviour policy becomes near-deterministic — which is exactly the failure Brunskill hints at.

That control contains evaluation as a subproblem, and that alternating the two converges. Asserted ('this typically involves as a sub-component evaluation'). Policy iteration is never named; its monotone improvement and finite convergence are never mentioned.

The full label-complexity hierarchy passive ~ n, active ~ log n, teaching ~ constant. Waved through in about thirty seconds. The notes should make each rate precise: PAC sample complexity O((1/eps) log(1/delta)) for thresholds; O(log(1/eps)) for binary-search active learning; and teaching dimension exactly 2 for threshold classifiers on the line (1 only under degenerate assumptions) — and note that the transcript's 'log n' is an informal restatement of a bound in 1/eps, not in a sample count n.

That imitation learning reduces RL to supervised learning, and what the reduction costs. The slide asserts the reduction; the transcript describes the failure mode (drift off the expert's circular helicopter trajectory into unsupervised territory) without stating the result. The notes must supply the compounding-error bound — behaviour cloning with per-step classification error epsilon suffers regret O(epsilon T^2) over horizon T, versus O(epsilon T) for DAgger-style interactive imitation — since this is the theorem the anecdote is a picture of.

That there is a fundamental gap between model-based and model-free RL. Cited to Microsoft Research New York and left as 'come ask me about that'. The notes should state the actual separation result (an exponential gap in sample complexity between model-based and model-free approaches in contextual decision processes with low Bellman rank) rather than the gesture.

That the state-representation size drives computational complexity, data requirements, and performance. Asserted on the slide as three bullets. No rate is given; the notes should supply at least the tabular sample-complexity dependence on |S| and |A| so the claim has content.

That over-generalization can strictly hurt. Asserted ('if you overshoot-overgeneralize you could overfit your prior experience'). The notes should formalize this as approximation error entering the value bound, e.g. the O(eps_approx/(1-gamma)) or (1-gamma)^-2 dependence in approximate policy iteration, so that the trade-off against the sample-efficiency benefit of generalization is quantitative.

That the indefinite-horizon-to-infinite-horizon-with-absorbing-states reduction is valid. Offered as 'one way to model it' with an explicit admission that it is tricky. The notes should give the construction and prove that the resulting infinite-horizon value equals the original expected total reward under the random stopping time, and identify when this needs a proper-policy assumption (as in stochastic shortest path).

That a bandit is a special case of an MDP. Asserted structurally by the taxonomy slides. The notes should give the formal embedding (a single state, or i.i.d.-resampled contexts with no transition dependence on the action) and show that delayed rewards vanish as a consequence, so that the H = 1 reduction is explicit rather than pictorial.

That doing all exploration up front is sometimes optimal or 'at least equivalent'. Asserted in a question answer with the honest hedge 'it depends on the decision process'. The notes should identify the regime — explore-then-commit achieving the right regret order in some bandit settings, versus its provable suboptimality relative to UCB/Thompson sampling in general — since the lecture leaves the claim unresolvable as stated.
algorithms: No algorithm is specified in enough detail to implement from this lecture alone; all named methods are forward references. The exceptions below are fully specified problem/model objects rather than procedures.

Mars rover MDP (fully specified, directly implementable): S = {s_1,...,s_7}; A = {left, right}; true reward r(s_1) = +1, r(s_7) = +10, r(s) = 0 otherwise. Agent-side (deliberately wrong) model: reward 0 in every state, and transitions that succeed with probability 0.5 and stay put with probability 0.5, i.e. P(s_1|s_1,right) = P(s_2|s_1,right) = 0.5, P(s_2|s_2,right) = P(s_3|s_2,right) = 0.5, and so on; boundary behaviour is unstated in both slides and transcript and must be chosen (self-loop at the ends is the natural reading). Policy pi(s) = right for all s. At gamma = 0, V^pi = (1,0,0,0,0,0,10).

Policy evaluation, at the level of a definition only: compute V^pi(s) = E[sum_{k>=0} gamma^k r_{t+k} | s_t = s]. Neither the Bellman equation, the iterative sweep, nor the linear-solve form is given; the lecture just displays the answer for gamma = 0.

Dynamic programming and tree search, named as the two ways to convert a known model into an action ('given a model of the world what is the right decision to make'). No recursion, no pseudocode, no complexity.

Model-based agents: maintain explicit p(s'|s,a) and r(s,a), then plan to obtain a policy. Model-free agents: maintain an explicit value function and/or policy and no model. Given as a classification of algorithms, not as algorithms.
Actor-critic, named as the archetype of the value-plus-policy intersection in David Silver's Venn diagram, with no update rule.
Behaviour cloning / imitation learning, described only as 'reduces RL to supervised learning' plus the drift failure mode; no loss, no dataset construction, no DAgger loop.
Belief-state filtering for POMDPs, alluded to as 'beliefs of world state, or RNN'; the Bayes filter update is never written.
Importance-sampling off-policy evaluation, alluded to as 'use data gathered from other policies to evaluate the counterfactual', with no estimator written down.
Named-only, deferred to later lectures: model-free control, deep RL / RL with function approximation, policy search, and exploration algorithms.
notation_introduced: a_t, o_t, r_t = the action taken, observation received, and reward received at discrete time step t
h_t = (a_1, o_1, r_1, ..., a_t, o_t, r_t) = the history, the complete interaction record up to and including step t

s_t = f(h_t) = the agent state, an arbitrary function of the history (the transcript says 'a function of the history'; the slide writes both s_t = f(h_t) and, on the Markov-assumption slide, s_t = (h_t))
world state (unnamed symbol) = the true environment state determining next observation and reward, typically hidden from the agent, distinct from the agent state
Markov condition: p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) = p(s_{t+1} | h_t, a_t)
s_t = o_t = the full-observability / MDP choice of state
s_t = h_t = the history-as-state choice, which is always Markov
S = state space, A = action space
p(s_{t+1} = s' | s_t = s, a_t = a) = transition / dynamics model
r(s_t = s, a_t = a) = E[r_t | s_t = s, a_t = a] = reward model (expected immediate reward)
pi : S -> A = policy; pi(s) = a for deterministic policies; pi(a|s) = Pr(a_t = a | s_t = s) for stochastic policies
V^pi(s_t = s) = E[r_t + gamma*r_{t+1} + gamma^2*r_{t+2} + gamma^3*r_{t+3} + ... | s_t = s] = state value function under pi
gamma = discount factor, stated to lie in [0,1], weighting immediate against future reward; gamma = 0 used for the rover example
'try left' / 'try right' = action labels emphasizing that the intended motion may fail (stochastic dynamics)
reward-convention notation r(s), r(s,a), r(s,a,s') for reward attributed to state, state-action, and transition respectively; the class defaults to r(s,a)
Agent taxonomy labels: model-based, model-free, value-based, policy-based, actor-critic; 'explicit' meaning retrievable without further computation
Horizon vocabulary: finite horizon, infinite horizon, indefinite horizon; stationary vs non-stationary policy; absorbing / sink / termination states
Bandit vs MDP vs POMDP as the three types of sequential decision process
Evaluation vs control (prediction vs optimization); on-policy vs off-policy evaluation
Named-only algorithm-analysis criteria: regret, sample complexity, computational complexity, empirical performance, convergence
Image-space cardinality 256^(100*200*3), used to motivate generalization
notation_hazards: Reward index shift vs Sutton and Barto. Brunskill writes V^pi(s_t = s) = E[r_t + gamma*r_{t+1} + ... | s_t = s], with r_t the reward at the *current* step, and the rover slide attaches reward to the state occupied. Sutton and Barto define G_t = R_{t+1} + gamma*R_{t+2} + ..., where the reward following a_t carries index t+1. The two conventions differ by one in every subscript. This is exactly the confusion behind the student's question 'why is it not s_6 that has value 10' — under Brunskill's convention V(s_6) = r(s_6) = 0 at gamma = 0, whereas a Sutton-and-Barto reader naturally expects the reward for the transition into s_7 to land at s_6. Downstream notes must pin one convention and translate.

History starts with an action. The slide defines h_t = (a_1, o_1, r_1, ..., a_t, o_t, r_t), so there is no initial observation o_0 and the agent's first action is taken with no observational input. Most treatments (and any practical implementation) begin with an observation. Harmless for the lecture, but it silently changes how you index a trajectory in code.

The state-function symbol is inconsistent. The transcript says the state is 'a function of the history'; the slides write s_t = f(h_t) in one place and s_t = (h_t) on the Markov slide, where the function symbol has been dropped by the PDF's font handling. Do not read the latter as an identity — the identity s_t = h_t is a separate, specific choice discussed under 'why is the Markov assumption popular'.

gamma in [0,1] is stated without the gamma = 1 caveat. She says the discount factor 'is going to be between zero and one' and the slide says nothing more. At gamma = 1 the infinite-horizon sum need not converge; the closed range is fine only for episodic or finite-horizon problems.

The Markov condition is stated for transitions only. p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) = p(s_{t+1}|h_t,a_t) says nothing about rewards, yet 'sufficient statistic of the history' is used as though it covered both. The reward-side condition is needed and is never written.

Markov-ness is a property of the representation, not of the world. She corrects a student on exactly this point and the correction is easy to miss: 'these particular models of the world are not Markov; there might be other models of the world that are'. Also note her explicit permission to run Markov algorithms on a knowingly non-Markov state while remaining aware of the violated assumption.

Auto-caption garbles that a reader should silently repair: 'markup decision process' throughout means Markov decision process, and 'the mark off setting' means the Markov setting; 'in state S7 you get S you get 10' means the reward in s_7 is +10; 'Neurex Conference' means NeurIPS/NIPS; 'distribution honorable RL' means distributional RL; 'invitation learning' means imitation learning; 'an oral agent' means an RL agent; 'one action prostate' means one action per state; 'discreet timer' means discrete time; 'partial aliasing' means perceptual (state) aliasing; 'stink states' means sink states; 'solitary without a rule book' means solitaire; 'it's a waiting' (of the value function) means a weighting; 'two courts of ice cream' means two quarts; 'Bev Wolf' means Beverly Woolf.

The Mars rover model's boundary transitions are never specified. The slide gives P(s_1|s_1,right) = P(s_2|s_1,right) = 0.5 and the analogous pattern inward, but says nothing about try-right at s_7 or try-left at s_1. Any implementation has to choose (self-loop is the natural reading), and the choice affects V^pi for every gamma > 0.

The rover has two different reward models in play simultaneously. The true reward is +1 at s_1 and +10 at s_7; the agent's *believed* reward model is identically 0 everywhere. The slides show both, several slides apart, with the same seven-cell diagram. Conflating them makes the value-function slide look wrong.

'log n' in the machine-teaching aside is loose. Active learning of a threshold gives a bound logarithmic in 1/epsilon (binary search on the boundary), not logarithmic in a sample count n; and the teaching requirement is two points in general, not one. She says 'one point or at most two points essentially constant', which is the right order but the wrong constant if quoted precisely.

animation_candidates.what: Discount-factor sweep on the 7-state Mars rover: hold pi = always-right fixed and animate gamma from 0 to 0.99, showing the value bar over each of s_1..s_7 morph from the myopic (1,0,0,0,0,0,10) profile into a smooth gradient that pulls the whole chain toward s_7.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture shows exactly one frame of this (gamma = 0) and then verbally promises the rest ('we'll see more of that next time'). A static slide cannot convey that gamma is the knob that decides whether the +1 at s_1 or the +10 at s_7 dominates, nor show the crossover gamma at which the optimal action in the middle states flips from left to right. One continuous parameter, one visible consequence — the ideal case for animation.
animation_candidates.visual_form: 7-cell chain with a value bar per cell, a gamma slider driving the frames, and a second panel showing the greedy action arrow per cell flipping as gamma crosses the threshold

animation_candidates.what: The s_6 puzzle: a shot-by-shot resolution of the student's objection, rendering all three reward conventions r(s), r(s,a), r(s,a,s') side by side on the same rover transition s_6 --right--> s_7 and showing where the +10 lands in each.
animation_candidates.why: This is the one moment in the lecture where a real conceptual confusion surfaces and is answered only verbally ('all of them are basically isomorphic'). Animating the reward token physically appearing at a different point in the (s, a, s') sequence under each convention makes the index shift visible instead of asserted, and pre-empts the single most common notation error a reader will carry into every later lecture.
animation_candidates.visual_form: three parallel timelines of the same transition, with a glowing +10 token attached to the state node, the state-action edge, or the arrival node respectively; then the three V^pi tables converging

animation_candidates.what: Perceptual aliasing walk through the two-corridor world: the robot traverses right-right-down-down-down while a live panel shows (a) the four-bit wall observation, (b) the growing history tape, and (c) a heat map of 'which cells are consistent with everything seen so far' collapsing from many to one.
animation_candidates.why: This is the lecture's only genuine proof by counterexample, and Brunskill delivers it by drawing on the board with an explicit apology that it is hard to see. The whole point is temporal — the observation is identical across many cells at one instant, and only accumulating history disambiguates — so a still image literally cannot express it. The collapsing consistency set is also the belief-state update the lecture skips, shown for free.
animation_candidates.visual_form: grid-world with a moving agent, a four-bit sensor readout, a scrolling history tape, and a shaded belief/consistency overlay on the grid

animation_candidates.what: Reward hacking in the artificial tutor: animate the tutor's item-selection distribution over episodes collapsing onto easy addition, with a second panel plotting cumulative agent reward rising while actual student mastery of subtraction flatlines at zero.
animation_candidates.why: The class was asked to predict this outcome, and the answer was delivered in one sentence. The failure is dynamic — the collapse happens *because* the student learns addition quickly, so reward and learning decouple over time — and the divergence of the two curves is the entire lesson. Two lines pulling apart is the clearest possible rendering of a misspecified objective.
animation_candidates.visual_form: stacked area chart of action frequencies over episodes, beside a dual-axis plot of cumulative reward vs true mastery, with the divergence point marked

animation_candidates.what: The four-axis taxonomy as an animated checklist: optimization / delayed consequences / exploration / generalization as four lamps, lit or dimmed in turn as the frame walks through RL, AI planning, supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and imitation learning.
animation_candidates.why: Brunskill uses the same four bullets on five consecutive slides with different items struck through, which is an animation rendered badly as five stills. Playing it as one figure that mutates makes the comparative structure — that each paradigm is RL minus something specific — legible in a way five separate slides never are.
animation_candidates.visual_form: four-lamp indicator row above a paradigm label that cycles, with the differing lamp highlighted on each transition

animation_candidates.what: Horizon countdown and the death of exploration: an agent in the five-dish restaurant with a visible 'days remaining' counter, animating its exploration probability decaying to exactly zero on the final day, contrasted against an infinite-horizon agent whose behaviour never changes.
animation_candidates.why: The claim 'on the last day you will always exploit' plus 'the finite-horizon optimal policy is non-stationary' is the most substantive theoretical statement in the lecture, and it is inherently about time. Showing the same state producing different actions at different remaining horizons is the definition of non-stationarity made visible, and the exploration probability hitting zero at the boundary is a one-frame proof of the zero-value-of-information claim.
animation_candidates.visual_form: side-by-side agents with a remaining-horizon counter, a per-step action choice, and a decaying exploration-probability bar that terminates at zero for the finite-horizon agent only

animation_candidates.what: Label complexity ladder for the threshold on a line: the same 1-D classification problem solved three times — random labels accumulating until the boundary is pinned (passive), binary-search queries halving the interval (active), and a cooperative teacher placing one plus and one minus (teaching).
animation_candidates.why: Thirty seconds of transcript encode three different asymptotic rates. Animating the shrinking uncertainty interval under each protocol turns n vs log n vs constant from three numbers into three visibly different rates of progress, and it is the only place in the lecture where a quantitative separation is claimed.
animation_candidates.visual_form: three stacked number lines, each with an uncertainty interval shrinking as labelled points appear, and a query counter per protocol

animation_candidates.what: Off-policy evaluation with a stochasticity dial: collect trajectories from a behaviour policy on the rover, then estimate V of the always-right target policy, while a dial reduces the behaviour policy's randomness and the estimator's confidence interval visibly explodes.
animation_candidates.why: Brunskill's caveat — 'you need to have some stochasticity in the actions you take' — is the load-bearing condition for the whole off-policy story and is stated in half a sentence. Animating the variance blow-up as coverage vanishes shows *why* the condition exists rather than that it exists, and it is the single most directly transferable idea in the lecture for anyone reusing logged execution traces.
animation_candidates.visual_form: trajectory sampler over the 7-state chain, a per-state action-coverage histogram, and a running value estimate with an error band that widens as the behaviour policy concentrates

code_experiment_candidates: Build the 7-state Mars rover as a plain transition tensor P[s, a, s'] and reward vector, with the agent's 0.5-success model, and reproduce V^pi = (1,0,0,0,0,0,10) for pi = always-right at gamma = 0 by iterative policy evaluation. Then sweep gamma over {0, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99} and plot the value profile; this both verifies the slide and generates the animation above. Requires choosing a boundary convention, which is itself a useful exercise since neither slides nor transcript specify one.

Numerically verify the claimed isomorphism of reward conventions: construct three versions of the same rover under r(s), r(s,a), and r(s,a,s'), apply the reductions r(s,a) = sum_s' p(s'|s,a) r(s,a,s') and the state-augmentation needed to go the other way, and check that V^pi agrees up to the index shift. Where it fails to agree, you have found the precise sense in which 'isomorphic' is too strong.

Corridor aliasing benchmark: implement the two-corridor world with a four-bit wall sensor and compare three agent-state choices — s = o_t, s = last k observations for k in {1,2,4}, and s = full history (or an exact belief filter) — measuring goal-reach rate and steps to goal. This turns the lecture's verbal counterexample into a quantitative statement about how much memory the domain actually needs, and directly tests her claim that 'the last four observations' is often enough.

Reward-hacking sandbox: a two-skill student simulator (Bayesian knowledge tracing, addition learned faster than subtraction) plus a tabular tutor. Train the tutor on (a) the lecture's +1/-1 immediate-correctness reward and (b) a learning-gain reward, and plot action distributions and terminal mastery for both. Reproduces the lecture's predicted collapse and demonstrates that the fix is in the reward, not the algorithm.

Finite vs infinite horizon side by side: solve the same MDP by backward induction (producing a time-indexed policy pi_k) and by value iteration to convergence (producing a stationary policy), then find and report every state where the two disagree and at which remaining horizons. Constructing an MDP where they disagree is the real content — it makes the non-stationarity claim concrete rather than asserted.

Bandit vs MDP ablation: take one reward table and two dynamics — one where the action determines the next state, one where the next state is resampled independently of the action — and run the same bandit algorithm (e.g. UCB over actions per state) on both. Shows empirically that the bandit assumption 'actions have no influence on next observations' is exactly the hypothesis whose violation causes failure, and gives the H=1 reduction operational meaning.

Off-policy evaluation and its coverage condition: collect trajectories on the rover under epsilon-greedy behaviour policies with epsilon in {0.5, 0.2, 0.05, 0.01}, estimate V of the always-right policy by ordinary and weighted importance sampling, and plot bias and variance against epsilon. Empirically recovers Brunskill's 'you need some stochasticity' caveat and the variance blow-up she does not mention.

Model error and its cost: perturb the rover's transition probabilities away from the true dynamics by a controlled amount delta, plan optimally in the wrong model, execute in the true one, and plot the value lost against delta. Empirically traces the simulation-lemma dependence that the lecture replaces with 'the model can be wrong but often can still be used in useful ways'.

Label complexity ladder: learn a threshold on [0,1] three ways — i.i.d. random labels, binary-search active queries, and a two-point cooperative teacher — and plot queries needed against target error. Confirms (and corrects the constants in) the lecture's n / log n / constant claim.

State-space size vs sample efficiency: take one underlying environment and vary the agent's state granularity from very coarse aggregation to full-history (one visit per state), then measure the data needed to reach a fixed policy quality. Makes the lecture's three-bullet assertion about computational complexity, data required, and resulting performance into a measured curve, including the pathological 'one data point per state' extreme she describes verbally.
dated_or_superseded: The Atari-2015 framing as *the* paradigm shift. Written from early 2019, the lecture's arc ends at pixel-input DQN. It predates AlphaZero/MuZero's consolidation of model-based planning with learned models, and entirely predates the shift of RL's centre of gravity to language models — RLHF (2020-2022), then the reasoning-RL family (PPO/GRPO and DPO-style offline alternatives, 2023-2025). A modern patch should state that by 2026 the largest-scale application of RL by compute is post-training of LLMs, not game playing.

'LSTMs and other things like that' as the technology loosening state-space assumptions. Superseded almost immediately by Transformers. The modern answer to 'how do I turn a history into an agent state' is a sequence model over the context — Decision Transformer, Trajectory Transformer, and in-context/meta-RL — and for LLM agents the agent state is literally the prompt/context window. The lecture's implicit assumption that a compact hand-designed sufficient statistic is preferable to the raw history has been substantially reversed by cheap long-context attention.

POMDP belief states 'or RNN'. Still correct in principle, but in practice belief filtering has been largely displaced by learned recurrent or attentional state encoders, and for LLM agents by retrieval plus context. The Bayes-filter framing is now taught as theory rather than as implementation guidance.

'We won't talk very much about multi-agent RL, but it's also a really important case.' This aside has aged into a central topic: multi-agent LLM systems, debate and self-play for reasoning, and agent-to-agent protocols are mainstream by 2026. The dismissal should be flagged rather than inherited.

Machine teaching as 'a really interesting new area that's been around for maybe 5-10 years' with the room reporting zero familiarity. The ideas have been absorbed into curriculum learning, data-centric ML, and above all teacher-student LLM distillation and synthetic-data generation, where a strong model deliberately constructs maximally informative training data for a weak one. The cooperative-teaching sample-complexity intuition is now routine engineering practice.

The Microsoft Research New York model-based vs model-free separation, cited as brand new. That line of work (Bellman rank / contextual decision processes, 2018-2019) has been subsumed by a more general theory — bilinear classes and the Decision-Estimation Coefficient (Foster et al., 2021 onward) — which gives a unified characterization of when statistical efficiency is achievable. Cite the modern framework, not the 2019 snapshot.

'There's now some interest in thinking about distributional RL.' Distributional RL was emerging in 2019; the C51/QR-DQN/IQN line is now standard practice and appears in default agent implementations. This is no longer a frontier remark.

Off-policy evaluation presented as a distinctive and somewhat aspirational strength of RL. By 2026 OPE (doubly-robust estimators, marginalized importance sampling) and offline RL (CQL, IQL, and the offline-to-online pipeline) are mature subfields with standard benchmarks. The lecture's one-sentence treatment understates how much machinery now exists — and understates the practical difficulty.

The exploration-first framing of RL as a whole. The lecture places exploration among the four defining features of RL. For the dominant contemporary application — RL on language models — the setting is overwhelmingly offline or imitation-first with a comparatively thin RL fine-tuning layer, and exploration is often deliberately constrained (KL penalties to a reference policy). The four-axis taxonomy still classifies correctly, but its weighting no longer reflects where RL is actually practised.

The prerequisite list ('have heard of MDPs before in an AI or ML class') and the claim that the course goes beyond anything else at Stanford. Purely a 2019 curricular artifact; irrelevant to a 2026 reader and safely ignorable.

relevance_to_user_research.why: Not critical — the lecture proves nothing and gives no algorithm, so nothing here is citable in an ARR submission. But it is more than background for this specific problem, for four concrete reasons. (1) It supplies the exact vocabulary for the formalization the user already has in mind, and one slide is a direct hit: the agent-state slide says the state may include 'meta information like ... how many decisions left until an episode ends', which is precisely the argument for putting node position in the DAG and remaining budget into the state rather than conditioning only on query features. (2) The finite-horizon non-stationarity claim (00:56:43) is the single most transferable statement: because the workflow has a finite horizon, the optimal fidelity policy is provably time-dependent, so a policy that maps query features to a fidelity without conditioning on depth/remaining-budget is structurally misspecified — and the corollary that exploration has zero value on the final decision says the last node should be scored purely greedily. (3) Brunskill's bandit definition — 'actions have no influence on the next observation' — is exactly the assumption that makes AEP-style query-level routing an H=1 bandit and exactly the assumption that node-level assignment violates, since a weak model at node k degrades the partial trace that node k+1 consumes. That gives the user a crisp one-line statement of why the node-level problem is not a stack of independent routing decisions, which is the framing their paper needs in its problem-setup section. (4) Two warnings apply directly: reward hacking (a terminal-accuracy-minus-lambda-times-cost reward will be gamed — at high lambda the policy collapses to all-weak, at low lambda to all-strong, and the interesting behaviour lives in a band that must be found rather than assumed), and the off-policy caveat that reusing execution traces to evaluate a different fidelity assignment requires the trace-collecting policy to have been stochastic with coverage over fidelities at each node. That last point has immediate infrastructure consequences on the Phoenix cluster, since re-running whole workflows under Qwen2.5-72B to evaluate each candidate assignment is the dominant cost and trace reuse is the obvious mitigation. What the lecture does *not* give them: any treatment of budget constraints (the lambda-weighted objective is a constrained MDP, never mentioned), any algorithm, any sample-complexity result, and nothing on the state-abstraction question of how to featurize a partial LLM execution trace. For those they need the later exploration and policy-search lectures, plus the constrained-MDP and OPE literature outside this course.

lecture_title: L02 - Given a Model of the World: Markov Processes, Markov Reward Processes, MDPs, Policy Iteration and Value Iteration
one_paragraph_summary: This is the planning lecture: the dynamics and reward function are handed to you, and the only question is how to act well when consequences are delayed. Brunskill builds the formalism in three stages. A Markov process is a state set plus a transition kernel in which the current state is a sufficient statistic of history; a Markov reward process adds a per-state reward and a discount factor, which lets her define the return (discounted sum of rewards to a horizon) and the value function (its expectation). She gives three ways to compute an MRP's value function and contrasts their costs: Monte Carlo rollouts (model-agnostic, error decaying like N^{-1/2}, exploits nothing about the Markov structure), the closed form V = (I - gamma P)^{-1} R (exact, one shot, but a matrix inversion costing roughly |S|^2 to |S|^3), and iterative dynamic programming via repeated Bellman backups (|S|^2 per sweep, cheaper per step, and the one that generalises once actions appear). Adding actions gives an MDP; fixing a policy collapses an MDP back to an MRP, so all three evaluation tools transfer directly to policy evaluation. The control half of the lecture establishes that the optimal value function is unique and that for an infinite-horizon discounted finite MDP some optimal policy is deterministic and stationary (though not necessarily unique), that brute-force enumeration over the |A|^{|S|} deterministic policies is possible but wasteful, and that policy iteration - evaluate, form Q^pi, act greedily - improves the policy monotonically. She walks the policy improvement proof on the board by repeatedly substituting the greedy action into the Bellman expansion until the new policy's own value function falls out, then argues termination from strict monotonicity plus the finiteness of policy space. Value iteration is presented as the alternative: it always holds an optimal k-step-to-go value rather than an exactly-evaluated suboptimal policy, and it converges because the Bellman optimality backup is a gamma-contraction in the sup norm, a fact she proves briefly by pulling the max outside a difference and bounding the transition-weighted sum. The finite-horizon case and the Banach fixed point argument are both deferred.
prerequisites: Lecture 1's informal definitions of a model, a policy, and a value function, and the agent-environment interaction loop
Linear algebra: matrix-vector products, transposes, matrix inversion, eigenvalues, and the fact that a row-stochastic matrix has rows summing to one
Vector norms, especially L1/L2/L-infinity, and what it means for a distance to shrink under a map
Probability: conditional distributions, expectation, marginalising over a next-state distribution, and sampling from a categorical distribution
Geometric series and the idea that a bounded reward with gamma < 1 gives a bounded infinite sum
Big-O reasoning about algorithmic cost (why |S|^3 inversion is worse than |S|^2 per sweep)
Comfort with the distinction between a random quantity (the return) and its expectation (the value)

concepts.name: Planning versus learning
concepts.one_line: Today the transition and reward models are given, so the entire problem is computing good behaviour; estimating the model from data is deferred to later lectures.

concepts.name: Delayed consequences
concepts.one_line: The central difficulty of the control problem is that maximising long-run reward may require deliberately forgoing immediate reward.

concepts.name: Markov assumption
concepts.one_line: A state is Markov when conditioning on it and the current action gives the same next-state distribution as conditioning on the entire history, i.e. the state is a sufficient statistic of the past.

concepts.name: Future independent of past given present
concepts.one_line: The Markov property is exactly the statement that a single aggregate summary of the present screens off everything that came before.

concepts.name: Markov process / Markov chain
concepts.one_line: A pair (S, P) with a (finite or infinite) state set and a next-state kernel P(s'|s); no actions and no rewards exist yet, so the agent is a passive observer of a stochastic process.

concepts.name: Transition matrix
concepts.one_line: With finitely many states the kernel is an |S| x |S| row-stochastic matrix, and the next-state distribution is obtained by multiplying a one-hot current-state vector by P (up to a transpose convention).

concepts.name: Mars Rover chain
concepts.one_line: A seven-state left-right corridor used throughout the lecture; e.g. from s1 the process self-loops with probability 0.6 and steps right with 0.4, and from s4 it splits 0.4/0.4/0.2 among s3, s5 and staying put.

concepts.name: Stationary distribution
concepts.one_line: Run a Markov chain long enough and its state distribution settles to a steady state that does not depend on where it started, which is why no initial state is specified in the chain definition.

concepts.name: Sampling an episode
concepts.one_line: Start at a state, multiply by P to get a next-state distribution, let nature draw one outcome from it, repeat; this generates a trajectory such as s4, s5, s6, s7, s7, s7.

concepts.name: Markov reward process
concepts.one_line: A tuple (S, P, R, gamma) that adds to a Markov chain a reward function R(s) equal to the expected immediate reward for occupying s, plus a discount factor; still no actions.

concepts.name: Mars Rover MRP rewards
concepts.one_line: R(s1) = 1, R(s7) = 10, and zero for the five interior states, so the corridor has a small reward at one end and a large one at the other.

concepts.name: Horizon
concepts.one_line: The number of time steps an episode runs for; it may be finite, in which case she calls the process finite-horizon, or infinite, as with a stock price one never stops observing.

concepts.name: Return G_t
concepts.one_line: The discounted sum of rewards accumulated from time t out to the horizon, weighting the reward k steps ahead by gamma^k; it is a random variable, not a number.

concepts.name: Value function as expected return
concepts.one_line: V(s) is the expectation of the return given that the process is in state s; return and value coincide only when the process is deterministic.

concepts.name: Discount factor semantics
concepts.one_line: gamma = 0 makes the agent myopic (immediate reward only), gamma = 1 weights all future rewards equally, and intermediate values match how people and firms empirically discount the future.

concepts.name: Discounting for mathematical convenience
concepts.one_line: A discount factor below one guarantees the infinite-horizon value stays bounded whenever the reward is bounded; if the horizon is certainly finite, gamma = 1 is harmless.

concepts.name: Why geometric discounting
concepts.one_line: A student asks whether the exponential schedule is forced; the answer is no, other schedules exist, but geometric discounting is the standard choice because of the mathematical properties it buys (contraction, stationarity).

concepts.name: Four-step return example
concepts.one_line: With gamma = 1/2 and horizon 4, the trajectory s4, s5, s6, s7 collects nothing until the last step, so its return is 10 times (1/2)^3 = 1.25.

concepts.name: Value estimation by simulation
concepts.one_line: Roll out many episodes from the start-state distribution and average their returns; this converges asymptotically to V and its error scales like one over the square root of the number of rollouts.

concepts.name: Simulation is Markov-agnostic
concepts.one_line: Monte Carlo estimation never uses the Markov property, which makes it robust when the assumed structure is wrong, but also means it throws away structure that could make estimation cheaper.

concepts.name: MRP Bellman decomposition
concepts.one_line: The Markov property lets the value split into immediate reward plus gamma times the transition-weighted average of the value at the next state: V(s) = R(s) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s) V(s').

concepts.name: Analytic MRP solution
concepts.one_line: Writing the Bellman decomposition in matrix form V = R + gamma P V and rearranging gives (I - gamma P) V = R, hence V = (I - gamma P)^{-1} R.

concepts.name: Cost of the matrix inverse
concepts.one_line: The closed form is exact and one-shot but costs roughly |S|^2 to |S|^3 depending on the inversion routine, and it requires a finite state space.

concepts.name: Self-loops are not circular
concepts.one_line: A state that can transition to itself does not make V(s) ill-defined; for an infinite-horizon process the value is stationary and the linear system remains well posed provided the matrix is invertible.

concepts.name: Invertibility of I - gamma P
concepts.one_line: Because P is stochastic its eigenvalues are bounded by one in magnitude, so I - gamma P is always invertible whenever gamma < 1 (answered later in the lecture after she deferred the student's question).

concepts.name: Iterative policy evaluation for an MRP
concepts.one_line: Initialise V_0 = 0 (any initialisation works), then repeatedly set V_k(s) = R(s) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s) V_{k-1}(s') for every state until the sup-norm change falls below epsilon; each sweep costs |S|^2.

concepts.name: Bootstrapping
concepts.one_line: The iterative method reuses the previous iterate's value estimate at the successor state rather than a true value, which is what makes each sweep cheap.

concepts.name: Three routes to an MRP value function
concepts.one_line: Simulation (no structure needed, slow, unbiased in the limit), analytic inversion (exact, finite states only, cubic-ish), and dynamic programming (cheap sweeps, generalises to control) are the three options, with only the last extending cleanly once actions appear.

concepts.name: Markov decision process
concepts.one_line: The tuple (S, A, P, R, gamma) where the dynamics P(s'|s,a) are indexed by action and the reward may be written R(s), R(s,a) or R(s,a,s'); the lecture uses R(s,a) from here on.

concepts.name: Why transitions are stochastic
concepts.one_line: Stochasticity is a stand-in for model uncertainty and unmodelled variables (a robot slipping on carpet, traffic on the way to the airport); enough extra state variables could in principle make it deterministic.

concepts.name: Mars Rover MDP
concepts.one_line: Two actions a1 and a2 that broadly push left and right, each with its own transition matrix, with self-loops at the corridor endpoints; deliberately not called left/right because the outcome need not be achieved.

concepts.name: Policy
concepts.one_line: A mapping from state to action, either deterministic or a distribution over actions; the lecture works mostly with deterministic policies until policy search appears later in the course.

concepts.name: MDP plus policy induces an MRP
concepts.one_line: Fixing a policy collapses an MDP to an MRP by averaging reward and dynamics over the policy's action distribution, so every MRP evaluation technique becomes a policy evaluation technique.

concepts.name: Bellman backup for a fixed policy
concepts.one_line: V^pi_k(s) = R(s, pi(s)) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s, pi(s)) V^pi_{k-1}(s'), i.e. the MRP backup with the reward and dynamics indexed by the policy's action.

concepts.name: Zero-discount evaluation example
concepts.one_line: With gamma = 0 the value of any policy is just the immediate reward vector, so V = (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10) regardless of what the transition model is - a deliberate trick question.

concepts.name: One Bellman backup at s6
concepts.one_line: Given V_k = (1,0,0,0,0,0,10), gamma = 1/2, and dynamics that keep the rover at s6 with probability 0.5 and move it to s7 with probability 0.5, one backup gives V_{k+1}(s6) = 0 + 0.5*(0.5*0 + 0.5*10) = 2.5.

concepts.name: Backward propagation of value
concepts.one_line: Successive backups let the knowledge that s7 is worth +10 flow leftward down the corridor: after one sweep values equal immediate rewards, and each further sweep pushes reward information one step further back.

concepts.name: MDP control
concepts.one_line: Control means computing an optimal policy rather than merely evaluating a given one; this lecture computes it from a known model rather than learning it.

concepts.name: Counting deterministic policies
concepts.one_line: A deterministic policy independently picks one of |A| actions in each of |S| states, giving |A|^{|S|} policies - 2^7 = 128 for the Mars Rover - exponential in the state space but finite.

concepts.name: State-dependent action sets
concepts.one_line: Real problems (medical interventions, for instance) restrict which actions are legal per state, in which case the count is a product of per-state action-set sizes; the lecture assumes a uniform action set for simplicity.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of the optimal value function
concepts.one_line: There is exactly one optimal value function: for each state a single scalar giving the maximum achievable expected discounted return, even though several policies may attain it.

concepts.name: Non-uniqueness of the optimal policy
concepts.one_line: Ties between actions mean the optimal policy need not be unique, in contrast to the optimal value function.

concepts.name: Optimal policies are deterministic and stationary
concepts.one_line: For an infinite-horizon discounted finite MDP there exists an optimal policy that is deterministic and time-independent, justifying the focus on deterministic policies.

concepts.name: Intuition for stationarity
concepts.one_line: If you act forever, then whenever you arrive in a state you still face an infinite future, so the optimal choice cannot depend on the clock.

concepts.name: Policy enumeration
concepts.one_line: Because the policy space is finite, one can evaluate all |A|^{|S|} deterministic policies independently and take the best; embarrassingly parallel, but wasteful serially.

concepts.name: Policy iteration
concepts.one_line: Initialise a policy at random, then alternate exact policy evaluation with greedy policy improvement, halting when the policy stops changing.

concepts.name: State-action value Q^pi
concepts.one_line: Q^pi(s,a) is the expected discounted return from taking action a now - possibly against the policy's advice - and following pi from the next step onwards: R(s,a) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) V^pi(s').

concepts.name: Policy improvement step
concepts.one_line: Compute Q^{pi_i}(s,a) for every state-action pair from the freshly evaluated V^{pi_i}, then set pi_{i+1}(s) = argmax_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a).

concepts.name: Greedy action is never worse
concepts.one_line: max_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a) is at least Q^{pi_i}(s, pi_i(s)) = V^{pi_i}(s), trivially, because the old action remains available to the max.

concepts.name: The subtlety of policy improvement
concepts.one_line: The Q argmax only certifies that deviating for one step and then reverting to the old policy is better, yet the new policy is committed to forever; that this still helps is the non-obvious content of the theorem.

concepts.name: No local optima in tabular policy iteration
concepts.one_line: Unlike gradient-based policy search, tabular policy iteration cannot get stuck at a local maximum and is guaranteed to reach the global optimum.

concepts.name: Policy improvement theorem
concepts.one_line: V^{pi_{i+1}}(s) >= V^{pi_i}(s) for every state, with strict inequality somewhere whenever pi_i was suboptimal.

concepts.name: Proof of monotonic improvement
