concepts.one_line: Bound V^{pi_i}(s) by max_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a), rewrite the max as the action pi_{i+1}(s), expand Q into reward plus discounted next-state value, re-bound that next-state V^{pi_i} by its own max over Q, and keep nesting; in the limit every step uses pi_{i+1}, so the whole chain of inequalities terminates at V^{pi_{i+1}}(s).

concepts.name: Policies never revisited
concepts.one_line: Once the policy stops changing it can never change again, and strict monotone improvement means no policy is ever repeated, so policy iteration halts in at most |A|^{|S|} iterations.

concepts.name: Value iteration
concepts.one_line: Initialise V_0 = 0 and repeatedly apply V_{k+1}(s) = max_a [ R(s,a) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) V_k(s') ] over all states until convergence (or out to a finite horizon).

concepts.name: Value iteration versus policy iteration
concepts.one_line: Policy iteration always holds a policy whose infinite-horizon value is exactly known but which may be poor; value iteration always holds an exactly optimal value for a k-step-to-go problem but for a horizon that is still too short - they compute different intermediate objects and meet at the same limit.

concepts.name: Finite-horizon reading of the iterate
concepts.one_line: V_k(s) is the optimal value of acting for exactly k more steps, which is why zero initialisation is the natural choice: with no steps left, value is zero, and the first backup selects the best single action.

concepts.name: Bellman equation
concepts.one_line: The self-consistency constraint that a value function must equal immediate reward plus the discounted expectation of its own value at the next state.

concepts.name: Bellman backup operator
concepts.one_line: Write B for the map taking an old value function to a new one via the max-over-actions backup, and B^pi for the version that fixes the action to pi(s); policy evaluation is then computing a fixed point of B^pi.

concepts.name: Contraction operator
concepts.one_line: An operator O is a contraction in a chosen norm if the distance between any two inputs does not grow (and generally shrinks) after applying it: ||OV - OV'|| <= ||V - V'||.

concepts.name: Bellman backup is a contraction
concepts.one_line: For gamma < 1 the Bellman optimality backup is a gamma-contraction in the sup norm, which is precisely why value iteration converges.

concepts.name: Proof of the contraction property
concepts.one_line: Take two arbitrary value vectors, write the difference of their backups, replace the two independent maxima with a single max over the difference (an upper bound), cancel the identical reward terms, bound each next-state difference by the sup-norm difference, pull it outside the sum, and use that the transition probabilities sum to one to leave a factor of gamma.

concepts.name: Contraction implies a unique fixed point
concepts.one_line: Because the backup contracts, repeated application converges to a single fixed-point value vector regardless of initialisation - stated and left as an exercise.

concepts.name: Course logistics
concepts.one_line: Open questions she could not settle live (matrix invertibility, contraction examples) are deferred to Piazza and office hours, and the finite-horizon material at the end of the deck is left unlectured for time.

theorems_stated: Markov property: P(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) = P(s_{t+1} | h_t, a_t), i.e. the state is a sufficient statistic of the history.
A Markov chain run long enough converges to a steady-state (stationary) distribution over states that is independent of the start state.
MRP Bellman equation: V(s) = R(s) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s) V(s').
Closed-form MRP value: V = (I - gamma P)^{-1} R for finite state spaces.
A stochastic matrix P has eigenvalues bounded by one in magnitude, hence I - gamma P is invertible for every gamma < 1.
Monte Carlo estimation of a value function has accuracy scaling like O(1/sqrt(N)) in the number of rollouts.
An MDP together with a fixed policy induces a Markov reward process, with reward and transitions averaged over the policy's action distribution.
The number of deterministic policies in a finite MDP is |A|^{|S|} - exponential in the state count but finite.
There exists a unique optimal value function V* for a finite discounted MDP.
For an infinite-horizon discounted finite MDP there exists an optimal policy that is deterministic and stationary (time-independent).
The optimal policy need not be unique: ties in the action values allow several distinct policies to achieve V*.
Policy improvement theorem: with pi_{i+1}(s) = argmax_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a), we have V^{pi_{i+1}}(s) >= V^{pi_i}(s) for all s, with strict inequality somewhere if pi_i is suboptimal.
max_a Q^{pi}(s,a) >= Q^{pi}(s, pi(s)) = V^{pi}(s) for all s.
Tabular policy iteration converges to the global optimum and, unlike gradient-based policy search, has no local optima to get trapped in.
If the policy is unchanged on one policy-iteration step it is unchanged forever, and no policy can be visited twice, bounding policy iteration by |A|^{|S|} iterations.
The Bellman optimality backup operator is a gamma-contraction in the L-infinity norm whenever gamma < 1.
A contraction operator has a unique fixed point, so repeated application of the Bellman backup converges to a single value function independent of initialisation.
If the reward function is bounded and gamma < 1, the infinite-horizon discounted value function is bounded.
When the horizon is guaranteed finite, gamma = 1 is mathematically safe.
proofs_given: Policy improvement theorem, walked through on the board (~00:59:50): the chain V^{pi_i}(s) <= max_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a) = Q^{pi_i}(s, pi_{i+1}(s)) = R(s, pi_{i+1}(s)) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s, pi_{i+1}(s)) V^{pi_i}(s') <= R(s, pi_{i+1}(s)) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(...) max_{a'} Q^{pi_i}(s', a'), then recursive re-expansion of the inner Q; unrolling indefinitely substitutes pi_{i+1} at every time step, so the right-hand side becomes V^{pi_{i+1}}(s). The two moves she isolates as the tricks are (a) V^{pi} is a lower bound on max_a Q^{pi}, and (b) rewriting that max as the definition of pi_{i+1}.

Bellman optimality backup is a gamma-contraction in the sup norm (~01:11:15), shown quickly for two arbitrary value vectors V_k and V_j: expand both backups, upper-bound the difference of the two independent maxima by a single max of the difference, cancel the identical R(s,a) terms, bound each |V_k(s') - V_j(s')| by the sup-norm distance, factor it out of the sum over s', and use sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) = 1 to leave gamma * ||V_k - V_j||_inf.
Derivation of the analytic MRP solution (~00:25:31): starting from V = R + gamma P V, subtract gamma P V, factor as (I - gamma P) V = R, and invert.

Invertibility of I - gamma P (~00:41:08), given as a one-line spectral argument: P is stochastic so its eigenvalues have magnitude at most 1, therefore I - gamma P has no zero eigenvalue for gamma < 1. Delivered as an answer to an earlier student question she had deferred; the eigenvalue bound itself is asserted, not derived.

Count of deterministic policies is |A|^{|S|} (~00:46:50), argued by explicit enumeration of the four policies (a1a1, a1a2, a2a1, a2a2) in a two-state, two-action MDP, to show the count is exponential rather than linear in |S|.

Policy iteration terminates (~01:03:56), argued informally: strict monotone improvement means a policy can never recur, and the policy space has size |A|^{|S|}, so the number of iterations is bounded.
proofs_skipped: Existence and uniqueness of the optimal value function V* is asserted flatly at ~00:43:05 with no argument; the standard proof (V* is the unique fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, by Banach) is never given.

Existence of a deterministic, stationary optimal policy for an infinite-horizon discounted finite MDP is asserted at ~00:48:51 with only the intuition that an infinitely long future looks the same at every time step. No argument is given that randomisation cannot help, nor that no history-dependent policy beats a Markov one.

The Banach fixed point theorem itself - that a contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point and that iterates converge to it geometrically - is explicitly handed off as an exercise at ~01:12:52 ('a good exercise to do').

That the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator equals V*, and that acting greedily with respect to V* yields an optimal policy. Both are used implicitly to justify value iteration but neither is stated as something requiring proof.

That policy iteration's terminating policy is globally optimal. Termination and monotone improvement are argued, but the step from 'the policy stopped changing' to 'this policy is optimal' (the fixed point of the greedy operator satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, hence its value is V*) is asserted at ~00:55:16 as 'guaranteed to converge to the global optima' without derivation.

That B^pi (the fixed-policy Bellman backup) is also a contraction, hence that iterative policy evaluation converges. Only the max-version contraction is proved; the policy-evaluation case is assumed by analogy, and is the one actually used earlier in the lecture.

Any convergence rate or stopping rule for value iteration. The algorithm halts when ||V_k - V_{k-1}||_inf < epsilon, but the standard bound ||V_k - V*||_inf <= gamma/(1-gamma) * ||V_k - V_{k-1}||_inf that makes this epsilon meaningful is never mentioned, nor is the gamma^k decay of the error.
Boundedness of the value function under bounded reward and gamma < 1. Cited at ~00:16:32 as a key benefit of discounting, but the geometric-series bound |V| <= R_max/(1-gamma) is never written down.

The Monte Carlo error rate O(1/sqrt(N)) is asserted at ~00:21:22, and the 'mathematical bounds you can use to say how many simulations you need' are gestured at without naming Hoeffding or Chernoff or stating any concentration inequality.

Existence and uniqueness of a stationary distribution independent of the start state (~00:07:01) is asserted with no hypotheses at all; irreducibility, aperiodicity and the Perron-Frobenius theorem are all omitted. The claim is in fact false for periodic or reducible chains.

That the induced MRP under a policy has R^pi(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) R(s,a) and P^pi(s'|s) = sum_a pi(a|s) P(s'|s,a), and that its value function equals V^pi of the original MDP. Stated verbally at ~00:32:36 as an obvious averaging construction, never verified.

The claim that P stochastic implies all eigenvalues have magnitude at most one - the load-bearing fact in the invertibility argument - is asserted, not proved (Gershgorin discs or the row-sum norm bound would do it).

That value iteration's k-th iterate V_k equals the optimal value of the k-step finite-horizon problem. Asserted at ~01:07:34; the induction on k is not carried out, and the finite-horizon material where it would be formalised is skipped for time.

That the tabular policy-iteration landscape has no local optima, in contrast to policy gradient (~00:55:16). Stated as fact with a wave at gradient methods; no argument for why the discrete greedy improvement operator cannot stall at a suboptimal fixed point.

That once the policy stops changing it can never change again. She says she is skipping the slide (~01:04:58) that would show Q^{pi} is identical on the next round, so the argument is only sketched by a student answer.

That geometric discounting is the schedule with 'really nice mathematical properties' (~00:17:00). Which properties (time consistency, preservation of stationarity, contraction) and why non-geometric schedules break them are all deferred to 'we'll see later'.

Complexity claims are given without justification: matrix inversion at |S|^2 to |S|^3, iterative policy evaluation at |S|^2 per sweep. The per-sweep cost of value iteration (|S|^2 |A|) and of policy iteration overall are never even stated.
That the three MRP evaluation methods (simulation, analytic, DP) all converge to the same quantity is assumed throughout and never shown.
Concrete examples of contraction operators are explicitly deferred to after class, office hours, or Piazza (~01:10:20).
The entire finite-horizon treatment - time-indexed value functions V_t, backward induction, and non-stationary optimal policies - is left in the slides and not lectured (~01:13:30).
Whether the initialisation of value iteration affects anything once converged is posed as an open exercise rather than answered.
algorithms: Episode sampling from a Markov chain: represent the current state as a one-hot vector, multiply by the transition matrix to get a next-state distribution, sample one successor from it, and repeat to build a trajectory.

Monte Carlo / simulation value estimation for an MRP: draw initial states from the start distribution, roll out full episodes, compute each episode's discounted return, average across rollouts; error decays like N^{-1/2}, and the method makes no use of the Markov property.

Analytic MRP value computation: form the reward vector R and transition matrix P, solve V = (I - gamma P)^{-1} R. One shot and exact; requires a finite state space and an inversion costing roughly |S|^2 to |S|^3.

Iterative policy evaluation (dynamic programming) for an MRP: set V_0(s) = 0 for all s, then repeat V_k(s) <- R(s) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s) V_{k-1}(s') for all s until ||V_k - V_{k-1}||_inf < epsilon. Cost |S|^2 per sweep; initialisation is irrelevant to the converged answer.

Policy evaluation for a fixed policy in an MDP: the same sweep with the policy's action substituted in - V^pi_k(s) <- R(s, pi(s)) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s, pi(s)) V^pi_{k-1}(s') - equivalently, run any of the three MRP methods on the policy-induced MRP.
Policy enumeration (brute-force policy search): list all |A|^{|S|} deterministic policies, evaluate each independently by any method, return the argmax. Trivially parallel, but hopeless serially.

Policy iteration: initialise pi_0 randomly; while the policy keeps changing, (1) evaluate pi_i to get V^{pi_i}, (2) compute Q^{pi_i}(s,a) = R(s,a) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) V^{pi_i}(s') for all state-action pairs, (3) set pi_{i+1}(s) = argmax_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a). Halts when pi_{i+1} = pi_i, in at most |A|^{|S|} iterations.

Value iteration: initialise V_0(s) = 0 for all s, then repeat V_{k+1}(s) <- max_a [ R(s,a) + gamma * sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) V_k(s') ] for all s until the sup-norm change is below epsilon (or until the finite horizon is reached). V_k is the optimal k-steps-to-go value; the greedy policy with respect to the converged V is optimal.

Bellman backup operators as first-class objects: B V applies the max-over-actions backup, B^pi V applies the fixed-policy backup; policy evaluation is computing the fixed point of B^pi and value iteration is computing the fixed point of B.
notation_introduced: s_t, a_t, r_t - state, action and reward at time step t
h_t - the history, i.e. the full sequence of prior states, actions and rewards up to time t
P(s'|s) - Markov chain transition kernel; P(s'|s,a) - MDP dynamics model indexed by action
P as an |S| x |S| row-stochastic transition matrix, with the next-state distribution obtained by multiplying a one-hot state vector by P (transposed depending on convention)
Markov process tuple (S, P)
Markov reward process tuple (S, P, R, gamma)
Markov decision process tuple (S, A, P, R, gamma)
R(s) = E[r_t | s_t = s] for an MRP; R(s,a) for an MDP; she also names the variants R(s,a,s')
R as a vector of per-state expected rewards when the state space is finite
gamma in [0,1] - discount factor
H - horizon, the number of time steps in an episode, possibly infinite
G_t - the return, the discounted sum of rewards from t to the horizon
V(s) = E[G_t | s_t = s] - value function; V as a vector over states
V^pi(s) - value of state s under policy pi; V^pi_k the k-th iterate of policy evaluation
Q^pi(s,a) - state-action value: take a now, follow pi thereafter
V* - the (unique) optimal value function; pi* - an optimal policy
pi(s) for deterministic policies, pi(a|s) for stochastic ones
V_k - value iteration index k; pi_i - policy iteration index i (subscript indexes which policy, not which state)
B - the Bellman backup operator, written BV; B^pi - the fixed-policy Bellman backup operator
||x|| - a norm on value vectors; the sup norm ||V_k - V_{k-1}||_inf is used as the convergence criterion
|S|, |A| - cardinalities of the state and action sets
V = R + gamma P V - the MRP Bellman equation in matrix form
notation_hazards: She calls a process with a finite horizon a 'finite Markov Decision Process' (~00:14:46). In Sutton and Barto and most of the literature, 'finite MDP' means finite state and action sets, not finite horizon. The academic notes should say 'finite-horizon' explicitly.

'Stationary' is used in two unrelated senses within twenty minutes: the stationary (steady-state) distribution of a Markov chain (~00:07:01), and a stationary policy or stationary value function meaning time-independent (~00:25:40, ~00:48:51). Worth disambiguating in writing.

Row-vector versus column-vector convention for P is never fixed. During the student Q&A she repeatedly hedges ('depending on the notation and whether you take the transpose... it will be on the left or the right') and says it should be obvious from context. Pin down one convention (V = R + gamma P V with P[s][s'] = P(s'|s)) before writing the notes.

In the s6 backup worked example (~00:41:49) the spoken arithmetic drops a factor of gamma: the caption reads '0 plus 0.5 times 0 plus 0.5 times 10', which parses as 5, but the equation she writes is 0 + gamma * (0.5 * V(s6) + 0.5 * V(s7)) with gamma = 0.5, giving 2.5. Use 2.5.
The policy-evaluation slide writes V_k where it should write V^pi_k; a student catches it and she confirms it is a typo (~00:42:10). Any reproduction of that slide should carry the pi superscript.

In the policy improvement proof the transcript writes R(s, pi_i+1(s)) and R(s, pi(a)) where the quantity being bounded is a Q value, not a bare reward; and pi_i(a) appears where pi_i(s) is meant (she corrects the second slip aloud). The auto-caption also renders 'reward' variously as 'word', 'return reward' and 'already credit'.
The MRP Bellman equation is introduced with R(s), and the MDP version silently switches to R(s,a) without restating the equation, so the reader must re-derive the action-indexed form.

Reward indexing differs from Sutton and Barto: she writes R(s) = E[r_t | s_t = s], indexing the reward at the same time step as the state, whereas S&B use R(s) = E[R_{t+1} | S_t = s]. This is an off-by-one in every return and Bellman expression relative to S&B.

The four-step return example (~00:19:28) discounts the reward at the fourth visited state by gamma^3, i.e. the first reward is undiscounted (gamma^0). Consistent within the lecture but worth stating, because horizon-4 with rewards at t = 0..3 is easy to misread as gamma^4.
'2 to the 7th' is |A|^{|S|}, not |S|^{|A|}. A student explicitly expresses surprise that the count is exponential rather than linear, so the exponent order is a known stumbling point.

Per-sweep complexity of iterative policy evaluation is given as |S|^2, which is right for an MRP or a fixed policy; for value iteration it is |S|^2 |A|, which she never states. Do not carry the |S|^2 figure over to value iteration.

She says the stationary distribution is 'independent of the start state' with no conditions attached; this is false for reducible or periodic chains, so the notes need the irreducible-aperiodic hypothesis.

'Value iteration says you always know what the optimal value and policy is, but only if you get to act for k time steps' - the greedy policy extracted mid-run is optimal for the k-step problem, not for the infinite-horizon one. Easy to misquote as 'value iteration maintains an optimal policy'.

The contraction is defined loosely as 'the distance doesn't get bigger and can shrink' (~01:09:50), which is a non-expansion, not a contraction. The proof actually establishes the strict gamma-contraction with gamma < 1; state the modulus explicitly.

animation_candidates.what: Reward information flowing backwards along the seven-state Mars Rover corridor as successive Bellman backups are applied, starting from V_0 = 0 and the +10 at s7.
animation_candidates.why: She spends real time on this verbally ('information about the fact that s7 is good is going to kinda flow backwards') because it is the single best intuition for why dynamic programming works, and it is exactly the thing static equations hide. A per-iteration bar chart makes the propagation front visible and shows why the number of sweeps needed scales with the diameter of the state graph.
animation_candidates.visual_form: 1-D grid-world value sweep: seven cells in a row, bar height (and colour ramp) per state, stepping through k = 0, 1, 2, ... with the changed cell highlighted each sweep

animation_candidates.what: The policy improvement proof as a term-by-term unrolling: V^{pi_i}(s) <= max_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a), rewritten as pi_{i+1}, expanded into reward plus discounted next value, then the inner V^{pi_i} re-bounded and re-expanded, repeating until V^{pi_{i+1}} emerges.
animation_candidates.why: This is the one genuinely non-obvious argument in the lecture, and she flags the subtlety herself ('here's the weird part', 'it should be at least a little unclear that this is a good thing to do'). The difficulty is that each substitution replaces one more time step's action with the new policy - a purely visual fact about which term got rewritten, which prose describes badly.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Term-level formula morph: the inequality chain stays on screen, with the substituted subterm highlighted and each newly-committed time step colour-coded, so the viewer watches pi_i turn into pi_{i+1} one time index at a time

animation_candidates.what: Two arbitrary value vectors being repeatedly hit with the Bellman backup, their sup-norm distance shrinking by a factor of gamma each application, both converging on the same fixed point.
animation_candidates.why: The contraction is the load-bearing convergence argument and she rushes it for time. Seeing two arbitrary starting points spiral to the same limit is what makes 'initialisation does not matter' and 'the fixed point is unique' obvious, and it directly answers the exercise she leaves hanging at the end of class.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two points in a low-dimensional projection of value space, connected by a distance bracket labelled with its sup norm, marching inward toward a marked fixed point; a side panel plots ||V_k - V*|| on a log axis to show the geometric rate

animation_candidates.what: Policy iteration and value iteration running side by side on the same Mars Rover MDP, with policy iteration's exact-evaluation jumps in policy space next to value iteration's incremental value sweeps.
animation_candidates.why: She draws the distinction verbally - policy iteration always holds a fully-evaluated but possibly poor policy, value iteration always holds an exactly-optimal-but-short-horizon value - and this is the comparison students most often blur. A synchronised split screen shows the two intermediate objects are genuinely different things converging to the same answer.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Split screen: left, a policy grid (arrows per state) that snaps discretely with a full value readout each time; right, a value bar chart that creeps upward every sweep with the implied greedy arrows flickering above it; a shared iteration counter and a shared distance-to-V* plot below

animation_candidates.what: The algebraic rearrangement of V = R + gamma P V into V = (I - gamma P)^{-1} R, shown as matrix blocks moving across the equals sign.
animation_candidates.why: The step is trivially short but the shapes are where students lose the thread - which object is a vector, which is |S| x |S|, and where the identity matrix comes from. Rendering R and V as tall thin blocks and P as a square block makes the factoring step self-evident in a way that inline symbols do not.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Matrix-block algebra: labelled rectangles sized to their true dimensions, sliding and factoring, with the identity matrix materialising when V is pulled out of V - gamma P V

animation_candidates.what: A continuous sweep of the discount factor from 0 to 1 on the Mars Rover corridor, reshaping the optimal value function and flipping the greedy policy's direction at some critical gamma.
animation_candidates.why: The corridor has +1 at one end and +10 at the other, so there is a genuine gamma at which the optimal action in the middle states reverses. This turns 'gamma trades off immediate versus future reward' from a slogan into a visible bifurcation, and it sets up discounting as a design decision rather than a formality.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Scatter-plus-curve: a gamma slider driving a value curve over the seven states, with arrow glyphs above each state recolouring as the argmax flips, plus a small bifurcation plot of optimal action versus gamma

animation_candidates.what: One step of MRP sampling: a one-hot state vector multiplied by P to yield a next-state distribution, then collapsed to a single sampled successor, repeated to grow a trajectory.
animation_candidates.why: The student Q&A in this lecture is dominated by confusion about exactly this - which dimension is the start state, why the agent cannot be in several states at once, what the transpose does. Animating the vector-matrix product followed by a visible sampling collapse resolves all three at once.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Vector-times-matrix animation feeding a probability histogram that collapses to a single highlighted cell, with the growing trajectory accumulating in a strip below

animation_candidates.what: Enumerating the deterministic policies of a two-state, two-action MDP as a branching tree, then scaling the same construction up to 2^7 for the Mars Rover.
animation_candidates.why: A student explicitly expected the policy count to be linear in the number of states and is surprised by the exponential. The tree makes the independence of the per-state choices - the reason the exponent is |S| and not |A| - immediate, and it motivates why policy iteration beats enumeration.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Tree expansion: one branch level per state, leaves enumerated as arrow-pair policies, then a zoom-out where the four leaves become 128 to show the growth

code_experiment_candidates: Build the seven-state Mars Rover MRP (transition matrix, reward vector, gamma = 0.5) and compute its value function three ways - Monte Carlo rollouts, the closed form (I - gamma P)^{-1} R, and iterative Bellman sweeps - then verify all three agree and plot Monte Carlo error against 1/sqrt(N) on log-log axes to confirm the rate she asserts.

Empirically test the contraction claim: draw many random pairs of value vectors, apply the Bellman optimality backup to each, and plot the ratio ||BV - BV'||_inf / ||V - V'||_inf against gamma. The ratio should sit at or below gamma, confirming the modulus and showing the bound is tight for adversarial pairs.

Compute the eigenvalues of P and the condition number of (I - gamma P) as gamma sweeps toward 1, to see the analytic solution stay valid but become numerically ill-conditioned - the concrete content behind the invertibility question she deferred to Piazza.

Implement policy iteration and value iteration on the Mars Rover MDP; instrument both to record the value function and greedy policy per iteration, verify they reach the same V*, and compare iteration counts and wall-clock time.

Instrument policy iteration to log every policy it visits and assert that no policy ever repeats and that V^{pi_{i+1}} >= V^{pi_i} componentwise at each step - a direct empirical check of the monotone improvement theorem and the |A|^{|S|} iteration bound.

Brute-force enumerate all 128 deterministic policies, evaluate each analytically, and confirm the maximum matches what policy iteration and value iteration return; also count how many distinct policies attain V* to exhibit the non-uniqueness she claims.

Verify the finite-horizon reading of value iteration: for small k, compare V_k from k Bellman sweeps against an exhaustive depth-k expectimax tree search, confirming V_k is exactly the optimal k-steps-to-go value.

Sweep gamma from 0 to 1 and plot the optimal policy for each interior state, locating the critical gamma at which the corridor's +1 end stops beating the +10 end - a concrete demonstration that the discount factor changes the optimal behaviour, not just its scale.

Construct a small MDP with a deliberate tie between two actions and confirm numerically that V* is unique while at least two distinct policies are optimal, plus check that different argmax tie-breaking rules give different but equally good policies.

Test the stopping rule she uses without justifying: run value iteration to machine precision to get V*, then plot the true error ||V_k - V*||_inf against the observed increment ||V_k - V_{k-1}||_inf, and check the standard gamma/(1-gamma) bound relating them.

Break the stationary-distribution claim: build a periodic chain (a two-state deterministic swap) and a reducible chain, and show empirically that the state distribution does not converge or that the limit depends on the start state - the counterexample to her unconditioned assertion.

Compare per-sweep cost empirically: time iterative policy evaluation, value iteration and matrix inversion as |S| grows, to check the |S|^2, |S|^2|A| and |S|^{2-3} scalings claimed or implied in lecture.
dated_or_superseded: The policy iteration bound is given as 'at most |A|^{|S|} iterations', which is correct but enormously loose. Ye (2011) showed policy iteration is strongly polynomial for a fixed discount factor, running in O(|S|^2|A|/(1-gamma) * log(|S|^2/(1-gamma))) iterations; in practice it converges in a handful of steps. Any modern notes should state the strongly-polynomial result alongside the trivial bound.

Matrix inversion is quoted at 'somewhere between N squared and N cubed'. The theoretical exponent is now around 2.37 (Alman-Williams and successors), though N^3 remains the practical figure for dense solves; more importantly, one would solve the linear system directly rather than forming an inverse.

Her aside that gradient-based policy methods can get stuck in local optima, in contrast to tabular policy iteration, predates the global-convergence results for policy gradient in the tabular and softmax settings (Agarwal, Kakade, Lee and Mahajan, 2021, and related work). The contrast is still pedagogically fine but the blanket claim about policy gradient needs a modern footnote.

The lecture's framing of 'given a model of the world' as a slightly artificial special case has aged in the opposite direction from what one might expect: model-based planning with learned models (MuZero-style latent dynamics, and increasingly world models used for planning) has made exact-planning semantics more relevant, not less, even though tabular value and policy iteration are essentially never run at scale.

Discounting is presented as partly principled and partly a convenience, with no mention of the now-standard critiques and alternatives: average-reward MDPs, the argument that gamma is a hyperparameter that distorts the objective being evaluated, and the practice in modern deep RL of using gamma close to 1 with explicit episode truncation and bootstrapping at the cut.

The dynamic-programming sweep is presented as synchronous over all states. Modern treatments would immediately mention asynchronous, in-place and prioritised sweeping, plus real-time dynamic programming, which change both the cost per iteration and the convergence analysis.

The claim about Monte Carlo error going as 1/sqrt(N) is fine but the surrounding treatment predates the now-routine use of variance-reduction and control-variate techniques (and, for planning specifically, MCTS with UCB) as the default sampling-based planners.

Nothing here covers constrained or budgeted MDPs, which is not so much dated as a gap that a 2026 reader working on cost-aware decision making would expect to see cross-referenced (Altman's constrained MDP framework, Lagrangian relaxation, and budget-augmented state).

relevance_to_user_research.why: This lecture supplies the exact formal object the user has already chosen to frame their problem as, and several of its results transfer directly to node-level fidelity assignment, but none of its algorithms is runnable on their setting without substantial modification. What transfers: (1) The finite-horizon reading of value iteration - V_k as the optimal value with k steps to go - is precisely the right algorithm shape for a workflow DAG with a bounded node count. Backward induction over a topological order of the DAG is the exact analogue, and it is the principled version of whatever greedy per-node heuristic they end up shipping. (2) Q^pi(s,a) defined as 'take action a now, then follow pi thereafter' is exactly the quantity their per-node ablations estimate: run node i at strong fidelity and let the current fidelity policy handle the rest. Naming it as a Q value gives them the vocabulary to say what their ablation measures and why it is not the same as the value of the globally-reassigned policy. (3) The policy improvement theorem and its proof are the template for the claim they will want to make in a method section - that an improvement step over per-node fidelity choices is monotone in end-to-end accuracy-minus-cost. Critically, the lecture also makes vivid the exact subtlety that will bite them: the greedy Q argmax only certifies a one-step deviation followed by reversion to the old policy, whereas they intend to change fidelities at many nodes simultaneously and run the new assignment throughout. Brunskill flags this as 'the weird part' and it is a real gap in the naive argument; a per-node ablation sweep followed by a simultaneous reassignment is not covered by the theorem as stated. (4) The |A|^{|S|} counting argument is the clean way to state why exhaustive fidelity search is hopeless: 2^N assignments for N nodes, or more with pruning as a third action - the same exponential that motivates policy iteration over enumeration. (5) Query-level routing as the H = 1 case is exactly the bandit special case the lecture's framework degenerates to. Honest limits on the transfer: the whole lecture assumes a known model, and they have neither a transition kernel (how a node's output distribution shifts under fidelity, and how that propagates downstream) nor a reward model (terminal accuracy) in closed form - both must be estimated from expensive rollouts, which puts them in the learning setting of later lectures, not this one. Their state is high-dimensional and effectively continuous (partial execution traces are text), so tabular DP is out and function approximation is required. Their reward is terminal-only and sparse, which is the credit-assignment problem this lecture sidesteps entirely by assuming per-step rewards. And the budget constraint makes their problem a constrained MDP, which this lecture does not touch at all - the lambda-weighted scalarisation they describe is a Lagrangian relaxation whose justification is nowhere in this material. So: read it for the vocabulary, the Bellman/Q decomposition, the improvement-theorem proof template, and the finite-horizon backward-induction shape. Do not expect an algorithm to lift.

lecture_title: Model-Free Policy Evaluation: Monte Carlo and Temporal Difference Learning
one_paragraph_summary: This lecture asks a single question — given a fixed policy, how do you estimate its value when nobody hands you the transition and reward models — and answers it three ways, then spends most of its energy on how the three answers differ. It first re-frames dynamic programming policy evaluation as an operation on a lookahead tree: DP takes the one-step expectation exactly (because the model is known) and bootstraps, i.e. it substitutes the previous iterate for the entire remaining subtree instead of rolling it out. Monte Carlo throws away the model and the bootstrap: it samples whole trajectories to termination and averages the realized returns, which needs no model and no Markov assumption but only works in episodic settings and is high variance. Temporal difference learning is the hybrid — it samples the next state (like MC) and bootstraps off the current value estimate (like DP) — giving an online, model-free, non-episodic update r + gamma*V(s') - V(s) that can be applied after every single transition. The lecture then builds the machinery to compare these: a recap of estimator bias, variance, and MSE, from which first-visit MC comes out unbiased and consistent, every-visit MC comes out biased (returns from repeated visits inside one episode are correlated, so the average is no longer over IID draws) but consistent and empirically lower variance, and TD(0) comes out biased (it bootstraps off a wrong estimate) but much lower variance and still consistent in the tabular case. A seven-state Mars rover episode is worked through numerically to show that MC updates every visited state at episode end while TD(0) updates only the state whose transition it just saw, so information about a distant reward propagates backward one state per repeated episode. Finally, the batch/offline setting is contrasted with the Sutton and Barto A/B example: given a fixed dataset, MC converges to the minimum mean-squared-error fit to the observed returns while TD(0) converges to the value of the maximum-likelihood (certainty-equivalent) MDP built from the same data, and these disagree — which is the right answer depends entirely on whether the world is actually Markov.
prerequisites: Markov processes, Markov reward processes, and Markov decision processes as defined in L02
Bellman expectation equation and iterative dynamic programming policy evaluation
Discounted return and the role of the discount factor gamma in (0,1]
State value function V^pi and state-action value function Q^pi, and why Q supports policy improvement
Basic probability: expectation, IID sampling, the law of large numbers
Estimator vocabulary: statistic, bias, variance, mean squared error, consistency (the lecture recaps this but assumes some fluency)
Norms on vectors (used for the DP convergence stopping criterion)
Comfort with the tabular / finite state-and-action setting

concepts.name: Course admin and framing
concepts.one_line: Only framing, no logistics: today covers DP policy evaluation (recap), Monte Carlo policy evaluation, and TD learning, plus criteria for comparing estimators; importance sampling for off-policy data is flagged as an end-of-class stretch goal and gets deferred; control comes next lecture.

concepts.name: Return G_t
concepts.one_line: The discounted sum of rewards accumulated from time t onward along one realized trajectory; it is a random variable, not a value.

concepts.name: State value function V^pi
concepts.one_line: The expectation of the return under policy pi starting from state s; distinct from any single realized return whenever the environment is stochastic (the recurring analogy: today's drive to the airport versus the average drive).

concepts.name: State-action value function Q^pi
concepts.one_line: Expected discounted return when you take action a in state s and follow pi afterward; useful because it lets you compare a one-step deviation against the policy, which is the engine of policy improvement.

concepts.name: Iterative DP policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: With known dynamics and reward, initialize V to zero and repeatedly apply V_k(s) = r(s, pi(s)) + gamma * sum_{s'} p(s'|s, pi(s)) V_{k-1}(s'), stopping when the norm of the change between successive iterates falls below epsilon.

concepts.name: DP iterate as an exact finite-horizon value
concepts.one_line: V_k under DP is not merely 'a step toward the answer' — it is exactly the k-horizon value of pi, i.e. the value you would get if you were only allowed to act for k more steps, and it doubles as an approximation of the infinite-horizon value that improves with k.

concepts.name: Lookahead tree / backup diagram
concepts.one_line: Draw the state at the root, the (single, policy-determined) action below it, the stochastic branching over next states below that, and recurse: every policy-evaluation algorithm in the course is a different strategy for approximating the expectation over this tree of possible futures.

concepts.name: Bootstrapping
concepts.one_line: Replacing an entire subtree of future rewards with a cached value estimate for its root instead of rolling the subtree out; DP bootstraps, MC does not, TD does.

concepts.name: Sampling versus bootstrapping as orthogonal approximations
concepts.one_line: Bootstrapping approximates the future discounted return by an estimate; sampling approximates the expectation over next states by drawing from it — DP does neither approximation of the expectation (it has the model) but bootstraps, MC samples but never bootstraps, TD does both.

concepts.name: Why DP's bootstrap costs no accuracy (with a caveat)
concepts.one_line: With a known model, substituting V_{k-1} introduces no sampling error because V_{k-1} is exactly the (k-1)-horizon value under pi — the lecturer's point that bootstrapping is 'free' is about approximation error from the substitution, not about V_{k-1} equalling V^pi.

concepts.name: DP requires a model and the Markov assumption
concepts.one_line: Bootstrapping off V(s') presupposes that s' summarizes the whole history — the value of a state must not depend on how you arrived there.

concepts.name: Stationarity of the infinite-horizon value function
concepts.one_line: Answering a student question: reusing the previous iterate across time steps is legitimate because in the infinite-horizon discounted setting there are always infinitely many steps remaining, so V^pi does not depend on t; the finite-horizon case is genuinely different and is set aside.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: Estimate V^pi(s) by sampling complete episodes under pi and averaging the realized returns from s; requires only the ability to sample from the environment, not a parametric model of it.

concepts.name: Properties of MC policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: Model-free, no bootstrapping, no Markov assumption needed, but restricted to episodic MDPs — you cannot average over lives if you only get one, so a robot that acts forever cannot be evaluated this way.

concepts.name: First-visit Monte Carlo policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: Maintain N(s) and a return total G(s); for each sampled episode compute G_{i,t} for every t, and for each state use only the first time step at which it was visited to increment N(s) and add G_{i,t}, then report V(s) = G(s)/N(s).

concepts.name: Repeated visits within one episode
concepts.one_line: Discretizing time finely means you can sit in the same state for several consecutive steps (three minutes stuck at a red light is three visits to the same state), which is exactly the situation that separates first-visit from every-visit MC.

concepts.name: Bias of an estimator
concepts.one_line: The gap between the expected value of the statistic (expectation taken over datasets drawn under the true parameter) and the true parameter.

concepts.name: Variance of an estimator
concepts.one_line: Expected squared deviation of the statistic from its own mean, under the data distribution induced by the true parameter.

concepts.name: Mean squared error decomposition
concepts.one_line: MSE of an estimator equals its variance plus the square of its bias; MSE is normally what you actually care about, and different algorithms sit at different points on the bias/variance trade-off curve.

concepts.name: First-visit MC is unbiased and consistent
concepts.one_line: Because each episode contributes one IID draw of the return from a state, the sample mean is unbiased, and by the law of large numbers it converges to V^pi as the number of episodes grows.

concepts.name: Bias is generally not computable
concepts.one_line: Answering a student: if you could compute bias exactly you would already know the true parameter and would not need the estimator; in practice you bound it, or use model-selection machinery (structural risk minimization) to compare estimators.

concepts.name: Every-visit Monte Carlo policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: Same bookkeeping as first-visit but you increment the count and add the remaining return for every occurrence of a state within an episode, which yields far more data points per episode.

concepts.name: Every-visit MC is biased but consistent
concepts.one_line: Returns from multiple visits to the same state inside one episode overlap and are therefore correlated, so the average is no longer over IID variables and the estimator picks up bias; it nevertheless converges to V^pi in the limit and empirically has substantially lower variance because it uses far more data.

concepts.name: When first-visit and every-visit coincide
concepts.one_line: If a state is essentially never revisited inside an episode the two estimators are the same; and at matched visit counts first-visit is preferable since it has comparable variance without the bias — the gain from every-visit comes from getting more counts per episode.

concepts.name: Incremental Monte Carlo
concepts.one_line: Keep a running mean and update V(s) toward the observed return with step size alpha; setting alpha = 1/N(s) reproduces every-visit MC exactly, while a constant alpha weights recent data more heavily.

concepts.name: Non-stationary environments
concepts.one_line: A constant step size is the practical hedge when the MDP itself drifts (wearing machinery, shifting user preferences in recommender systems) — old data is then actively misleading, which is why production systems are retrained frequently; the course otherwise assumes stationarity.

concepts.name: MC still requires the full return before updating
concepts.one_line: A self-correction in lecture: incremental MC is 'online' only in the sense of not storing all returns — you still must wait until the episode terminates to compute G_{i,t}.

concepts.name: Mars rover worked example (MC)
concepts.one_line: Seven states, reward +1 at s1 and +10 at s7 and zero elsewhere, policy a1 everywhere, gamma = 1, and the single observed episode s3 -> s2 -> s2 -> s1 with rewards 0,0,0,+1; first-visit MC gives V = [1,1,1,0,0,0,0] and every-visit MC gives V(s2) = 1 as well (N = 2 and total return 2).

concepts.name: MC as a backup diagram
concepts.one_line: MC approximates the expectation over the whole tree by walking one full branch down to a terminal leaf and summing the rewards along it; it never touches p(s'|s,a) and never reuses a cached value.

concepts.name: MC variance and rare events
concepts.one_line: Answering a student: MC estimators are high variance and you may need many rollouts to see rare futures — though rollout-based methods are far from useless in practice (AlphaGo is cited), and how badly rare events hurt depends on what alternatives you have.

concepts.name: Discounting versus guaranteed termination
concepts.one_line: If the process is certain to terminate, returns are finite and gamma < 1 is not needed for MC; but gamma cannot rescue you from a loop that may never terminate, so MC is simply inapplicable there.

concepts.name: Temporal difference learning
concepts.one_line: The hybrid of MC and DP: model-free, samples the next state rather than taking an exact expectation, bootstraps off the current value estimate rather than rolling out, works in both episodic and continuing settings, and updates immediately after each transition.

concepts.name: From incremental MC to TD
concepts.one_line: Take the incremental MC update, which moves V(s_t) toward the sampled return G_{i,t}, and replace the return you would have to wait for with the one-step estimate r_t + gamma * V(s_{t+1}); that single substitution is the whole idea of TD.

concepts.name: TD(0) update rule
concepts.one_line: V(s_t) <- V(s_t) + alpha * (r_t + gamma * V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)), applied after observing each (s, a, r, s') tuple with a = pi(s) during policy evaluation.

concepts.name: TD target
concepts.one_line: The quantity r_t + gamma * V(s_{t+1}) that TD moves its estimate toward; it replaces the Bellman expectation's explicit sum over s' with the single next state that was actually observed.

concepts.name: TD error
concepts.one_line: delta_t = r_t + gamma * V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t), the discrepancy between the one-step bootstrapped target and the current estimate of the state you left.

concepts.name: TD error does not vanish
concepts.one_line: Even with infinite data the TD error does not go to zero unless the transition is deterministic, because the target is a single sampled future while V(s_t) is an expectation over futures (hit traffic versus not).

concepts.name: Step-size conditions for TD convergence
concepts.one_line: Convergence requires mild conditions on a decaying alpha (roughly 1/t suffices); a very small constant alpha is also generally fine, but alpha = 1 discards the previous estimate entirely and can oscillate indefinitely.

concepts.name: TD is biased
concepts.one_line: Bootstrapping off a value estimate that is not yet V^pi injects bias in a systematic direction; DP does not suffer this because with a known model its bootstrap target is the genuine value, whereas TD's is only an approximation.

concepts.name: TD bias is not an initialization artifact
concepts.one_line: Answering a student: you could initialize differently and TD would still be biased — the bias comes from substituting an approximate V^pi(s') into the target, not from the starting values.

concepts.name: TD(0) pseudocode
concepts.one_line: Choose a step-size schedule, initialize V, then loop: sample a transition under pi, apply the TD(0) update to the state you just left, and move on; the tuple is discarded unless you keep a replay buffer.

concepts.name: Mars rover worked example (TD)
concepts.one_line: On the same single episode with alpha = 1, TD(0) yields V = [1,0,0,0,0,0,0]: only s1, the state from which the +1 was actually observed, changes, because by the time the reward appears TD has already discarded the fact that s3 and s2 were visited.

concepts.name: Backward propagation of reward information under TD
concepts.one_line: Repeating the same trajectory moves the learned +1 backward roughly one state per pass (s1, then s2, then s3), so how fast information travels depends on the transition dynamics — this is the price of not doing MC's episode-end sweep.

concepts.name: Replay buffers and update order
concepts.one_line: Naive TD is memoryless and throws each tuple away, which is what you want under tight memory; deep RL instead stores transitions and resamples them, and in a batch the order in which you replay tuples materially affects convergence (a backward sweep propagates reward much faster).

concepts.name: TD is Q-learning with the policy fixed
concepts.one_line: Answering a student: Q-learning is the control analog that also chooses over actions; TD policy evaluation is what you get when the action is pinned to pi(s).

concepts.name: The TD-to-MC continuum
concepts.one_line: The '0' in TD(0) marks the shortest member of a family: you can sum the first n observed rewards and only then bootstrap, sweeping continuously from one-step TD to never-bootstrapping MC; the lecture flags this and does not develop it.

concepts.name: Comparison table: DP, MC, TD
concepts.one_line: Model-free: DP no, MC yes, TD yes. Continuing/non-episodic: DP yes, MC no, TD yes. Tolerates non-Markov: DP no, MC yes, TD no. Converges to V^pi in the tabular limit under mild conditions: all three yes. Unbiased: MC yes (first visit), TD no, DP ill-posed because it is not a sampling estimator at all.

concepts.name: Unbiased versus consistent
concepts.one_line: Unbiasedness is a finite-sample statement (on average across datasets the estimate equals the truth); consistency is an asymptotic one (bias and error vanish as data goes to infinity) — TD is consistent but biased, which shows the two are genuinely different properties.

concepts.name: Failure under violated Markov assumption
concepts.one_line: Applied to a non-Markov environment, DP and TD converge to something simply wrong no matter how much data you collect — the lecturer cites her group's intelligent-tutoring-system work on a fractions tutor — whereas MC just averages realized returns and is safe in partially observable settings.

concepts.name: Divergence under function approximation
concepts.one_line: Everything in this lecture assumes a tabular value function; once you leave the tabular case many model-free evaluation methods are not guaranteed to converge to anything at all, let alone to the right thing — deferred to a later lecture.

concepts.name: Bias-variance summary of the three methods
concepts.one_line: MC: unbiased, high variance, consistent, episodic only. TD: biased, much lower variance, consistent in the tabular case, online. DP: exact given a model, but only for the finite horizon it has iterated to.

concepts.name: Batch / offline policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: Given a fixed set of K episodes collected under pi, repeatedly resample episodes and apply MC or TD until the estimates stop moving — trading extra computation for better use of a fixed and expensive dataset.

concepts.name: Sutton and Barto A/B example
concepts.one_line: Two states, gamma = 1, eight episodes: one is (A, r=0) then (B, r=0); six are (B, r=1); one is (B, r=0). Both methods agree that V(B) = 6/8 = 3/4, but in the batch limit MC gives V(A) = 0 while TD gives V(A) = 0 + 1 * V(B) = 3/4.

concepts.name: Batch MC converges to the minimum-MSE fit
concepts.one_line: Batch Monte Carlo converges to the value function that minimizes squared error against the observed returns, which for A means the single realized return of 0 and nothing else.

concepts.name: Batch TD(0) converges to the certainty-equivalent MDP value
concepts.one_line: Batch TD(0) converges to the solution dynamic programming would give on the maximum-likelihood MDP fitted by counting from the data (P(B|A) = 1, expected reward at B = 3/4), so it exploits Markov structure that MC ignores.

concepts.name: Which batch answer is better depends on the Markov property
concepts.one_line: If the world really is Markov, TD's answer is a strict win — it transfers the six observations about B onto A even though A was visited once; if the world is not Markov, converging to the Markov-model answer is converging to the wrong thing and MC is safer.

concepts.name: Certainty equivalence
concepts.one_line: Estimate P-hat and r-hat from counts, then run exact dynamic programming on the fitted model; suggested as an exercise, and noted to be often far more data-efficient than model-free MC or TD.

concepts.name: Off-policy evaluation via importance sampling
concepts.one_line: Flagged as the technique for evaluating pi from data collected under a different policy, promised if time permitted, and explicitly pushed to a later lecture.

theorems_stated: DP policy evaluation's k-th iterate V_k^pi(s) is exactly the k-horizon value of state s under pi, and equivalently an approximation to the infinite-horizon value that improves with k.
In the infinite-horizon discounted setting V^pi is stationary (independent of the time index), which is what licenses reusing a single value function across all time steps.
MSE of an estimator = variance + bias squared (stated in lecture as a sum of bias and variance, which is a slip).
The first-visit Monte Carlo estimator is an unbiased estimator of V^pi.
The first-visit Monte Carlo estimator is consistent, converging to V^pi by the law of large numbers.
The every-visit Monte Carlo estimator is biased, because returns from repeated visits within a single episode are correlated and therefore not IID.
The every-visit Monte Carlo estimator is nonetheless consistent, and empirically has substantially lower variance than first-visit MC.
Incremental MC with step size alpha = 1/N(s) is exactly equivalent to every-visit Monte Carlo.
At an equal number of counts per state, first-visit MC dominates every-visit MC (same variance, no bias); every-visit's advantage is purely that it accumulates counts faster.
TD(0) is a biased estimator of V^pi, because it bootstraps off a value estimate that is not equal to V^pi.
TD(0) has lower variance than Monte Carlo, and is consistent (converges to V^pi) in the tabular case under mild step-size conditions such as alpha_t on the order of 1/t.
A constant step size of alpha = 1 makes TD ignore its previous estimate and can cause the estimates to oscillate without converging.

The TD error r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t) does not converge to zero even with infinite data unless the environment is deterministic, because it compares a single sampled successor against an expectation over successors.

Monte Carlo policy evaluation does not require the Markov property; dynamic programming and TD both do, and applied to non-Markov data they converge to an incorrect value regardless of how much data is collected.
In the tabular Markov case all three of DP, MC and TD converge to the true V^pi in the limit under mild assumptions.
Unbiasedness and consistency are distinct: an estimator (TD) can be biased at every finite sample size yet have its bias vanish asymptotically.
In the batch/offline setting, Monte Carlo converges to the value function minimizing mean squared error against the observed returns.
In the batch/offline setting, TD(0) converges to the dynamic-programming solution of the maximum-likelihood (certainty-equivalent) MDP estimated by counting from the data.
Batch MC and batch TD(0) can therefore converge to different value functions on the same dataset (the A/B example: V(A) = 0 versus V(A) = 3/4).
Once tabular representations are replaced by function approximation, model-free policy evaluation methods may fail to converge at all, not merely converge to a wrong value.
proofs_given: Numerical verification of the first-visit MC estimate on the Mars rover episode: V = [1,1,1,0,0,0,0], with the class walking state by state and self-correcting V(s4) from 1 to 0.

Numerical verification that every-visit MC gives V(s2) = 1 on the same episode, by explicitly noting N(s2) = 2 and the accumulated return G(s2) = 2, and observing that both visits produced identical returns only because gamma = 1 and the rewards in between were zero.
Numerical verification that TD(0) with alpha = 1 on the same episode updates only s1, by stepping through each (s, a, r, s') tuple in order and showing each earlier update writes a zero.

Explicit computation of the A/B batch example: V(B) = 6/8 under both MC and TD (because B always terminates, so it is effectively a one-step problem), then V(A) = 0 under MC (the only observed A-trajectory returned 0) and V(A) = 0 + 1 * 3/4 = 3/4 under TD (bootstrapping off V(B)) — a concrete counterexample demonstrating that batch MC and batch TD do not agree.

Informal argument for why every-visit MC loses unbiasedness: first-visit gives one IID return per episode; multiple visits within an episode yield overlapping and hence correlated returns, so the sample mean is no longer an average of IID draws.

Informal argument for why TD is biased and DP with a known model is not: DP's bootstrap target is the genuine value of the policy for the horizon it has reached, whereas TD substitutes an approximation of V^pi(s'), and any error there propagates into the update in a systematic direction.
proofs_skipped: Convergence of iterative DP policy evaluation. The Bellman expectation operator being a gamma-contraction in the sup norm, and Banach's fixed-point theorem giving existence, uniqueness, and a geometric convergence rate, are never stated; only the epsilon stopping criterion appears.
That V^pi is the unique fixed point of the Bellman expectation equation, and that (I - gamma P^pi) is invertible so V^pi = (I - gamma P^pi)^{-1} r^pi exists in closed form.
The induction showing that the k-th DP iterate is exactly the k-horizon value of pi. This is asserted as an interpretation with no proof.

The relationship between the epsilon stopping threshold and the actual distance to V^pi (i.e. that a small successive difference implies a bounded error, via the standard epsilon*gamma/(1-gamma) bound).

Unbiasedness of first-visit MC. That E[G_{i,t} | s_t = s] = V^pi(s) is asserted, never derived; in particular the subtlety that the first-visit times are themselves random (the inspector's-paradox worry a student raises) is explicitly left as an open question the lecturer says she will look into.

The law-of-large-numbers argument for MC consistency is invoked by name only; which LLN (weak/strong), what integrability and independence conditions are needed, and whether convergence is in probability or almost sure are all unspecified.

That every-visit MC is biased. Only the correlation intuition is offered. No derivation of the bias, no statement of its sign, and no rate (the standard result, Singh and Sutton 1996, is that the bias is O(1/n) in the number of episodes and that the estimator is consistent).
That every-visit MC is consistent. Asserted flatly with no argument, despite the estimator not being an average of IID variables.

That every-visit MC has lower variance than first-visit MC. Justified only as 'empirically' and 'intuitively, more data points'; no variance comparison is derived, and the claim is not universally true.
The claim that at matched counts first-visit is better because it has 'basically the same variance' without the bias. Asserted in response to a student question, with no supporting analysis.
The MSE = variance + bias^2 decomposition. Stated (and garbled as a plain sum) with no derivation of the cross-term vanishing.
The equivalence of incremental MC with alpha = 1/N(s) to the batch sample mean. Asserted; the one-line induction showing the running-mean recursion reproduces the average is skipped.

Convergence of tabular TD(0). The stochastic-approximation proof (Robbins-Monro conditions sum alpha_t = infinity and sum alpha_t^2 < infinity, plus the Jaakkola-Jordan-Singh / Dayan / Tsitsiklis machinery) is entirely absent; even the Robbins-Monro conditions themselves are not written down, only the example alpha_t = 1/t.
Quantification of TD(0)'s bias. It is argued to exist and to be directional, but no expression, bound, or asymptotic rate is given, and no statement of how it interacts with the step-size schedule.

That TD has lower variance than MC. Asserted repeatedly with a hand-wave about bootstrapping 'averaging over variability'; no variance calculation, and no statement of when this fails (it does not always hold).

That constant alpha causes oscillation or convergence only to a neighborhood of V^pi. Asserted for alpha = 1; the standard result that constant alpha gives convergence in distribution to a ball whose radius scales with alpha is not stated.

That the TD error does not vanish except under deterministic dynamics. Argued verbally via the traffic example; never formalized as E[delta_t | s_t] = 0 at the fixed point while delta_t itself has nonzero variance.
That batch Monte Carlo converges to the minimizer of squared error against the observed returns. Asserted; the argument that the sample mean is the least-squares solution is not spelled out.

That batch TD(0) converges to the certainty-equivalence estimate, i.e. to the exact value of the maximum-likelihood MDP. This is the most consequential unproved claim in the lecture; the proof (that the batch TD fixed point satisfies the Bellman equation of the empirical model) is entirely omitted.

That certainty-equivalence model-based evaluation is more data-efficient than MC or TD. Asserted as 'often much more data efficient' with no sample-complexity comparison; the reader is told to work out the construction themselves.
Why exactly the certainty-equivalent model's DP solution is a sensible estimator at all — no discussion of when the plug-in model estimate is consistent or of its own bias.

That MC is valid without the Markov property. Asserted; what exactly MC converges to in a partially observable or history-dependent environment (the return averaged over the state-occupancy distribution induced by pi, which need not equal any per-observation value) is never characterized.

That DP and TD converge to a wrong answer under violated Markov assumptions 'no matter how much data'. Supported by an anecdote about a fractions intelligent tutoring system; no bound on the resulting bias, no criterion for testing Markovianity, and no discussion of how to detect the failure.
The claim that TD learning is the analog of Q-learning with the policy fixed. Stated as an aside; no derivation of the correspondence between the TD(0) and Q-learning updates.
The n-step / TD(lambda) continuum between TD(0) and MC. Mentioned as existing; no update rule, no bias-variance characterization as a function of n or lambda, no forward/backward view equivalence.

Divergence of model-free policy evaluation under function approximation. Asserted as a preview; no counterexample (e.g. Baird's star), no statement of the deadly triad, no conditions under which linear TD does converge (on-policy linear TD does converge, and this qualification is not made).
How the order of updates in the batch setting affects convergence speed. Acknowledged to matter absolutely; no analysis, and the backward-sweep advantage is only gestured at.

How many samples are needed to propagate reward information back through a chain of states under TD. A student asks directly; the answer is 'it depends on the dynamics' with no bound, and no mention of the mixing-time or effective-horizon dependence.
Any concentration inequality bounding the deviation of an MC or TD estimate from its mean. Concentration inequalities are named in passing as a tool for variance but never applied.
Structural risk minimization as a way to reason about estimator bias. Named (as 'structural risk maximization') and deferred to office hours.
Importance sampling for off-policy policy evaluation. Announced as the intended final topic and dropped entirely; the estimator, its unbiasedness, and its variance blow-up are all absent.
algorithms: Iterative dynamic programming policy evaluation. Initialize V_0 = 0. Repeat for k = 1, 2, ...: for all s, V_k(s) = r(s, pi(s)) + gamma * sum_{s'} p(s' | s, pi(s)) * V_{k-1}(s'). Stop when ||V_k - V_{k-1}|| < epsilon. Requires known dynamics and reward; each iterate is exactly the k-horizon value of pi.

First-visit Monte Carlo policy evaluation. Initialize N(s) = 0, G(s) = 0, V(s) = 0 for all s. Loop over episodes i: generate s_1, a_1, r_1, ..., s_T under pi; compute G_{i,t} = r_t + gamma*r_{t+1} + ... + gamma^{T-t}*r_T for every t. For each state s, let t be the FIRST time step in episode i at which s occurs (skip s if it never occurs): N(s) <- N(s) + 1; G(s) <- G(s) + G_{i,t}; V(s) <- G(s)/N(s). Ignore all later occurrences of s within the same episode.

Every-visit Monte Carlo policy evaluation. Identical bookkeeping, but the inner loop runs over EVERY time step t at which s occurs in the episode, so a state visited three times contributes three (correlated) returns and three increments to N(s).

Incremental Monte Carlo policy evaluation. For each visit (first-visit or every-visit as chosen), update V(s) <- V(s) + alpha * (G_{i,t} - V(s)). With alpha = 1/N(s) this is algebraically identical to every-visit MC; with alpha held constant the estimate becomes an exponentially weighted average favouring recent episodes, which is the recommended variant for non-stationary environments. Note: you still must wait for the episode to terminate before you can form G_{i,t}.

TD(0) policy evaluation. Choose a step-size schedule alpha_t (decaying, e.g. on the order of 1/t, for convergence guarantees). Initialize V arbitrarily (e.g. zero). Loop forever: observe the current state s_t, take a_t = pi(s_t), observe r_t and s_{t+1}; update V(s_t) <- V(s_t) + alpha_t * (r_t + gamma * V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)); set s_t <- s_{t+1}. The bracketed quantity is the TD error; r_t + gamma*V(s_{t+1}) is the TD target. In its naive form the transition tuple is then discarded; the replay-buffer variant stores tuples and resamples them for repeated updates.

Batch (offline) policy evaluation. Given a fixed set of K episodes collected under pi, repeatedly sample an episode from the set and apply either the MC update or the TD update to it, sweeping many times until estimates converge. MC and TD have different fixed points in this regime. Update order within the batch materially affects convergence speed (a backward sweep propagates reward much faster than a forward one).

Certainty-equivalence (model-based) policy evaluation. From the batch data, form maximum-likelihood estimates by counting: P-hat(s'|s,a) = count(s,a,s') / count(s,a), and r-hat(s,a) = mean observed reward at (s,a). Then run exact dynamic programming (or solve the linear system) on the fitted MDP to obtain V-hat^pi. Presented as an exercise and claimed to be often substantially more data-efficient than model-free MC or TD; it is also the fixed point that batch TD(0) converges to.
notation_introduced: G_t = discounted return from time t: r_t + gamma*r_{t+1} + gamma^2*r_{t+2} + ..., a random variable along one trajectory
gamma in [0,1], the discount factor; the lecture sets gamma = 1 in both worked examples to keep arithmetic clean
V^pi(s) = E[G_t | s_t = s] under policy pi, the state value function
Q^pi(s,a) = E[G_t | s_t = s, a_t = a, then follow pi], the state-action value function
V^pi_k, the k-th iterate of DP policy evaluation, interpreted as the exact k-horizon value under pi; also written informally as V_{k+1} and V_k when emphasizing iteration order
||V^pi_k - V^pi_{k-1}|| < epsilon as the DP convergence criterion (norm left unspecified)
p(s' | s, a), the dynamics / transition model (the lecture uses 'dynamics' and 'transition model' interchangeably); r(s, a) the reward model
N(s), the visit count for state s; G(s), the accumulated return total for state s
G_{i,t}, the return computed from time step t within episode i
alpha, the step size / learning rate, possibly a function of the time step
theta, a model parameter; theta-hat(x), a statistic that is a function of the observed data and estimates theta
Bias(theta-hat) = E[theta-hat] - theta; Var(theta-hat) = E[(theta-hat - E[theta-hat])^2]; MSE = Var + Bias^2
(s, a, r, s') transition tuple, the unit of experience TD consumes
TD target: r_t + gamma * V^pi(s_{t+1})
TD error (temporal difference error): r_t + gamma * V^pi(s_{t+1}) - V^pi(s_t)
TD(0), where the 0 denotes bootstrapping after one observed reward, marking the shortest member of a family of n-step methods
P-hat and r-hat, the maximum-likelihood (count-based) model estimates used in certainty equivalence
notation_hazards: MSE is stated in lecture as 'the sum of its bias and its variance'. The correct decomposition is variance plus bias SQUARED. Corrected silently above.
'Structural risk maximization' is said aloud; the technique is structural risk MINIMIZATION.

The Q-function is introduced as 'the expected reward if we follow pi but start by taking a' — it is the expected discounted RETURN, not a single reward. Similar loose use of 'reward' for 'return' recurs throughout.

V^pi_k is overloaded. In the DP section it is the exact k-horizon value function (a well-defined mathematical object). In the TD section the lecturer explicitly notes there is no clean global V_k any more, because TD updates one entry of a single value table asynchronously rather than producing a coherent sweep of iterates; she nevertheless keeps the k-1 subscript on the board. Downstream notes should distinguish 'synchronous iterate' from 'current table'.
The transcript garbles the DP backup as 'V^pi_{k-1}, the best part' — the trailing words are caption noise, not mathematics; the intended object is just V^pi_{k-1}(s').

The claim that 'you don't get biased in dynamic programming because that V^pi you bootstrap is actually V^pi' is imprecise. In DP, V_{k-1} is the exact (k-1)-horizon value, which is NOT the infinite-horizon V^pi; the lecture itself concedes this later when filling in the comparison table. The precise statement is that DP's bootstrap introduces no SAMPLING error, and that the bias it does carry is a horizon-truncation bias that vanishes geometrically in k.

The reward layout of the Mars rover is stated confusingly ('reward is in state S_1, one and state S_7 it's plus 10'). Intended: r(s1) = +1, r(s7) = +10, r = 0 elsewhere, and taking any action from s1 or s7 collects that reward and terminates.
The TD Mars rover answer 'one followed by all zeros' only holds for alpha = 1, which the transcript never states explicitly. With a smaller alpha the answer is [alpha, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0].
In the A/B batch example the spoken numbers slide between '6 divided by 8', 'three quarters' and 'V of B is equal to 3- 6 8ths'. All refer to the same value 3/4.

The lecturer says both 'six of eight episodes gave reward 1' and separately describes 'in two of them we got a zero' — the dataset is one A-episode ending in B with reward 0, six B-only episodes with reward 1, and one B-only episode with reward 0, so B is visited eight times and yields reward 1 exactly six times.
'It converges to the true estimate' is said where 'the true value' is meant.

Sutton and Barto write the Bellman expectation backup as a sum over actions weighted by pi(a|s); this lecture assumes a deterministic policy throughout and writes r(s, pi(s)) directly. Reconciling with the textbook requires reinstating the outer expectation over actions.
'Asymptotically no under minor assumptions' is caption noise for 'asymptotically, under mild assumptions'.
'Important sampling' in the transcript is importance sampling.

Alpha = 1/N(s) is said to make incremental MC 'identical to every visit Monte Carlo'; this is correct only when N(s) is the every-visit count. With the first-visit count it reproduces first-visit MC instead. The step size and the counting rule are independent choices.

animation_candidates.what: Three backup diagrams drawn on one shared lookahead tree, with DP, MC, and TD(0) each lighting up only the nodes they touch.
animation_candidates.why: This is the organizing idea of the entire lecture and it is inherently spatial: DP fans out one full level and stops at cached values, MC drills one branch all the way to a terminal leaf, TD(0) touches exactly one edge. Static text has to describe three things serially that the viewer needs to compare simultaneously; a single tree with three overlays makes the sampling-versus-bootstrapping axes visible at a glance.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Backup diagram: a fixed state-action tree rendered once, then three timed passes highlighting visited nodes, with a two-axis badge (samples? bootstraps?) filling in as each pass completes.

animation_candidates.what: The Mars rover strip of seven states with the single episode s3 -> s2 -> s2 -> s1, showing first-visit MC, every-visit MC, and TD(0) writing into the value vector.
animation_candidates.why: The punchline is that identical data produces [1,1,1,0,0,0,0] under MC and [1,0,0,0,0,0,0] under TD, and the reason is purely about WHEN each algorithm writes. Watching MC wait for termination and then sweep backward over the whole episode, versus TD writing a zero at each step and only catching the +1 at the very end, converts an abstract 'TD does not propagate information backward' into something you see happen.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Grid-world value sweep: a 1x7 strip of value cells with a moving agent token, a running return accumulator for MC, and cell-flash animations on each write.

animation_candidates.what: Repeating the same Mars rover episode three times under TD(0) so the +1 crawls backward one state per pass.
animation_candidates.why: This is the single most common misconception about TD — students believe the update is 'just DP but sampled' and do not internalize that reward information travels at one state per episode. Three consecutive passes shown as a filmstrip makes the propagation speed, and therefore the motivation for n-step returns, eligibility traces, and backward replay sweeps, immediately obvious.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Filmstrip of three value-vector states side by side, with an arrow tracing the +1 moving leftward, then a fourth panel showing what MC produced after one episode for contrast.

animation_candidates.what: Sampling distributions of first-visit MC, every-visit MC, and TD(0) estimates of one state's value, animated as the number of episodes grows.
animation_candidates.why: Bias, variance, consistency, and MSE are four distinct properties that students routinely collapse into 'accuracy'. Watching MC's cloud stay centered on the truth but wide, TD's cloud sit tight but visibly offset and then slide onto the truth, and every-visit MC's cloud narrow while carrying a shrinking offset, separates unbiasedness from consistency in a way that the lecture's verbal Q&A struggled to.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Scatter plus fitted density curves over the estimate axis, with a vertical line at the true V^pi, an episode-count slider driving the animation, and an MSE = variance + bias^2 bar decomposing alongside.

animation_candidates.what: The A/B batch example: eight episode strips fed into two engines that produce different answers for V(A).
animation_candidates.why: This is the lecture's sharpest result and its proof is a construction, not an argument. Animating the same eight episodes flowing into an MC engine (which only ever looks at the one A-trajectory and returns 0) and a TD engine (which builds the empirical graph A -> B, learns V(B) = 3/4, then backs it up into A) makes the certainty-equivalence claim concrete rather than a slogan.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Tree expansion / dataflow: eight episode rows on the left, splitting into two panels — a returns-averaging panel and an estimated-MDP-graph panel with edge probabilities being counted in, then a backup arrow filling V(A) = 3/4.

animation_candidates.what: Term-by-term morph of the update rule from DP backup, through incremental MC, into TD(0).
animation_candidates.why: The lecture derives TD in one spoken sentence ('replace G with r + gamma V(s')'), which is exactly the kind of substitution that is trivial once seen and opaque when read. A morph that holds the surrounding algebra fixed while one term slides out and another slides in shows that MC and TD are the same update with different targets, and that DP is the same target with the sample replaced by an expectation.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Term-level formula morph: three aligned equations with color-coded terms, cross-fading the target term while the V(s) <- V(s) + alpha(target - V(s)) scaffold stays fixed.

animation_candidates.what: The TD error as a persistent sample-versus-expectation gap, on the two-branch traffic example.
animation_candidates.why: Students expect the TD error to go to zero at convergence, by analogy with a residual. Showing a converged V(s) with two possible successors, and delta_t alternating between two nonzero values forever while its mean sits at zero, kills that misconception in one shot and motivates why step sizes must decay.
