animation_candidates.visual_form: Two-branch chart with a live delta_t trace: a running plot that keeps oscillating while its running mean flatlines at zero, contrasted against a deterministic-environment panel where delta genuinely collapses.

animation_candidates.what: A slider sweeping the bootstrap depth n from 1 (TD(0)) to episode length (MC), with bias and variance meters responding.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture names this continuum and drops it. Since the whole point of the lecture is a bias-variance trade-off, and the continuum is the trade-off made continuous, one interactive control does more work than the entire comparison table.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Interactive tree where the sampled prefix (solid path) grows and the bootstrapped tail (collapsed cached node) shrinks, with two live gauges for bias and variance.

code_experiment_candidates: Implement the 7-state Mars rover as a tabular MRP with a chosen stochastic transition matrix, compute the exact V^pi by solving (I - gamma*P)V = r, then run first-visit MC, every-visit MC, and TD(0) and plot RMSE against V^pi versus number of episodes on shared axes. This is the load-bearing experiment: it reproduces the lecture's whole comparison table empirically in about forty lines.

Reproduce the lecture's single-episode calculation exactly as a unit test: assert first-visit MC yields [1,1,1,0,0,0,0], every-visit MC yields V(s2) = 1, and TD(0) with alpha = 1 yields [1,0,0,0,0,0,0]. Cheap, and it pins the semantics of the three update rules before any of the statistical experiments run.

Measure the bias of every-visit versus first-visit MC directly. Build a chain with a deliberate self-loop so states are revisited many times per episode, run each estimator 2000 independent times at each of several episode budgets, and plot (mean estimate - true value) versus budget. Should show every-visit's bias decaying roughly like 1/n while first-visit's hovers at zero, which is the result the lecture asserts without proof.

Reproduce the A/B batch example verbatim (two states, gamma = 1, the eight specified episodes), run batch MC and batch TD(0) to convergence with a small constant alpha over many sweeps, and confirm V(A) converges to 0 and 3/4 respectively while both give V(B) = 0.75. Then add the certainty-equivalence solver and confirm it agrees with batch TD to numerical precision — this turns the lecture's biggest unproved claim into a checkable fact.

Step-size study for TD(0): compare constant alpha in {1.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01}, alpha = 1/N(s), and alpha_t = 1/t^0.6 on the same environment; plot the error trace to show alpha = 1 oscillating, small constant alpha converging to a noisy band whose width scales with alpha, and Robbins-Monro schedules converging.

Reproduce Sutton and Barto's 5-state random walk (Example 6.2): RMS error of MC versus TD across a sweep of alpha values and episode counts. It is the canonical figure this lecture is implicitly describing and gives a reference plot to check the implementation against.

n-step TD sweep: implement n-step returns and plot final RMSE as a function of n from 1 to the episode length, at several alpha values. Directly instantiates the TD(0)-to-MC continuum the lecture names and drops, and yields the U-shaped bias-variance curve.

Certainty-equivalence versus model-free sample efficiency: at each of several dataset sizes, fit P-hat and r-hat by counting, solve exactly, and compare RMSE against batch TD and batch MC on the same data. Tests the lecture's unproved claim that the model-based route is often far more data-efficient.

Markov-violation demo: construct a chain where two genuinely different states emit the same observation (state aliasing), then run MC and TD on the observation sequence. MC should converge to the correct expected return per observation while TD converges to a persistently wrong value regardless of data volume, reproducing the intelligent-tutoring-system failure the lecture only tells an anecdote about.

Variance measurement: run 500 independent seeds of MC and TD, and plot the empirical variance (not just the mean error) of the value estimate versus episode count, to make the 'TD has much lower variance' claim quantitative rather than asserted.

Batch replay ordering: on a fixed dataset, compare forward sweeps, backward sweeps, and uniformly random replay of TD updates, plotting sweeps-to-convergence. Makes concrete the lecturer's remark that update order 'absolutely affects your convergence' and previews prioritized replay.
dated_or_superseded: 'Probably TD learning is the most popular' — still broadly true, but the modern default for policy evaluation inside deep RL is not plain TD(0). It is a neural critic trained with a target network and replay (the DQN lineage) or, for policy-gradient methods, GAE(lambda), which is precisely the TD(0)-to-MC continuum the lecture mentions and does not develop. GAE has been the practical answer since 2015 and is what PPO ships with.

'For things like AlphaGo they use Monte Carlo' — AlphaGo (2016) did blend MCTS rollouts with a value network, but AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero (2017-2018) removed the rollouts entirely, using the learned value at the leaf instead, and MuZero (2019-2020) learns a latent dynamics model and plans in it. The modern lesson is closer to 'learned bootstrapped values replaced Monte Carlo rollouts' than to 'Monte Carlo works fine'.

The replay-buffer remark is DQN-era. Current practice adds prioritized experience replay, n-step returns inside the buffer, distributional value learning (C51, QR-DQN, IQN), and off-policy corrections such as Retrace and V-trace for when the buffer's behaviour policy drifts from the target policy. None of these existed in the form assumed by 'you resample and do this update'.

Certainty equivalence is presented as a side exercise; since 2019 model-based RL has become a major area, and the data-efficiency claim has been formalized — plug-in model-based estimation is now known to be minimax-optimal for tabular policy evaluation in the generative-model setting, and Dreamer / MBPO style methods carry the idea into deep RL. The lecture's 'often much more data efficient' is now a theorem plus a large empirical literature rather than a hunch.

Off-policy evaluation via importance sampling, deferred here, has moved substantially. Naive per-trajectory importance sampling is now rarely competitive; doubly-robust estimators, weighted/per-decision IS, and marginalized importance sampling (the DICE family) are the standard tools, along with a mature offline-RL literature (CQL, IQL) built on top of them.

The function-approximation warning is still correct but is now framed as the 'deadly triad' (bootstrapping + off-policy + function approximation), with known partial remedies — gradient-TD and emphatic TD give convergence guarantees under linear function approximation, and on-policy linear TD was already known to converge. The bare 'they might not converge to anything' understates what is now known.

The bias-variance treatment of every-visit MC is fine but the modern reference point is that every-visit MC's bias is O(1/n) and it is consistent (Singh and Sutton 1996), a result that predates the lecture and could simply have been cited instead of left as intuition.

relevance_to_user_research.why: This is the first lecture in the sequence whose content actually distinguishes the user's new problem from the one they already solved. Query-level routing (AEP) is H=1: there is no future to estimate, so MC and TD coincide and the whole lecture collapses to 'average the observed reward'. Node-level fidelity assignment is H>1 with a purely terminal reward (task accuracy is only observed after the DAG finishes) minus per-node token costs incurred along the way — which is exactly the credit-assignment setting this lecture is about, and the MC-versus-TD choice becomes a real design decision rather than a formality. Three things transfer concretely. First, the Markov warning is load-bearing and is the most likely place for the user to be quietly wrong: their proposed state includes 'partial execution trace', which in practice will be some hand-engineered summary of generated text, and any such summary almost certainly violates the Markov property. The lecture's point is that under aliasing, bootstrapped estimators converge to a confidently wrong value no matter how much data you collect, whereas MC-style terminal-return credit assignment stays honest. If they train a per-node critic with TD over hand-crafted features, they need to know this failure mode exists and should design a probe for it (the state-aliasing experiment above is a two-hour sanity check). Second, the bias-variance framing is the right lens for the actual trade-off they face: rollouts are extremely expensive (each episode is a full multi-node workflow of vLLM calls on the A100 nodes), so MC's high variance costs real GPU hours, while a bootstrapped critic buys variance reduction at the price of a bias they cannot easily measure. The n-step / GAE continuum, which the lecture names and skips, is very likely the practical answer given DAG depths of roughly 3-15 nodes. Third, their setting is fundamentally batch/offline — they will collect workflow rollouts once and want to evaluate many fidelity policies against that fixed dataset — so the A/B example and certainty equivalence are directly on point: with a small discrete action space (weak / strong / prune) and a bounded node count, a plug-in empirical model over node outcomes is genuinely tractable and may well beat model-free evaluation on their data budget. What keeps this from 'critical' is that the lecture is entirely tabular and on-policy, and neither of those survives contact with their problem. Their state space is not enumerable, their reward has a budget constraint that this lecture's unconstrained discounted formulation does not express, and the technique they most need — off-policy evaluation, so they can score alternative fidelity assignments against logged rollouts without re-running the workflow — is exactly the topic that gets announced and then dropped at the end of this lecture. Treat L03 as the conceptual foundation that tells them which questions to ask, and get the answers from the off-policy-evaluation and function-approximation lectures downstream.

lecture_title: Lecture 4 - Model-Free Control (Monte Carlo control, SARSA, Q-learning, maximization bias)
one_paragraph_summary: This lecture closes the loop from model-free *evaluation* (L03) to model-free *control*: how an agent improves its policy when it has neither a dynamics nor a reward model and refuses to build one. The organizing device is generalized policy iteration with the model surgically removed. Two substitutions do all the work. First, evaluate Q rather than V, because greedy improvement from Q is argmax_a Q(s,a) and needs no model, whereas greedy improvement from V needs a one-step Bellman backup through P and R. Second, since a deterministic greedy policy would only ever sample one action per state and therefore learn nothing about alternatives, replace greedy with epsilon-greedy. Brunskill then proves on the board the one result the lecture actually establishes: epsilon-greedy improvement is monotonic, i.e. the epsilon-greedy policy w.r.t. Q^{pi_i} is at least as good as pi_i, provided Q^{pi_i} is exact. The algebra hinges on rewriting max_a Q as an upper bound on any convex combination of Q values whose weights are (pi_i(a|s) - eps/|A|)/(1-eps). Around that core she assembles the algorithm family: Monte Carlo on-policy Q evaluation, GLIE Monte Carlo online control with eps_k = 1/k, SARSA (on-policy TD control, bootstrapping on the action actually taken), and Q-learning (off-policy TD control, bootstrapping on the max). Convergence for all three is *asserted* under GLIE plus Robbins-Monro step sizes, with a crucial asymmetry made explicit for Q-learning: infinite visits plus admissible step sizes suffice for Q -> Q*, but making the *followed* policy optimal additionally requires GLIE. The lecture ends on maximization bias: in a single-state, two-action MDP with zero-mean stochastic rewards, each empirical Q is unbiased yet E[max_a Q-hat] >= max_a E[Q-hat] = V* by Jensen, so greedy value estimates are systematically optimistic on finite samples; double Q-learning fixes this by decoupling action selection from action evaluation across two independently-updated Q tables.
prerequisites: MDP formalism: states, actions, transition model P(s'|s,a), reward model R(s,a), discount gamma, expected discounted return
Value functions V^pi and Q^pi, the Bellman expectation and Bellman optimality equations
Policy iteration and value iteration with a known model, including the policy improvement theorem (proved in an earlier lecture and reused here as a black box)
Monte Carlo policy evaluation for V^pi: first-visit vs every-visit, unbiasedness of first-visit, variance/bias trade-off
TD(0) policy evaluation for V^pi, and the two ideas it combines: sampling the expectation over s' and bootstrapping on the current estimate
Incremental / running-average updates and the role of a learning rate alpha
Basic probability: expectations, unbiased estimators, convexity and Jensen's inequality
Familiarity with the 7-state Mars rover toy MDP used throughout CS234

concepts.name: Course sessions, homework, office hours
concepts.one_line: Optional structured deep-dive sessions announced on Piazza carry 1% extra credit tracked via in-session attendance codes; the last one is recorded over Zoom for SCPD students, and homework 1 plus regular office hours are running.

concepts.name: Scope of model-free control
concepts.one_line: Today the agent must choose actions to maximize expected discounted return while knowing neither dynamics nor reward, and while deliberately declining to estimate either - learning happens directly from experience in the value function.

concepts.name: Which of the RL difficulties are in play
concepts.one_line: This lecture adds optimization and exploration to the delayed-consequence problem already present in evaluation; generalization (function approximation) is explicitly postponed.

concepts.name: TD-Gammon as historical motivation
concepts.one_line: Tesauro's backgammon player (early 1990s, dated in the talk as roughly 1994) trained a neural network by model-free RL and was the first convincing demonstration that this style of learning scales to a nontrivial game.

concepts.name: When model-free is the right choice
concepts.one_line: Model-free methods are motivated not only by an unknown model but also by a known-yet-ruinously-expensive one, e.g. climate or sustainability simulators where each rollout costs as much as a real-world robot trial.

concepts.name: On-policy vs off-policy learning
concepts.one_line: On-policy learning estimates and improves the same policy that generated the data; off-policy learning uses data gathered under one behavior to estimate the value of a different policy, e.g. splicing together the (s1,a1) and (s1,a2) experiences to reason about an action sequence never actually executed.

concepts.name: Generalized policy iteration recap
concepts.one_line: With a known model: initialize pi arbitrarily, compute V^pi by policy evaluation, then set pi'(s) = argmax_a [R(s,a) + gamma sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) V^pi(s')], and repeat - the improvement step is precisely the step that needs the model.

concepts.name: Finite termination of policy iteration
concepts.one_line: Because each round either strictly improves the policy or leaves it fixed, and there are at most |A|^|S| deterministic policies over finite S and A, policy iteration terminates after finitely many improvement steps.

concepts.name: Two ways to drop the model
concepts.one_line: Either estimate P-hat and R-hat from data and plan in the estimated MDP (model-based, acknowledged as reasonable and personally favored but set aside), or estimate Q directly and improve greedily from it (model-free, taken today).

concepts.name: Why Q rather than V for model-free control
concepts.one_line: Greedy improvement from V requires a one-step lookahead through the unknown dynamics and reward, whereas greedy improvement from Q is a pure argmax over the stored table, so Q is the object that makes improvement model-free.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo on-policy Q evaluation
concepts.one_line: Run the V-version of Monte Carlo evaluation with every S replaced by the pair (S,A): maintain N(s,a) and a running total G(s,a) of returns, update on first (or every) visit to a state-action pair within each episode, and set Q^pi(s,a) = G(s,a)/N(s,a).

concepts.name: Greedy policy improvement from Q
concepts.one_line: Given an estimate Q^{pi_i}, the improved policy is simply pi_{i+1}(s) = argmax_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a), with no model access at all.

concepts.name: The no-exploration failure of deterministic greedy policies
concepts.one_line: A deterministic policy visits exactly one action per state, so Q^pi(s,a) is only ever estimated at a = pi(s); every other entry stays at its initialization and the argmax step is therefore vacuous, however much data is collected.

concepts.name: Optimistic initialization (deferred)
concepts.one_line: Initializing Q high everywhere makes untried actions look attractive and drives systematic exploration; with the right initialization this yields provable bounds on the data needed to reach the optimal policy, but the analysis is postponed to the exploration lecture.

concepts.name: Markov caveat on the policy class
concepts.one_line: Everything here assumes policies that map the current state to actions; if the real environment is not Markov in that state, one is optimizing within a restricted policy class and may be unable to represent the genuinely best history-dependent behavior.

concepts.name: Epsilon-greedy policy
concepts.one_line: With probability 1-eps take argmax_a Q(s,a) and with probability eps sample uniformly from all |A| actions, so pi(a|s) = eps/|A| for non-greedy actions and 1 - eps + eps/|A| for the greedy one - the random branch is not required to exclude the greedy action.

concepts.name: Mars rover Monte Carlo Q example
concepts.one_line: With R(s,a1) = (1,0,0,0,0,0,10), R(s,a2) = (0,0,0,0,0,0,5), gamma = 1, greedy policy a1 everywhere and eps = 0.5, one sampled epsilon-greedy trajectory (s3,a1,0; s2,a2,0; s3,a1,0; s2,a2,0; s1,a1,1; terminal) gives every visited pair a first-visit return of 1 and leaves all unvisited pairs at 0.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo splits experience across actions
concepts.one_line: Taking the max over the two Q rows recovers the same value vector Monte Carlo produced for V in the previous lecture, but the same episode now has to be shared out among |A| tables, so each entry is estimated from fewer samples.

concepts.name: First-visit vs every-visit in this example
concepts.one_line: Every-visit changes nothing here because both visits to s3 have identical return-to-go of 1; the two estimators only diverge when repeated visits within an episode carry different remaining returns.

concepts.name: Monotonic improvement of epsilon-greedy policy improvement
concepts.one_line: If pi_{i+1} is epsilon-greedy with respect to the exact Q^{pi_i} of an epsilon-greedy pi_i, then Q^{pi_i}(s, pi_{i+1}(s)) >= V^{pi_i}(s) for every s, and hence V^{pi_{i+1}} >= V^{pi_i} pointwise.

concepts.name: Board proof of epsilon-greedy improvement
concepts.one_line: Expand Q^{pi_i}(s,pi_{i+1}(s)) = (eps/|A|) sum_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a) + (1-eps) max_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a), multiply the max term by (1-eps)/(1-eps), replace the implicit 1 by sum_a [pi_i(a|s) - eps/|A|]/(1-eps) (which is a valid probability vector since pi_i is epsilon-soft), push Q inside the sum so the max becomes a weighted average and the inequality flips to >=, then cancel the two identical eps/|A| terms to leave exactly sum_a pi_i(a|s) Q^{pi_i}(s,a) = V^{pi_i}(s).

concepts.name: Exactness caveat on monotonic improvement
concepts.one_line: The guarantee holds only when Q^{pi_i} is computed exactly; with a sampled or function-approximated Q a single unlucky rollout of a rarely-tried action can make the improvement step move the policy backwards, which is why the guarantee evaporates once approximation enters.

concepts.name: Greedy in the Limit of Infinite Exploration (GLIE)
concepts.one_line: A policy sequence is GLIE if every state-action pair is visited infinitely often and the behavior policy converges to the greedy one, pi_i(a|s) -> 1[a = argmax_a Q(s,a)] with probability 1; decaying eps_i = 1/i is a sufficient construction.

concepts.name: GLIE Monte Carlo control converges
concepts.one_line: GLIE Monte Carlo online control converges to the optimal state-action value function Q*, and hence to an optimal policy.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo online control algorithm
concepts.one_line: Initialize Q = 0, N = 0, eps = 1, k = 1, pi = epsilon-greedy(Q); repeatedly sample a full episode under pi, update N(s,a) and G(s,a) at each (first) visit, set Q(s,a) = G(s,a)/N(s,a), then increment k, set eps = 1/k, and rebuild pi as epsilon-greedy(Q).

concepts.name: Mars rover greedy and epsilon-greedy readout
concepts.one_line: From the learned Q table the greedy policy is a1 at s1, a2 at s2, a1 at s3 and an arbitrary tie-break elsewhere; at k = 3 with eps = 1/k the agent acts greedily two-thirds of the time, and breaking ties randomly at query time is preferable empirically to freezing one tie-break.

concepts.name: TD ingredients recap
concepts.one_line: TD(0) updates V(s) <- V(s) + alpha[r + gamma V(s') - V(s)], combining sampling (a single draw of s') with bootstrapping (reusing the current estimate); Monte Carlo samples but does not bootstrap, and TD's payoff is being able to update mid-episode.

concepts.name: SARSA
concepts.one_line: On-policy TD control: from s_t take a_t ~ epsilon-greedy(Q), observe r_t and s_{t+1}, choose a_{t+1} ~ epsilon-greedy(Q), then Q(s_t,a_t) <- Q(s_t,a_t) + alpha[r_t + gamma Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) - Q(s_t,a_t)], and immediately re-derive the epsilon-greedy policy at s_t.

concepts.name: Why the second A in SARSA matters
concepts.one_line: The bootstrap target uses the action actually selected next, so the update must wait until that choice is made; this is what makes SARSA on-policy and makes its target reflect the exploration the agent will really do.

concepts.name: Dropping the pi superscript on Q
concepts.one_line: Once control begins, Q is no longer indexed by a fixed policy because the behavior policy changes during learning and the estimate averages over samples generated by a whole sequence of policies.

concepts.name: SARSA convergence conditions
concepts.one_line: SARSA converges to Q* in finite-state-action MDPs if the policy sequence is GLIE and the step sizes satisfy the Robbins-Monro conditions sum_t alpha_t = infinity and sum_t alpha_t^2 < infinity, e.g. alpha_t = 1/t.

concepts.name: Why step sizes need both Robbins-Monro conditions
concepts.one_line: alpha = 1 discards all past experience so the estimate never settles, alpha = 0 freezes it entirely, and the two Robbins-Monro conditions formalize the middle ground: enough total movement to reach any value, decaying fast enough to damp the noise.

concepts.name: Ergodicity caveat on GLIE
concepts.one_line: GLIE is unachievable when the environment is non-ergodic - crash the helicopter and the states beyond that point are permanently unreachable - so such domains are usually recast as episodic with a termination condition, at the cost of only bounded exploration.

concepts.name: Q-learning
concepts.one_line: Off-policy TD control: Q(s_t,a_t) <- Q(s_t,a_t) + alpha[r_t + gamma max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a') - Q(s_t,a_t)], which needs only (s,a,r,s') and can therefore update before the next action is chosen, with policy improvement touching only the state just visited.

concepts.name: SARSA vs Q-learning early behavior
concepts.one_line: SARSA's target is realistic about the random exploratory actions the agent will actually take while Q-learning's max is optimistic, so in the Sutton and Barto cliff walk SARSA earns more online reward early; in most other domains the optimism helps exploration, both converge to the same limit, and the two can be mixed.

concepts.name: Q-learning convergence, split into two claims
concepts.one_line: Visiting all state-action pairs infinitely often plus Robbins-Monro step sizes suffices for Q -> Q*, but ensuring the policy being followed is itself optimal additionally requires GLIE - so one can learn the optimal Q while never acting optimally.

concepts.name: Initialization is asymptotically irrelevant, empirically decisive
concepts.one_line: Under the convergence conditions the limit is independent of how Q was initialized, yet optimistic initialization frequently dominates zero or random initialization in practice.

concepts.name: Backup speed of Q-learning vs Monte Carlo
concepts.one_line: A Q-learning step only rewrites the entry for the state-action pair just visited, so a large reward late in an episode propagates backwards one step per update, whereas Monte Carlo credits the entire episode at once - slower information flow, but cheaper and lower-variance per step.

concepts.name: Maximization bias
concepts.one_line: In a single-state MDP with two actions whose rewards are zero-mean and stochastic, so Q*(s,a1) = Q*(s,a2) = V*(s) = 0, the empirical per-action estimates are individually unbiased yet V-hat = E[max_a Q-hat(s,a)] >= max_a E[Q-hat(s,a)] = V*, so greedy value estimates are positively biased.

concepts.name: Jensen proof of maximization bias
concepts.one_line: The max is a convex function of its arguments, so by Jensen's inequality E[max(Q-hat(a1), Q-hat(a2))] >= max(E[Q-hat(a1)], E[Q-hat(a2)]) = max(0,0) = 0 = V^pi, with the gap arising because finite samples let one arm look accidentally positive and the argmax immediately exploits that noise.

concepts.name: Maximization bias in general MDPs
concepts.one_line: The same effect is not an artifact of the one-state example; it propagates through Markov decision processes, with worked cases in a paper by Mannor, Tsitsiklis and coauthors cited from the podium.

concepts.name: Double Q-learning
concepts.one_line: Maintain two independently-updated estimates Q1 and Q2; on each step flip a fair coin to decide which one to update, and form its target by selecting the action with one table and reading its value off the other, so that the value used is an unbiased estimate of the selected action's value.

concepts.name: Empirical payoff of double Q-learning
concepts.one_line: In a domain contrasting a stochastic but genuinely worse action against a deterministic better one, Q-learning takes the bad action a large fraction of the time on small data while double Q-learning largely avoids it, at the cost of only a second Q table.

concepts.name: Takeaways stated at the close
concepts.one_line: Know how to run Monte Carlo on-policy control, SARSA and Q-learning; know how fast each updates, both in whether it must wait for the episode to end and how quickly reward information propagates backwards; and know the conditions under which each converges to Q*.

theorems_stated: Policy improvement theorem (restated from an earlier lecture, used as a black box): if Q^pi(s, pi'(s)) >= V^pi(s) for all s, then V^{pi'}(s) >= V^pi(s) for all s.

Finite termination of policy iteration: over finite S and A there are at most |A|^{|S|} deterministic policies, each round either strictly improves or repeats the previous policy, so the procedure halts after finitely many improvement steps.

Monotonic improvement under epsilon-greedy: for an epsilon-soft pi_i and pi_{i+1} epsilon-greedy w.r.t. the exact Q^{pi_i}, Q^{pi_i}(s, pi_{i+1}(s)) >= V^{pi_i}(s) for all s, and therefore V^{pi_{i+1}} >= V^{pi_i}.
GLIE Monte Carlo control converges to the optimal state-action value function Q*.
SARSA convergence: for finite-state-action MDPs, SARSA converges to Q* if the policy sequence is GLIE and the step sizes satisfy sum_t alpha_t = infinity, sum_t alpha_t^2 < infinity.

Q-learning convergence (two-part): visiting every (s,a) infinitely often together with Robbins-Monro step sizes suffices for Q -> Q*; ensuring the executed policy is optimal requires the additional GLIE condition.
Asymptotic independence from initialization: under the stated convergence conditions the limiting Q is unaffected by how Q was initialized.
Maximization bias: for unbiased per-action estimates Q-hat of a Q whose entries are all equal to V*, E[max_a Q-hat(s,a)] >= max_a E[Q-hat(s,a)] = V*, so the greedy value estimate is upward-biased.
Existence of a step-size / exploration-rate schedule achieving GLIE: eps_i = 1/i (equivalently eps_k = 1/k per episode) is sufficient.
SARSA and Q-learning converge to the same limit despite differing early behavior.
proofs_given: Monotonic improvement of epsilon-greedy policy improvement: the full algebraic derivation is done on the board, including the multiply-by-(1-eps)/(1-eps) step, the rewriting of 1 as sum_a [pi_i(a|s) - eps/|A|]/(1-eps) using the fact that action probabilities sum to one, and the key inequality obtained by replacing max_a Q^{pi_i}(s,a) with the weighted average of Q^{pi_i}(s,a) under those weights.
Maximization bias in the single-state two-action example: the Jensen's inequality argument E[max_a Q-hat] >= max_a E[Q-hat] = max(0,0) = 0 = V^pi is written out explicitly.
Finite termination of policy iteration: proved by the informal counting argument over the |A|^{|S|} deterministic policies together with the monotonic-improvement-or-fixed-point dichotomy.

Worked derivation (not a theorem, but done in full): the first-visit Monte Carlo Q table produced by one epsilon-greedy Mars rover trajectory, including which entries stay at zero and why every-visit gives the same answer here.
proofs_skipped: The policy improvement theorem itself. The board proof only establishes the pointwise inequality Q^{pi_i}(s, pi_{i+1}(s)) >= V^{pi_i}(s); the step from there to V^{pi_{i+1}} >= V^{pi_i} (the telescoping/repeated-substitution argument, or a monotonicity argument on the Bellman operator) is imported from an earlier lecture and never re-derived here. The academic notes must supply it, since it is where the actual improvement claim lives.

The epsilon-soft precondition in the epsilon-greedy improvement proof is never checked. The step that rewrites 1 as sum_a [pi_i(a|s) - eps/|A|]/(1-eps) requires pi_i(a|s) >= eps/|A| for every a, i.e. pi_i must itself be epsilon-soft with the same eps, and requires those weights to sum to 1. Neither condition is verified, and the case where eps changes between iterations (which it does under the eps_k = 1/k schedule) is not addressed at all.

Whether the epsilon-greedy improvement result gives convergence of the whole iteration, as opposed to a single monotonic step. A student asks this directly and is told it will be handled 'in a second'; what follows is the GLIE statement, not a convergence proof. The fact that the fixed point of epsilon-greedy policy iteration is the optimal epsilon-soft policy (not the optimal policy) is never mentioned.
Convergence of GLIE Monte Carlo control to Q*. Asserted flatly with no argument. The notes need the law-of-large-numbers-plus-GLIE argument, or the standard stochastic approximation treatment.

Convergence of SARSA to Q* under GLIE plus Robbins-Monro. Asserted only. The underlying result (Singh, Jaakkola, Littman and Szepesvari, 2000) is not named or sketched, and the stochastic-approximation machinery behind it is not touched.

Convergence of Q-learning to Q*. Asserted only. Neither the gamma-contraction property of the Bellman optimality operator nor the Robbins-Monro / Dvoretzky-style stochastic approximation argument (Watkins and Dayan, 1992; Jaakkola, Jordan, Singh 1994) is given.

Why the Robbins-Monro conditions sum alpha_t = infinity and sum alpha_t^2 < infinity are the right ones. Motivated purely by the degenerate endpoints alpha = 1 and alpha = 0; no argument that divergence of the sum is needed to reach an arbitrary starting offset and convergence of the squared sum is needed to suppress noise accumulation. The claim that these are 'one sufficient set of conditions' is not accompanied by any necessity discussion.

That eps_i = 1/i actually implies GLIE. Asserted as sufficient. When a student presses for a general characterization of which decay schedules are GLIE, the answer is explicitly a guess ('I think it's probably exactly the same'). The notes should state and prove the actual condition (each action retains probability bounded below by something whose visitation counts diverge, e.g. via a Borel-Cantelli argument), which is genuinely nontrivial because eps -> 0 while requiring infinitely many visits to every pair.

That optimistic initialization yields provable sample-complexity guarantees for reaching a near-optimal policy. Asserted twice and deferred wholesale to the exploration lecture; no bound, no algorithm, no conditions.

That SARSA and Q-learning converge to the same limit. Asserted. This is only true when SARSA's behavior policy is GLIE - with fixed eps > 0 SARSA converges to the optimal epsilon-soft policy, not Q*. The distinction is elided.

The cliff-walk claim that SARSA accrues more online reward than Q-learning in the early regime. Attributed to Sutton and Barto, described qualitatively via optimism vs realism, but not analyzed and not shown on a plot.

That maximization bias also arises in genuine MDPs, not just the one-state example. Attributed to a cited paper and immediately dropped; no construction, no MDP exhibited, no bound on the size of the bias.

That double Q-learning is unbiased. The central claim - using one estimator to select and the other to evaluate produces an unbiased estimate of the selected action's value - is asserted without proof. The independence assumption required (and the fact that double Q-learning is in general negatively biased rather than exactly unbiased) is not discussed, nor is the convergence of double Q-learning stated. van Hasselt (2010) is not cited.

The claim, made in a Q&A aside, that first-visit Monte Carlo control needs no step-size conditions because the estimator is unbiased and converging for all returns. Stated informally; the interaction between a nonstationary policy and the running average is not examined.
The carried-over claim that every-visit MC is a biased but lower-variance estimator relative to first-visit. Restated in passing, never proved (inherited from L03).
The claim that one can converge to the optimal Q function while never converging to the optimal policy (keeping eps high). Stated as an interesting fact; the separation is not demonstrated.

The claim that a non-Markov environment reduces the state-only policy class to a genuinely restricted one that may exclude the optimal behavior. Asserted in response to a student question; no example, no formal statement.
The claim that asymptotic convergence is independent of Q initialization. Asserted; follows from the convergence theorems, but since those are unproved, so is this.

Whether reaching a fixed policy is a valid stopping criterion in the model-free setting. A student asks whether, as in exact policy improvement, arriving at the same policy means you are done; the answer redirects to convergence conditions and never actually resolves the stopping question - which matters, because with approximate Q a repeated policy proves nothing.
algorithms: Generalized policy iteration with a known model: alternate exact policy evaluation of V^pi with greedy improvement pi'(s) = argmax_a [R(s,a) + gamma sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) V^pi(s')].

Monte Carlo on-policy Q evaluation: given pi, sample an episode, compute the return G_{i,t} for every timestep, and for each state-action pair visited (first-visit or every-visit) increment N(s,a), add G_{i,t} to the running total G(s,a), and set Q^pi(s,a) = G(s,a)/N(s,a).

Epsilon-greedy policy construction from Q: assign probability 1 - eps + eps/|A| to argmax_a Q(s,a) and eps/|A| to every other action (the random branch samples uniformly over all actions, greedy action included).

Monte Carlo online control (GLIE MC control): initialize Q(s,a) = 0, N(s,a) = 0, k = 1, eps = 1, pi = epsilon-greedy(Q); loop { sample episode k under pi; for each first visit to (s,a) in the episode: N(s,a) += 1, G(s,a) += G_{k,t}, Q(s,a) = G(s,a)/N(s,a); k += 1; eps = 1/k; pi = epsilon-greedy(Q) }.

SARSA (on-policy TD control): initialize Q and an epsilon-greedy pi; from s_t take a_t ~ pi, observe (r_t, s_{t+1}), select a_{t+1} ~ pi, apply Q(s_t,a_t) <- Q(s_t,a_t) + alpha[r_t + gamma Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) - Q(s_t,a_t)] (equivalently Q <- (1-alpha)Q + alpha * target), then rebuild pi as epsilon-greedy at s_t; repeat with t <- t+1.

Q-learning (off-policy TD control): from s_t take a_t under a behavior policy that is epsilon-greedy w.r.t. the current estimate of Q*, observe (r_t, s_{t+1}), and apply Q(s_t,a_t) <- Q(s_t,a_t) + alpha[r_t + gamma max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a') - Q(s_t,a_t)]; no next action is required, so the update can be issued immediately and only pi(s_t) needs refreshing.

Double Q-learning: maintain Q1 and Q2; on each transition flip a fair coin, and update the chosen table by selecting the greedy next action with that table while reading the value of that action from the other table, so selection and evaluation use independent samples.

Robbins-Monro step-size schedule: alpha_t = 1/t as the canonical theoretical choice, with the practical note that constant or slowly-decaying alpha is usually preferred empirically and is domain-dependent.
notation_introduced: Q^pi(s,a): expected discounted return from taking a in s and following pi thereafter - the central object of the lecture, replacing V^pi because argmax over it is model-free
N(s,a): visit count for a state-action pair, replacing the state count N(s) used in L03
G(s,a): running accumulator of returns for a state-action pair (a sum across episodes, NOT a single return)
G_{i,t}: the return from timestep t of episode i - the quantity actually added into G(s,a)
|A|: cardinality of the (assumed finite and known) action set, used as the denominator in epsilon-greedy
eps (epsilon): exploration probability; pi(a|s) = eps/|A| for non-greedy a and 1 - eps + eps/|A| for the greedy a
pi_i, pi_{i+1}: successive policies in the improvement sequence, with i indexing improvement rounds
k: episode index in Monte Carlo online control, with eps_k = 1/k
GLIE: Greedy in the Limit of Infinite Exploration - infinite visits to every (s,a) plus pi_i -> greedy w.r.t. Q with probability 1
alpha, alpha_t: TD learning rate / step size, with the Robbins-Monro conditions sum alpha_t = infinity, sum alpha_t^2 < infinity
SARSA tuple (s_t, a_t, r_t, s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}): the five quantities the on-policy TD control update consumes, and the source of the algorithm's name
Unindexed Q (no pi superscript): deliberately introduced from SARSA onwards, signalling that the estimate is no longer tied to one fixed policy
Behavior policy vs greedy policy: the policy generating data vs the policy that is greedy w.r.t. the current Q, whose separation defines off-policy learning
Q1, Q2: the two independently-maintained tables of double Q-learning
V-hat, Q-hat: empirical (finite-sample) estimates, used in the maximization-bias argument
notation_hazards: The auto-captions repeatedly render the TD/SARSA update as 'Q + (1 - alpha) r + ...'. This is mathematically impossible. The two legitimate forms are Q <- Q + alpha[target - Q] and Q <- (1-alpha)Q + alpha*target; the lecturer explicitly notes they are equivalent and asks students to flag her board typos. Any note derived from this transcript must not copy the caption's arithmetic.

'one minus Epsilon divide by one minus Epsilon' and 'one over Epsilon divided by one over Epsilon' in the proof are caption noise for the single algebraic move of multiplying the max term by (1-eps)/(1-eps). Reading the captions literally makes the proof incoherent.

Epsilon-greedy's greedy-action probability is 1 - eps + eps/|A|, not 1 - eps, because the random branch includes the greedy action. Two separate students have to raise this before it is stated cleanly; slides and speech elsewhere use the sloppier 1 - eps.
'greedy in the limit of infinity exploration' and later 'greedy in the limit of information' are both garbles of Greedy in the Limit of Infinite Exploration (GLIE).
'argotic' in the ergodicity aside is 'ergodic'.

G is overloaded. Sutton and Barto reserve G_t for the return from time t; here G(s,a) is a cross-episode running SUM of returns used as a numerator, while G_{i,t} is the return proper. Conflating them silently turns the Monte Carlo update into nonsense.

The Q superscript is dropped mid-lecture. Up to Monte Carlo control everything is Q^{pi_i}; from SARSA onward it is bare Q. This is a deliberate and meaningful change (the target policy is moving), but it means the same symbol denotes an on-policy value in the proof and a moving estimate in the algorithms.

In the Mars rover exercise the transcript elides the tail of the sampled trajectory. It has been reconstructed as (s3,a1,0; s2,a2,0; s3,a1,0; s2,a2,0; s1,a1,1; terminal) from the answers given later - specifically that the greedy action at s2 comes out as a2, that s3 is visited exactly twice with identical return-to-go, and that max_a Q ends as (1,1,1,0,0,0,0).

The transcript records a student's answer that only Q(s1,a1) becomes nonzero, and the lecturer says that would be correct 'for the TD case'. She means a single TD/Q-learning update sweep, not TD in general; a reader could mistake this for a claim about TD's fixed point.
'we could do Monte Carlo improvement by setting pi to an epsilon-greedy version of Q pi' - 'Monte Carlo improvement' is spoken where 'policy improvement' is meant.

The maximization-bias citation is garbled as 'Johnson Tsitsiklis and Shie Mannor'. Almost certainly Mannor, Simester, Sun and Tsitsiklis on bias and variance in value function estimation. Double Q-learning's actual source (van Hasselt, 2010) is never named at all.

In the SARSA convergence discussion the caption produces 'if alpha is equal to 1, generally your Q-function is not gonna converge' immediately followed by 'if alpha is 0, then you're not updating' - these are the two degenerate endpoints, not a claim that alpha = 1 diverges in every setting.
A student's clarification about the SARSA target index is transcribed as 'Q ST one A be plus one be ST plus one'; the intended object is Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}).

The lecturer writes the Monte Carlo Q update and the epsilon-greedy proof with epsilon fixed, but the algorithm decays eps with k. The proof as given does not cover a changing eps, and the transcript does not flag this.

animation_candidates.what: The epsilon-greedy monotonic improvement derivation, animated term by term: expand the expectation, multiply the max term by (1-eps)/(1-eps), morph the implicit 1 into sum_a [pi_i(a|s) - eps/|A|]/(1-eps), then visually 'push Q inside' so that max_a Q collapses into a weighted average and the equals sign tips over into >=, and finally cancel the two identical eps/|A| terms leaving V^{pi_i}.
animation_candidates.why: This is the only real proof in the lecture and every step is an algebraic sleight of hand that looks unmotivated in static text. Animation can show the two eps/|A| terms as physically identical objects that annihilate, and can show the max-to-average step as a single bar in a bar chart being replaced by a weighted mixture of all the bars - which is exactly the geometric content of the inequality and is invisible on a page.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Term-level formula morph with a synchronized bar chart of Q^{pi_i}(s,a) across actions, where the max bar visibly dominates the weighted-average line

animation_candidates.what: One Mars rover episode, three learners: replay the identical trajectory (s3,a1; s2,a2; s3,a1; s2,a2; s1,a1 -> +1) three times side by side and light up the Q cells that change under first-visit Monte Carlo, SARSA, and Q-learning.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture's own closing summary says the thing to internalize is how fast each method updates and how quickly reward information propagates backwards. That is a temporal property and text can only assert it. Animation makes it literal: MC flashes every visited cell simultaneously at episode end, SARSA and Q-learning light exactly one cell per step and need repeated episodes for the +1 to crawl back from s1 to s3.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Three synchronized 2-by-7 Q-table grids with cell highlighting, driven by a shared trajectory scrubber, plus an episode counter showing the backward crawl

animation_candidates.what: Maximization bias made visible: draw n samples from two N(0,1) arms, plot the two empirical means as dots converging on zero, and simultaneously build a histogram of max(Q-hat(a1), Q-hat(a2)) across many repetitions - showing it centred strictly above zero while each individual mean is centred at zero.
animation_candidates.why: Jensen's inequality is a one-line statement that students accept and do not feel. Watching two unbiased estimators produce a visibly biased maximum, with the bias shrinking as n grows, converts an abstract inequality into an observed phenomenon and shows exactly why the effect is a finite-sample pathology.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Scatter of per-arm sample means over increasing n, paired with a live histogram of the max whose mean line sits above the true V* = 0

animation_candidates.what: Cliff walk: animate the two policies SARSA and Q-learning converge to under a fixed eps, with the agent occasionally taking a random step, and overlay the online-return curves.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture asserts the SARSA-beats-Q-learning-early result and defers to Sutton and Barto without showing anything. The mechanism is entirely spatial - Q-learning learns the optimal path hugging the cliff edge, then eps-greedy exploration periodically shoves the agent off it, while SARSA's target has priced that risk in and it learns a safe interior path. A gridworld animation shows this in about four seconds; prose takes a paragraph and still does not land.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Gridworld with two agents tracing their learned paths, random-action steps flashed in a distinct color, plus a paired online-reward line chart

animation_candidates.what: Double Q-learning's decoupling: two Q tables side by side, a coin flip picking which one gets updated, an arrow from the selecting table's argmax pointing at the corresponding cell in the evaluating table.
animation_candidates.why: The selection/evaluation split is the entire idea and is genuinely hard to state without confusing which table does what. A single animated arrow crossing between the two tables resolves it instantly, and replaying the maximization-bias example with the split in place shows the bias disappearing.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two Q-table grids with a coin-flip gate and a crossing selection-to-evaluation arrow, replayed against the biased single-table version

animation_candidates.what: GLIE as two conditions holding at once: run eps_k = 1/k and animate, on one side, a visit-count heatmap over all (s,a) filling in without bound, and on the other, the action-probability distribution at a fixed state sharpening onto the argmax.
animation_candidates.why: Students routinely read GLIE as a single condition and then cannot see why decaying eps does not kill exploration. Showing the counts still diverging while the distribution collapses - because 1/k decays slowly enough that its sum diverges - makes the tension and its resolution simultaneous and obvious.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Split screen: visit-count heatmap with a divergence counter, alongside an animated probability-simplex or bar distribution over actions

animation_candidates.what: Backup diagrams for SARSA, Q-learning, and expected SARSA drawn as trees and animated in sequence from the same root (s_t, a_t).
animation_candidates.why: The single distinction that separates these three algorithms is which nodes at depth two the target reads from - one sampled node, the max node, or an expectation over all of them. A static diagram shows this but an animation that grows the same tree three different ways makes the family structure, and where SARSA's on-policy character comes from, immediate.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Backup diagram tree expansion, three variants from a shared root, with the selected depth-two nodes highlighted

animation_candidates.what: The off-policy stitching picture from the opening: two trajectories collected under different behavior, with a new path assembled from segments of both to evaluate a sequence never actually executed.
animation_candidates.why: Brunskill draws this at the very start to motivate off-policy learning and it is the conceptual seed of Q-learning, but the transcript's version is nearly unreadable. Animating the splice - segments detaching from their source trajectories and joining into a new one - carries the whole intuition in one gesture.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two trajectory ribbons through a small state graph, with segments detaching and recombining into a third highlighted path

code_experiment_candidates: Implement the 7-state Mars rover with R(s,a1) = (1,0,0,0,0,0,10), R(s,a2) = (0,0,0,0,0,0,5), gamma = 1, and reproduce the lecture's hand-computed first-visit Monte Carlo Q table from the exact trajectory (s3,a1; s2,a2; s3,a1; s2,a2; s1,a1) as a unit test, then run GLIE MC control with eps_k = 1/k and watch the greedy policy stabilize.

Run first-visit MC control, SARSA and Q-learning on the same Mars rover with an identical random seed and episode stream, and plot per-episode L-infinity distance of Q from the true Q* (computable exactly by value iteration) to quantify the propagation-speed claim from the lecture's closing summary.

Reproduce the Sutton and Barto cliff walk: SARSA vs Q-learning at fixed eps = 0.1, plotting online sum-of-rewards per episode to recover the crossing behavior, then repeat with eps_k -> 0 to demonstrate that both greedy policies converge to the same optimum - directly testing the lecture's asserted-but-unproved 'both converge to the same thing'.

Monte Carlo study of maximization bias: for n = 1..1000 samples per arm from two N(0,1) arms, estimate E[max_a Q-hat] over many repetitions and plot the bias decaying in n; overlay the double-estimator version to show the bias removed (and, if done carefully, the negative bias it introduces instead).

Reproduce the Sutton and Barto maximization-bias MDP (the two-state example with a stochastic action of negative expected value) and plot the fraction of left actions taken by Q-learning vs double Q-learning against episode number, matching the plot flashed at the end of the lecture.

Step-size ablation on a small random MDP: Q-learning with alpha_t = 1/t, alpha_t = t^{-0.6}, alpha_t = t^{-1.5} and constant alpha, checking empirically that only the schedules satisfying both Robbins-Monro conditions converge, and that alpha_t = t^{-1.5} stalls short of Q* while constant alpha oscillates.

Empirically verify the epsilon-greedy monotonic improvement theorem: compute Q^{pi_i} exactly by solving the linear system for a small MDP, apply epsilon-greedy improvement, and assert V^{pi_{i+1}} >= V^{pi_i} pointwise; then repeat with Q^{pi_i} estimated from k rollouts and count how often monotonicity is violated as a function of k - a direct experimental probe of the lecture's exactness caveat.

Test whether eps_k = 1/k actually delivers GLIE in practice: instrument visit counts N(s,a) over a long run and plot min_{s,a} N(s,a) against k for eps_k = 1/k, 1/sqrt(k) and 1/k^2, showing where the infinite-visitation condition silently fails.

Initialization sweep: zero, random, and optimistic Q initialization on the Mars rover and on a sparse-reward chain MDP, measuring episodes-to-optimal-policy - demonstrating the lecture's claim that initialization is asymptotically irrelevant but empirically decisive.

Fixed-eps SARSA vs Q-learning fixed points: run both to convergence with eps pinned at 0.1 and show that SARSA's limit is the optimal epsilon-soft policy while Q-learning's is Q*, exposing the gap the lecture glosses over.
dated_or_superseded: Double Q-learning is presented as a small tabular trick with 'pretty small overhead'. Since 2015 its deep counterpart (Double DQN, van Hasselt, Guez and Silver, AAAI 2016) has been standard, and the overestimation story has been refined considerably: clipped double Q-learning in TD3 (Fujimoto et al., 2018) and the twin-critic minimum in SAC are now the default treatment of maximization bias in continuous control, and the effect is understood as interacting with function-approximation error, not just finite-sample noise.

The framing of Q-learning as an off-policy method whose only subtlety is exploration predates the offline-RL literature. With a fixed dataset and no ability to visit new state-action pairs, the max operator becomes actively harmful (extrapolation error on out-of-distribution actions), which is the entire motivation for CQL, IQL, BCQ and related methods. Anyone applying this lecture to logged data needs that patch, and the lecture's convergence conditions - which require infinite visits to every pair - quietly rule out exactly that setting.

TD-Gammon (dated in the talk as roughly 1994; the well-known versions are 1992 and 1995) as the flagship model-free success is a 2019-era choice that already looked backward-looking. The natural modern anchors are DQN on Atari, AlphaZero, and RLHF/RLVR fine-tuning of language models, where the model-free control machinery in this lecture reappears as PPO and GRPO.

The claim that 'empirically, generally, you want to do Q-learning' over SARSA reflects pre-2019 practice in small discrete domains. In deep RL the on-policy/off-policy choice is now made on sample-efficiency-vs-stability grounds, and on-policy policy-gradient methods (PPO) dominate several of the highest-profile applications, including LLM post-training.

The tabular convergence guarantees (GLIE plus Robbins-Monro) are stated as the theory of the field. Modern practice runs almost entirely in the function-approximation regime where the deadly triad (bootstrapping, off-policy, approximation) can diverge and none of these guarantees survive; the lecture flags that function approximation is coming but not that it invalidates the theorems just stated.

Epsilon-greedy with eps_k = 1/k as the exploration mechanism is theoretically convenient and now rarely used unmodified; count-based and pseudo-count bonuses, RND, Thompson sampling and bootstrapped DQN are the standard alternatives, and the lecture's own admission that optimistic initialization has better guarantees points at the gap.

relevance_to_user_research.why: Not critical, but meaningfully more than background - three specific pieces bear directly on node-level fidelity assignment. (1) Maximization bias is the sharpest transfer. Your node-level assignment picks argmax over per-node value estimates of {weak, strong, prune}, and those estimates come from a small number of expensive, high-variance rollouts whose reward is terminal accuracy minus lambda times token cost. The single-state two-action example in this lecture IS your query-level AEP bandit with two arms, and its conclusion - that individually unbiased estimates produce a systematically optimistic max on finite samples - predicts a concrete failure mode you should expect: the weak model will look better than it is at exactly the nodes where it happened to get lucky, and your policy will lock onto that. Double Q-learning (or any select-with-one-sample, evaluate-with-another split) is a cheap, directly implementable mitigation, and this is worth an ablation in the paper. (2) The on-policy/off-policy distinction governs whether you can reuse traces. Every rollout costs real A100 time on Qwen2.5-72B, so you will want to collect under one fidelity policy and evaluate others without re-executing the DAG. Q-learning's off-policy property is precisely the license to do that, and SARSA vs Q-learning is a real design choice for you, not a textbook curiosity - SARSA's realism about the exploration you will actually perform matters if your deployed policy stays stochastic. (3) The Q-over-V argument is the reason your method is even formulable: choosing a fidelity at a node is argmax_a Q(node-state, a), which needs no model of how the downstream workflow will behave. Where the lecture stops short of your problem: it is tabular, so nothing here tells you how to represent a state made of query features, DAG position, partial trace and remaining budget - you will need function approximation, which is explicitly deferred. It offers no treatment of the budget constraint (your lambda-penalized objective is fine, but a hard token budget as a state variable in a finite-horizon MDP is not covered). Most importantly, GLIE is unusable for you: infinite visits to every (node-context, fidelity) pair is exactly the resource you do not have, and the lecture concedes that finite-sample exploration guarantees are a later topic. Your real bottleneck - learning a good assignment policy from very few expensive rollouts - is the thing this lecture names and postpones. Read it for the maximization-bias result and the off-policy framing; do not expect it to supply your algorithm or your analysis.

one_paragraph_summary: This lecture drops the tabular assumption that carried lectures 1-4 and replaces the value table with a parameterized function V̂(s;w) or Q̂(s,a;w), motivated by state spaces (Atari pixels, robot sensors) too large to enumerate. The organizing move is to recast policy evaluation as regression: if an oracle handed us (s, V^π(s)) pairs we would minimize a mean squared loss by stochastic gradient descent, and for a linear approximator V̂ = x(s)ᵀw the gradient collapses to the features themselves, giving the update Δw = α(target − x(s)ᵀw)x(s). The whole lecture is then that one update with three different targets plugged into the "target" slot: the true value (oracle), the Monte Carlo return G_t (unbiased, no Markov assumption, episodic only), and the bootstrapped TD target r + γx(s')ᵀw. Brunskill then asks what these converge to, weighting error by the stationary distribution d(s) induced by the policy: she states without proof the Tsitsiklis-Van Roy results that on-policy MC with linear VFA reaches the minimum-MSVE weights and TD(0) reaches within a factor 1/(1−γ) of that minimum, and works the corollary that with one-hot (tabular) features both errors are exactly zero. The second half turns to control — Q̂ with joint state-action features, MC/SARSA/Q-learning targets, interleaved with ε-greedy improvement — and to why this can break: TD with function approximation is not true gradient descent, and although the Bellman backup is a contraction, the projection back onto the representable function class can be an expansion, so the composition need not have a fixed point. Baird's 7-state, 8-feature counterexample runs throughout as the concrete vehicle: benign for on-policy MC and TD updates, divergent once the data comes from a behavior policy whose state distribution differs from the target policy's, even after discarding action-mismatched tuples. The closing summary is the deadly triad (function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy) and the warning that stability is not enough — what a method converges to, which depends on the objective and the features, matters as much as whether it converges.
prerequisites: MDP formalism: states, actions, transition model P(s'|s,a), reward model, discount factor γ, policies (deterministic and stochastic)
V^π and Q^π as expected discounted sums of reward; Bellman expectation and Bellman optimality equations
Dynamic programming: policy evaluation, policy iteration, value iteration, and the fact that the Bellman backup is a γ-contraction with a unique fixed point (established in earlier lectures)
Model-free policy evaluation: first-visit vs every-visit Monte Carlo, TD(0), the distinction between sampling and bootstrapping, bias-variance contrast between MC and TD (L03)
Model-free control: SARSA, Q-learning, ε-greedy exploration, on-policy vs off-policy (L04)
Multivariable calculus: gradients, chain rule, taking derivatives of a scalar loss with respect to a parameter vector
Gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent, learning rates
Linear regression / ordinary least squares and the normal equations w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy
Supervised learning basics: hypothesis class capacity, overfitting, bias-variance trade-off (structural risk minimization is referenced by name)
Elementary Markov chain vocabulary: transition matrices, the notion of a limiting distribution (helpful, not assumed)

concepts.name: Course admin
concepts.one_line: Homework 1 due, homework 2 (on function approximation) released this week; a TensorFlow tutorial and deep-learning background sessions are provided since deep learning is not a prerequisite, though gradient descent and differentiation are assumed.

concepts.name: Why go beyond tabular representations
concepts.one_line: Everything so far assumed a finite state/action space small enough to store a lookup table of values or models, but real problems (Atari frames as raw pixels) have state spaces so large that both memory and the data needed to visit every entry are infeasible.

concepts.name: Generalization as the central requirement
concepts.one_line: Because an agent will constantly land in state-action pairs it has never seen exactly before, it must transfer value estimates from similar prior experience rather than look them up, and that transfer is what function approximation buys.

concepts.name: Parameterized value function
concepts.one_line: Replace the table by a function V̂(s;w) (or Q̂(s,a;w)) mapping a state into a scalar value through a parameter vector w, which may be the weights of a deep network, a polynomial, or anything else.

concepts.name: Three resources saved by approximation
concepts.one_line: A compact representation reduces memory, reduces computation, and reduces the amount of experience (data) the agent must gather, and the same argument applies to approximating dynamics models and policies, not just value functions.

concepts.name: Capacity versus resources trade-off
concepts.one_line: The choice of approximator defines a hypothesis class, so a very compact representation is cheap to fit but may be unable to express any good policy — the degenerate limit being 'assume every video-game frame is the same state', which is maximally compact and useless.

concepts.name: Relation to bias-variance and structural risk minimization
concepts.one_line: In answer to a student, restricting representational capacity induces a permanent bias (the true value function is simply not in the class) while lowering variance, so this is the same capacity-versus-data trade-off as structural risk minimization in supervised learning, not an orthogonal one.

concepts.name: Choice of function approximator
concepts.one_line: Almost every supervised-learning approximator has been tried in RL (neural nets, decision trees, nearest neighbours, wavelet bases); the class focuses on differentiable ones because they have smooth optimization properties, but differentiability is not always the right criterion.

concepts.name: Interpretability motivates non-differentiable approximators
concepts.one_line: For clinical decision support a decision tree that justifies why a treatment is recommended can beat a more accurate deep network, and a hybrid is possible: fit the deep network first, then fit a tree to it for post-hoc interpretability.

concepts.name: Why start with linear value function approximation
concepts.one_line: Linear VFA is both the best theoretically studied approximator in RL and a useful lens on deep networks, which can be read as computing a complicated feature map followed by a linear head.

concepts.name: Gradient descent review
concepts.one_line: For a differentiable objective J(w), the gradient ∇_w J(w) is the vector of partial derivatives with respect to each parameter, and the descent step is w ← w − α∇_w J(w); iterated enough times with a suitable learning rate this reaches a local optimum, which matters because 'local' is all RL will generally guarantee.

concepts.name: Oracle formulation of policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: Imagine an oracle that returns the true V^π(s) for any queried state; then fitting V̂ to the resulting (s, V^π(s)) pairs is ordinary supervised regression, and this idealization is the scaffold onto which every real algorithm in the lecture is later grafted.

concepts.name: Mean squared value error objective
concepts.one_line: J(w) = E_π[(V^π(s) − V̂(s;w))²], where the expectation is over the distribution of states encountered while executing π — a point a student presses on and which becomes central once the stationary distribution is introduced.

concepts.name: Gradient of the MSE objective
concepts.one_line: Differentiating gives Δw = −½α∇_w J(w) = α E[(V^π(s) − V̂(s;w))∇_w V̂(s;w)], with the factor ½ chosen to cancel the 2 from the square.

concepts.name: Stochastic gradient descent on the value objective
concepts.one_line: Drop the expectation and evaluate the gradient at a single sampled state, giving Δw = α(V^π(s) − V̂(s;w))∇_w V̂(s;w); the expected SGD update equals the full gradient update, which is what makes this legitimate.

concepts.name: Feature vector representation of state
concepts.one_line: A state is summarized by a feature vector x(s) ∈ R^n whose entries are whatever measurements or engineered quantities the designer chooses.

concepts.name: Laser range finder robot example
concepts.one_line: A robot with a 180-degree laser scanner has the obvious feature vector of 180 distances to the nearest obstacle, one per degree.

concepts.name: Feature aliasing breaks the Markov property
concepts.one_line: That 180-ray representation is not Markov because many positions in a hallway — and the identical hallway on another floor — produce the same reading, so the features alias distinct underlying states; augmenting the state with history can restore Markovianity, and in general any aliased representation is non-Markov though it may still support decent decisions.

concepts.name: Feature engineering versus learned features
concepts.one_line: Pre-deep-learning RL invested heavily in hand-designing features (e.g. detecting corners from raw range data), and the appeal of deep networks is that they push the feature-selection problem back into learning, accepting high-dimensional raw sensor input directly.

concepts.name: Linear value function approximation
concepts.one_line: V̂(s;w) = x(s)ᵀw = Σ_j x_j(s)w_j, one weight per feature.

concepts.name: Two ways to build state-action features
concepts.one_line: For Q̂ one can either keep a separate weight vector per action or fold the action into the feature vector as x(s,a) with a single shared w; these differ in how much statistical strength is shared across actions.

concepts.name: Linear VFA gradient update
concepts.one_line: Since ∇_w x(s)ᵀw = x(s), the update becomes Δw = α(V^π(s) − x(s)ᵀw)x(s), which factors interpretably as step size × prediction error × feature value.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo return as an unbiased target
concepts.one_line: G_t, the sum of rewards from t to the end of the episode, is an unbiased but noisy sample of V^π(s_t), so it can be substituted wherever the oracle value was needed.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo value function approximation
concepts.one_line: Treat the collected (s_t, G_t) pairs as a supervised regression dataset: Δw = α(G_t − x(s_t)ᵀw)x(s_t), applied once per first visit to a state within each episode.

concepts.name: First-visit versus every-visit carries over
concepts.one_line: The same distinction as in tabular MC applies unchanged: the algorithm shown is first-visit, every-visit is also valid and is biased but asymptotically consistent.

concepts.name: Discounting in the episodic case
concepts.one_line: In episodic problems γ = 1 is safe because guaranteed termination already bounds the return (bounding is the main reason for γ < 1), though including γ is equally fine.

concepts.name: Updates are per state, not per episode
concepts.one_line: In response to repeated student questions: within one sampled episode the weight vector is updated once for each distinct first-visited state, and this incremental scheme converges to the same solution as batching all the data and fitting once.

concepts.name: Baird's counterexample: setup
concepts.one_line: Seven states and eight features; action a₁ (solid) deterministically moves to s₇ from anywhere, action a₂ (dashed) sends you uniformly to one of s₁..s₆; all rewards are zero so V^π ≡ 0 for every policy, yet the setting will later exhibit divergence.

concepts.name: Baird feature vectors
concepts.one_line: For i = 1..6, x(s_i) has a 2 in slot i and a 1 in slot 8; x(s₇) has a 1 in slot 7 and a 2 in slot 8 — so there are more features (8) than states (7), a legitimate and deliberately near-tabular-looking representation.

concepts.name: Worked Monte Carlo update on Baird
concepts.one_line: With w initialized to all ones, V̂(s₁) = 2+1 = 3; on an episode giving G = 0 with α = 0.5, Δw = 0.5(0−3)x(s₁) = (−3,0,…,0,−1.5), so w becomes (−2,1,1,1,1,1,1,−0.5) — only the two nonzero features of s₁ change.

concepts.name: Termination hack for the MC variant
concepts.one_line: Baird's chain is continuing, so to run Monte Carlo she adds a small terminating probability from s₇ (stay with probability 0.99, terminate with 0.01) so that episodes end.

concepts.name: Stationary distribution under a policy
concepts.one_line: Fixing a policy turns an MDP into a Markov reward process; running that chain long enough yields a stationary distribution d(s) over states, a probability distribution summing to one describing the long-run fraction of time spent in each state.

concepts.name: Balance equation
concepts.one_line: d(s') = Σ_s d(s) Σ_a π(a|s) P(s'|s,a): pushing the distribution through one step of the policy-induced chain leaves it unchanged.

concepts.name: Mixing time is problem-dependent and unknown
concepts.one_line: The balance equation says nothing about how long convergence takes — it can be a few steps or millions depending on the transition structure — and there is no easy test for whether collected data has actually reached stationarity; the lecture explicitly declines to treat this.

concepts.name: Mean squared value error weighted by d
concepts.one_line: MSVE(w) = Σ_s d(s)(V^π(s) − V̂(s;w))², weighting error by how often each state is actually visited, on the reasoning that error in rarely visited states matters less.

concepts.name: Tsitsiklis and Van Roy convergence for Monte Carlo
concepts.one_line: On-policy Monte Carlo policy evaluation with a linear approximator converges to the weights minimizing MSVE — the best the hypothesis class can do, which need not be zero error.

concepts.name: Batch Monte Carlo value function approximation
concepts.one_line: Given a whole dataset of (s_i, G_i) pairs, solve the least-squares problem analytically rather than incrementally: differentiate, set to zero, and get the normal-equation solution — ordinary linear regression on returns.

concepts.name: When batch is and is not worth it
concepts.one_line: The closed form costs a matrix inverse and requires holding the full design matrix, which is infeasible at web scale, so it suits small feature dimensions and settings where all data is already in hand; mini-batches are the middle ground and can propagate information much faster than single incremental steps.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo makes no Markov assumption
concepts.one_line: Because MC uses the full realized return rather than a bootstrapped one-step backup, batch MC VFA remains valid in non-Markov environments — an easily missed but important caveat given the aliasing discussion earlier.

concepts.name: Three approximations, still on-policy
concepts.one_line: TD with VFA stacks function approximation, bootstrapping, and sampling, but as long as learning stays on-policy the data resembles the IID supervised setting closely enough that convergence behaves well.

concepts.name: TD(0) with linear value function approximation
concepts.one_line: Substitute the bootstrapped target r + γx(s')ᵀw for the oracle value, giving Δw = α(r + γx(s')ᵀw − x(s)ᵀw)x(s), applied after every transition tuple.

concepts.name: TD(0) versus TD(λ) naming
concepts.one_line: Everything in this course is the TD(0) variant; Sutton and Barto discuss a family TD(λ), so readers should not confuse them.

concepts.name: Worked TD update on Baird
concepts.one_line: On the same tuple (s₁, a₁, r=0, s₇) with γ = 0.9 and all-ones weights, V̂(s₁) = V̂(s₇) = 3, so the TD error is 0 + 0.9(3) − 3 = −0.3, ten times smaller than Monte Carlo's −3, illustrating TD's smaller, more local updates.

concepts.name: TD(0) convergence bound
concepts.one_line: On-policy TD(0) with linear VFA converges to weights whose MSVE is within a factor 1/(1−γ) of the minimum achievable MSVE — worse than Monte Carlo's guarantee, but still bounded.

concepts.name: Tabular features make both errors zero
concepts.one_line: With one-hot features (one per state) the class can represent V^π exactly, so min_w MSVE = 0; the TD bound is a multiple of that minimum, hence also zero, and both MC and TD converge to the exact V^π at every state.

concepts.name: Where 1/(1−γ) comes from, informally
concepts.one_line: 1/(1−γ) is roughly the effective horizon, and bootstrapping propagates approximation error backwards so that per-step error accumulates over that horizon; when the approximator has no error there is nothing to accumulate and TD matches MC.

concepts.name: MC versus TD speed with approximation
concepts.one_line: Asked which converges faster, she says it is not really understood theoretically, though in practice TD's bootstrapping often helps.

concepts.name: Control with value function approximation
concepts.one_line: Represent Q̂(s,a;w) = x(s,a)ᵀw with joint state-action features and interleave approximate policy evaluation with ε-greedy policy improvement; this is where instability begins.

concepts.name: The Deadly Triad
concepts.one_line: Combining function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy learning is the configuration under which methods can fail to converge or converge somewhere bad; of the three, off-policy learning appears to be the dominant culprit.

concepts.name: Changing policies destroy the stationary distribution argument
concepts.one_line: The clean on-policy guarantees rested on a fixed policy inducing a fixed stationary distribution; in control the policy changes as learning proceeds, so the state distribution is non-stationary and the analysis no longer applies.

concepts.name: MC, SARSA and Q-learning control targets
concepts.one_line: The same update Δw = α(target − x(s,a)ᵀw)x(s,a) with three targets: G_t for Monte Carlo, r + γx(s',a')ᵀw for SARSA, and r + γ max_{a'} x(s',a')ᵀw for Q-learning — differing only in the form of bootstrapping and whether a max is taken.

concepts.name: TD with function approximation is not a gradient method
concepts.one_line: The TD update does not follow the gradient of any objective function (it is a semi-gradient), which is deferred to Sutton and Barto chapter 11 and the course notes.

concepts.name: Projection operator
concepts.one_line: A Bellman backup applied to a representable value function generally lands outside the approximator's function class, so the algorithm implicitly projects it back — TD with VFA is the composition of an approximate sampled Bellman backup with a projection Π.

concepts.name: Contraction versus expansion
concepts.one_line: An operator is a contraction if applying it to two value functions never increases their distance (in max norm), which is what guarantees convergence to a fixed point in dynamic programming; an expansion increases that distance, and the projection step under linear VFA can be an expansion, so the composition need not converge.

concepts.name: Gordon's averagers
concepts.one_line: Geoff Gordon's 1995 work on averagers is cited as the early treatment of exactly this issue — of which function approximators are and are not non-expansions.

concepts.name: Off-policy Baird divergence setup
concepts.one_line: Target policy π always takes a₁; behavior policy takes a₂ with probability 6/7 and a₁ with probability 1/7; γ = 0.99; the naive correction is to simply discard every tuple whose action disagrees with π.

concepts.name: Why discarding mismatched actions is not enough
concepts.one_line: Every retained tuple is action-consistent with π, yet under π you would enter s₇ and stay there almost always, while the behavior policy keeps teleporting you back into s₁..s₆, so the state visitation distributions differ sharply — and it is that mismatch, unaccounted for, that makes the TD weights blow up.

concepts.name: Divergence of off-policy TD
concepts.one_line: Running TD learning on this filtered off-policy data causes the weights to diverge, despite the true value function being identically zero and easily representable.

concepts.name: Convergence summary table
concepts.one_line: Tabular: everything converges. Linear on-policy: MC and TD converge, and control converges up to 'chatter' (bounded oscillation rather than a single point). Linear off-policy Q-learning: can diverge. Nonlinear: essentially no guarantees — though this is an oversimplification given two decades of subsequent work.

concepts.name: Stability is not the same as quality
concepts.one_line: An algorithm can converge, with weights that never blow up, to a genuinely bad approximation; the critical determinants of what it converges to are the objective function chosen and the feature representation.

concepts.name: Geometry of value function approximation
concepts.one_line: The Sutton and Barto figure depicts a plane of representable value functions, a Bellman update leaving that plane, and the projection back onto it; different distances measured in that picture define different objectives (value error, Bellman error, projected Bellman error), and the MSVE used all lecture is only one choice and not necessarily the one that yields the best real-world performance.

theorems_stated: Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (c. 1997): on-policy Monte Carlo policy evaluation with a linear value function approximator converges, in the limit of infinite data, to the weight vector w_MC minimizing the stationary-distribution-weighted mean squared value error, i.e. MSVE(w_MC) = min_w Σ_s d(s)(V^π(s) − x(s)ᵀw)².

On-policy TD(0) with a linear value function approximator converges to weights w_TD satisfying MSVE(w_TD) ≤ (1/(1−γ)) · min_w MSVE(w) — within a constant factor of the best representable approximation, where 1/(1−γ) plays the role of an effective horizon.

Corollary worked in class: if the features are a one-hot (tabular) encoding then min_w MSVE = 0, hence both the Monte Carlo and TD(0) limits have exactly zero mean squared value error and recover V^π at every state.
The expected stochastic gradient descent update equals the full (batch) gradient update, which is the justification for sampling the gradient at a single state.
G_t (the realized return from time t) is an unbiased estimator of V^π(s_t); every-visit Monte Carlo is biased but asymptotically consistent, while first-visit is unbiased.
