The Bellman backup operator is a contraction in the max norm and therefore has a unique fixed point to which repeated backups converge (recalled from the dynamic programming lecture).

A projection operator onto the span of a linear value function approximator can be an expansion in the max norm, so the composition of Bellman backup and projection need not be a contraction (attributed to Gordon 1995 on averagers).
TD learning with function approximation does not follow the gradient of any objective function (it is a semi-gradient method) — asserted, with the treatment deferred to Sutton and Barto chapter 11.
Off-policy TD learning on Baird's counterexample diverges (weights grow without bound) even when action-mismatched tuples are discarded and the true value function is exactly representable.

Convergence summary asserted as a table: tabular representations converge for MC, SARSA and Q-learning; linear on-policy MC and TD converge, with control exhibiting bounded 'chatter'; linear off-policy Q-learning can diverge; nonlinear approximation has essentially no guarantees.
Fixing a policy in an MDP yields a Markov reward process whose chain, run long enough, converges to a stationary distribution d satisfying the balance equation d(s') = Σ_s d(s) Σ_a π(a|s) P(s'|s,a).
In episodic settings γ = 1 is admissible because guaranteed termination already bounds the return.
proofs_given: Derivation of the stochastic gradient update from the mean squared value error objective for a general differentiable approximator: differentiate J(w) = E[(V^π(s) − V̂(s;w))²], apply the chain rule, absorb the factor 2 into the ½, and drop the expectation to sample at one state — carried out fully on the board.

Specialization of that derivation to the linear case: because ∇_w x(s)ᵀw = x(s), the general update collapses to Δw = α(V^π(s) − x(s)ᵀw)x(s), decomposed interpretably as step size × prediction error × feature value.

The same derivation carried through twice more by substitution — once with G_t replacing the oracle value (Monte Carlo VFA) and once with r + γx(s')ᵀw replacing it (TD(0) VFA) — establishing that all three algorithms share a single update form.

Short but complete argument that one-hot features drive the minimum MSVE to zero: with one feature per state the weight vector can store the exact value of each state independently, an infinite-data Monte Carlo average recovers each such value, hence min_w MSVE = 0; then, since the TD limit is bounded by a multiple of that minimum, the TD error is zero too.

Fully worked numeric Monte Carlo update on Baird's counterexample: from w = 1 (all ones), V̂(s₁) = 3, return G = 0, α = 0.5, giving Δw = −1.5·x(s₁) = (−3,0,…,0,−1.5) and new weights (−2,1,1,1,1,1,1,−0.5), including the observation that only features with nonzero value in s₁ are updated.

Fully worked numeric TD(0) update on the same tuple: V̂(s₁) = V̂(s₇) = 3, TD error 0 + 0.9(3) − 3 = −0.3, contrasted quantitatively against Monte Carlo's error of −3 to show TD makes far smaller local updates.

Informal but complete causal argument for the off-policy failure on Baird: tracing the trajectory distribution under the target policy (absorbed into s₇) against that under the behavior policy (repeatedly scattered back over s₁..s₆) to show that action-level filtering leaves the state distribution badly mismatched.

Verbal argument (in response to a student) that the effective horizon 1/(1−γ) multiplies the per-step approximation error because bootstrapping propagates that error backwards, whereas Monte Carlo does not — an intuition sketch, not a derivation.
proofs_skipped: The Tsitsiklis-Van Roy theorem that on-policy Monte Carlo linear policy evaluation converges to the minimum-MSVE weights. Stated as a fact with attribution and a historical anecdote; no proof, no statement of the regularity conditions (step-size schedule, feature linear independence, ergodicity of the induced chain).

The 1/(1−γ) bound for on-policy TD(0) with linear VFA. Explicitly deferred — a student asks directly where the constant comes from and the answer is 'in the interest of time, I'm not gonna go through it too much, I encourage you to read the Tsitsiklis paper' (approx. 01:08:04). Only an effective-horizon intuition is given. This is the single most important gap for the academic notes.

That the projection operator Π onto the span of a linear feature map can be an expansion in the max norm. Asserted, attributed to Gordon (1995) on averagers, with no construction of an expanding example and no discussion of why the ‖·‖_D-weighted projection is a non-expansion in the on-policy case (which is precisely what rescues on-policy TD and is never mentioned).
That the composition ΠB therefore need not be a contraction and may have no fixed point. Stated as the consequence of the previous item; the actual failure mode is never exhibited.

That TD with function approximation is not the gradient of any objective. Explicitly deferred to Sutton and Barto chapter 11 and the course lecture notes. The semi-gradient decomposition (dropping the dependence of the target on w) is not written down.

The divergence of off-policy TD on Baird's counterexample. Asserted with an intuitive distribution-mismatch story; the geometric blow-up of the weights is never computed, simulated, or proved. Baird's original argument (showing the update matrix has an eigenvalue outside the unit disc) is not touched.

Existence and uniqueness of the stationary distribution d. The balance equation is written down but the conditions guaranteeing a solution exists, is unique, and is actually reached (irreducibility, aperiodicity, positive recurrence; Perron-Frobenius) are never stated. The lecture says 'I'm not gonna get into any of that in this class.'

Mixing-time bounds. A student asks for proven bounds; the answer is 'not that I know of, there might be some.' No treatment of how long data must be collected before it approximates the stationary distribution, nor of how the finite-sample error depends on the mixing time.

That the batch least-squares solution actually minimizes the objective. She says 'you take the derivative, you set it to zero, it's linear regression, you can solve for this analytically' without carrying out the derivation, writing the normal equations w = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀG explicitly, or discussing invertibility / rank conditions / regularization when XᵀX is singular.

That the incremental (SGD) Monte Carlo procedure converges to the same weights as the batch analytic solution. Asserted flatly in reply to a student ('it ends up converging to the same thing'); no argument, no step-size conditions.

That gradient descent converges to a local optimum. Asserted; the required step-size conditions are waved at ('there may be some conditions on the learning rate') and never stated (Robbins-Monro: Σα_t = ∞, Σα_t² < ∞).
That E[SGD update] = full gradient update, and that this implies convergence. The first is stated as obvious; the second is not established at all.
That G_t is an unbiased estimator of V^π(s_t). Asserted as the licence for the whole Monte Carlo VFA construction; never proved (it is one line, but the notes should contain it).
That every-visit Monte Carlo is biased but asymptotically consistent. Asserted as carried over from the tabular lecture; neither the bias nor the consistency is argued here.

That the Bellman backup operator is a γ-contraction in the max norm and hence has a unique fixed point. Referred back to the dynamic programming lecture as already known; the Banach fixed-point argument is not restated even though the contrast with the expansion result is the conceptual heart of this lecture.

That an aliased state representation is necessarily non-Markov. A student asks whether this generalizes and gets a bare 'yes'; no precise statement (this is really a claim about the observation process, and the careful version needs the distinction between belief states and observation histories), and the claim that adding history restores Markovianity is likewise unargued.

That γ = 1 is always safe in the episodic case. Justified only by 'the episodic case is always guaranteed to be bounded'; the actual requirement (termination with probability one, plus bounded per-step rewards) is not formalized, and the student question about summing returns over episodes of varying length is answered informally.

The convergence and 'chatter' behaviour of MC control and SARSA with linear VFA. Presented as a summary table entry; no conditions, no definition of chatter beyond 'some oscillation', no result cited.
Divergence of Q-learning with linear VFA under off-policy updating. Table entry only, with the Baird example gestured at rather than instantiated for Q-learning.

The existence of modern algorithms with convergence guarantees, including 'recent work on batch RL which can converge with nonlinear approximators'. Mentioned in one sentence with no algorithm named, no result stated, no citation.

The relationships among the competing objectives in the Sutton and Barto chapter 11 geometry figure (mean squared value error, Bellman error, projected Bellman error) and which projections/distances they correspond to. Shown as a picture and described qualitatively; no definitions, no inequalities between them.
The claim that minimizing MSVE is not necessarily the best objective for real task performance. Asserted at the very end; no counterexample and no alternative criterion given.
The relative sample efficiency or convergence speed of MC versus TD under function approximation. Explicitly stated as not understood: 'to my knowledge that's not really understood.'

The stationary-distribution approach to off-policy evaluation she references as 'a really cool paper that just came out about a month ago' (marginalized importance sampling over state distributions rather than per-step ratios). Mentioned in passing with no result, and its connection to the Baird failure — which it directly addresses — is never drawn.
algorithms: Stochastic gradient descent for oracle-supervised value function approximation: sample a state s, query the true V^π(s), update w ← w + α(V^π(s) − V̂(s;w))∇_w V̂(s;w). Scaffold only — the oracle does not exist — but every later algorithm is this with the oracle value replaced.

Incremental first-visit Monte Carlo linear VFA policy evaluation: initialize w = 0; repeat { sample a full episode s₁,a₁,r₁,…,s_T under π; for each time t, if s_t is first-visited in this episode, compute G_t = Σ_{k=t}^{T} r_k and update w ← w + α(G_t − x(s_t)ᵀw)x(s_t) }. Episodic only; one weight update per first-visited state, not one per episode; every-visit variant is legal with the usual bias/consistency caveat.

Batch (analytic) Monte Carlo linear VFA policy evaluation: collect N episodes, form the dataset {(x(s_i), G_i)}, and solve argmin_w Σ_i (G_i − x(s_i)ᵀw)² in closed form by ordinary least squares (differentiate, set to zero, invert). Costs a matrix inverse and storage of the full design matrix; makes no Markov assumption, so it is valid in non-Markov environments.

TD(0) with linear VFA for policy evaluation (semi-gradient TD): initialize w; repeat { observe a transition tuple (s,a,r,s') generated by π; update w ← w + α(r + γx(s')ᵀw − x(s)ᵀw)x(s) }. Updates after every transition rather than every episode; handles continuing (non-episodic) tasks.

Monte Carlo control with Q value function approximation: use joint state-action features x(s,a) and target G_t defined from the first visit to a state-action pair, update w ← w + α(G_t − x(s,a)ᵀw)x(s,a), interleaved with ε-greedy improvement of the induced policy.
SARSA with linear Q function approximation: on tuple (s,a,r,s',a') update w ← w + α(r + γx(s',a')ᵀw − x(s,a)ᵀw)x(s,a), with ε-greedy action selection.

Q-learning with linear Q function approximation: on tuple (s,a,r,s') update w ← w + α(r + γ max_{a'} x(s',a')ᵀw − x(s,a)ᵀw)x(s,a). Structurally identical to SARSA except for the max, and the off-policy element that makes it the divergence-prone member of the family.

Naive off-policy correction by filtering: given data from a behavior policy, discard every tuple whose executed action disagrees with the target policy's action, then run TD on what remains. Presented explicitly as the simple thing one might try, and then shown to fail on Baird because it corrects the action distribution but not the state distribution.

Two constructions of state-action features: (a) a separate weight vector per action over state features x(s), versus (b) a single shared weight vector over joint features x(s,a) that encode state and action together. Different sharing properties; the lecture uses (b).
notation_introduced: w — the parameter (weight) vector; always treated as a column vector, possibly the weights of a deep network or of a linear model
V̂(s;w) — parameterized approximation to the state value function; written V̂(s,w) and V̂^π(s;w) interchangeably
Q̂(s,a;w) — parameterized approximation to the state-action value function
x(s) ∈ R^n — feature vector of state s; x_j(s) its j-th component
x(s,a) — joint state-action feature vector used for control
V̂(s;w) = x(s)ᵀw = Σ_{j=1}^{n} x_j(s) w_j — linear value function approximation
J(w) = E_π[(V^π(s) − V̂(s;w))²] — mean squared prediction objective, expectation over states visited under π
∇_w J(w) — gradient of the objective with respect to the parameter vector
Δw = −½ α ∇_w J(w) — the weight increment, with ½ chosen to cancel the 2 from differentiating the square
α — learning rate / step size, generally required to decay over time for convergence
G_t — return from time t, the sum (or discounted sum) of rewards to the end of the episode
d(s) — stationary distribution over states induced by policy π; Σ_s d(s) = 1
d(s') = Σ_s d(s) Σ_a π(a|s) P(s'|s,a) — the balance equation characterizing d
MSVE(w) = Σ_s d(s)(V^π(s) − V̂(s;w))² — mean squared value error, the lecture's error metric
TD target: r + γ V̂(s';w) = r + γ x(s')ᵀw
TD(0) — the one-step temporal difference variant used throughout, explicitly distinguished from the TD(λ) family in Sutton and Barto
B (Bellman backup operator) and Π (projection operator onto the representable function class); TD with VFA is described as the composition Π∘B
Contraction: an operator O with ‖O V₁ − O V₂‖ ≤ ‖V₁ − V₂‖ (max norm); an expansion is the reverse inequality
1/(1−γ) — the effective horizon, appearing as the multiplicative slack in the TD(0) error bound
'Deadly triad' — the combination of function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy learning
Baird counterexample notation: states s₁..s₇, action a₁ (solid arrows, deterministic to s₇), action a₂ (dashed arrows, uniform over s₁..s₆), eight-dimensional features
notation_hazards: The auto-captions render −½α as '1.5 alpha' throughout the gradient derivation (e.g. 'W- delta W is equal to 1.5 alpha to P pi of S minus S W times X'). The intended expression is Δw = −½α∇_w J(w) = α(V^π(s) − x(s)ᵀw)x(s). Relatedly, 'P pi of S' is V^π(s) and 'S W' or 'v of sw' is V̂(s;w).

Baird's feature vectors are badly garbled because the lecturer reads slot indices aloud while pointing at the board: '200013', 'two, two, three, four, five, six, seven', 'S2 looks like zero to one, two, three, four, five', '200001'. The actual vectors are x(s_i) = 2e_i + e_8 for i = 1..6, and x(s₇) = e₇ + 2e_8, in R⁸. This reconstruction is confirmed by the arithmetic she does use: with w = 1 (all ones), V̂(s₁) = 2 + 1 = 3 and V̂(s₇) = 1 + 2 = 3, both of which she states explicitly. Similarly, the post-update weight vector transcribed as 'minus two, one, two, three, four, five, six minus 0.5' is w = (−2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, −0.5) — she is counting off the six unchanged ones. 'Initialize our weights to 1111' means the all-ones vector in R⁸.

The discount factor is inconsistent between the two Baird worked examples: γ = 0.9 in the TD(0) update (yielding the TD error 0 + 0.9(3) − 3 = −0.3), but γ = 0.99 in the later off-policy divergence setup. Sutton and Barto's canonical version uses 0.99 throughout. The 0.9 appears to be a convenience for mental arithmetic; it does not affect the qualitative point.

She twice slips between the TD bound as an inequality and as an equality. The result is MSVE(w_TD) ≤ (1/(1−γ)) min_w MSVE(w), but in the tabular argument she says 'this is just equal to MSVE of the Monte Carlo times one over one minus Gamma'. Only the ≤ direction is needed (and true) for the conclusion that the tabular error is zero.

'TD Gamma' in the naming aside is TD(λ). 'Umberto Chapter 11' and 'Sutton Umberto' are Sutton and Barto chapter 11. 'batch URL' is batch RL. 'Jeff Gordon' is Geoff Gordon, and 'a really nice paper on averages from 1995' is his work on averagers (Stable Function Approximation in Dynamic Programming).

'It's only when we get into the control case ... where in this example and many others, things start to go right' — 'right' should be 'wrong'. Likewise 'setting the bar to often call it The Deadly Triad' is 'Sutton and Barto often call it the deadly triad', and 'mark off' throughout is 'Markov'.
'Wave function' appears once for 'value function'; 'e-greedy' is ε-greedy; 'partial aliasing' is the lecturer's phrasing for what is usually called perceptual or state aliasing.

She writes the balance equation first in one direction then flips it mid-sentence ('let me just flip this, I think it's a little bit easier to think about it the other way around'), so the transcript contains a half-finished version before the correct d(s') = Σ_s Σ_a form. The sum over actions is there specifically to accommodate stochastic policies.

The expectation in the MSE objective is repeatedly asked about by students and answered loosely — sometimes as 'over the policy', sometimes 'over states'. It is over the stationary state distribution d induced by π. This matters: the whole convergence story is stated with respect to that weighting, and the lecture never uses any other weighting even though she concedes control would want a different one.

The sign convention on α is deliberately left loose ('I'm gonna be a little bit loose on those ... you can flip it and be positive or negative'), in response to a student catching a sign. Notes should fix one convention: with the error written (target − prediction), the update adds αδx.

V̂ versus V^π is verbally conflated throughout — 'the value' sometimes means the true value and sometimes the current estimate, and in the Baird MC walkthrough she notes mid-stream that 'it depends on if you've already updated your w then your value will already be different', which is the first-visit ordering subtlety rather than a notational one.

animation_candidates.what: The single update rule with three interchangeable targets: start from J(w) = E[(V^π(s) − x(s)ᵀw)²], differentiate term by term so ∇_w V̂ visibly collapses to x(s), then swap the target slot three times — oracle V^π(s), Monte Carlo G_t, bootstrapped r + γx(s')ᵀw — while the rest of the expression stays frozen.
animation_candidates.why: This is the entire architecture of the lecture and the transcript literally repeats the derivation three times because the identity is hard to see in static notation. An animated morph that holds the invariant part fixed and animates only the target makes the point in one shot, and pre-empts the common misreading that MC-VFA and TD-VFA are structurally different algorithms.
animation_candidates.visual_form: term-level formula morph with a highlighted 'target' slot that cross-fades between three expressions

animation_candidates.what: Baird's 7-state MDP with the weight vector rendered as eight live bars, running MC and TD(0) side by side from w = 1 on the same transition (s₁, a₁, 0, s₇) with α = 0.5.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture spends ten minutes on hand arithmetic (Δw = −1.5·x(s₁) for MC versus a TD error of −0.3) precisely to make the magnitude contrast felt. Showing only two of eight bars move, and MC's moving ten times further, converts a tedious board calculation into an immediate visual, and establishes the state diagram that the divergence shot later reuses.
animation_candidates.visual_form: graph of 7 nodes with solid/dashed action arrows, plus a synchronized 8-bar weight chart per algorithm

animation_candidates.what: Off-policy divergence on Baird: run filtered TD and animate the eight weight bars growing geometrically off-screen, juxtaposed against two state-visitation histograms — the target policy's spike on s₇ versus the behavior policy's spread over s₁..s₆ — with the true V ≡ 0 drawn as a flat line the estimates race away from.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture asserts divergence and explains it verbally but never shows it; this is the lecture's dramatic climax delivered entirely on trust. Seeing weights explode while the true value function is identically zero and exactly representable is the moment the deadly triad stops being an abstraction. Pairing it with the two histograms puts the cause on screen next to the effect, which the verbal explanation cannot do.
animation_candidates.visual_form: dual-panel: diverging weight traces on a log axis beside two animated visitation histograms

animation_candidates.what: Contraction versus expansion in function space: two value functions as points, the Bellman backup B pulling them together but off the plane of representable functions, then the projection Π snapping both back onto the plane — and pushing them further apart than they started.
animation_candidates.why: This is the conceptual heart of why control breaks, it is asserted without proof, and it is irreducibly geometric — the lecture is describing a picture out loud. Animating the two-step B-then-Π cycle with the inter-point distance measured after each step shows exactly where the contraction guarantee is lost, which no amount of prose does efficiently.
animation_candidates.visual_form: 2D/3D function-space schematic with a shaded representable plane, two tracked points, and a live distance readout after each operator

animation_candidates.what: Mixing to the stationary distribution: a histogram over Baird's seven states evolving under d ← (P^π)ᵀd until it stops changing, with the balance equation's terms highlighting as they are applied; then a second, deliberately slow-mixing chain run alongside.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture states that mixing time is problem-dependent, unknown, and untestable, then declines to discuss it — leaving students with a definition and a warning but no feel for either. Watching one chain settle in a few steps while another is still visibly drifting after hundreds makes 'you can't just wait 100 steps' concrete, and it motivates why d appears in the MSVE definition at all.
animation_candidates.visual_form: animated bar histogram driven by repeated matrix-vector products, with equation terms lighting up in sync

animation_candidates.what: Horizon amplification: sweep γ from 0 to 0.99 and plot both min_w MSVE and the TD bound (1/(1−γ))·min_w MSVE, with a toggle that switches the feature set from a coarse linear basis to one-hot.
animation_candidates.why: Two separate ideas collapse into one picture here — that the TD penalty blows up with the effective horizon, and that the entire penalty vanishes when the approximator is exact. The lecture answers a student question about where 1/(1−γ) comes from with pure intuition; watching the gap open as γ→1 and then collapse to zero when the toggle flips to tabular delivers the intuition and the corollary together.
animation_candidates.visual_form: animated curve pair on shared axes with a feature-representation toggle

animation_candidates.what: Feature aliasing: a robot in a hallway casting a 180-ray fan, with the resulting feature vector shown as a strip; move the robot to a different position and then to an identical hallway on another floor, and show the two distinct world states collapsing onto the same point in feature space.
animation_candidates.why: Aliasing is the lecture's justification for the claim that a natural representation can be non-Markov, and it is what connects feature choice to everything downstream. The failure is spatial and instantaneous when animated — two robots, one feature vector — whereas the verbal version required the lecturer to field two follow-up questions before it landed.
animation_candidates.visual_form: side-by-side floor plans with ray-casting, feeding a shared feature-space scatter where two states merge into one dot

animation_candidates.what: Information propagation per update: one trajectory, with Monte Carlo shown walking all the way to termination to form G_t before updating, versus TD(0) updating immediately from a one-step backup — animated as how far backward along the trajectory a single update carries reward information.
animation_candidates.why: It grounds the recurring MC-versus-TD contrast (variance, bootstrapping, why TD's updates are small, and why batch methods 'propagate information a lot more quickly') in a single reusable picture, and it sets up why bootstrapping is the mechanism that compounds approximation error over the 1/(1−γ) horizon.
animation_candidates.visual_form: trajectory strip with backward-flowing highlight of differing reach per update

code_experiment_candidates: Implement Baird's counterexample exactly (7 states, 8 features, x(s_i) = 2e_i + e_8 and x(s₇) = e₇ + 2e_8, all rewards zero, γ = 0.99) and reproduce all three regimes in one script: on-policy MC converging, on-policy TD(0) converging, and off-policy TD with action-filtered data diverging. Plot all eight weight traces on a log axis. This is the lecture's central unproved claim and it is about forty lines of numpy.

Empirically verify both Tsitsiklis-Van Roy results on a small random MDP: solve for the exact V^π by matrix inversion, compute the stationary distribution d as the dominant left eigenvector of P^π, compute min_w MSVE by d-weighted least squares, then run MC-SGD and TD(0)-SGD to convergence and check that MSVE(w_MC) ≈ the minimum and MSVE(w_TD) ≤ minimum/(1−γ). Sweep γ ∈ {0.5, 0.9, 0.99} to see how loose the bound actually is in practice — the lecture never says whether it is tight.

Directly exhibit the expansion the lecture asserts but does not construct: build the d-weighted projection Π for a given feature matrix, sample random pairs of value functions V₁, V₂, and compute ‖ΠBV₁ − ΠBV₂‖_∞ / ‖V₁ − V₂‖_∞, searching for pairs where the ratio exceeds 1. Then repeat with the projection weighted by the on-policy stationary distribution to show why on-policy TD is rescued — the piece of the story the lecture omits entirely.

Tabular-as-one-hot sanity check: run the identical linear VFA code path with one-hot features on a small MDP and confirm MSVE → 0 for both MC and TD, reproducing the in-class exercise and validating the implementation before trusting it on harder feature sets.

Incremental versus batch Monte Carlo VFA: verify numerically that the SGD solution and the closed-form least-squares solution w = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀG agree (the lecture asserts this in reply to a student without argument), then benchmark wall-clock and memory as the feature dimension grows to make the 'Facebook can't do this' scaling claim quantitative. Include a singular XᵀX case to expose the invertibility condition never mentioned in class.

Stationary-distribution weighting ablation: compute d numerically, measure empirical mixing time from a random start, and compare the argmin weights and resulting value estimates under d-weighted versus uniformly-weighted MSVE. Shows concretely that the choice of state weighting changes which approximator is 'best' — the point the lecture raises via a student question and then drops.

Deadly-triad ablation grid on a small gridworld: cross {tabular, linear, small MLP} × {MC, TD(0)} × {on-policy, off-policy}, run many seeds, and log the divergence rate and final MSVE for each cell. This turns the lecture's asserted summary table into measured data, including the 'chatter' cell, which is described only as 'some oscillation'.

Compare the two state-action feature constructions on a small control problem — a separate weight vector per action versus one shared weight vector over joint x(s,a) features — measuring sample efficiency and cross-action interference. The lecture notes the two options and says they give 'different forms of sharing' without ever quantifying the trade-off.

Add proper importance weighting to the Baird off-policy experiment (per-step ratios, and then a marginalized state-distribution ratio) and show which of them actually stops the divergence. This directly connects the lecture's naive filtering failure to the off-policy-evaluation paper she mentions in passing but never ties back to Baird.
dated_or_superseded: The homework infrastructure is TensorFlow (a TF tutorial is promised for the following week). PyTorch has been the standard for RL research code since roughly 2020, and JAX-based stacks are common for scale; any modern reimplementation should ignore the TF framing entirely.

The convergence summary table ('linear off-policy can diverge, nonlinear all bets are off') is presented as near-final with a one-line hedge. It has been substantially refined since: gradient-TD methods (GTD2/TDC) and emphatic TD give convergent off-policy linear algorithms with explicit objectives; van Hasselt et al. (2018) empirically dissected which triad component actually drives divergence in deep RL and found target networks and multi-step returns matter more than the triad framing suggests. The lecture alludes to 'algorithms now that do have convergence guarantees' without naming any.

The claim that TD-with-VFA follows no gradient is correct but incomplete as taught: the modern framing is that the Bellman error is not identifiable from off-policy samples at all (Chen and Jiang, 2019), which is a sharper and more useful statement than 'it's a semi-gradient' and reframes the whole choice-of-objective discussion at the end of the lecture.

The 'batch RL that can converge with nonlinear approximators' mentioned as brand-new work is now the mature field of offline RL (BCQ, CQL, IQL, and the pessimism/concentrability theory behind them). Crucially, that literature answers the exact question she flags as important and leaves open — not just whether a method converges but what it converges to — via coverage assumptions on the behavior data, which is precisely the Baird failure mode formalized.

The off-policy evaluation paper described as 'came out like a month ago' about using stationary-distribution differences rather than per-step ratios is Liu et al. (2018), Breaking the Curse of Horizon. This spawned the DICE family (DualDICE, GenDICE, GradientDICE) and marginalized importance sampling now has finite-sample theory. It is no longer a curiosity to mention in passing; it is the standard answer to the Baird divergence story the lecture tells thirty minutes later.

LSTD and LSPE are conspicuously absent. The lecture presents the closed-form batch solution for Monte Carlo but never gives the analogous batch solution for TD, which is the natural companion and is standard in any modern treatment of linear VFA.

The framing of deep networks as 'a complicated feature map followed by linear function approximation' is still a defensible reading of the final layer, and remains the right pedagogical bridge, but it understates how much representation learning and value learning interact in practice (representation collapse, the value-improvement path, auxiliary tasks). Worth a modern footnote rather than a correction.
Baird's counterexample itself is entirely current and remains the canonical divergence example; nothing here needs patching.

relevance_to_user_research.why: About half this lecture maps directly onto node-level fidelity assignment, and the mapping is unusually concrete. The user's state — (query features, node position in the DAG, partial trace, remaining budget) — is a high-dimensional, largely textual object, so a tabular value table is out from the start and some V̂(s;w) or Q̂(s,a;w) over engineered or embedding-derived features is mandatory. The most transferable single piece is batch Monte Carlo VFA: their offline data will be a fixed set of workflow rollouts, each yielding a terminal return (accuracy minus lambda times token cost), and fitting a linear head on frozen Qwen embeddings by weighted least squares against realized returns is a cheap, stable, genuinely competitive baseline for fidelity assignment — one they can implement in an afternoon and defend in an ARR submission as the obvious thing a reviewer will ask why they did not try. The lecture's remark that Monte Carlo makes no Markov assumption matters more for them than for most students: a 'partial execution trace' summarized into features is almost certainly non-Markov, and the hallway-aliasing example is a precise account of their likely failure mode (two traces with identical summaries but different continuations). The off-policy half is the other genuinely load-bearing part. Their rollout data will come from some behavior policy — all-strong, AFlow's default assignment, or random fidelity — while they want to evaluate a different one, and Baird is exactly the lesson that filtering to action-matched tuples is insufficient because the state distribution is still wrong. In their setting this is not hypothetical: if the behavior policy runs the strong model at node 1, the traces arriving at node 2 are systematically different from those under a weak-at-node-1 policy, so naive per-node value estimates are biased by construction. That single insight is worth the lecture. Against this: the second half's pathologies are substantially defused by their problem structure. With H roughly 3-10 operators, a terminal-only reward, and gamma effectively 1, the 1/(1−gamma) horizon-amplification bound is close to vacuous, and they can plausibly avoid bootstrapping entirely by regressing on terminal returns — which sidesteps the deadly triad, the contraction/expansion argument, and the divergence results altogether. Their actual bottlenecks are elsewhere: rollout cost on the A100 budget (sample efficiency, not asymptotic convergence), per-node credit assignment across a DAG rather than a chain, and the budget constraint, none of which this lecture addresses. So: the regression-on-returns machinery and the distribution-mismatch warning transfer cleanly and should shape their method; the convergence theory is background they can cite but will likely never be bitten by. Useful, not critical.

one_paragraph_summary: This lecture is the bridge from linear value function approximation to deep RL. Brunskill first argues why linear features are limiting (you must hand-design the right basis, and the true value function may not lie in its span) and why non-parametric alternatives such as kernel/k-NN approximators, despite the beautiful property of being averagers (non-expansions, so a Bellman backup composed with them stays a contraction and therefore converges), do not scale because the number of points needed to cover a space grows exponentially in its dimension. She then gives a compressed introduction to deep networks as compositions of differentiable layers, with the chain rule giving backpropagation and autodiff removing the hand derivation, plus the universal approximation property and a depth-efficiency claim. CNNs are motivated purely as a parameter-reduction device that exploits image structure: a 1000x1000 image would need ~10^6 weights per fully connected unit, whereas a shared 5x5 filter needs 25 weights reused across the whole image, buying translation invariance for free; stride, zero-padding, multiple filter banks, pooling and a fully connected head are sketched. The historical arc is TD-Gammon's early success, then the mid-1990s deadly-triad results (function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy control can diverge, with concrete failure cases), then a long retreat, then DeepMind's Atari results. The core technical content is DQN: state is the last four frames (an approximate Markov statistic that fails on memory games like Montezuma's Revenge), 4-18 discrete actions, reward is score change, one architecture and hyperparameter set across ~50 games learned from scratch. Two pathologies motivate the two innovations - correlated, non-IID consecutive samples and a non-stationary regression target - answered by experience replay (a ~1M-tuple buffer, minibatch resampling, reusing each transition many times) and fixed Q-targets (a frozen weight copy w-minus used only inside the bootstrap term, refreshed every n steps). The published ablation is the punchline: on Breakout, replay alone moves performance from single digits to 241, dwarfing the contribution of the deep architecture or the target network. She closes with three immediate successors - Double DQN (decouple action selection from action evaluation to fight maximization bias), prioritized replay (motivated by a Mars Rover exercise showing that replaying backups in reverse order propagates a terminal reward in two updates while forward order propagates nothing, and by a result that oracle ordering gives exponential convergence speedup), and dueling DQN (split the head into V(s) and A(s,a), which is not identifiable without an added constraint) - and stresses that none of this has convergence guarantees.
prerequisites: MDPs, policies, value functions, and the Bellman operators
The fact that the Bellman backup is a gamma-contraction in sup norm, and what a contraction/fixed point buys you
Tabular TD(0) and tabular Q-learning, including the off-policy max in the Q-learning target
Monte Carlo return G_t as an unbiased but high-variance value target, versus the biased low-variance bootstrapped TD target
Linear value function approximation from the previous lecture: features x(s), V-hat = x(s)^T w, the MSE objective, and the resulting weight update
Stochastic gradient descent and the chain rule from multivariable calculus
Epsilon-greedy exploration
Maximization bias and tabular double Q-learning, introduced briefly in an earlier lecture
The 7-state Mars Rover chain used as the course's running toy MDP

concepts.name: Course admin
concepts.one_line: Homework 2 is released and must be submitted in TensorFlow (the autograder assumes it); weekend sessions will cover deep learning background for students without it; default project descriptions drop tomorrow with proposals due in about a week; Azure credits and a machine-setup tutorial are available.

concepts.name: Why function approximation at all
concepts.one_line: Interesting RL problems have observation spaces so large (raw pixels, rich patient/student/customer records) that you will essentially never revisit an identical state, so models, value functions or policies must be represented by parameterized functions that generalize across states rather than by tables.

concepts.name: Differentiable approximator + MSE + SGD recap
concepts.one_line: Represent V-hat(s;w) or Q-hat(s,a;w) with a differentiable parameterization, define the loss J(w) as the expected squared error between the true value and the approximation, and descend it with SGD; because the expectation of the stochastic update equals the full gradient update, per-tuple or per-episode updates are unbiased.

concepts.name: The unknown-target problem
concepts.one_line: The MSE objective references the true V^pi, which is exactly the object you are trying to learn, so in practice you substitute a proxy target: the Monte Carlo return G_t from the full episode, or the bootstrapped TD target r + gamma * V-hat(s';w).

concepts.name: Limits of linear value function approximation
concepts.one_line: Linear VFA works very well given the right features and is the best-understood case theoretically, but choosing those features is the whole problem, and a poor feature set makes the true value function unrepresentable for some states no matter how long you train.

concepts.name: Deep nets as learned features plus a linear last layer
concepts.one_line: A deep network used for Q-learning is best read as an elaborate learned feature extractor whose final fully connected layer performs linear regression on those features, which is why deep VFA is a strict generalization of linear VFA rather than a different animal.

concepts.name: Kernel and non-parametric approximators
concepts.one_line: k-nearest-neighbour and kernel methods are non-parametric approximators whose representation size grows with the number of data points, and they carry much stronger RL convergence results than linear VFA, but they are rarely used at scale.

concepts.name: Curse of dimensionality for non-parametric methods
concepts.one_line: To make every point in a d-dimensional space lie within epsilon of some stored data point you must effectively grid the space, so the number of points needed grows exponentially in d, hurting computation, memory and sample complexity simultaneously.

concepts.name: Averagers are non-expansions
concepts.one_line: Averager-type approximators (which return convex combinations of stored values) are non-expansions in sup norm, so composing one with the gamma-contracting Bellman backup yields an operator that is still a contraction, giving guaranteed convergence - unlike linear VFA, where the composed operator need not be a contraction and iterated backups can blow up.

concepts.name: Deep network as a composition of functions
concepts.one_line: Write y = h_n(h_{n-1}(...h_1(x;w_1)...;w_{n-1});w_n) with a loss J on top; each h is a linear map or a nonlinear activation applied to one, and all that is required is differentiability.

concepts.name: Backpropagation via the chain rule
concepts.one_line: dJ/dw_k factors as (dJ/dh_n)(dh_n/dh_{n-1})...(dh_{k+1}/dh_k)(dh_k/dw_k), so a single backward pass propagates the output error into every layer's weights; she derived this on the board and noted she once had to do it by hand for every architecture.

concepts.name: Automatic differentiation as the enabling innovation
concepts.one_line: The practical unlock of the last several years is autodiff in frameworks like TensorFlow: you specify the network and the loss, and gradients for arbitrarily deep architectures come for free, which is what made very deep models usable by non-specialists.

concepts.name: Activation functions and ReLU's non-differentiable kink
concepts.one_line: Layers alternate linear maps with nonlinear activations such as sigmoid or ReLU; a student objected that ReLU is not differentiable, and the resolution given was that it fails at exactly one point and its flat region simply contributes zero gradient - which is also the seed of the vanishing-gradient problem in very deep nets, deferred to session.

concepts.name: Universal function approximation
concepts.one_line: A network with at least one hidden layer and sufficiently many nodes can represent any function, so unlike linear VFA there is no representational capacity barrier preventing you from expressing the true value function.

concepts.name: Depth efficiency
concepts.one_line: A deep network can represent the same function with exponentially fewer nodes or parameters than a shallow one, which is the practical argument for depth over a very wide single hidden layer.

concepts.name: Parameter blow-up motivating CNNs
concepts.one_line: A 1000x1000 image has 10^6 pixels, so a single fully connected hidden unit needs 10^6 weights, and a bank of such units run in parallel gives an intractable parameter count while ignoring everything we know about the structure of images.

concepts.name: Filter / receptive field and weight sharing
concepts.one_line: Instead of connecting a unit to the whole image, connect it to a local patch and reuse the identical weight vector as you slide that patch over the image, so a 5x5 filter costs 25 weights total rather than 10^6 per unit.

concepts.name: Stride and zero-padding, with an output-size example
concepts.one_line: Stride is how far the patch moves between applications and zero-padding is how many zeros to append at the border; a 28x28 input convolved with a 5x5 filter at stride 1 with no padding produces a 24x24 output map from 25 shared weights.

concepts.name: Translation invariance as the inductive bias
concepts.one_line: The same weights applied everywhere means a feature detector (an edge, say) is found wherever it occurs, encoding the belief that the salient content of an image does not change when you shift your head slightly - the same belief that motivated hand-built features like SIFT before deep learning.

concepts.name: Filter banks and pooling
concepts.one_line: Multiple filters are learned in parallel to detect different features, and pooling layers (max pooling, or averaging) downsample so the network can funnel a very high-dimensional image toward a low-dimensional output such as a scalar Q value.

concepts.name: Fully connected head
concepts.one_line: The final layer is typically fully connected and behaves like linear regression on the learned convolutional feature representation, emitting the prediction - for DQN, one Q value per discrete action.

concepts.name: Historical arc: TD-Gammon to the deadly triad to Atari
concepts.one_line: Neural RL had an early success in backgammon in the early 1990s, then mid-1990s theory plus concrete failing test cases showed that function approximation combined with bootstrapping and off-policy control can diverge, which chilled the area for a decade until deep learning's compute-and-data era let DeepMind revisit it around 2013-2014.

concepts.name: The deadly triad
concepts.one_line: Function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy control together can fail to converge - and even where iterates do converge, the fixed point reached need not be a good solution.

concepts.name: Did deep learning solve the 1990s problems?
concepts.one_line: Asked directly whether the divergence problem was resolved or merely brute-forced, she answered honestly that gradient-TD style algorithms (Sutton and Barto ch. 11) are true SGD methods that do converge but not necessarily to the optimal policy, while DQN's contributions are heuristic stability devices, and understanding the triad remains open.

concepts.name: Q-learning with function approximation is a semi-gradient method
concepts.one_line: The DQN weight update is not a true gradient of any objective because the target term also depends on w and its dependence is ignored; these are approximations to gradient descent that work surprisingly well, and true-gradient variants (GTD/TDC) exist separately.

concepts.name: Atari as an RL problem
concepts.one_line: State is the game screen, action is one of roughly 4-18 discrete joystick/button positions (small action space, enormous pixel state space), and reward is the change in game score, which can be dense or extremely sparse depending on the game.

concepts.name: Four-frame stacking as an approximate Markov state
concepts.one_line: A single frame lacks velocity, so DQN stacks the last four frames to recover position and velocity; this is far cheaper than carrying the full history but is provably insufficient for games with hidden inventory or long-range dependencies such as Montezuma's Revenge.

concepts.name: One architecture, fifty games
concepts.one_line: The Nature paper's methodological contribution was using the same network architecture and the same hyperparameters across ~50 games (learning separate weights per game from scratch) rather than the usual three hand-tuned benchmark domains, and releasing the source code.

concepts.name: Pathology 1: correlated samples
concepts.one_line: Consecutive tuples (s,a,r,s') and (s',a',r',s'') are strongly dependent - in a deterministic system the only difference between their returns is one reward - so naive online updates violate the IID assumption that SGD analysis relies on.

concepts.name: Pathology 2: non-stationary targets
concepts.one_line: Unlike supervised learning, there is no oracle supplying fixed labels: the regression target is computed from the current Q estimate, which changes every time you update the weights, which changes the policy, which changes the target again.

concepts.name: Experience replay
concepts.one_line: Store transitions in a finite buffer (typically the most recent ~1M tuples), and repeatedly sample minibatches from it to perform Q-learning updates; because Q changes between visits, replaying the same tuple later yields a genuinely different update, so data is reused rather than discarded after one use.

concepts.name: Replay is not the same as a longer frame stack
concepts.one_line: A student asked whether replay is equivalent to keeping more frames; it is not - more frames enrich the state representation, whereas replay revisits an old transition from a genuinely different current Q function and so produces a different weight update.

concepts.name: Infinite replay converges to the certainty-equivalent model solution
concepts.one_line: In the tabular case, sweeping TD learning over a fixed dataset infinitely many times converges to the same answer you would get by fitting the maximum-likelihood transition and reward model from that data and then planning exactly in it; replay moves you along that spectrum toward model-based planning.

concepts.name: Compute versus experience trade-off
concepts.one_line: Replay trades computation for data - should the agent think harder about old transitions or go collect new ones? - which she flags as an open, under-studied metacomputation/metacognition question currently settled by fixed heuristic replay-to-environment-step ratios.

concepts.name: Buffer eviction policy
concepts.one_line: In answer to a student: the buffer is finite and usually first-in-first-out over the most recent samples, but which transitions to retain is a genuinely open design choice whose right answer depends on how non-stationary the environment is.

concepts.name: Fixed Q-targets
concepts.one_line: Maintain two weight vectors for one network: w, updated by SGD every step, and w-minus, a frozen older copy used only to compute the bootstrap term in the target r + gamma * max_a' Q(s',a';w-minus); w-minus is refreshed to w every n steps.

concepts.name: Why freezing the target helps
concepts.one_line: Freezing reduces the noise/variance in the regression target, turning the problem back into something closer to ordinary supervised learning with fixed labels; the degenerate limit makes it vivid - a constant target is perfectly stable and trivially learnable, just useless.

concepts.name: The freeze-versus-propagate tension
concepts.one_line: n=1 recovers standard Q-learning while n=infinity never updates the target at all, and a student correctly pointed out that freezing directly blocks the backward propagation of newly discovered reward through the chain, so the target period is a hyperparameter trading stability against information flow.

concepts.name: These fixes are not deep-net-specific
concepts.one_line: Asked whether replay and target freezing are peculiar to neural networks, she said no - both apply to any value function approximator, including linear; they were emphasized in DQN because instability was more feared with very expressive approximators.

concepts.name: Full DQN algorithm
concepts.one_line: Act epsilon-greedily, store (s,a,r,s') in replay memory D, sample a random minibatch from D, compute targets with w-minus, take an SGD step on the mean squared error between Q(s,a;w) and those targets, and periodically copy w into w-minus - with no sophisticated exploration in the original paper.

concepts.name: Breakout demo and reward exploitation
concepts.one_line: The learned agent progresses from flailing to discovering the tunnel strategy - punching a hole at the side and bouncing the ball behind the wall - illustrating that an agent asked to maximize a reward will find the maximizing strategy, including ones humans take a while to discover.

concepts.name: Why the paddle jitters
concepts.one_line: The visible twitching is exploration plus indifference: with no movement cost the agent gets identical reward for staying still or shuffling, so it cannot distinguish those actions; adding a movement penalty would clean it up.

concepts.name: Human-level performance is asymptotic
concepts.one_line: The famous human-level bar refers to final performance after training, not to sample efficiency - the agent consumes enormous amounts of experience, as students will discover in homework 2 - and a long tail of hard-exploration games sits far below human level.

concepts.name: The DQN ablation
concepts.one_line: On Breakout the reported ablation gives roughly 3 with neither trick, ~10 with fixed targets only, 241 with replay only, and a further gain with both: replay is overwhelmingly the dominant ingredient, and simply reusing each data point matters more than the depth of the approximator.

concepts.name: Deep features with a linear last layer refit
concepts.one_line: Prompted by a student noticing the ablation table lacks a linear-plus-replay row, she pointed to work (including her own) that trains a deep trunk and then fits the last layer by explicit linear or Bayesian linear regression, which is cheaper and gives calibrated uncertainty while keeping a rich representation.

concepts.name: Maximization bias
concepts.one_line: The max over noisy estimated state-action values is a biased estimator of the true max, systematically overestimating it, because the max operator preferentially selects whichever action's estimate happened to be inflated by noise.

concepts.name: Double Q-learning (tabular)
concepts.one_line: Maintain two Q tables, act using an average of the two, and on each transition flip a coin: with probability one half select the greedy next action according to Q1 but evaluate it with Q2 when updating Q1, and symmetrically otherwise - decoupling selection from evaluation.

concepts.name: Double DQN
concepts.one_line: Reuse the two weight sets DQN already maintains: select the greedy next action with the current online weights w and evaluate that action's value with the frozen target weights w-minus, so the target becomes r + gamma * Q(s', argmax_a' Q(s',a';w); w-minus) - a few lines of code for a large empirical gain across Atari.

concepts.name: Mars Rover replay-ordering exercise
concepts.one_line: Given the trajectory s3,a1,0,s2 / s2,a1,0,s2 / s2,a1,0,s1 / s1,a1,+1,term, students vote and find that replaying backup 3 first sets V(s2) = 0 + gamma*V(s1) = 1 and then backup 1 sets V(s3) = 1, recovering the full Monte Carlo estimate in two updates, whereas the forward order propagates nothing - so which tuples you replay and in what order both matter.

concepts.name: Oracle replay ordering gives exponential speedup
concepts.one_line: A 2016 result shows that on chain-structured MDPs, an oracle that picks the optimal replay order needs exponentially fewer updates to converge than uniform sampling; computing that order is intractable, but it justifies trying to approximate it.

concepts.name: Prioritized experience replay
concepts.one_line: Attach to each stored tuple a priority p_i equal to the magnitude of its DQN/TD error (its prediction error, with the max in the target), refresh p_i whenever that tuple is replayed, and sample tuple i with probability proportional to p_i^alpha, where alpha=0 recovers uniform sampling and alpha to infinity recovers always replaying the single worst-fit tuple.

concepts.name: Freezing versus ordering interaction
concepts.one_line: A student objected that if w-minus is frozen you cannot keep propagating reward backwards; she agreed, and added that ordering still matters because the buffer may hold a million tuples while the target refreshes every ~50 steps, so w does change many times within one pass over the buffer.

concepts.name: Dueling DQN
concepts.one_line: Split the network head into one stream estimating V(s) and another estimating the advantage A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s), then recombine them into Q; the architectural point is to concentrate learning signal on which action is better rather than on the absolute worth of the state.

concepts.name: Non-identifiability of the dueling decomposition
concepts.one_line: The V/A split is not identifiable - you can add any constant to V and subtract it from every advantage without changing Q - so the architecture must impose an extra default assumption on the advantage stream; she flagged this explicitly and deferred the details for lack of time.

concepts.name: Cumulative gains stack
concepts.one_line: The Atari comparisons layer: DQN < double DQN < double DQN with prioritized replay < dueling on top of that, each contributing a substantial performance gain within roughly two years of the original paper.

concepts.name: Practical implementation advice
concepts.one_line: Do not start by throwing deep Q-learning at Atari: get the linear Q-learning case fully working first, because even a small game like Pong can take ~12 hours before you learn that nothing was learned - this is why the assignment is staged that way; further practical tips are credited to John Schulman.

theorems_stated: Universal function approximation: a network with one hidden layer and enough nodes can represent any function, so representational capacity is not the bottleneck for deep VFA.
Depth efficiency: a deep network can represent a given function with exponentially fewer nodes/parameters than a shallow network.
Averager approximators are non-expansions in sup norm; composed with the gamma-contracting Bellman backup they yield a contraction, hence guaranteed convergence of the resulting fitted iteration.
Linear value function approximation composed with a Bellman backup is not in general a contraction, which is why repeated backups can diverge.
Deadly triad: function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy control can fail to converge, and where it converges the fixed point may be far from optimal.
Curse of dimensionality for non-parametric approximators: the number of stored points needed to keep every query within epsilon of a neighbour scales exponentially in the input dimension.
The expectation of the stochastic gradient descent update equals the full-batch gradient update.
Maximization bias: the max over noisy estimated state-action values is a biased (upward) estimator of the max of the true values.

Tabular TD learning run to convergence over a fixed dataset (equivalently, infinite replay) reaches the same solution as fitting the maximum-likelihood transition and reward model from that data and planning exactly in it.
Oracle-ordered replay achieves an exponential reduction in the number of updates required for value-function convergence on chain-like MDPs relative to naive ordering (2016 result).
The dueling decomposition Q(s,a) = V(s) + A(s,a) is not identifiable without an additional constraint on the advantage stream.
Gradient-TD style algorithms (Sutton and Barto ch. 11) are genuine stochastic gradient methods and do converge, though not necessarily to the optimal policy.
Monte Carlo returns are unbiased estimators of V^pi but high variance; bootstrapped targets are biased but lower variance.
proofs_given: Backpropagation: she wrote out the chain-rule factorization dJ/dw_k = (dJ/dh_n)(dh_n/dh_{n-1})...(dh_{k+1}/dh_k)(dh_k/dw_k) on the board for a composed network, which is a genuine (if informal) derivation of the backward pass.

Informal covering argument for exponential scaling of non-parametric methods: to have every point on a line within epsilon of a stored point you need a fixed number of points; do it on a square and you need that number squared; iterating gives the exponential-in-dimension conclusion.

Worked numeric derivation of the Mars Rover replay backups: replaying (s2,a1,0,s1) gives V(s2) = 0 + gamma*V(s1) = 1, then replaying (s3,a1,0,s2) gives V(s3) = 0 + gamma*V(s2) = 1, matching the first-visit Monte Carlo estimate; the reverse order leaves V(s3) unchanged. This constitutes a proof by counterexample that replay order changes the resulting value function.

Reductio for why fixed targets stabilize: taking the freeze to its extreme, a constant target (say zero) makes the regression a fixed supervised problem that provably converges to w=0 - demonstrating stability at the cost of usefulness, and isolating target non-stationarity as the source of instability.

ReLU gradient argument: on the flat branch the derivative is exactly zero, so gradient descent is well defined there (and the single kink is a measure-zero nuisance) - a short argument in answer to a student objection.
proofs_skipped: Universal function approximation theorem is asserted with no statement of hypotheses (which activation classes, which function classes, uniform approximation on compacta) and no proof or citation (Cybenko/Hornik).

The depth-efficiency claim ('exponentially fewer nodes than a shallow net') is asserted with no construction, no function class, and no citation; she explicitly offers to discuss it offline or on Piazza.

That averagers are non-expansions, and that non-expansion composed with a gamma-contraction is a gamma-contraction, is asserted without the sup-norm argument (Gordon 1995 fitted value iteration). The proof is three lines and belongs in the notes.

The exponential covering-number scaling for kernel/k-NN approximators is only gestured at with a picture; no formal statement in terms of covering numbers, no sample-complexity bound, no statement of what smoothness assumption makes the epsilon-ball argument valid.

The deadly-triad divergence result is cited as '1995 to 1998 results' with no counterexample worked on the board - neither Baird's star MDP nor the Tsitsiklis-Van Roy two-state example is shown, and no divergence proof is given.

No statement or proof of the positive counterpart: on-policy TD with linear function approximation converges, and its fixed point is within 1/(1-gamma) (or 1/sqrt(1-gamma^2)) of the best representable approximation. This is exactly the contrast the triad result needs.

The claim that gradient-TD / GTD / TDC are true stochastic gradient methods with convergence guarantees is deferred entirely to Sutton and Barto chapter 11 - no objective function (MSPBE), no derivation, no convergence statement.
E[SGD update] = full gradient update is asserted as a reminder, never derived.

The claim that tabular TD run to convergence over a fixed dataset equals the certainty-equivalence (maximum-likelihood model) solution is asserted as something 'we talked about a long time ago' but not proved. This is a substantive theorem (Sutton's batch-TD result) and its proof is a fixed-point argument worth writing out.

Maximization bias is asserted without the one-line Jensen argument E[max_a X_a] >= max_a E[X_a], without any quantification of the bias magnitude as a function of the number of actions and estimator variance, and without proof that the double estimator is unbiased (or that it is in fact negatively biased).
That Double DQN actually reduces overestimation is supported only by 'it gives you a huge benefit in many cases for Atari' - no analysis, no bound.

Q-learning with function approximation is described as 'not a true gradient descent method' but the residual-gradient decomposition is never shown: the true gradient of the mean squared Bellman error has a second term through the target, and that term is dropped. Why dropping it is nevertheless usually benign (and when it is not) is entirely unaddressed.

No convergence claim of any kind is offered for DQN with replay and target networks - she states explicitly that these have no convergence guarantees. The notes should state the modern partial results (neural fitted Q-iteration analyses, convergence of target-network Q-learning under two-timescale assumptions).

The claim that fixed targets 'reduce noise in the target' is only intuition; no bias/variance decomposition of the bootstrapped target as a function of the target-update period n is given, and no analysis of the resulting stability/propagation-speed trade-off.
The oracle-ordering exponential-speedup result (2016) is cited with no MDP class specified, no statement of what is being compared against, and no proof sketch.
Why prioritizing by |TD error| approximates the oracle ordering is never argued - it is presented purely as intuition. The notes should address why this is a reasonable surrogate and where it fails.

The importance-sampling correction that prioritized replay requires (sampling non-uniformly from the buffer biases the expected update; Schaul et al. reweight by (1/(N*P(i)))^beta) is not mentioned at all. This is a genuine omission, not just a deferred proof.

Non-identifiability of Q = V + A is asserted ('it is not identifiable, I'm happy to talk about that offline'); the one-line argument (add c to V, subtract c from every A) and the two standard fixes (subtract the max advantage, giving V = max_a Q; or subtract the mean advantage, which is what the paper actually uses and which changes the semantics of V) are all skipped.

That the last four frames constitute an approximately Markov statistic is asserted; no discussion of the POMDP formalism, belief states, or what is actually lost. Montezuma's Revenge is offered as an informal counterexample only.

The interaction between experience replay and off-policyness is never analyzed: replaying data collected under old policies makes DQN an off-policy algorithm with a growing behaviour/target policy mismatch, which is precisely one leg of the triad the tricks are supposed to be mitigating. The tension is never named.
No justification is given for why the same architecture and hyperparameters transfer across ~50 games, nor any analysis of what the reported 'human-level' normalization actually measures.
algorithms: Stochastic gradient descent for value function approximation: given a tuple or episode, update w by alpha times the prediction error times the gradient of V-hat (or Q-hat) with respect to w.
Linear VFA with a Monte Carlo target: w <- w + alpha*(G_t - x(s)^T w)*x(s).
Linear VFA with a TD target: w <- w + alpha*(r + gamma*x(s')^T w - x(s)^T w)*x(s).
Backpropagation / reverse-mode automatic differentiation over a composed network h_n(...h_1(x)).

Convolutional forward pass: slide a shared filter of size f over the input with a given stride and zero-padding, producing an output map (28x28 input, 5x5 filter, stride 1, no padding -> 24x24); repeat with a bank of filters; interleave pooling layers for downsampling; finish with a fully connected head.
Q-learning with function approximation (semi-gradient): w <- w + alpha*(r + gamma*max_a' Q-hat(s',a';w) - Q-hat(s,a;w)) * grad_w Q-hat(s,a;w), where all weights on the right-hand side are the same w.

DQN: epsilon-greedy behaviour policy; store (s,a,r,s') in replay memory D; sample a random minibatch from D; compute targets y = r + gamma*max_a' Q(s',a';w-minus) using the frozen weights; take an SGD step on the mean squared error between Q(s,a;w) and y; copy w into w-minus every n steps.
Tabular double Q-learning: maintain Q1 and Q2; act epsilon-greedily on their average; with probability 1/2 update Q1 using the action argmax under Q2 evaluated by Q2 (and symmetrically for Q2).
Double DQN: target y = r + gamma * Q(s', argmax_a' Q(s',a';w); w-minus) - select with online weights, evaluate with target weights.

Prioritized experience replay (proportional variant): store priority p_i = |TD/DQN error| for each tuple, refresh on replay, sample i with probability p_i^alpha / sum_j p_j^alpha; alpha=0 gives uniform replay, alpha -> infinity gives greedy replay of the worst-fit tuple.
Dueling DQN: shared convolutional trunk splits into a scalar V(s) stream and a per-action A(s,a) stream, recombined into Q(s,a) with an identifiability constraint on A.

Deep trunk with a refit linear/Bayesian-linear last layer: train the network, then solve exactly for the final-layer weights by (Bayesian) linear regression on the learned features, for efficiency and uncertainty estimates.
notation_introduced: w = parameter vector of the function approximator; V-hat(s;w) and Q-hat(s,a;w) = approximate state and state-action value functions
J(w) = objective, taken as the expected squared error between the true value and the approximation
x(s) = feature vector of state s; linear VFA writes V-hat(s;w) = x(s)^T w
G_t = return from time t, used as the Monte Carlo value target
TD target r + gamma*V-hat(s';w); Q-learning target r + gamma*max_a' Q-hat(s',a';w)
'prediction error' / 'TD error' = target minus current estimate; in the prioritized-replay section she calls it the 'DQN error' to flag that it contains the max
h_1, ..., h_n = layer functions of a deep network; y = h_n(h_{n-1}(...h_1(x))) with per-layer weights w_1,...,w_n
'activation function' = the nonlinear h (sigmoid, ReLU)
filter / receptive field = the shared local weight patch; stride = the step size when sliding it; zero-padding = border zeros added before convolving
pooling layer (max pooling / average pooling) = downsampling operator
w-minus = the frozen older copy of the network weights used only inside the bootstrapped target; w = the online weights being updated
n = target-network update period (copy w into w-minus every n steps or episodes)
D = replay memory / replay buffer
p_i = replay priority of tuple i; alpha = prioritization exponent in P(i) proportional to p_i^alpha
A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s), the advantage function
epsilon-greedy exploration with a schedule on epsilon
notation_hazards: alpha is overloaded within a single lecture: it is the SGD learning rate throughout (e.g. 'TD estimate with alpha equal one' in the Mars Rover example) and then, without warning, the prioritization exponent in prioritized replay's P(i) proportional to p_i^alpha. Rename one of them in the notes.

In the fixed-Q-targets section she repeatedly writes the target as 'r + gamma*V(s')' when the object being frozen is really max_a' Q(s',a';w-minus). The V/Q slippage is harmless in speech but must be tightened for a control algorithm.

'Function approximation plus offline off policy control plus bootstrapping' - the caption reads 'offline', but the deadly triad is function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy, and 'offline' is a transcription artifact of 'off-policy'.
The lecture says Atari has 'there's 80 joystick button positions'. This is a caption garble for 18 - consistent with her own repeated statement that the action space is between 4 and 18 actions.
She says deep nets 'happen a lot in unsupervised learning like predicting whether or not something is a cat' - that is supervised learning; the transcript preserves a verbal slip.

The prioritized-replay description says new tuples have their priority 'set to zero'. In Schaul et al. new transitions are given maximal priority precisely so they are replayed at least once; a zero priority would starve them forever under the proportional rule. Correct this silently in the notes.
The advantage stream is dictated as 'Q of s. One minus V of s' - a caption break for Q(s,a1) - V(s), Q(s,a2) - V(s), and so on.
'pulling layer' throughout the student Q&A is 'pooling layer'.
'prime number if you guys have heard about this' is a garble, almost certainly 'raise your hand if you've heard of this'.

Dates are loose: TD-Gammon is placed in 1994 (Tesauro's results are 1992 and 1995), and the DeepMind Atari work is repeatedly placed 'around 2014' (the NIPS deep learning workshop paper is December 2013 and the Nature paper is February 2015; she does correctly cite the Nature paper as 2015 later).

Sutton and Barto conventions differ in two places worth flagging: S&B write the target-network weights as w (or theta-minus following the DQN paper) and reserve w-bar for other uses, and S&B are explicit that these are semi-gradient methods - a term the lecture never uses even though it describes exactly that property.

The Mars Rover backups are numbered 1-4 verbally only, with the vote outcome given as 'the 3s have it' then 'the ones have it'; the numbering refers to position in the trajectory (1 = the s3 transition, 4 = the terminal s1 transition), which is easy to lose without the board.

animation_candidates.what: The Mars Rover 7-state chain with the four stored transitions, replayed in forward order versus reverse order, with each state's value lighting up as a backup fires.
animation_candidates.why: This is the single clearest 'aha' in the lecture and it is entirely spatial-temporal: forward order produces literally zero change while reverse order carries the terminal +1 back two states in two updates. Static text can state 'order matters'; only motion makes the reader feel the reward failing to travel.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Grid-world / chain value sweep: seven cells in a row, a replay buffer strip below showing which tuple is being fired, values animating in place, run twice side by side (forward vs reverse) with a sweep counter.

animation_candidates.what: Weight sharing in a convolution: a 5x5 filter sliding over a 28x28 grid producing a 24x24 map, with a running parameter counter comparing 25 shared weights against 10^6 fully connected weights.
animation_candidates.why: The whole justification for CNNs in this lecture is a parameter-count argument plus translation invariance, and both are geometric. Watching the identical weight patch physically reused at every location conveys 'shared' in a way that the phrase 'weight sharing' does not.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Sliding-window overlay on a pixel grid, with the output map filling in cell by cell, a persistent weight-count ticker, and a second pass showing a filter bank producing stacked feature maps then a pooling downsample.

animation_candidates.what: The bootstrapped target chasing itself: two copies of the same Q-network, one online and one frozen, with the regression target visualized as a moving dot. Run once with no freezing (target moves every step, weights oscillate) and once with a target period of n (target holds still, then jumps).
animation_candidates.why: 'Non-stationary target' is an abstraction until you see the label you are regressing toward move every time you take a step toward it. The freeze-versus-propagate tension a student raised is also purely temporal: freezing visibly stops reward from travelling back through the chain.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two-panel side-by-side: a loss landscape / target-dot animation on the left, a value-propagation chain on the right, with a target-period slider stepping n through 1, 10, 100, infinity.

animation_candidates.what: Term-level morph of the Q-learning target from r + gamma*max_a' Q(s',a';w) into the DQN target r + gamma*max_a' Q(s',a';w-minus) and then into the Double DQN target r + gamma*Q(s', argmax_a' Q(s',a';w); w-minus).
animation_candidates.why: All three algorithms differ by which weight vector sits in which slot. Written as three separate display equations they look like three unrelated formulas; animated as one formula with symbols recoloring and swapping, the reader sees that Double DQN is a one-symbol edit to the target, exactly as the lecture claims.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Term-level formula morph with the selection slot and the evaluation slot color-coded and animated apart.

animation_candidates.what: Maximization bias: N noisy Q estimates drawn around equal true values, with the sampling distribution of max_a Q-hat drifting rightward as N grows, then the double estimator's split of selection and evaluation collapsing the drift.
animation_candidates.why: The bias is a statement about a distribution of estimators, not about a single number; showing the histogram of max_a Q-hat separating from the dashed true max as the action count grows makes the effect quantitative and shows why it worsens with larger action spaces.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Scatter of estimates plus an animated histogram/curve of the max statistic, with a second panel for the double estimator, swept over N.

animation_candidates.what: The dueling head's non-identifiability: a shared trunk splitting into V and A, with a slider that adds a constant c to V and subtracts c from every advantage while the recombined Q values stay frozen.
animation_candidates.why: Non-identifiability is exactly the statement 'this knob moves without changing the output', which is a slider, not a sentence. The lecture explicitly ran out of time here, so the animation fills a stated gap.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Backup/architecture diagram with two streams and a live constant-shift slider, then a second beat showing the mean-subtraction constraint locking the slider.

animation_candidates.what: The DQN ablation as an animated bar chart on Breakout: 3, then ~10 with fixed targets, then 241 with replay, then the combination.
animation_candidates.why: The magnitude gap is the whole point and it is a factor of ~25 between the two tricks. Bars growing on a shared axis make the asymmetry visceral in a way the table in the paper does not.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Animated bar chart with a log-scale toggle and the two axes (replay on/off, target on/off) laid out as a 2x2 rather than a list.

animation_candidates.what: The deadly triad as three overlapping conditions, with a small linear-FA MDP whose weights are shown diverging to infinity once all three are switched on, and settling once any one is removed.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture asserts divergence and cites 1990s results but never shows a failure. Watching weights blow up when the third switch flips, and stabilize when it flips back, converts a cited theorem into an experienced fact.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Three toggles feeding a live weight-trajectory plot on a Baird-style star MDP.

code_experiment_candidates: Replay/target-network 2x2 ablation on CartPole or a small gridworld: run {replay on/off} x {target network on/off} with everything else fixed, five seeds each, and reproduce the qualitative finding that replay dominates. This is the lecture's central empirical claim and it is cheap to reproduce.

Mars Rover replay-ordering search: hard-code the 7-state chain and the four-transition trajectory, enumerate all orderings of k replayed backups, and measure updates-to-convergence for uniform, reverse-order, TD-error-prioritized, and brute-force-oracle orderings. Extend the chain length and plot updates-to-convergence versus chain length to see the exponential separation the 2016 result claims.

Baird's star counterexample: implement linear TD/Q-learning on the standard divergent MDP and plot the weight norm exploding; then add a target network with period n and show that it delays but does not remove divergence, and that on-policy sampling removes it. This supplies the counterexample the lecture only cites.

Semi-gradient versus residual gradient: implement both the dropped-term (semi-gradient) update and the full gradient of the mean squared Bellman error on a small MDP, and compare stability and fixed points - making concrete the 'these are not true gradient descent methods' remark.

Maximization bias sandbox: N actions with equal true value and Gaussian estimate noise; empirically measure E[max_a Q-hat] - max_a E[Q-hat] as a function of N and sigma, then measure the double estimator's residual (negative) bias. Then run tabular Q-learning versus double Q-learning on the classic two-state maximization-bias MDP.
Prioritized replay with a sum-tree: sweep alpha in {0, 0.4, 0.6, 1.0, 2.0} and, separately, toggle the importance-sampling correction on and off to show the bias the lecture never mentions.
