Dueling head with and without the identifiability constraint: train both, then log V(s) and mean_a A(s,a) over training to show the unconstrained version's V stream drifting arbitrarily while Q stays correct; compare mean-subtraction against max-subtraction.

Target-update-period sweep: n in {1, 10, 100, 1000, infinity} on a small control task, plotting both final performance and a measure of value-propagation speed, to make the stability-versus-propagation trade-off she describes into a curve.

Frame-stack ablation: k in {1, 2, 4, 8} on a velocity-dependent toy environment (a Pong-like or a moving-target gridworld) to show where Markov-ness breaks, plus a partially observable variant with hidden inventory to reproduce the Montezuma-style failure.

Batch/infinite replay versus certainty-equivalence: on a small tabular MDP, collect a fixed dataset, run TD(0) repeatedly to convergence over it, and separately fit the maximum-likelihood model and solve it exactly - verifying numerically that the two agree, which is the theorem the lecture asserts without proof.

Deep trunk plus refit linear last layer: train a DQN, then periodically solve the final layer in closed form by ridge or Bayesian linear regression on the frozen features, comparing sample efficiency and the quality of the resulting uncertainty estimates against vanilla DQN.

Compute-versus-experience sweep: vary the replay-updates-per-environment-step ratio over several orders of magnitude and plot final performance against both wall-clock and environment steps - the metacomputation trade-off she flags as under-studied.
dated_or_superseded: The three 'immediate improvements' presented here (Double DQN, prioritized replay, dueling) were consolidated shortly after into Rainbow (Hessel et al., AAAI 2018), which combines them with n-step returns, distributional value learning and noisy-net exploration; the modern baseline is Rainbow or a distributional agent, not vanilla DQN plus one trick.

Value-distribution methods (C51, QR-DQN, IQN) postdate this lecture and change what the network predicts - a return distribution rather than its mean - which is a more fundamental departure than any of the three extensions covered.

'Human-level on Atari' as the benchmark is superseded on both axes: Agent57 (2020) exceeded human on all 57 games including the hard-exploration tail she points at, and the field's attention moved to sample efficiency (Atari-100k), where model-based agents like MuZero/EfficientZero and self-supervised auxiliary-loss methods (CURL, SPR, DrQ) dominate. DQN's asymptotic-only human-level claim is no longer the interesting frontier.

Hard-exploration games at the bottom of her plot (Montezuma's Revenge, Pitfall) were subsequently addressed by intrinsic-motivation and archive methods - RND, Never Give Up, Go-Explore - so the lecture's 'we'll talk about exploration later' cliffhanger has concrete modern answers.

The four-frame stack as a Markov surrogate has been largely displaced by recurrent agents (R2D2) and, more recently, transformer-based sequence models (Decision Transformer, Trajectory Transformer), which handle exactly the memory failures she illustrates with Montezuma's Revenge.

Experience replay taken to its limit became offline / batch RL as a subfield after 2019, with a problem DQN does not face: extrapolation error from querying the Q function at actions absent from the buffer. BCQ, CQL and IQL are the standard responses. Any modern reader thinking about 'reuse logged data' needs this, and it did not exist in 2019.

'We have almost no theoretical guarantees for the rest of the day' is less true now: there are convergence analyses for target-network Q-learning under two-timescale assumptions, neural fitted Q-iteration results, and van Hasselt et al. (2018) 'Deep RL and the Deadly Triad' which empirically dissects exactly which leg does the damage in DQN.

The mandated TensorFlow 1.x for homework 2 is thoroughly dated; PyTorch is the default in RL research and JAX (with Flax/Optax, and RL stacks like Acme, CleanRL, Stable-Baselines3) is the performance choice. The autodiff point she makes stands; the framework does not.

The CNN architecture presented (a few conv layers, pooling, FC head) is the 2015 Nature DQN torso; modern pixel-based agents use IMPALA-style residual CNNs or vision transformers, and typically no pooling at all.

Kernel and nearest-neighbour approximators are dismissed as unscalable, but episodic-memory and retrieval-augmented RL (Neural Episodic Control, MFEC, and retrieval-augmented policies generally) revived exactly that idea with learned embeddings doing the dimensionality reduction she says is missing.

The prioritized-replay presentation predates the standard understanding that proportional prioritization requires importance-sampling correction with an annealed beta; that correction is now considered part of the algorithm, not an optional refinement.

relevance_to_user_research.why: Genuinely useful, though not the critical lecture, and the useful parts are not the ones the title advertises. Ignore the CNN half outright - it is a parameter-counting argument about images with no bearing on node-level fidelity assignment. The DQN half maps onto the user's setting more tightly than most RL lectures do, for four specific reasons. (1) Their action space is exactly DQN's regime: a tiny discrete set per node (weak / strong / prune), with a high-dimensional structured state (query embedding, DAG position, partial trace, remaining budget). A Q-network over that state with 3 outputs is the obvious first non-bandit baseline above their AEP query-level router, and the value-based framing generalizes their H=1 case to H>1 without changing the machinery. (2) The ablation result is a direct prescription, not trivia: replay swamped everything else because each environment interaction was expensive. In their setting one 'environment step' is a real workflow execution burning Qwen2.5-72B tokens on A100s, so the marginal value of reusing each logged trajectory many times is far higher than it was for Atari, where the emulator is free. Whatever they build should be replay-heavy or fully offline from a fixed pool of logged executions. (3) The Mars Rover ordering exercise is the most transferable ten minutes in the lecture. Their reward is terminal (task accuracy minus lambda times cost, revealed only after the whole DAG runs), which is precisely the sparse-terminal-reward chain where forward-order updates propagate nothing and reverse-order updates propagate the signal immediately. Backing up from the terminal node of the DAG is the right default, and prioritizing by TD error is the right refinement. (4) The dueling motivation is almost a restatement of their research question: they do not care about the absolute value of being at node k with query q, they care which fidelity is better there, i.e. the advantage. That argues for an advantage-parameterized or directly policy-gradient method over a raw Q head. Two honest caveats that keep this at 'useful' rather than 'critical'. First, their horizon is short - a searched AFlow workflow is maybe 5-15 operators - so bootstrapping error compounds far less than over an Atari episode, and fitted-Q-iteration over logged data, or even a per-node contextual bandit with a budget constraint, may match a full DQN stack at a fraction of the engineering cost. Second, and more importantly, the algorithm they actually need is offline RL, not online DQN: they will be learning from a fixed pool of logged workflow executions, where the binding problem is extrapolation error on fidelity assignments the logging policy never tried - a failure mode that postdates this lecture entirely and that DQN's two tricks do not address. The deadly triad discussion is the right warning to carry forward (they will have function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy data simultaneously), but the 2019 remedies are the wrong ones. Treat this lecture as the vocabulary and the cautionary tale, and get the actual algorithm from CQL/IQL.

lecture_title: CS234 Lecture 7: Imitation Learning (with a recap of DQN extensions)
one_paragraph_summary: The lecture has two halves. The first ~20 minutes finish the deep value-based material from the previous class: it re-derives why Double DQN differs from vanilla DQN (two weight sets that can be swapped every step, rather than one target set frozen for tens of episodes, so information propagates faster while still decoupling action selection from action evaluation and avoiding maximization bias), recaps prioritized experience replay (priority proportional to TD error magnitude, with an exponent alpha that collapses to uniform sampling at alpha = 0), and recaps dueling networks (split the head into V and A = Q - V, motivated by the observation that the features that determine state value differ from the features that determine relative action quality). It then makes the identifiability point: the (V, A) decomposition is not unique, since adding a constant to both leaves A unchanged, so one must pin the gauge by forcing the advantage of the chosen/greedy action to zero, or, as a heuristic, by subtracting the mean advantage. Rainbow is cited as evidence that these gains are roughly additive, and Montezuma's Revenge as evidence that none of them address hard exploration. The second half pivots to sample efficiency: tabular MDP lower bounds say that worst-case exploration is expensive, so the lecture asks what other supervision is available and answers "demonstrations". It sets up the demonstration-learning problem (known state/action spaces, unknown dynamics, no reward function, a set of trajectories from an assumed-optimal teacher) and splits it into behavior cloning (learn pi directly), inverse RL (recover R), and apprenticeship learning (recover R, then plan with it). Behavior cloning is presented as plain supervised learning and then broken: under i.i.d. supervised learning a per-step error rate epsilon gives about epsilon*T mistakes over a horizon T, but in an MDP a single mistake moves the agent off the expert's state distribution, where the supervised guarantee no longer applies, so errors compound to O(epsilon * T^2). DAgger is the fix: iteratively roll out the current policy, have the expert label every state actually visited, aggregate into one growing dataset, and retrain; the price is a human expert in the loop at every step, which the lecturer argues makes it impractical for high-frequency control. Inverse RL is then shown to be ill-posed even with infinite data: R identically zero makes every policy optimal, so infinitely many reward functions explain any demonstration. The lecture's constructive response is feature matching under a linear reward R(s) = w^T x(s): the value of a policy factors as V^pi = w^T mu(pi), where mu(pi) is the discounted expected feature vector (a discounted, feature-space analogue of the stationary state distribution), so if a learner's mu matches the expert's mu closely then its value is close to the expert's value for every admissible w, i.e. regardless of the true unknown reward. That yields the Abbeel-Ng style iterative max-margin apprenticeship algorithm (find w making the teacher look better than all previously found policies, solve the MDP for that w, add the resulting mu, repeat until the margin is small). The lecture closes by naming the modern successors that break the ambiguity differently: MaxEnt IRL (least-commitment distribution over trajectories subject to matching feature counts), GAIL (use a learned discriminator as a surrogate for occupancy-measure matching when the state space is too high-dimensional to write mu down), Bayesian IRL (put a prior over rewards if you genuinely want the reward rather than the policy), and imitation-plus-RL combinations that can exceed a suboptimal demonstrator.
prerequisites: MDP formalism: states, actions, transition model, discount factor, policy, value function V^pi and Q^pi
Q-learning and the notion of a bootstrapped TD target, including the maximization-bias problem in tabular double Q-learning
Value function approximation, especially linear approximation over state features, and Baird's divergence counterexample
DQN mechanics: experience replay, target networks, minibatch SGD, Adam
Supervised learning basics: hypothesis/policy class, empirical risk minimization, and the i.i.d. assumption behind generalization guarantees
Stationary state distributions induced by a policy, and the idea of a discounted state occupancy measure
Enough linear algebra and analysis to follow a Cauchy-Schwarz / Holder bound on an inner product; helpful (for the notes) to know convex duality and maximum-entropy modeling
Familiarity with GANs for the GAIL discussion

concepts.name: Course admin
concepts.one_line: Homework 2 is underway with optional deep-learning background sessions; projects may be self-designed or drawn from a suggested list (including a default bandits/warfarin project), and pinned Piazza FAQs should be consulted before office hours.

concepts.name: DQN recap: experience replay plus fixed Q targets
concepts.one_line: DQN = Q-learning with a deep network, stabilized by (i) sampling minibatches of (s,a,r,s') from a replay buffer to break temporal correlation and (ii) holding the target-network weights fixed for an interval so the regression target behaves like a stationary supervised-learning label.

concepts.name: Maximization bias
concepts.one_line: Using the same estimator both to choose the argmax action and to evaluate that action makes E[max] exceed max E, so Q values are systematically overestimated; decoupling selection from evaluation removes this bias.

concepts.name: Double DQN
concepts.one_line: Select the action with the online weights w and evaluate it with a second set w-, i.e. target = r + gamma * Q(s', argmax_a Q(s',a; w); w-), where crucially the two weight sets can be swapped every step or minibatch instead of one being frozen for 50-100 episodes.

concepts.name: Why Double DQN differs from vanilla DQN's target network
concepts.one_line: Vanilla DQN already uses w- for the target but takes the max under w- as well, and staleness means the last 50 episodes of data are not used to improve the target; Double DQN's symmetric two-network swap both decouples selection from evaluation and propagates new information into both networks quickly.

concepts.name: Stability versus speed of information propagation
concepts.one_line: A student asks whether there is a principled tradeoff between how fast information propagates and how unstable learning becomes; the lecturer concedes this is uncharacterized and that current practice is heuristic benchmark tuning across Atari/MuJoCo, flagging it as open theory.

concepts.name: Prioritized experience replay
concepts.one_line: Sample replay transitions with probability increasing in |TD error|^alpha rather than uniformly; alpha = 0 recovers uniform replay, and the originating paper claims optimal prioritization could give an exponential speedup in convergence but is computationally intractable.

concepts.name: Advantage function
concepts.one_line: A^pi(s,a) = Q^pi(s,a) - V^pi(s), the excess value of taking action a in state s relative to just following pi from s; introduced by Baird, the same author as the linear-function-approximation divergence counterexample.

concepts.name: Dueling DQN architecture
concepts.one_line: Split the network head into a scalar V(s) branch and a per-action A(s,a) branch and recombine to form Q, on the reasoning that the features predicting a state's value (e.g. game score) differ from those predicting relative action quality.

concepts.name: Non-identifiability of the value/advantage decomposition
concepts.one_line: Q does not determine a unique (V, A) pair: shifting V by any constant c and Q by the same c leaves A = Q - V unchanged, so the dueling architecture needs an extra gauge-fixing constraint.

concepts.name: Gauge fixing in dueling networks
concepts.one_line: Identifiability is restored by forcing the advantage of the greedy/selected action to be zero (subtract max_a' A(s,a')); the paper also reports that subtracting the mean advantage works empirically, which the lecturer labels a heuristic with no accompanying analysis.

concepts.name: Rainbow
concepts.one_line: Combining double Q-learning, prioritized replay, dueling, noisy nets and other recent advances gives gains that are largely additive, which is informative because overlapping tricks often turn out to be redundant; still requires ~200M frames of experience.

concepts.name: Montezuma's Revenge as a hard-exploration counterexample
concepts.one_line: After 50M frames DQN clears only the first two rooms, and dueling+prioritized+double gives essentially no improvement, showing these tricks improve credit propagation and training stability but not directed exploration under sparse reward.

concepts.name: Sample-complexity hardness of RL
concepts.one_line: There are pathological tabular MDPs whose learning requires very large amounts of data; the lecturer states that essentially tight upper and lower bounds are now known for the tabular case, and that even far better-than-epsilon-greedy exploration cannot escape them.

concepts.name: Motivation for imitation learning
concepts.one_line: When data is expensive, parallelization is impossible, or failure is intolerable (helicopters, medicine, driving), pure trial-and-error RL is impractical, so extra supervision in the form of demonstrations is a way to buy sample efficiency.

concepts.name: Reward specification is hard and brittle
concepts.one_line: Hand-designing a reward for something like driving requires enumerating many competing desiderata, and any misspecification will be exploited by the optimizer; demonstrating the desired behavior is often far easier than writing its reward down.

concepts.name: Problem setup for learning from demonstration
concepts.one_line: Given state space S, action space A, an unknown transition model, NO reward function, and a set of demonstration trajectories (s_0,a_0,s_1,a_1,...) from a teacher assumed optimal, learn either the teacher's policy, the teacher's reward, or both.

concepts.name: Three problem variants: behavior cloning, inverse RL, apprenticeship learning
concepts.one_line: Behavior cloning fits pi* directly from (s,a) pairs; inverse RL recovers R from demonstrations; apprenticeship learning recovers R and then computes a good policy under it, and is the setting used for the rest of the lecture.

concepts.name: When you want only the reward function
concepts.one_line: Recovering R alone is scientifically useful for inferring the goals or preferences of an agent you cannot control (animal behavior, commuting choices, purchasing preferences) even when you never intend to optimize it.

concepts.name: Behavior cloning as supervised learning
concepts.one_line: Fix a policy class (neural net, decision tree, etc.), treat each demonstrated (state, action) pair as an input/label example, and fit a classifier from states to actions with standard supervised learning, ignoring temporal structure.

concepts.name: ALVINN
concepts.one_line: An early (roughly 30-year-old) neural-network road-following driving system trained in part by supervised imitation of human driving trajectories, cited as the canonical early behavior-cloning success.

concepts.name: Supervised learning error over a horizon
concepts.one_line: If (s,a) pairs are i.i.d. and the learned classifier errs with probability epsilon, then over T decisions the expected number of mistakes is epsilon * T, which grows only linearly in the horizon.

concepts.name: Distribution shift: actions determine the data distribution
concepts.one_line: In an MDP the learner's own actions determine which states it subsequently visits, so once it deviates from the expert it is evaluated on a state distribution its training data never covered, and the i.i.d. supervised generalization guarantee simply does not apply.

concepts.name: Compounding error bound for behavior cloning
concepts.one_line: Because a single mistake at time t can put the agent off-distribution for all remaining T - t steps, the expected number of mistakes for behavior cloning in an MDP is O(epsilon * T^2) rather than epsilon * T, a result attributed to Ross and Bagnell.

concepts.name: Recurrence of the state-distribution-mismatch theme
concepts.one_line: The gap between the state distribution induced by the policy you follow and the one induced by the policy you want to evaluate is flagged as a foundational issue that will reappear repeatedly in RL (off-policy evaluation, policy gradients, safe policy improvement).

concepts.name: DAgger (dataset aggregation)
concepts.one_line: Iterate: roll out the current learned policy, query the expert for the correct action at every state actually visited, append all newly labeled pairs to one ever-growing dataset, and refit the policy by supervised learning on the aggregate.

concepts.name: DAgger's guarantee
concepts.one_line: DAgger is asserted to converge to a good policy under its own induced state distribution, i.e. the training distribution is forced to match the test distribution, removing the quadratic-in-horizon blowup; the guarantee is stated but not proved.

concepts.name: Cost of a human in the loop
concepts.one_line: DAgger needs an expert able to label every visited state, which is intractable at real-time control rates and is why the lecturer judges it less influential in practice than one-shot-demonstration methods; it is reasonable when decisions are slow and sparse, or via an expert who intervenes only on disagreement.

concepts.name: Inverse RL with no optimality assumption is vacuous
concepts.one_line: If nothing is assumed about the demonstrator's optimality with respect to the true reward, the demonstrations carry no information about that reward at all (you may still infer something about the demonstrator's own internal reward if you assume they are rational with respect to it).

concepts.name: Degeneracy of inverse RL
concepts.one_line: Even with an optimal teacher and infinite data, the reward function is not identifiable: R identically zero makes every policy optimal, and constant shifts and other transformations give infinitely many rewards consistent with the same behavior; observed by Ng and Russell (ICML 2000).

concepts.name: Linear feature-based reward
concepts.one_line: Assume R(s) = w^T x(s) for a known feature map x(s) and unknown weight vector w, so learning the reward reduces to learning a finite-dimensional w from demonstrations.

concepts.name: Discounted feature expectations mu(pi)
concepts.one_line: Starting from V^pi = E[sum_t gamma^t R(s_t) | pi] and substituting the linear reward, the constant w pulls outside the expectation, giving V^pi = w^T mu(pi) with mu(pi) = E[sum_t gamma^t x(s_t) | pi]: a discount-weighted, feature-space analogue of the stationary state distribution.

concepts.name: Reformulating IRL as a comparison over state distributions
concepts.one_line: Because V^pi = w^T mu(pi), comparing policies under an unknown linear reward becomes comparing their discounted feature-occupancy vectors, so the problem moves out of reward space and into occupancy space.

concepts.name: Sufficient condition for identifying w
concepts.one_line: If the demonstrations come from pi*, then V^{pi*} >= V^pi for all pi, so it suffices to find w* with w*^T mu(pi*) >= w*^T mu(pi) for every other policy pi, an infinite set of linear constraints on w.

concepts.name: Feature-matching value bound
concepts.one_line: If ||mu(pi) - mu(pi*)|| is small and the reward weights are norm-bounded, then |V^pi - V^{pi*}| = |w^T(mu(pi) - mu(pi*))| is small for EVERY admissible w, i.e. matching feature expectations gives near-expert value no matter what the true reward is.

concepts.name: Why the norm constraint on w is needed
concepts.one_line: The bound is obtained by applying a Holder/Cauchy-Schwarz step to the inner product w^T(mu - mu*) and using boundedness of w to keep the resulting value error finite; the lecturer sketches this and explicitly says she would have to check the details.

concepts.name: Occupancy matching claimed to imply policy identity
concepts.one_line: The lecturer asserts that if a learner visits every state with exactly the expert's discounted frequency then the two policies are identical, so one can abandon reward recovery entirely and still reproduce the expert's behavior.

concepts.name: Apprenticeship learning / max-margin algorithm
concepts.one_line: Repeat: find a w making the teacher's mu score higher than the mu of every policy found so far (a max-margin / SVM-like step), solve the MDP under that w to get a new policy and its mu (via the known transition model or Monte Carlo rollouts), add it to the set, and stop when the margin is small.

concepts.name: Choice of the L1 norm in the feature-matching condition
concepts.one_line: The L1 norm on mu(pi) - mu(pi*) forces the error to be small summed over all states rather than at a few, and L1/L-infinity pairs are the convenient ones for bounding value error; other norms change the analysis.

concepts.name: Maximum Entropy inverse RL
concepts.one_line: Among all trajectory distributions that reproduce the expert's expected feature counts, choose the maximum-entropy one, i.e. commit as little as possible beyond the data (deliberate underfitting) to break the reward ambiguity; from Ziebart and Bagnell's group.

concepts.name: Extension to unknown transition models
concepts.one_line: These methods extend to the unknown-dynamics case if you have a simulator or real-world access: roll out candidate policies, estimate their state-feature distributions empirically, and compare those to the demonstrator's.

concepts.name: GAIL: discriminator as an occupancy-matching surrogate
concepts.one_line: When the state space is high-dimensional (images, many-joint robots) writing down mu is infeasible, so train a discriminator to distinguish expert trajectories from agent-generated trajectories; inability to discriminate certifies occupancy matching, and the agent gathers fresh data each round.

concepts.name: Bayesian inverse RL
concepts.one_line: Frequentist IRL cannot pin down the reward, but placing a structured prior over reward functions and doing Bayesian updating yields a posterior that can exclude degenerate solutions like R = 0 and encode domain knowledge; related to Thompson-sampling-style priors used for exploration.

concepts.name: Going beyond the demonstrator
concepts.one_line: Because demonstrations (e.g. scraped from YouTube) are of unknown quality, the practical recipe is to use imitation to bootstrap and then continue with RL, which can exceed the demonstrator; cited work also treats demonstrations as noisy observations of an optimal path.

concepts.name: Open challenge: no optimal policy exists in the data
concepts.one_line: In healthcare, education and customer-facing domains the whole point is to beat existing behavior, so the assumed-optimal-teacher premise fails, and the open problem is combining inverse RL with safe online exploration.

theorems_stated: Non-identifiability of the dueling decomposition: for a fixed Q, the pair (V, A) with A = Q - V is not unique, because adding a constant to V and the same constant to Q leaves A invariant.
Supervised-learning horizon bound: under i.i.d. (s,a) data with per-decision error probability epsilon, the expected number of errors over T steps is epsilon * T.

Behavior cloning compounding-error bound: in an MDP, where the learner's actions determine its future state distribution, the expected number of errors is O(epsilon * T^2), quadratic rather than linear in the horizon (attributed to Ross and Bagnell, ~2010/2011).
DAgger convergence: iterative dataset aggregation with expert relabeling converges to a good policy measured under the state distribution the learned policy itself induces.
Vacuousness of IRL without an optimality assumption: demonstrations from an agent with no assumed relationship to the true reward carry zero information about that reward.

Degeneracy of inverse RL: R identically zero makes every policy optimal, so for any set of optimal demonstrations there exist infinitely many consistent reward functions; the reward is not identifiable even with infinite data (Ng and Russell, 2000).
Linear-reward value factorization: for R(s) = w^T x(s), V^pi = w^T mu(pi) where mu(pi) = E[sum_t gamma^t x(s_t) | pi] is the discounted expected feature vector.
Sufficient condition for the reward weights: if the teacher is optimal, any w* satisfying w*^T mu(pi*) >= w*^T mu(pi) for all pi is consistent with the demonstrations.

Feature-matching value bound: if ||mu(pi) - mu(pi*)||_1 <= epsilon and the reward weights are norm-bounded, then |V^pi - V^{pi*}| <= epsilon uniformly over all admissible w, i.e. independent of the unknown true reward.
Occupancy-implies-policy claim: a policy whose discounted state visitation frequencies exactly match the expert's is claimed to be identical to the expert policy.

Tabular RL sample-complexity: essentially matching upper and lower bounds are known for tabular MDPs, and there exist MDPs requiring an amount of data that scales prohibitively (stated, not quantified).
Prioritized replay claim: an optimal prioritization of replay backups can in some cases give an exponential speedup in convergence, but computing it is intractable.
Rainbow empirical claim: the gains from double Q-learning, prioritized replay, dueling, noisy nets and related extensions are approximately additive rather than redundant.
proofs_given: Non-identifiability of the advantage decomposition, by explicit construction: shift Q and V by the same constant and observe A = Q - V is unchanged, hence infinitely many decompositions realize the same Q.

Degeneracy of inverse RL, by counterexample elicited from the class: set R = 0 everywhere; then every policy attains the same (zero) return, so every policy is optimal and the observed demonstrations are consistent with it.

Derivation of V^pi = w^T mu(pi), done on the board: start from V^pi = E[sum_t gamma^t R(s_t) | pi], substitute R(s) = w^T x(s), and pull the constant vector w outside the expectation and the discounted sum, leaving the discounted expected feature vector mu(pi).

Sufficiency of feature matching for near-expert value, argued at the level of the inner product: since both values share the same unknown w, their difference is w^T(mu(pi) - mu(pi*)), which is small whenever the feature-expectation gap is small and w is norm-bounded (the norm inequality step is sketched, not carried out).

Informal argument for compounding errors, via the 'walk out the wrong door' example: one classification mistake places the learner in a region of state space with no training coverage, where the supervised guarantee is void and every subsequent decision may err, giving up to T additional errors per mistake.
proofs_skipped: The formal statement and proof of the O(epsilon * T^2) behavior-cloning bound (Ross and Bagnell). The lecture gives only the door/racecourse intuition. The notes must state the reduction precisely: with a policy whose 0-1 error under the expert's state distribution is at most epsilon and a task cost bounded in [0,1], the expected cost of the cloned policy is bounded by J(expert) + O(epsilon * T^2), and must exhibit the matching lower-bound construction showing the quadratic term is tight and not an artifact of loose analysis.

The DAgger guarantee itself. The lecture says only 'there are nice formal properties, you can be guaranteed to converge to a good policy under the induced state distribution'. The notes must supply: the reduction of DAgger to online learning (Follow-the-Leader over the aggregated dataset), the no-regret property of the resulting online convex program, and the resulting bound J(pi) <= J(expert) + O(epsilon * T) plus a regret term that vanishes as the number of iterations N grows.

The role of the mixing coefficient beta_i in DAgger. A student asks whether the expert's actions or the learner's actions drive the rollout; the lecturer answers that it is 'like tossing a coin' and says she would have to double-check. The notes must formalize pi_i = beta_i * pi_expert + (1 - beta_i) * pi_hat_i, show why beta_i must decay to zero (e.g. beta_i = p^{i-1}) for the state distribution to converge to the learner's own, and show why the naive beta_i = 1 version reduces to behavior cloning.

The precise norm inequality behind the feature-matching bound. The lecturer says 'I think you basically use Holder's inequality and then the fact that w is bounded' and explicitly declines to verify it. The notes must do the algebra: |w^T(mu(pi) - mu(pi*))| <= ||w||_q * ||mu(pi) - mu(pi*)||_p for conjugate exponents, and pin which pairing is actually being used, since the lecture states the constraint in L1 on mu but names L2 boundedness for w (these are not conjugate).

Why a norm constraint on w is required at all. The lecturer speculates it is to keep backup errors bounded and to keep the Bellman operator a contraction, then says 'you can check that'. The notes should show that without it the constraint set w^T mu(pi*) >= w^T mu(pi) is a cone (scale-invariant), so the optimization is unbounded and the margin is meaningless; the norm ball is what makes the max-margin problem well posed, and separately what converts a feature-expectation gap into a value gap.

Termination and iteration complexity of the max-margin apprenticeship algorithm (Abbeel and Ng, 2004). The lecture describes the loop and says 'repeat until the gap is sufficiently small' with no convergence claim. The notes must supply the theorem that the algorithm terminates after O(k / ((1-gamma)^2 * epsilon^2) * log(k / ((1-gamma) * epsilon))) iterations for a k-dimensional feature map, and note that the returned object is a mixture over the policies found, not a single deterministic policy.

The claim that matching discounted state-visitation frequencies implies identical policies. This is asserted twice and is FALSE as stated for general feature maps: matching mu(pi) only matches k linear functionals of the occupancy measure, and even matching the full discounted occupancy measure d^pi identifies a unique stationary policy only via pi(a|s) = d^pi(s,a) / sum_a' d^pi(s,a'), which requires state-action occupancy, not state occupancy. The notes must state the correct version (occupancy measures are in bijection with stationary policies on the state-action polytope; feature expectations are not) and give a counterexample with two distinct policies sharing the same mu.

The full characterization of the solution set in inverse RL (Ng and Russell, 2000). Only the R = 0 corner is exhibited. The notes should give the complete linear-programming characterization: pi = a_1 is optimal iff (P_{a_1} - P_a)(I - gamma P_{a_1})^{-1} R >= 0 for all a, so the consistent rewards form a convex polyhedral cone, and should present the standard tie-breaking objectives (maximize the margin by which a_1 beats the runner-up, plus an L1 penalty on R for sparsity).

Reward-shaping invariance. The lecturer gestures at 'you can always shift your rewards by a constant and it will not change your policy'. The notes should state and prove the actual result (Ng, Harada and Russell, 1999): potential-based shaping R'(s,a,s') = R(s,a,s') + gamma * Phi(s') - Phi(s) preserves the optimal policy set, and this is the necessary as well as sufficient form; and separately clarify that an additive constant on the reward does preserve the optimal policy in the discounted infinite-horizon setting but shifts all values by c / (1 - gamma).

The MaxEnt IRL derivation. Only the least-commitment slogan is given. The notes must derive it: maximize the entropy of a distribution over trajectories subject to the expected feature counts matching the empirical ones, form the Lagrangian, and obtain P(tau) proportional to exp(w^T mu(tau)); then show the log-likelihood is convex in w with gradient equal to empirical minus model-expected feature counts, and describe the forward-backward / soft-value-iteration computation of the model expectation.

The GAIL theory. Only the discriminator intuition is given. The notes must state the occupancy-measure result: the composition of IRL with a convex reward regularizer psi and subsequent RL is equivalent to minimizing psi*(rho_pi - rho_expert) over occupancy measures, and that the particular choice of psi corresponding to the GAN loss makes the objective the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the learner's and expert's occupancy measures, whose unique minimizer is rho_pi = rho_expert.

Why decoupled selection and evaluation removes maximization bias. Double DQN's correctness is asserted from the earlier tabular double Q-learning discussion but never proved here. The notes should give the standard argument: with independent estimates, E[Q_2(argmax_a Q_1(s,a))] is an unbiased estimate of Q(s, argmax_a Q_1(s,a)) rather than of max_a Q(s,a), and quantify the bias of the single-estimator version (e.g. the m-armed identical-value example where the overestimate grows with the number of actions).

Justification of the mean-subtraction baseline in dueling networks. The lecturer states the max-based gauge and then says the mean 'is more of a heuristic'. The notes should show that Q = V + A - mean_a A still uniquely determines (V, A) given Q (i.e. it is a valid gauge) but that V no longer equals the state value; and discuss why it is empirically more stable than the max version.

The prioritized-replay claims: neither the exponential-speedup result for optimal prioritization nor the bias analysis of non-uniform sampling is given. The notes must show that sampling with probability proportional to |delta|^alpha changes the expected gradient, and derive the importance-sampling correction weights (1/(N * P(i)))^beta with beta annealed to 1, which the lecture omits entirely.

The tabular sample-complexity bounds are asserted but never stated. The notes should give the actual minimax result (e.g. Omega(S * A * H^3 / epsilon^2) style lower bounds and the matching upper bounds for optimistic algorithms) so the claim 'RL is fundamentally data-hungry' is quantitative rather than rhetorical.

Bayesian IRL is named but not formalized: no likelihood model (e.g. the Boltzmann-rational P(a|s,R) proportional to exp(beta * Q_R(s,a))), no prior specification, no posterior-inference algorithm, and no statement of what identifiability is or is not recovered by the prior.

Baird's counterexample for linear value function approximation is referenced ('this is the same Baird') but not restated or reproved, even though the divergence phenomenon underlies the boundedness discussion.

The claim that imitation-plus-RL can exceed the demonstrator is asserted with pointers to Abbeel's and Levine's groups but with no formal condition under which the learner provably surpasses a suboptimal expert (e.g. the noisy-expert model where the demonstration is a perturbation of an optimal path).
algorithms: DQN: Q-learning with a deep network, an experience replay buffer of (s,a,r,s') tuples sampled in minibatches, a target network whose weights w- are refreshed every N steps/episodes, and SGD (Adam in the assignment) on the squared TD error.

Double DQN: maintain two weight sets; select the action with one set and evaluate it with the other, target = r + gamma * Q(s', argmax_a Q(s',a; w); w-), swapping the roles frequently (every step or minibatch) rather than freezing one set for many episodes.

Prioritized experience replay: assign each stored transition a priority p_i increasing in |TD error|, sample with probability proportional to p_i^alpha (alpha = 0 recovers uniform), optionally stochastically rather than greedily.
Dueling DQN: a shared trunk feeding two heads, V(s) and A(s,a), recombined as Q(s,a) = V(s) + A(s,a) - max_a' A(s,a') (or with the mean in place of the max as a heuristic).
Rainbow: the ensemble of double Q-learning, prioritized replay, dueling, noisy networks and other contemporaneous improvements applied together, evaluated at ~200M frames.

Behavior cloning: fix a policy class, form a supervised dataset of (state, expert action) pairs from demonstrations, and fit a classifier/regressor from states to actions by ERM, ignoring temporal structure.

DAgger (dataset aggregation): initialize D empty and pi_1 arbitrary; for i = 1..N, roll out pi_i (in practice mixed with the expert), query the expert for the correct action at every visited state, append those labeled pairs to D, and retrain pi_{i+1} by supervised learning on all of D; return the best policy found.

Apprenticeship learning via max-margin feature matching (Abbeel and Ng): estimate mu(pi*) from demonstrations; repeat { find w (norm-bounded) maximizing the margin by which w^T mu(pi*) exceeds w^T mu(pi_j) for all previously found pi_j; solve the MDP under reward w^T x(s) to get pi_{new}; estimate mu(pi_new) by rollouts or by using the known transition model } until the margin falls below a threshold.

Maximum Entropy inverse RL: fit a trajectory distribution of the form P(tau) proportional to exp(w^T mu(tau)) by maximizing likelihood / entropy subject to matching the expert's expected feature counts, using dynamic programming to compute expected state-visitation frequencies.

GAIL (generative adversarial imitation learning): alternate between training a discriminator to separate expert trajectories from agent trajectories, and improving the agent with a policy-gradient method whose reward is derived from the discriminator's output, thereby matching occupancy measures without ever writing down mu explicitly.
notation_introduced: w = online/current Q-network weights used for action SELECTION; w- = older or second weight set used for action EVALUATION (the target)
A^pi(s,a) = Q^pi(s,a) - V^pi(s), the advantage of action a in state s under policy pi
alpha = prioritization exponent in prioritized replay; alpha = 0 gives uniform sampling
pi* = the teacher's / expert's policy, assumed optimal with respect to the unknown true reward
tau = (s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, ...) a demonstration trajectory; the demonstration set is a collection of such trajectories
epsilon = per-decision error probability of the supervised classifier trained on demonstrations
T = horizon, i.e. the number of decisions in an episode; epsilon * T is the supervised bound, epsilon * T^2 the MDP bound
x(s) = feature vector of state s (written variously as phi/x in the lecture); R(s) = w^T x(s) is the linear reward model
w = reward weight vector in the IRL half of the lecture (SAME SYMBOL as the Q-network weights from the first half, different object)
mu(pi) = E[sum_{t=0}^{inf} gamma^t x(s_t) | pi], the discounted expected feature vector ('discounted weighted frequency of state features') under policy pi
V^pi = w^T mu(pi), the linear-reward factorization of policy value
mu(pi*) or mu_E = the expert's discounted feature expectation, estimated empirically from the demonstrations
||w|| <= 1 = the norm constraint on the reward weights that makes the max-margin problem well posed and the value bound finite
||mu(pi) - mu(pi*)||_1 <= epsilon = the L1 feature-matching condition
D = the aggregated dataset in DAgger
notation_hazards: The symbol w is overloaded across the two halves of the lecture: in the DQN recap it is the neural network parameter vector, and in the IRL half it is the linear reward weight vector. The notes should rename one of them (e.g. theta for the network, w for the reward).

The captions garble the DQN target repeatedly. 'r_t + gamma max over a Q of sta, st plus one' should read r_t + gamma * max_a Q(s_{t+1}, a; w-), and the trailing 'minus the current s' should read minus Q(s_t, a_t; w). Likewise 'queuing network' means Q-network throughout.

The dueling identifiability argument is stated as 'if you add a constant to both Q and V then you can get the same advantage function'. That is correct as a statement about invariance of A = Q - V, but the transcript immediately conflates it with a different invariance ('you can shift your rewards by a constant and it will not change your policy, it will change your value function'). These are two distinct facts and should be separated in the notes.

The gauge-fixing rule is stated as 'force the advantage for state and action to be zero if A is the action taken', where A denotes an ACTION here and is the same letter used for the advantage function two sentences earlier. The intended constraint is A(s, a*) = 0 for the greedy action a*, realized as Q = V + A - max_a' A.

The L1 discussion is mathematically wrong as transcribed: 'when you sum up all of those errors it has to be one'. The L1 norm is the sum of absolute per-component errors and the condition is that this sum be SMALL (bounded by epsilon), not equal to one.

The norm bookkeeping is inconsistent. The lecture states the feature-matching condition in L1 on mu but describes the constraint on w as an L2 ball, and then invokes Holder's inequality. Holder pairs L1 with L-infinity (and Cauchy-Schwarz pairs L2 with L2). The notes must pick one consistent pairing; the Abbeel-Ng original uses ||w||_2 <= 1 with ||mu(pi) - mu_E||_2 <= epsilon.

mu is described as being 'of s', i.e. as though it were a distribution over states. It is a vector indexed by FEATURE, of dimension k = dim(x(s)); it coincides with a discounted state distribution only when x is the one-hot/indicator encoding of the state. This distinction is exactly what makes the 'matching mu implies identical policies' claim false in general.

mu is called 'the stationary distribution with a discount factor on top'. The precise object is the normalized discounted occupancy measure d^pi(s) = (1 - gamma) * sum_t gamma^t P(s_t = s | pi); the lecture's mu omits the (1 - gamma) normalization, so it is an unnormalized discounted feature count, not a probability distribution.

Sutton and Barto write the advantage and the occupancy measure differently: S&B use mu(s) for the on-policy state distribution and eta(s) for expected visits, whereas this lecture uses mu for a FEATURE-space discounted count. Readers moving between the two will collide on this symbol.

Names are garbled by the captioner: 'Sergei Lamin' is Sergey Levine; 'Gail' is the acronym GAIL; 'generative adversarial inverse imitation learning' is Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (Ho and Ermon, 2016); 'Stephane Ross' and 'Drew Bagnell' (J. Andrew Bagnell) are correct. The Ng-Russell inverse RL paper is dated '1999, 2000' in the talk; it is ICML 2000.

T is used for the horizon throughout the imitation analysis but the same lecture uses t for time indices and, in the DQN part, 't + 100' for a target-refresh interval. Distinguish the horizon T from the refresh period.

The lecture says demonstrations tell you 'nothing' about the reward absent an optimality assumption, then immediately concedes you can infer something about the demonstrator's OWN reward under a rationality assumption. The two claims are compatible only once you distinguish the true global reward from the demonstrator's internal reward; the notes should make that split explicit.

animation_candidates.what: Compounding error: epsilon*T versus epsilon*T^2
animation_candidates.why: The whole intellectual payload of the behavior-cloning half is that a linear bound becomes quadratic purely because the data distribution is endogenous. Static text states two formulas; animation can show the mechanism - the moment the learner leaves the expert's support, the guarantee evaporates and the remaining T-t steps go dark. The 'area under the triangle' reading of T^2 (each of T possible first-mistake times contributes up to T subsequent errors) is a genuinely visual argument.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Split screen. Left: an i.i.d. supervised setting where errors are isolated red dots on a flat strip, counted linearly. Right: a corridor/racetrack where the expert's demonstrated trajectory is a bright ribbon; the learner tracks it, then at step t a single misclassification kicks it off the ribbon and a shaded 'no data' cone opens and swallows the rest of the rollout. Then abstract away: a T-by-T grid where the cell (t, t') lights up if a mistake at t causes an error at t' >= t, filling a triangle whose area is ~T^2/2, with the epsilon prefactor shown as the density of lit rows.

animation_candidates.what: DAgger's aggregation loop closing the distribution gap
animation_candidates.why: DAgger is easy to state and easy to misunderstand as 'just get more data'. The key is WHICH states get labeled: the learner's own visited states, not the expert's. An animation can show the training distribution physically migrating toward the test distribution over iterations, which is precisely what the theorem is about, and can simultaneously make the labeling cost visible (the point the lecturer says kills it in practice).
animation_candidates.visual_form: A 2D state space with two overlaid density clouds: expert occupancy (blue) and current-learner occupancy (orange). Iteration 1: clouds barely overlap, dataset D is a small blue blob. Each iteration, orange rollout points appear, an 'expert' icon stamps a label on each one, they turn blue and drop into D (which visibly grows as a stack), the policy is refit, and the orange cloud slides toward blue. A counter tracks |D| and total expert queries so the cost blows up on screen at the same time the error goes down.

animation_candidates.what: Term-level morph from V^pi = E[sum gamma^t R(s_t)] to V^pi = w^T mu(pi)
animation_candidates.why: This three-line derivation is the hinge of the second half - it is what converts an unidentifiable reward-learning problem into a tractable geometry problem in occupancy space. It is a perfect formula-morph: substitute, then commute a constant vector out through an expectation and an infinite sum. Seeing w physically slide out of the sum makes the resulting definition of mu feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Single equation centered on screen. Step 1: R(s_t) highlights and expands into w^T x(s_t). Step 2: the w^T factor detaches from inside the sum, glides left past the summation sign and past the expectation operator (each of which briefly glows to justify the move by linearity), and docks outside. Step 3: the remaining E[sum gamma^t x(s_t)] collapses into a single boxed symbol mu(pi), with a side panel showing mu as a k-slot bar chart of accumulated feature mass.

animation_candidates.what: Feature-expectation space, the max-margin step, and the apprenticeship iteration
animation_candidates.why: The Abbeel-Ng algorithm is described in the lecture as a verbal loop and is genuinely hard to hold in your head from prose. But it is entirely geometric: every policy is a point, the expert is a point, w is a direction, and the algorithm is repeated separation-then-best-response. Animating it also exposes the termination criterion (the margin shrinking) that the lecture waves at without proving.
animation_candidates.visual_form: A 2D projection of mu-space. The expert's mu* is a starred point; previously found policies are grey dots. Each iteration: a hyperplane with normal w swings until it maximally separates mu* from the grey dots (SVM-style, with the margin drawn as a corridor); the reward direction w is drawn as an arrow; then 'solve the MDP under w' spawns a new dot at the best-response mu, which lands closer to mu*. Repeat; the margin corridor visibly narrows toward zero. A side inset shows the induced reward as a heatmap over a gridworld changing with w.

animation_candidates.what: IRL degeneracy: one behavior, many rewards
animation_candidates.why: The R = 0 answer lands as a joke in lecture, but the real content is that the consistent-reward set is a whole cone, not two points. Animation can show many distinct reward landscapes all producing the identical optimal trajectory, which is far more convincing than the single degenerate example the lecture gives, and it sets up why MaxEnt/Bayesian tie-breaking is needed.
animation_candidates.visual_form: A small gridworld with one fixed demonstrated trajectory drawn in white, held constant throughout. Beneath it, a reward heatmap that continuously morphs through a family of consistent rewards - a sharp goal-at-the-corner reward, a smooth potential-shaped version, a constant-offset version, and finally fading to flat zero - while a 'policy optimal? YES' badge stays lit the entire time. Then zoom out to a polytope diagram: the cone of consistent w vectors, with the demonstrated constraints as its faces and R = 0 sitting at the apex.

animation_candidates.what: Double DQN: frozen target versus alternating weight sets
animation_candidates.why: The lecturer spends several minutes and three student questions on exactly this, because the difference from vanilla DQN is subtle and purely about update timing. An animation that runs the two schedules side by side on a timeline makes the 'you are throwing away 50 episodes of information' complaint immediate.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two parallel timelines of 100 steps. Top (DQN): a single w node updating continuously while a w- node sits greyed out, then snaps to copy w at step 50 and 100 - and a 'stale information' meter fills between snaps. Bottom (Double DQN): two nodes that alternate roles each step, with a small badge flipping between SELECT and EVALUATE, and information pulses propagating into both. Overlay: a running estimate of max_a Q showing the single-estimator curve biased above the true value and the decoupled curve tracking it.

animation_candidates.what: GAIL as occupancy matching through a discriminator
animation_candidates.why: The lecture motivates GAIL by saying mu is unwritable in high dimensions - so the surrogate is a learned function. That substitution (replace an explicit distributional distance with a trained classifier's confusion) is exactly the kind of idea that is one picture and many paragraphs.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Left: two trajectory bundles (expert, agent) feeding into a discriminator box that outputs a confidence dial. Early on the dial pegs at 'agent - easy'; the resulting reward signal pushes the agent bundle to deform toward the expert bundle; the dial drifts to 0.5 and the two bundles become visually indistinguishable. An inset shows the corresponding occupancy densities converging, making explicit that the discriminator's failure IS the matching certificate.

code_experiment_candidates: Measure the quadratic blowup directly: build a gridworld or a simple continuous 'racetrack' with a known optimal expert, train behavior cloning to a controlled per-step error rate epsilon (e.g. by label-noising or by limiting model capacity), then evaluate total mistakes as a function of horizon T for T in {10, 20, 50, 100, 200}. Fit log(errors) against log(T) and check the slope is near 2 for behavior cloning and near 1 for the same classifier evaluated i.i.d. on expert-distributed states. This turns the lecture's central theorem into a measured exponent.

Implement DAgger on the same environment and overlay its error-versus-T curve on the behavior-cloning curve, confirming the slope drops from ~2 to ~1. Additionally sweep the mixing schedule beta_i (constant beta = 1, constant beta = 0.5, decaying beta_i = 0.9^i) to show empirically why beta must decay - the constant-beta = 1 variant should degenerate to behavior cloning. Also plot expert-query count against performance to reproduce the labeling-cost objection the lecturer raises.

Visualize distribution shift as a KL or Wasserstein distance: at each DAgger iteration, estimate the discounted state occupancy of the learner and of the expert on a discretized state space and plot the divergence shrinking, alongside the task return. This makes the 'training distribution converges to the test distribution' claim measurable rather than asserted.

Enumerate the IRL solution polytope on a tiny MDP (3-5 states, 2 actions, known dynamics): given a target optimal policy, solve the Ng-Russell linear feasibility system (P_{a1} - P_a)(I - gamma P_{a1})^{-1} R >= 0 for all a, and either enumerate vertices or sample the cone. Show that R = 0 is a vertex, that many qualitatively different rewards are feasible, and that adding the max-margin plus L1-sparsity objective picks out a sensible one. This makes non-identifiability concrete instead of anecdotal.

Refute the 'matching mu implies identical policies' claim with a constructed counterexample: design a small MDP and a low-dimensional feature map x(s) where two demonstrably different stationary policies have identical mu vectors, and verify numerically. Then show that if x is the one-hot state encoding AND you match state-ACTION occupancy, the policy is recovered uniquely via pi(a|s) = d(s,a) / sum_a' d(s,a'). This is the single highest-value corrective experiment for this lecture.

Implement the full Abbeel-Ng apprenticeship loop on a gridworld with known dynamics: estimate mu_E from sampled expert rollouts, run the max-margin QP (or the simpler projection variant) to get w, value-iterate under w^T x(s), compute the new mu by exact discounted occupancy solve, and iterate. Plot the margin t_i versus iteration and check it decays as the theory predicts; also plot the recovered reward heatmap against the true one to show that value is matched even when the reward is not recovered.

Implement MaxEnt IRL (Ziebart) on the same gridworld: the exponential-family trajectory model, the convex log-likelihood in w, the forward-backward computation of expected state visitation frequencies, and gradient ascent on empirical-minus-expected feature counts. Compare its recovered reward with the max-margin one and confirm it is better behaved under a suboptimal/noisy expert, which is exactly the regime the lecture says max-margin handles poorly.

Reproduce the maximization-bias experiment: a toy MDP where all actions have identical true value, comparing single-estimator Q-learning against double Q-learning as the number of actions grows, plotting the overestimation of max_a Q. Then port the same comparison to a small DQN on CartPole to show the effect persists with function approximation.

Ablate the dueling gauge: train a dueling head with (a) Q = V + A - max A, (b) Q = V + A - mean A, and (c) no gauge fixing at all, on a small control task. Track training stability and, critically, check whether the learned V branch actually equals the true state value in each case - it should under (a) and should not under (b), which is the point the lecture leaves as a heuristic.

Train GAIL on CartPole or a small MuJoCo task with a two-layer MLP discriminator and a PPO generator, seeded with a handful of expert trajectories, and compare against behavior cloning at matched demonstration counts. Plot return against number of expert trajectories: behavior cloning should degrade sharply in the low-data regime where GAIL's environment access rescues it.

Ablate replay prioritization: implement uniform replay, proportional prioritization with alpha in {0, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0}, and prioritization WITH versus WITHOUT the importance-sampling correction weights that the lecture omits. Show that the uncorrected version is biased on a task where the bias matters, closing the gap the lecture leaves open.
dated_or_superseded: The lecture's claim that none of the DQN extensions solve hard exploration, and that Montezuma's Revenge remains open (with a passing 'we can basically solve Montezuma's now'), was overtaken within a year: Go-Explore (Ecoffet et al., 2019; Nature 2021) and Agent57 (Badia et al., 2020) exceeded human performance on Montezuma's Revenge and, in Agent57's case, on all 57 Atari games. Notes should present the lecture's pessimism as a 2019 snapshot.

Rainbow (2018) as the state of the art in value-based deep RL is superseded. Distributional methods matured (C51 -> QR-DQN -> IQN), and sample efficiency improved by orders of magnitude via model-based planning (MuZero, EfficientZero, DreamerV3) and via data-efficient off-policy methods (Rainbow-DQN at 100k frames, SPR, BBF). The lecture's '200 million frames is a lot of data' framing is still true but the frontier moved from ~200M to ~100k frames on Atari.

The lecturer's judgement that DAgger 'has been less influential' because it needs a human in the loop has been reversed in the LLM era, where the expert is another MODEL rather than a person. On-policy distillation, rejection-sampling SFT, RLAIF, and iterative self-correction pipelines are all DAgger-shaped: sample from the student, have a stronger teacher label or correct the student's own visited states, aggregate, retrain. The query cost objection dissolves when the expert is a callable API. This is the single most important modernization for these notes.

Max-margin apprenticeship learning (Abbeel and Ng, 2004) is essentially historical, as the lecturer half-concedes ('not something most people use anymore'). The live line runs MaxEnt IRL -> Guided Cost Learning -> GAIL -> AIRL -> f-divergence and distribution-matching imitation (ValueDICE, IQ-Learn, primal Wasserstein imitation), and more recently to expressive policy classes (diffusion policies, action-chunking transformers) where plain behavior cloning is again competitive.

The pessimistic reading of behavior cloning needs a caveat as of 2026. The O(epsilon * T^2) bound is worst-case; with very large demonstration corpora, high-capacity policies, and action chunking, behavior cloning is the workhorse of modern robot learning (RT-1/RT-2, Octo, OpenVLA, pi-0) and of LLM instruction tuning. The correct modern statement is that compounding error is a real failure mode that data scale, expressive multimodal policies, and on-policy correction mitigate - not that behavior cloning is fundamentally broken.

Inverse RL's centre of gravity moved from trajectory demonstrations to preference data. Deep RL from Human Preferences (Christiano et al., 2017) and the RLHF stack made reward modeling the dominant practical form of 'learn the reward from human behavior', and DPO and its successors then showed the reward model can be bypassed entirely for the alignment use case. The lecture's MaxEnt formulation is in fact the theoretical ancestor of both (the Boltzmann-rational likelihood is the Bradley-Terry model in disguise), which is worth making explicit.

The Bayesian-IRL aside ('put a prior so R = 0 is excluded') is now a well-developed area under reward learning and assistance games / CIRL (Hadfield-Menell et al., 2016), including formal treatments of reward identifiability up to potential shaping and of the risks of reward misspecification. The lecture's throwaway treatment understates a now-substantial literature.

The tabular sample-complexity claim ('we now have basically tight upper and lower bounds') was accurate in 2019 for the leading order but the minimax picture was completed shortly after (Azar et al. 2017 for regret, Zhang et al. 2020 for horizon-free bounds, and the model-based/model-free equivalence results), so the notes can now state the bounds rather than gesture at them.

GAIL's practical dominance has eroded: adversarial imitation is notoriously unstable, and non-adversarial distribution-matching objectives (IQ-Learn, ValueDICE) and simple filtered behavior cloning often match or beat it. GAIL should be taught as the conceptual bridge from feature matching to occupancy matching rather than as a recommended method.

relevance_to_user_research.why: Two results here bear directly on node-level fidelity assignment, and the rest does not. First, the compounding-error result is the cleanest available theoretical statement of the user's core risk: if a weak model executes a node with per-node error rate epsilon, and each error shifts the partial execution trace off the distribution the downstream operators were tuned or prompted for, then failures do not accumulate as epsilon * depth but closer to epsilon * depth^2, because a corrupted intermediate output puts every subsequent operator into an input distribution it has no competence over. That is exactly the argument for why fidelity assignment must be per-node and depth-aware rather than a flat global budget split, and it gives the paper a citable, non-hand-wavy reason that early/upstream nodes in the DAG deserve strong-model execution disproportionately. It also predicts a testable phenomenon on their Qwen2.5-72B/7B setup: the accuracy gap between all-strong and mixed-fidelity workflows should widen superlinearly with DAG depth, which is a cheap experiment and a good figure. Second, DAgger is a structural template for their allocation policy read as 'call the expensive model at states the cheap model reaches', with the modern twist that the expert is Qwen2.5-72B rather than a human, so the labeling-cost objection the lecture treats as fatal becomes merely a budget term - which is precisely the lambda * token-cost term in their objective. A DAgger-flavored training loop (roll out the weak-model workflow, have the strong model relabel the nodes where the trace degraded, train the router on those labels) is a plausible and defensible method section. What does NOT transfer: the entire IRL half. The user's reward is directly observable (terminal task accuracy minus lambda times token cost), so reward identifiability, feature-expectation matching, max-margin apprenticeship, MaxEnt and GAIL solve a problem they do not have. The Double DQN / dueling / prioritized-replay recap is standard background with no specific bearing. And a caveat on the theory itself: the epsilon * T^2 bound is worst-case and assumes an unrecoverable state, whereas many agentic workflows have self-correcting operators (verifiers, revision loops, ensembling) that make errors partially recoverable, so the user should cite the bound as motivation for depth-awareness rather than as a quantitative prediction. Rating is 'useful' rather than 'critical' because the transferable content is one theorem and one algorithmic analogy, not a framework; the lectures on policy gradients, off-policy evaluation, and especially budget-constrained exploration will matter more to their formulation.

one_paragraph_summary: This lecture pivots the course from value-function approximation to directly parameterizing the policy itself, pi_theta(a|s), and optimizing theta against a scalar objective. Brunskill first argues why one would want this at all: a policy parameterization can be the more natural place to inject domain knowledge, it scales to continuous/high-dimensional action spaces, and crucially it can represent stochastic policies, which are strictly necessary outside the tabular-MDP setting (adversarial games such as rock-paper-scissors, and partially observable domains with state aliasing, illustrated by an aliased gridworld where every deterministic policy over the observed features gets stuck). She then surveys the optimization side: gradient-free search (CMA-ES, demonstrated by Steve Collins' human-in-the-loop exoskeleton optimization that cut metabolic cost about 24 percent in roughly an hour) and finite-difference policy gradients (Kohl and Stone's AIBO gait optimization over 12 continuous gait parameters, learned on real robots in a few hours), before committing to analytic gradients. The mathematical core is the likelihood-ratio derivation: writing V(theta) as a sum over trajectories of P(tau;theta)R(tau), applying the multiply-and-divide trick to convert grad P into P times grad log P, and then decomposing log P(tau;theta) into log mu(s0) plus a sum of log transition terms plus a sum of log policy terms - at which point the first two families vanish under differentiation in theta, giving a completely model-free gradient estimator whose only ingredient is the score function grad_theta log pi_theta(a|s). She states (without proof, deferring to Sutton and Barto Chapter 13) the policy gradient theorem that generalizes this to average-reward and average-value objectives with a Q-weighting, then derives the first variance-reduction technique - exploiting temporal structure/causality by rearranging a double sum so that each score term is multiplied only by the reward-to-go G_t rather than the whole-trajectory return - which yields the REINFORCE algorithm. The lecture closes with three policy classes whose score functions are analytic: softmax-linear for discrete actions, fixed-variance Gaussian for continuous actions, and neural networks. Baselines, the second variance-reduction technique, are explicitly deferred to the next lecture.
prerequisites: MDP formalism: states, actions, transition model, reward, horizon, policy, and the value functions V^pi and Q^pi
The result from Lecture 1 that a finite/tabular MDP always admits a deterministic optimal policy
Monte Carlo policy evaluation, the return G_t, and the bias-variance tradeoff between MC and TD/bootstrapping (Lectures 3-4)
Value function approximation with parameters w, and stochastic gradient ascent/descent on a parameterized objective (Lectures 5-6)
Basic calculus: chain rule and specifically the log-derivative identity d/dx log f = f'/f
Probability: expectation, marginalization, Markov chains and their stationary distributions, unbiasedness of Monte Carlo estimators
Softmax and Gaussian density functions and the ability to differentiate their logs
Intuitive familiarity with partial observability / POMDPs and belief states
Helpful but not required: importance sampling and per-decision importance sampling, which the causality argument closely parallels

concepts.name: Course admin
concepts.one_line: Homework 2 in progress, project proposals via office hours/Piazza, an anonymous mid-quarter class feedback survey posted on Piazza, and Homework 3 (hands-on policy gradients) to be released after the midterm.

concepts.name: From parameterized value functions to parameterized policies
concepts.one_line: Writing Q(s,a;w) already commits you to a structural prior (linear = strong, deep net = weak); the same move can be made one level up by writing pi_theta(a|s) directly, and the chosen parameterization defines exactly the class of policies that can ever be learned.

concepts.name: Taxonomy: value-based, policy-based, actor-critic
concepts.one_line: Value-based methods learn V or Q and extract a policy; policy-based methods search directly in policy space; actor-critic methods explicitly maintain both a parameterized policy (actor) and a parameterized value function (critic).

concepts.name: Advantages and disadvantages of policy-based RL
concepts.one_line: Pros: sometimes a policy class is easier to specify than a value class, works well in high-dimensional or continuous action spaces, can represent stochastic policies, and (arguably) has better convergence behavior; cons: typically only local optima, and gradient estimation from rollouts is often sample-inefficient and high-variance.

concepts.name: Deterministic optimality in tabular MDPs
concepts.one_line: In a tabular MDP there always exists a deterministic policy that attains the optimal value, so stochasticity buys nothing there - which is why the motivating examples for stochastic policies must leave the tabular-MDP setting.

concepts.name: Rock-paper-scissors: stochasticity against an adversary
concepts.one_line: In a two-player zero-sum game the environment is not indifferent to your policy and can adapt, so any deterministic policy is exploitable, while the uniform random policy is unexploitable and hence optimal.

concepts.name: Aliased gridworld: stochasticity under partial observability
concepts.one_line: When the agent observes only wall-presence features (N/E/S/W), two distinct gray cells are indistinguishable, so any deterministic policy over observations must take the same action in both and can oscillate forever, whereas going east/west with probability 1/2 in the aliased cells reaches the goal quickly and has a strictly better value.

concepts.name: Is a stochastic policy always better under partial observability?
concepts.one_line: No - a student asks and Brunskill answers that a POMDP policy tracking a belief state over the true underlying state can disambiguate and act deterministically, doing better than blind randomization; randomizing is a cheap surrogate for belief tracking, not an optimum.

concepts.name: Policy search objectives
concepts.one_line: Three objectives are named: the episodic value V(theta) = E[sum of rewards from the start-state distribution], the average value J_avV = sum_s d^{pi_theta}(s) V^{pi_theta}(s) under the stationary distribution of the induced Markov chain, and the average reward per time step J_avR; the lecture works almost exclusively in the episodic case.

concepts.name: Gradient-free policy optimization
concepts.one_line: Because V(theta) is just a scalar function of theta, black-box optimizers (hill climbing, genetic algorithms, CMA-ES) can search for the maximum without differentiability, and they parallelize well, but they ignore all MDP/temporal structure and are sample-inefficient.

concepts.name: Exoskeleton human-in-the-loop optimization (Collins lab)
concepts.one_line: Each candidate control law is applied to a walking human while respiratory data is collected; a first-order dynamical model is fit to about two minutes of transient data to estimate steady-state metabolic cost, and CMA-ES proposes the next generation, cutting energy cost by about 24 percent versus no assistance after roughly an hour.

concepts.name: Gradient-based policy search
concepts.one_line: Ascend the objective as theta <- theta + alpha * grad_theta V(theta), structurally identical to value-function SGD except the derivative is taken with respect to policy parameters rather than critic parameters, and only a local maximum is guaranteed.

concepts.name: Finite-difference policy gradient
concepts.one_line: Perturb each of the k coordinates of theta by a small epsilon, re-evaluate the policy by rollouts, and form a coordinate-wise difference quotient; noisy and costing k evaluations per gradient, but it requires no differentiability of the policy at all.

concepts.name: AIBO gait optimization (Kohl and Stone, Robocup)
concepts.one_line: A quadruped walking gait is encoded as an elliptical locus with 12 continuous parameters injecting heavy domain knowledge, and finite-difference policy gradient run on 3 real robots (about 15 policies per iteration, 3 evaluations each, roughly 7.5 minutes per iteration) beat all hand-tuned gaits within a few hours and only tens-to-hundreds of policy evaluations.

concepts.name: What actually drives finite-difference policy search performance
concepts.one_line: Initial parameters matter because only local optima are reachable (hence random restarts or domain knowledge), the perturbation size matters, and most critical of all is the policy parameterization, since a bad policy class makes learning impossible regardless of the optimizer.

concepts.name: Open-loop policy
concepts.one_line: A policy need not be a state-to-action mapping; an open-loop policy is a fixed sequence of actions (a plan) executed regardless of what is observed, which is essentially what a fixed gait is.

concepts.name: Trajectories and the trajectory-level objective
concepts.one_line: With tau = (s_0,a_0,r_0,...,s_{T-1},a_{T-1},r_{T-1};s_T) and R(tau) the sum of rewards along it, V(theta) = E_{tau~pi_theta}[R(tau)] = sum over tau of P(tau;theta) R(tau), so theta enters only through the distribution over trajectories.

concepts.name: Likelihood-ratio (log-derivative) trick
concepts.one_line: Multiply and divide by P(tau;theta) inside the gradient: grad_theta V = sum_tau R(tau) grad_theta P = sum_tau P(tau;theta) R(tau) [grad_theta P / P] = E_tau[R(tau) grad_theta log P(tau;theta)], converting a gradient of a distribution into an expectation that can be sampled.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo estimator of the policy gradient
concepts.one_line: Roll out pi_theta m times and estimate grad_theta V ~= (1/m) sum_{i=1}^m R(tau_i) grad_theta log P(tau_i;theta), the uniform weighting arising because the sampled trajectories are already drawn from P(.;theta).

concepts.name: Geometric intuition for the score-weighted update
concepts.one_line: Treating R as a scoring function over sample space, the update raises the log-probability of each sampled trajectory in proportion to how good it was, so probability mass migrates toward high-reward regions of trajectory space.

concepts.name: Decomposition of the trajectory log-likelihood
concepts.one_line: P(tau;theta) = mu(s_0) * prod_{t=0}^{T-1} P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) pi_theta(a_t|s_t), and taking the log turns the product into a sum of an initial-state term, transition terms, and policy terms.

concepts.name: Dynamics and initial-state terms vanish (model-free gradient)
concepts.one_line: Only the policy factors depend on theta, so grad_theta log P(tau;theta) = sum_{t=0}^{T-1} grad_theta log pi_theta(a_t|s_t): the policy gradient can be computed with no knowledge of the transition model or the start-state distribution.

concepts.name: Why policy-dependent trajectories do not reintroduce the dynamics
concepts.one_line: A student objects that the dynamics depend on the policy; the answer is that the policy influences which trajectories occur only through the action-selection factor, since conditional on (s,a) the environment's transition is policy-independent - this decoupling is what makes the cancellation legitimate.

concepts.name: How P(tau|theta) is actually evaluated
concepts.one_line: A student proposes estimating the trajectory probability by empirical counts i/m; the answer is no - each sampled trajectory's log-probability is computed analytically (reducing to a sum of log pi terms) and then averaged, since in a stochastic domain no two sampled trajectories will generally coincide.

concepts.name: Score function
concepts.one_line: The score function is grad_theta log pi_theta(a|s); it is the only quantity the estimator needs, and choosing a policy class with an analytic score is what makes the whole method practical.

concepts.name: Assembled vanilla policy gradient estimator
concepts.one_line: grad_theta V(theta) ~= (1/m) sum_i R(tau_i) sum_{t=0}^{T-1} grad_theta log pi_theta(a_t^i | s_t^i), evaluated at every state-action pair observed, with no dynamics model required.

concepts.name: Policy gradient theorem
concepts.one_line: For any of the three objectives (episodic value, average reward per step, average value), grad_theta J(theta) = E_{pi_theta}[ grad_theta log pi_theta(s,a) * Q^{pi_theta}(s,a) ], generalizing the trajectory derivation from the raw return to a Q-weighting; stated without proof and referred to Sutton and Barto Chapter 13.

concepts.name: Unbiased but noisy
concepts.one_line: The Monte Carlo policy gradient is an unbiased estimate of the true gradient but has high variance, exactly analogous to Monte Carlo value estimation, which motivates the variance-reduction agenda.

concepts.name: Variance reduction menu
concepts.one_line: Two remedies are named - exploiting temporal structure and using baselines - and a student's suggestion of bootstrapping (replacing the return with a TD-style target, trading bias for variance) is endorsed as the route to actor-critic.

concepts.name: Temporal structure / causality
concepts.one_line: For a single reward r_{t'}, grad_theta E[r_{t'}] = E[r_{t'} * sum_{t=0}^{t'} grad_theta log pi_theta(a_t|s_t)] - the score terms after t' drop out, because r_{t'} is determined by the truncated trajectory up to t'.

concepts.name: Reordering the double sum into reward-to-go form
