Full regret derivation for UCB on the board: (i) write regret as sum of Q(a*) - Q(a_t); (ii) add and subtract U_t(a_t); (iii) argue the resulting sum of Q(a*) - U_t(a_t) is at most zero by the key lemma and discard it; (iv) replace U_t(a_t) - Q(a_t) by the Hoeffding width; (v) upper bound log(t^2/delta) by log(T^2/delta) and factor it out; (vi) regroup the time sum into a per-arm sum over pull indices; (vii) apply sum of 1/sqrt(n) <= 2*sqrt(N); (viii) substitute the worst-case uniform allocation N_i = T/m; (ix) collect terms to obtain the O(sqrt(m T log(T^2/delta))) bound.

Constructive counterexample showing greedy can commit permanently to a suboptimal arm: with overlapping reward distributions there is nonzero probability the single initialization sample from the better arm is lower than that from the worse arm, after which the argmax never changes.

Worked greedy and epsilon-greedy traces on the three-armed broken-toe bandit, computing the per-step regret sequence (0, 0.05, 0.85, ...) and the selection probabilities after the initialization samples 1, 1, 0.

Argument that greedy never re-selects the zero-estimate Bernoulli arm: rewards are bounded below by 0 so that arm's estimate cannot decrease, while the other arms retain strictly positive empirical means, so it is never again the argmax.
proofs_skipped: Hoeffding's inequality is stated as a 'refresher' and used as a black box. No Chernoff/moment-generating-function derivation, no discussion of why bounded support is required, and no statement of the sub-Gaussian generalization that the bandit literature actually relies on. The academic notes should supply the MGF proof and note that boundedness in [0,1] is an assumption the lecture says will recur in 'most of the proofs that we do'.

The Lai-Robbins-style asymptotic lower bound (regret/log t >= sum over suboptimal arms of gap / KL(R_a || R_{a*})) is quoted from prior work with no proof and no citation on the board. Worse, the lecturer is uncertain on camera about its exact form, telling a student she would have to check the original paper for whether it holds per time step or only asymptotically, and speculating there are 'transitory constant terms'. Both the precise statement and its change-of-measure proof are open work for the notes.

Sum over t = 1 to infinity of t^-2 = pi^2/6 is offered as a 'fun fact' with no proof (the Basel problem). Only the weaker consequence (< 2) is used, and that weaker bound has an elementary telescoping proof worth including.
Sum over n = 1 to N of n^(-1/2) <= 2*sqrt(N) is asserted with 'you use an integral argument, I'm happy to talk about it offline'. The comparison-with-integral proof is never shown.

The claim that sum over arms of sum over n=1..N_i of n^(-1/2), subject to sum of N_i = T, is maximized at the uniform allocation is justified only by the remark that 1/sqrt(n) is decreasing. Decreasingness alone does not establish it; the real argument is concavity of N -> 2*sqrt(N) plus Jensen, and this gap should be closed explicitly.

The step bounding U_t(a_t) - Q(a_t) by the confidence width drops a factor of 2. On the good event this quantity is Qhat_t(a_t) + u_t - Q(a_t), which is bounded by 2*u_t, not u_t. The lecturer only patches a constant when a student objects and then explicitly says 'I'll be a little loose with constants', so the constant bookkeeping through the whole derivation is unverified.

Linear regret for greedy is demonstrated only by a single unlucky-sample anecdote. There is no proof that the probability of locking onto a suboptimal arm is bounded away from zero as a function of the gap and the reward distributions, and no formal worst-case construction.

Linear regret for fixed-epsilon epsilon-greedy is argued informally from 'a bad arm gets pulled infinitely often'. The explicit bound Regret(T) >= (epsilon/m) * (sum over a of gap(a)) * T is never written, and the matching upper bound is never given either.

Linear regret for uniform random exploration ('explore forever') is asserted from a reproduced figure attributed to David Silver's slides, with no derivation of the constant (which is just the mean gap).

The strongly implied but never stated positive result that epsilon-greedy with a decaying schedule achieves logarithmic regret. The lecturer repeatedly qualifies with 'if epsilon is fixed', inviting the contrast, and never delivers the Auer-Cesa-Bianchi-Fischer epsilon_t proportional to m/(d^2 t) result or its analysis. This is a conspicuous hole for the notes.

Why the upper confidence bounds of every arm, not just the pulled one, must be refreshed each step. The lecture answers 'in terms of the theory we often have to do that in order to account for high probability bounds' and half-shows the reason (the log t^2 numerator is shared across arms and the union bound ranges over arm-time pairs). A clean statement of what breaks if you only update the pulled arm is missing.

The gap-dependent (problem-dependent) UCB bound of order sum over suboptimal arms of log(T)/gap(a) is explicitly acknowledged to exist and be 'much nicer and tighter', and is then never derived. This is arguably the more informative bound and belongs in the notes alongside the problem-independent one proved here.

The expected-regret version of the UCB analysis from the original UCB paper is mentioned and deliberately skipped in favour of the high-probability version, on the grounds that the latter was easier to present in class. The relationship between the two (and how to integrate the high-probability bound into an expectation) is not shown.

Whether the derived O(sqrt(m T log T)) upper bound is tight is never addressed. The minimax lower bound of order sqrt(m T) is not stated, so a student cannot tell whether the log factor is intrinsic or an artifact of the proof technique. The notes must supply the minimax lower bound and identify the log gap.

The identity 'total regret = sum over arms of E[N_t(a)] * gap(a)' is asserted as 'another way to think about it which is equivalent' with no derivation. The regrouping by arm and the interaction between the expectation and the random counts N_t(a) deserve at least a line.

The choice of delta/t^2 as the per-step failure budget is deferred at the moment it is made ('we'll see why we might want to choose that particular probability shortly') and then only retroactively justified by summability. Alternatives are never compared: delta/(m t^2) to absorb the arm union, a union bound over pull counts n rather than time steps, or time-uniform / law-of-the-iterated-logarithm bounds that avoid the union bound entirely.

The Bernoulli-greedy claim that arms one and two can never see their empirical means reach exactly zero, hence the third arm at zero is never re-selected, is stated as intuition. It depends on bounded support and a strictly positive first sample, and the contrasting Gaussian case (where estimates can cross later) is mentioned but not analysed.

The deterministic-reward aside — that greedy then suffers only constant initial regret and zero regret thereafter — is asserted in reply to a student and not proved, nor is it reconciled with the general lower bound (which assumes nondegenerate distributions).

Exploiting variance or higher-moment knowledge for tighter bounds (Bernstein-style bounds, UCB-V) is raised by a student, acknowledged as possible, and explicitly excluded from coverage. No statement of what the improvement looks like.

The entire Bayesian half of the agenda: Bayesian regret, probability matching, and Thompson sampling are named at the start and again in the closing minute, but receive no definition, no algorithm box, no guarantee and no proof. The promised numerical UCB walkthrough of the broken-toe example is also deferred.

Contextual bandits are raised twice (a student asks about patient heterogeneity; the lecturer says the default project involves it) and deferred by 'we'll probably get to this in a couple lectures'. No formulation, no LinUCB, no regret statement.
Risk-sensitive and safe bandits are mentioned as active work in the lecturer's own group, with the heavy-tail-of-bad-outcomes motivation sketched, but no criterion, algorithm or guarantee is given.

The claim that 'regret is going to be unbounded unfortunately in these cases' for any algorithm is asserted as a general fact. It is really a corollary of the quoted logarithmic lower bound and should be derived as such rather than left as an aside.
algorithms: Greedy bandit: pull each of the m arms once in round-robin, maintain Qhat_t(a) as the sample mean of the rewards observed for arm a, and thereafter always select argmax_a Qhat_t(a), breaking ties uniformly at random. Worst-case regret linear in T.

Epsilon-greedy bandit: same estimates and same round-robin initialization, but at each step select the greedy arm with probability 1 - epsilon and otherwise select uniformly among all m arms, so the greedy arm is actually chosen with probability 1 - epsilon + epsilon/m. With epsilon held fixed, regret is linear in T.

Uniform random exploration ('explore forever'): select an arm uniformly at random at every step, ignoring all data. Regret is linear in T with constant equal to the average gap. Mentioned as the degenerate baseline.

Hoeffding-UCB (the lecture's UCB1-style algorithm): (1) pull each arm once; (2) at each step t, for every arm a compute U_t(a) = Qhat_t(a) + sqrt( log(t^2/delta) / (2 * N_t(a)) ); (3) select a_t = argmax_a U_t(a); (4) observe r_t sampled from the true reward distribution of a_t; (5) update Qhat and N for the selected arm and recompute U_t(a) for ALL arms (the log t^2 numerator changes every step); (6) repeat. Achieves regret O(sqrt(m T log(T^2/delta))) with probability at least 1 - 2*m*delta.

Generic optimism-under-uncertainty template: maintain, for each action, any statistic that upper bounds the true value with high probability and whose width decreases in the number of times that action has been taken, then act greedily with respect to that upper bound. The lecture presents this as the reusable pattern that will later carry over from bandits to MDPs and to function approximation.

Thompson sampling / probability matching (named only, algorithm deferred to the next lecture): maintain a prior over each arm's reward parameter, update it to a posterior with observed rewards, and use the posterior to decide how to act.
notation_introduced: m = number of arms (the bandit analogue of the action set size |A|); arms are used interchangeably with actions
P(r | a), written R^a in the standard literature = the unknown stochastic reward distribution of arm a; rewards assumed bounded in [0,1] throughout the proofs
Q(a) = E[r | a] = the true mean reward (action value) of arm a; unknown to the agent
a* = argmax_a Q(a) = the optimal arm; V* = Q(a*) = the optimal value. The lecturer writes both V* and (garbled in captions as 'B star') for the same quantity
a_t = the arm selected at step t; r_t = the reward sampled from arm a_t's distribution at step t
per-step regret l_t = E[ V* - Q(a_t) ] = one-step opportunity loss
total regret L_t = E[ sum over tau = 1 to t of (V* - Q(a_tau)) ]
N_t(a) = number of times arm a has been pulled up to time t
gap(a), written Delta_a = V* - Q(a); zero for a*, strictly positive otherwise
Qhat_t(a) = empirical mean reward of arm a from its N_t(a) observed samples
U_t(a) = upper confidence bound on Q(a) at time t; U_t(a) = Qhat_t(a) + sqrt( log(t^2/delta) / (2 N_t(a)) )
u (rendered as 'mu'/'nu' by the captions) = the Hoeffding confidence half-width added to an empirical mean; a scalar, not a mean
delta = per-step-per-arm failure-probability parameter; the final regret bound holds with probability at least 1 - 2*m*delta
n = number of samples of one specific arm (the argument to Hoeffding), versus t = total number of steps taken on any arm; the lecture explicitly flags that these are different
T (capital) = the horizon / total number of steps, versus t (lowercase) = the running step index
KL(. || .) = Kullback-Leibler divergence between two arms' reward distributions, appearing only in the quoted lower bound
i = index over arms in the regret decomposition, so N_T(i) is the final pull count of arm i
notation_hazards: The confidence half-width u is transcribed throughout as 'mu' or 'nu'. This is dangerous because mu is the standard symbol for an arm's MEAN in the bandit literature (Lattimore and Szepesvari, Auer et al.), where the lecture uses Q(a) for that role. Read every 'mu' in this transcript as a confidence radius, never as a mean.
'Sum over t = 1 to infinity of t to the minus t' is a caption garble; it must be t^(-2), which is the Basel sum equal to pi^2/6.

The square root in the UCB bonus covers the whole expression. The transcript at one point renders it as 'Qhat + 1 over 2 N_t(a) times log of t squared over delta', which without the radical is dimensionally and numerically wrong. The correct form is Qhat_t(a) + sqrt( log(t^2/delta) / (2 * N_t(a)) ).
'Exponential minus 2 n u squared' means exp(-2 n u^2), with the entire product in the exponent, not exp(-2n) * u^2.
V* is occasionally spoken as 'B star' by the captions; the lecturer herself acknowledges going back and forth between V* and Q(a*) for the same quantity and invites students to ask.

In the union-bound line the failure event is written with the hat on the wrong symbol ('the probability that Qhat of a_t is greater than U'). The failure event is that the TRUE mean Q(a) exceeds the upper confidence bound U_t(a); the empirical mean is by construction below its own bound.

t is overloaded: inside the bonus it is the running step count, but in the final theorem T is the horizon. The proof silently switches by upper-bounding log(t^2/delta) with log(T^2/delta), a step a student has to ask about explicitly.

n versus t is a live confusion the lecturer preempts: n = pulls of the specific arm (drives the shrinking 1/sqrt(n) factor), t = total steps on any arm (drives the growing log factor). Mixing them destroys the whole 'two competing rates' intuition.
'Regret' is used for both the per-step opportunity loss and the cumulative sum without consistent subscripting. The board writes both as 'regret'.

Constants are explicitly not tracked: the lecturer says 'I'll be a little loose with constants, but definitely catch me on them', and a student has to supply a missing factor of 2 mid-proof. Do not treat any numeric constant in the final bound as verified.

The lecture's answer 'this is all for an infinite horizon case' refers to the union bound being taken out to t = infinity so that the confidence bounds hold forever; the regret THEOREM is still stated for a finite T. These are different senses of horizon.

Sutton and Barto is a poor cross-reference here. Chapter 2 of S&B evaluates bandits by percent-optimal-action and average reward, barely mentions regret, and writes its UCB bonus as c*sqrt(ln t / N_t(a)) with a free tuning constant c. This lecture's bonus, sqrt(ln(t^2/delta)/(2 N_t(a))) = sqrt((2 ln t + ln(1/delta))/(2 N_t(a))), is the same shape with the constant pinned by an explicit failure budget. The conventions here follow Silver / Lattimore-Szepesvari, not S&B.

In the epsilon-greedy worked example the transcript's '1 - epsilon over 2' is about splitting the greedy probability between two TIED arms, not about the epsilon-greedy rule itself. The exploration split across all arms is epsilon/m (here epsilon/3).

'Regret is going to be unbounded' means it grows without bound as T grows, not that it is infinite at any finite T. The same sentence is used for both the lower-bound consequence and the linear-regret failure of epsilon-greedy, which are different claims.
dated_or_superseded: The motivating sample-complexity figure — 'two to ten million steps for DQN to play Pong' — is the 2015-2018 state of the art and has been badly beaten. EfficientZero (2021) reaches above-human median Atari performance in 100k environment steps, and BBF (2023) and DreamerV3 (2023) are the current data-efficiency references. The lecture's rhetorical point (that naive deep RL is far too sample-hungry for people-in-the-loop settings) survives intact, but the number should be updated and the model-based / replay-ratio reasons for the improvement noted.

The problem-independent bound proved here is O(sqrt(m T log T)). The log factor is not intrinsic: MOSS (Audibert and Bubeck, 2009) attains the minimax-optimal O(sqrt(m T)), and KL-UCB (Cappe et al., 2013) attains the Lai-Robbins constant exactly in the problem-dependent regime. The lecture leaves the impression that sqrt(m T log T) is what optimism buys you, which understates the modern picture.

Thompson sampling is presented in 2019 as the not-yet-analysed Bayesian alternative to be covered next lecture. By now it has strong frequentist regret guarantees (Agrawal and Goyal 2012; Kaufmann, Korda and Munos 2012, showing asymptotic optimality for Bernoulli arms), so the Bayesian/frequentist split the lecture sets up is much less sharp than presented.

Lattimore and Szepesvari's Bandit Algorithms (2020) postdates the lecture and is now the standard reference; it supersedes the ad hoc constant-tracking here and gives the concentration, lower-bound and information-theoretic machinery in one place.

The lecture's 'best algorithm' framing is purely stochastic-bandit. Best-of-both-worlds algorithms (Tsallis-INF, Zimmert and Seldin 2019 onward) now achieve near-optimal regret simultaneously in the stochastic and adversarial settings, collapsing a distinction the course treats as separate settings.

Optimism as THE exploration principle has partly ceded ground in deep RL to posterior-sampling and ensemble methods (bootstrapped DQN, randomized value functions) and to intrinsic-motivation bonuses such as RND (2018, contemporaneous but unmentioned). Optimism remains the theoretically cleanest story, not the empirically dominant one at scale.

Contextual bandits, deferred here, have since become the standard formulation for exactly the user's problem class: LinUCB-style and neural contextual bandits (NeuralUCB, 2020) and, directly, LLM-routing-as-contextual-bandit work from 2023 onward (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT-style cascades, hybrid routing). Anyone reading this lecture for routing purposes should treat it as the H=1, non-contextual, unconstrained special case and go straight to the contextual literature.

Budget-constrained bandits (Bandits with Knapsacks, Badanidiyuru, Kleinberg and Slivkins) are not mentioned at all, which matters because any real cost-constrained deployment — including token budgets — is a knapsack-bandit problem, not a plain one.

Best-arm identification / pure exploration (simple regret, successive elimination, LUCB) is absent. For offline evaluation on a fixed benchmark set, simple regret rather than cumulative regret is the right criterion, and the lecture's framework does not cover it.

animation_candidates.what: Greedy locking onto the wrong arm: two overlapping reward densities, samples dropping one at a time, running empirical means as moving markers, and the argmax pointer snapping to the worse arm and then freezing while the true means stay fixed and visibly contradict it.
animation_candidates.why: The failure mode is entirely about sampling luck unfolding over time. A static figure of two overlapping Gaussians cannot show that ONE unlucky draw permanently ends learning; the freeze is the point, and only motion conveys 'and it never moves again'.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two-density plot with animated sample drops, running-mean markers, and an argmax pointer that latches and locks

animation_candidates.what: The two competing rates inside the UCB bonus: per-arm error bars shrinking as 1/sqrt(N_t(a)) while the shared log(t^2/delta) numerator lifts every bar slightly on every step, including arms that were not pulled.
animation_candidates.why: This is exactly why the algorithm must refresh ALL arms' bounds each step, which the lecture asserts but only half-explains. Seeing an unpulled arm's bar creep upward while the pulled arm's bar contracts makes the mechanism obvious in a way the formula does not.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Bar chart of m arms with animated confidence whiskers over simulated time, unpulled bars tinted to highlight that they still move

animation_candidates.what: The add-and-subtract regret manipulation as a term-level formula morph: start from sum of [Q(a*) - Q(a_t)], split the U_t(a_t) term in and out, highlight the bracket [Q(a*) - U_t(a_t)], stamp it '<= 0 on the good event' via a callback to the lemma, then grey it out and let it fall away.
animation_candidates.why: This is the single most important algebraic move in the lecture and it is the canonical shot-by-shot case: each frame is one legal rewriting, and the payoff (the unobservable a* disappearing from the expression) is a visual event, not a verbal one.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Term-level formula morph with colour-tagged terms and a dropped-term animation

animation_candidates.what: The two-case lemma on a value number line: plot Q(a*), Q(a_t), U_t(a*), U_t(a_t) as points on a vertical axis, then play case one (a_t = a*) and case two (a_t != a*), sliding U_t(a_t) above U_t(a*) above Q(a*) with the argmax and validity arrows drawn as they are used.
animation_candidates.why: The proof is two short inequalities chained, and students conflate 'UCB of the selected arm' with 'UCB of the optimal arm' (a student in the lecture does exactly this). A number line makes the chain and the distinction unmissable.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Vertical value number line with animated point placement and labelled inequality arrows

animation_candidates.what: A live regret race on the broken-toe bandit: cumulative regret curves for uniform random, greedy, epsilon-greedy and UCB drawn simultaneously as the simulation runs, with the log-t lower bound drawn as a floor.
animation_candidates.why: 'Linear versus sublinear' is a statement about asymptotic shape that only becomes visceral when you watch three curves stay straight while one bends over, against a floor that nobody can go below. Static endpoint plots hide the divergence.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Animated multi-series cumulative-regret plot over a running simulation, with a shaded infeasible region below the lower bound

animation_candidates.what: The integral argument for sum of 1/sqrt(n) <= 2 sqrt(N): unit-width rectangles of height 1/sqrt(n) appearing one at a time, then the curve 1/sqrt(x) sliding underneath and the antiderivative 2 sqrt(x) sweeping out the bounding area.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture literally punts this ('happy to talk about it offline'), and it is a 15-second picture. Animating the rectangles-under-curve comparison closes a stated gap at almost no cost.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Riemann-rectangle overlay on 1/sqrt(x) with a sweeping area fill

animation_candidates.what: The equal-allocation worst case: a bar chart of pull counts N_i with the total pinned at T, morphing from a lopsided allocation to the uniform one while a readout of the objective sum of 2 sqrt(N_i) climbs to its maximum.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture's justification ('1/sqrt(n) is decreasing') is not actually the argument; the real reason is concavity. Watching the objective rise as the bars level out IS the Jensen picture, and it repairs a genuine hole in the proof visually.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Constrained bar-chart morph with a live objective readout and the concave sqrt curve shown alongside

animation_candidates.what: The union bound as a stacking budget: a strip of failure-probability blocks of size delta/t^2 for t = 1, 2, 3, ..., accumulating leftward into a total bar that visibly converges and stops short of the 2*m*delta ceiling.
animation_candidates.why: Students accept union bounds mechanically without feeling why the t^-2 decay is what makes an infinite-horizon guarantee possible. Showing the blocks shrink fast enough that the stack terminates makes the design choice of delta/t^2 look inevitable rather than arbitrary.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Accumulating probability-budget bar with a convergence ceiling line

code_experiment_candidates: Reproduce the lecture's central claim end to end: implement the three-arm Bernoulli broken-toe bandit (0.95 / 0.90 / 0.10) and run uniform random, greedy, fixed-epsilon epsilon-greedy, decaying-epsilon epsilon-greedy, and Hoeffding-UCB with the exact bonus sqrt(log(t^2/delta)/(2 N_t(a))). Plot mean cumulative regret over 1000 seeds with confidence bands and overlay the log-t lower bound. The deliverable is the linear-versus-sublinear separation as a figure the student generated rather than read.

Empirically audit the confidence bounds: with the true means known, log at every step and for every arm whether Q(a) > U_t(a), and compare the observed total failure count against the theoretical 2*m*delta. This directly tests whether the union bound is as conservative as the lecture admits, and how much slack the all-arms requirement costs.

Verify the key lemma numerically: at every step assert U_t(a_t) >= V* and record the margin. Plot the margin over time; it should be positive throughout on non-failure runs and should shrink as the algorithm concentrates. This turns an abstract two-case argument into an observable invariant.

Test the claimed scaling exponents: sweep T over several decades and m over 2, 5, 10, 50, fit log(regret) against log(T) and log(m), and check whether the slopes match the predicted 1/2 in each. Also sweep delta to confirm the sqrt(log(1/delta)) dependence. This is where the 'loose with constants' warning gets checked.

Fill the lecture's biggest hole: implement epsilon-greedy with epsilon_t proportional to 1/t and with the Auer-style m/(d^2 t) schedule, and show empirically that decaying epsilon recovers logarithmic regret while fixed epsilon does not. The lecture repeatedly implies this and never states it.

Gap-dependence experiment: run UCB on the easy instance (means 1.0 and 0.001) and the hard instance (means 0.530 and 0.525) and measure both cumulative regret and time-to-identify-the-best-arm. This makes the problem-dependent versus problem-independent distinction concrete and shows the regret bound proved in lecture is blind to a difference that dominates practice.

Preview the next lecture by implementing Thompson sampling with Beta(1,1) priors on the same Bernoulli bandit and racing it against UCB on identical seeds. Useful both as a bridge and as a check on the lecture's framing that these are two genuinely different approaches with comparable guarantees.

Ablate the 'update all arms' requirement: run a variant of UCB that only refreshes the pulled arm's bound and compare regret and empirical bound-failure rate against the correct version. This answers the question the lecture waves off, and it is a cheap, decisive experiment.

Directly relevant to the user's research: cast query-level model routing as a two-armed bandit (weak Qwen2.5-7B versus strong Qwen2.5-72B) with reward = task accuracy minus lambda times token cost, run UCB against an always-strong oracle, and sweep lambda to watch the gap between the two arms flip sign. The interesting regime is exactly the small-gap regime the lecture flags as hard, which is a testable claim about when routing is learnable at all.

relevance_to_user_research.why: This is the closest CS234 gets to the user's stated H=1 special case: query-level routing between a weak and a strong model IS a stochastic bandit, with arms = fidelities and reward = accuracy minus lambda times token cost. Three things transfer concretely. (1) The gap concept is the right lens on when routing is even learnable: the decision-relevant quantity is the gap between weak-model and strong-model expected reward on a query class, and the lecture's intuition that means of 0.530 versus 0.525 are hard to separate while 1.0 versus 0.001 is easy maps exactly onto the user's hardest regime — the queries where the weak model is nearly as accurate as the strong one but far cheaper are precisely the small-gap, high-sample-cost cases, and lambda is a knob that literally moves the gap and can flip its sign. That is a paper-grade framing the user does not appear to have yet. (2) The lecture's demonstration that fixed-epsilon exploration has LINEAR regret is a direct warning against the default epsilon-greedy or fixed-temperature exploration that routing and workflow-search papers habitually use, and it gives a principled reason to prefer an optimism or posterior-sampling rule. (3) Regret decomposed as sum over arms of E[N(a)] times gap(a) is a clean way to report ablations: how many nodes got the expensive fidelity unnecessarily, weighted by how much that cost. Honest limits, which is why this is 'useful' and not 'critical'. The lecture's setting is non-contextual, online, unconstrained and cumulative-regret-scored, and the user's setting is none of those four. Their routing decision is contextual (query features are the whole point), their evaluation is offline on a fixed benchmark where simple regret / best-arm identification is the right criterion rather than cumulative regret, their token budget is a hard constraint putting them in bandits-with-knapsacks territory, and their action space is a per-node choice across a DAG, so it is combinatorial and sequential rather than m flat arms. Contextual bandits and budget constraints are exactly what this lecture defers or omits. The specific technical payload here — the Hoeffding-UCB proof with its union bound and sqrt-sum manipulations — is not machinery the ACL/NAACL paper will need to reproduce. Read this lecture for vocabulary and for the gap/regret framing of the H=1 case, then go to contextual bandits, BwK, and the 2023-onward LLM-routing literature for anything the paper will actually cite.

lecture_title: Fast Reinforcement Learning II: Bayesian Bandits, Thompson Sampling, PAC, and Optimistic Tabular MDP Exploration
one_paragraph_summary: This lecture completes the bandit story and carries its three organizing axes (setting, evaluation framework, algorithmic style) into tabular MDPs. It opens by recapping optimism-under-uncertainty and stating the gap-dependent logarithmic regret bound for UCB, contrasting it with the gap-free bound proved in L11 and using it to introduce the idea of problem-dependent bounds: the algorithm need not know the gaps, but its regret is governed by them. A three-armed Bernoulli "broken toe" instance is worked numerically to show how the UCB bonus sqrt(2 ln t / N_t(a)) causes the algorithm to alternate between the two plausibly-optimal arms while assigning exactly zero probability to the clearly bad arm, unlike epsilon-greedy which spreads epsilon/|A| mass everywhere. A short argument shows that acting greedily on the highest LOWER confidence bound can incur linear regret through a confirmation-bias lock-in, which is the lecture's justification for optimism specifically. The second half switches from frequentist to Bayesian: maintain a posterior over each arm's reward parameters, use conjugacy (Beta-Bernoulli, with alpha and beta read as pseudo-counts of ones and zeros) to keep updates in closed form, define Bayesian regret as regret averaged over the prior, and note that probability matching -- select an arm with the probability it is optimal -- is intuitively right but has no obvious computation. Thompson sampling is then presented as the surprisingly simple algorithm that implements probability matching exactly: draw one parameter vector from the posterior, act greedily as if that draw were the truth, observe, update. The same broken-toe instance is re-traced under Thompson sampling with Beta(1,1) priors, showing it commits to the best arm far faster than UCB. The lecture then introduces PAC as an alternative framework that bounds the NUMBER of non-small mistakes rather than their cumulative sum, which matters when a few catastrophic errors and many trivial ones are not morally equivalent. Finally it moves to tabular MDPs: optimistic initialization at Rmax/(1-gamma) has no guarantee by itself; Even-Dar and Mansour showed Q-learning becomes PAC only under an absurdly larger initialization that is exponential in the number of updates; Jin et al. recently obtained regret bounds for model-free Q-learning with UCB-style bonuses; and model-based methods -- especially MBIE-EB, which fits MLE dynamics and rewards from counts and adds a beta/sqrt(N(s,a)) reward bonus before planning -- are shown to be PAC with a sample complexity polynomial in |S|, |A|, 1/(1-gamma), 1/epsilon and 1/delta.
prerequisites: Markov decision processes: states, actions, transition and reward models, discount factor gamma, policies
Value functions V and Q, the Bellman optimality equations, and value iteration
Model-free control: Q-learning, SARSA, and Monte Carlo control, including learning-rate schedules
The bound V*(s) <= Rmax/(1-gamma) for discounted MDPs, derived from a geometric series
Stochastic multi-armed bandits, regret, and the UCB algorithm and its analysis from L11
Hoeffding's inequality, union bounds, and the idea of a high-probability confidence interval
Basic probability distributions: Bernoulli, Gaussian, Beta, Dirichlet, and the exponential family
Bayes' rule, priors, likelihoods, posteriors, and maximum likelihood estimation
Asymptotic notation and the distinction between linear, logarithmic, and polynomial growth

concepts.name: Course admin
concepts.one_line: Students on the default project need not submit anything special for the project milestone; no other logistics were discussed.

concepts.name: Stochastic multi-armed bandit recap
concepts.one_line: A bandit is an MDP stripped of state: a fixed action set, each action having an unknown stationary reward distribution, from which one iid sample is drawn each time that action is chosen.

concepts.name: Censored (bandit) feedback
concepts.one_line: The problem is not supervised learning because you observe the reward only for the arm you actually pulled, never the counterfactual outcomes of the arms you passed over.

concepts.name: Regret is about expectations, not realizations
concepts.one_line: Drawn with two overlapping Gaussians: a single draw from the inferior arm can exceed the mean of the superior arm, so regret is defined on expected values and only makes sense averaged over many rounds.

concepts.name: Gap of an action
concepts.one_line: Delta_a = Q(a*) - Q(a), the expected loss per round from playing a instead of the optimal arm.

concepts.name: Optimism under uncertainty as a two-case progress argument
concepts.one_line: Acting greedily on an upper confidence bound yields either zero regret (the optimal arm was chosen) or, with high probability, a downward revision of the chosen arm's bound, so every mistake buys information that shrinks the mistake's cause.

concepts.name: Interval estimation (Kaelbling, 1993)
concepts.one_line: Historical note: interval estimation applied optimism to MDPs and worked well empirically long before anyone proved it was a good idea, an inversion of the usual theory-then-practice order.

concepts.name: Gap-dependent regret bound for UCB
concepts.one_line: With high probability UCB's cumulative regret grows like the sum over suboptimal arms of log T / Delta_a, i.e. logarithmically in the horizon with a constant governed by the instance's gaps.

concepts.name: Problem-dependent vs problem-independent bounds
concepts.one_line: A key distinction is whether unknown quantities like the gaps appear in the ALGORITHM or only in the ANALYSIS; UCB needs no knowledge of the gaps yet automatically performs better on easier instances, which is the property one wants from an adaptive algorithm.

concepts.name: Broken-toe toy bandit
concepts.one_line: Three Bernoulli arms modelling treatments for a broken toe: surgery p=0.95, buddy taping p=0.9, doing nothing p=0.1, used as the running instance for both UCB and Thompson sampling.

concepts.name: UCB bonus and worked instantiation
concepts.one_line: With UCB(a) = empirical mean + sqrt(2 ln t / N_t(a)), after one pull of each arm (t=3, outcomes 1,1,0) the two good arms tie at 1 + sqrt(2 ln 3) and the bad arm sits at sqrt(2 ln 3), so it is never selected.

concepts.name: Denominator-driven arm switching
concepts.one_line: After pulling a1 a second time (t=4, N(a1)=2) its bonus shrinks to sqrt(2 ln 4 / 2) while a2 keeps sqrt(2 ln 4 / 1), so a2 is selected next regardless of whether a1's second draw was a 0 or a 1 -- the switch is caused purely by the count, not by the reward.

concepts.name: Support comparison, UCB vs epsilon-greedy
concepts.one_line: At this point UCB puts nonzero probability on exactly two arms and zero on the visibly bad one, whereas epsilon-greedy with epsilon=0.1 puts 0.1/3 on every non-greedy arm including the bad one -- UCB allocates exploration strategically, epsilon-greedy uniformly.

concepts.name: Regret trace for UCB
concepts.one_line: For the action sequence a1,a2,a3,a1,a2 the per-round regrets are 0, 0.05, 0.85, 0, 0.05, computable only because the simulator knows the true means.

concepts.name: Confidence bounds are high-probability objects
concepts.one_line: A UCB can and sometimes does fall below the true mean, which is exactly why the L11 proof had to condition on the event that all bounds hold and pay a delta for the failure event.

concepts.name: Pessimism (highest lower bound) yields linear regret
concepts.one_line: Selecting the arm with the largest LOWER confidence bound can lock onto a suboptimal arm forever: its interval tightens around its own true mean, which stays above the untried arm's lower bound, so the hypothesis is never disproved and regret grows linearly.

concepts.name: Optimistic initialization as a cheap substitute for UCB
concepts.one_line: Rather than maintaining bounds, pretend each arm was already pulled once with an enormous reward and average that fake pull into the running empirical mean; simple and often effective, but calibrating how optimistic the fake pull must be is the hard part.

concepts.name: Regret-rate summary across bandit strategies
concepts.one_line: Greedy: linear. Fixed-epsilon greedy: linear. Decayed-epsilon greedy: sublinear but only under a schedule that depends on the unknown gaps, so unachievable in practice without an oracle. Sufficiently optimistic initialization: sublinear, but 'sufficiently' is delicate.

concepts.name: Bayesian bandits
concepts.one_line: Instead of assuming only bounded rewards, assume a parametric reward family and maintain an explicit posterior over its parameters given the history of pulls and rewards, then use that posterior to steer exploration.

concepts.name: Posterior update via Bayes' rule
concepts.one_line: For an arm i with unknown reward parameter phi_i, p(phi_i | r) = p(phi_i) p(r | phi_i) / p(r); the whole difficulty is whether the three pieces admit a closed form.

concepts.name: Conjugate priors
concepts.one_line: A prior is conjugate to a likelihood when the posterior lies in the same parametric family as the prior, which turns Bayesian updating into arithmetic on a few sufficient statistics; exponential families are the canonical source of such pairs.

concepts.name: Beta-Bernoulli conjugacy
concepts.one_line: If theta ~ Beta(alpha, beta) and r ~ Bernoulli(theta), the posterior after observing r=1 is Beta(alpha+1, beta) and after r=0 is Beta(alpha, beta+1).

concepts.name: Alpha and beta as pseudo-counts
concepts.one_line: Starting from Beta(1,1), alpha equals one plus the number of observed successes and beta one plus the number of failures, so the prior is literally a ledger of imagined prior pulls -- which is also how domain knowledge is injected.

concepts.name: The posterior is over theta, not over rewards
concepts.one_line: A student question forces the clarification that the Bernoulli parameter theta IS the arm's mean, and the Beta distribution expresses uncertainty about that mean, not about any individual binary reward.

concepts.name: Bayesian regret
concepts.one_line: Regret additionally averaged over the prior on parameters: how well does the algorithm do on average across the ensemble of worlds the prior deems possible, rather than in the single fixed world of frequentist regret.

concepts.name: Probability matching
concepts.one_line: A selection rule that plays each arm with exactly the posterior probability that it is the optimal arm given the history; intuitively appealing and automatically optimistic, since poorly-known arms are more likely to be best, but with no obvious way to compute the required probability.

concepts.name: Thompson sampling
concepts.one_line: Each round, draw one parameter vector from the current posterior, compute the implied action values, play the argmax as though the draw were truth, observe the reward, and update the posterior by Bayes' rule.

concepts.name: Thompson sampling implements probability matching
concepts.one_line: Posterior sampling followed by greedy selection reproduces exactly the probability-matching distribution, because the probability that a is optimal equals the posterior expectation of the indicator that a is the argmax of the sampled action values.

concepts.name: Thompson sampling worked trace
concepts.one_line: From Beta(1,1) priors, sampled thetas 0.3/0.5/0.6 select the bad arm, which returns 0 and moves it to Beta(1,2); the next draw 0.7/0.5/0.3 selects the good arm, which returns 1 and drives it through Beta(2,1), Beta(3,1), Beta(4,1), after which it is repeatedly chosen -- arm 2 is never pulled at all in this trace.

concepts.name: Informative vs uninformative priors
concepts.one_line: Beta(1,1) is uniform and neutral; a sharper prior like Beta(3,4) acts like fake pulls that accelerate learning when correct and mislead for a long stretch when wrong, which motivates asking how robust an algorithm is to prior misspecification.

concepts.name: A confident arm is not an absorbing state
concepts.one_line: Even after one arm's posterior concentrates, a rival arm with a flat posterior retains nonzero probability of drawing a near-1 sample, and if the leading arm's true mean is only moderate its posterior collapses toward that mean and the rivals catch up -- the prior matters early but is outweighed eventually.

concepts.name: Conjugate families beyond Bernoulli
concepts.one_line: Real-valued rewards call for a Gaussian likelihood with a Gaussian (or normal-inverse-gamma) prior; categorical rewards call for a multinomial likelihood with a Dirichlet prior. The recipe is: identify the reward family, then find its conjugate prior.

concepts.name: Thompson sampling attains the Lai-Robbins lower bound
concepts.one_line: Thompson sampling matches the classical asymptotic lower bound on bandit regret, and its Bayesian regret bound is of the same logarithmic order as UCB's -- with the caveat that this holds when the prior is correct.

concepts.name: Optimism can be too optimistic for too long
concepts.one_line: Illustrated by a robot that has hit the same door thirty thousand times and whose upper bound still argues for one more attempt; Thompson sampling's advantage in practice is that it is less optimistic than UCB, and frequentist analyses of Thompson sampling usually recover UCB-like optimism as a proof device.

concepts.name: PAC-Bayes as a hybrid framework
concepts.one_line: Named as the line of work that seeks guarantees behaving Bayesianly when the prior is good and frequentist-ly when the prior is wrong -- best of both worlds -- but not developed further.

concepts.name: Contextual bandits
concepts.one_line: A state is observed and affects which arm is best, but unlike an MDP the chosen action does not influence the next state -- e.g. how you treat this patient does not determine who walks in next.

concepts.name: Empirical case for Thompson sampling, and delayed feedback
concepts.one_line: Chapelle and Li's news-recommendation study showed Thompson sampling beating UCB and other baselines, and it is more robust under delayed outcomes because deterministic UCB keeps repeating one action while the pending feedback is outstanding, whereas Thompson sampling's stochasticity keeps the batch diverse.

concepts.name: Probably Approximately Correct for decision making
concepts.one_line: An algorithm is PAC(epsilon, delta) if, with probability at least 1-delta, it selects an epsilon-optimal action on all but a polynomial number of time steps, where the polynomial depends on the domain parameters and is computable in advance.

concepts.name: Why PAC and regret say different things
concepts.one_line: Cumulative regret cannot distinguish many tiny errors from a few catastrophic ones -- giving everyone a headache scores the same as harming a handful of patients severely -- whereas PAC counts only the mistakes larger than epsilon.

concepts.name: PAC applied to the toy trace
concepts.one_line: With epsilon = 0.05, playing surgery (0.95) or taping (0.9) both count as epsilon-optimal, so only pulls of the do-nothing arm (0.1) register as mistakes; the optimism run and the Thompson run are then compared by counting those.

concepts.name: Carrying the framework into tabular MDPs
concepts.one_line: Regret, Bayesian regret, PAC, optimism and probability matching all transfer to tabular MDPs, but the analysis becomes substantially more subtle even without function approximation.

concepts.name: Optimistic initialization in MDPs
concepts.one_line: Initialize every Q(s,a) to Rmax/(1-gamma) -- provably an upper bound on Q* -- then run Monte Carlo, Q-learning or SARSA; this encourages systematic coverage by treating every unvisited state-action as wonderful until disproved, but carries no performance guarantee on its own.

concepts.name: Even-Dar and Mansour (2002): PAC Q-learning
concepts.one_line: Purely greedy Q-learning with a suitable learning-rate schedule is PAC provided the initialization is Rmax/(1-gamma) divided by the product of all the learning rates -- a quantity exponential in the number of updates (with alpha=0.1 fixed, roughly 10^T), so sufficient in theory and useless in practice.

concepts.name: Jin et al. (NeurIPS 2018): model-free Q-learning can be efficient
concepts.one_line: With a milder, UCB-style optimistic initialization and carefully chosen learning rates, model-free Q-learning admits sublinear regret bounds -- not yet tight, but the first evidence that model-free methods can compete with the model-based theory that dominated the field.

concepts.name: Model-based strategy 1: optimistic until confident
concepts.one_line: Assume every state-action pair yields Rmax/(1-gamma) and keep assuming it until enough samples have accumulated that the MLE model for that pair is provably close to the truth, then switch to the empirical estimate; among the earliest PAC results for MDPs, but empirically weak because it ignores contrary evidence until the threshold is hit.

concepts.name: Model-based strategy 2: confidence sets over models
concepts.one_line: Maintain confidence regions over both the reward and the transition parameters and plan optimistically within them -- the direct MDP analogue of interval estimation for bandits.

concepts.name: Model-based strategy 3: reward bonuses, and why they generalize
concepts.one_line: Use the plain MLE model but add an exploration bonus to the reward; this is preferred because writing confidence sets over a deep-network dynamics model is intractable, whereas a bonus drops straight into model-free deep RL, and empirically bonuses do about as well as explicit confidence sets.

concepts.name: MBIE-EB algorithm
concepts.one_line: Track N(s,a), N(s,a,s') and the reward sum Rc(s,a); form the MLE reward Rc(s,a)/N(s,a) and transition N(s,a,s')/N(s,a); solve by value iteration the MDP whose reward is the MLE reward plus beta/sqrt(N(s,a)); set unvisited pairs to Qmax = 1/(1-gamma); act greedily and repeat.

concepts.name: The exploration bonus decays with experience
concepts.one_line: The beta/sqrt(N(s,a)) term is effectively infinite at zero count and shrinks toward zero as data accumulates, so the planner is pulled toward under-sampled state-action pairs and converges to the empirical model where data is plentiful.

concepts.name: PAC for reinforcement learning, and greedy's failure
concepts.one_line: An RL algorithm is PAC if on all but N steps its action is epsilon-close to optimal, with N polynomial in |S|, |A|, 1/(1-gamma), 1/epsilon and 1/delta; greedy exploration does not satisfy this and can require exponentially many steps.

concepts.name: MBIE-EB is PAC
concepts.one_line: Averaging counts and bolting on a square-root bonus suffices to guarantee near-optimal action selection on all but a polynomial number of time steps, with the bound inversely dependent on epsilon and polynomial in the state and action counts.

concepts.name: Empirical ordering of exploration strategies
concepts.one_line: On small hand-constructed hard domains, bonus- and confidence-set-based methods (MBIE-EB, MBIE) beat optimistic-until-confident methods, which in turn beat greedy by a wide margin -- so the provably efficient methods are also the empirically strong ones here.

theorems_stated: Gap-dependent regret bound for UCB: with high probability the cumulative regret is O(sum over suboptimal arms of log T / Delta_a), where Delta_a = Q(a*) - Q(a); the algorithm never needs the gaps, only the bound mentions them.
Greedy action selection incurs linear cumulative regret; epsilon-greedy with a fixed epsilon also incurs linear regret.
Epsilon-greedy with an appropriately decayed epsilon achieves sublinear (logarithmic) regret, but the required schedule depends on the unknown gaps, making it unimplementable without an oracle.
Sufficiently optimistic initialization achieves sublinear regret in bandits; the threshold for 'sufficiently' is not specified.

Greedy selection with respect to the highest LOWER confidence bound can incur linear regret, via lock-in on a suboptimal arm whose own interval tightens correctly while the optimal arm is never sampled.

Beta(alpha, beta) is a conjugate prior for the Bernoulli likelihood: observing r=1 gives Beta(alpha+1, beta) and r=0 gives Beta(alpha, beta+1); consequently alpha and beta are pseudo-counts of successes and failures.
Thompson sampling implements probability matching exactly: the induced action distribution equals the posterior probability that each action is optimal given the history.
Thompson sampling achieves the Lai-Robbins asymptotic lower bound on bandit regret.
The Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling is of the same (logarithmic) order as the regret bound of UCB, when the prior is correctly specified.
For a discounted MDP with rewards bounded by Rmax, V*(s) <= Rmax/(1-gamma), so initializing Q(s,a) = Rmax/(1-gamma) is guaranteed optimistic.

Even-Dar and Mansour (2002): purely greedy Q-learning under a suitable learning-rate schedule alpha_i, initialized to Rmax/(1-gamma) divided by the product of the learning rates, is PAC. The initialization is exponential in the number of updates.

Jin et al. (NeurIPS 2018): model-free Q-learning with a UCB-style optimistic bonus and carefully chosen learning rates achieves sublinear regret in tabular MDPs; the bounds are not yet minimax-optimal.
Early (2002-era) model-based 'optimistic until confident' algorithms for MDPs are PAC.
MBIE-EB is PAC: on all but a number of steps polynomial in |S|, |A|, 1/(1-gamma), 1/epsilon and 1/delta, it selects an epsilon-optimal action with probability at least 1-delta.
Greedy exploration in MDPs is not PAC and can require a number of suboptimal steps that is exponential in the problem size.
proofs_given: Informal correctness argument for optimism in bandits: at each round either the optimal arm is selected (zero instantaneous regret) or a suboptimal arm is selected, in which case its upper confidence bound is with high probability above its true mean and will be revised downward, so every mistake produces information that shrinks the cause of the mistake.

Verbal proof by construction that lower-confidence-bound selection yields linear regret in the two-arm case: if arm 2's true mean lies above arm 1's lower bound, sampling arm 2 concentrates its interval around its own (suboptimal) mean, arm 1 is never sampled, its interval never tightens, and the wrong hypothesis is never refuted.
Explicit numerical instantiation of the UCB rule at t=3 on the broken-toe instance, showing the two good arms tie and the bad arm is strictly dominated so it receives zero selection probability.

Explicit numerical instantiation at t=4 showing that after a second pull of a1 the bound flips to a2 because the count in the denominator grew, together with the check that this flip occurs whether a1's second draw was 0 or 1 (i.e. it is count-driven, not reward-driven).

Computation of epsilon-greedy selection probabilities: the greedy arm gets 1 - epsilon + epsilon/|A| and each other arm gets epsilon/|A| = 0.1/3 (approximately 0.033), used to contrast with UCB's zero mass on the bad arm.
Step-by-step regret accounting for the UCB action sequence a1,a2,a3,a1,a2 giving 0, 0.05, 0.85, 0, 0.05, and for the Thompson sampling sequence a3,a1,a1,a1,a1 giving 0.85, 0, 0, 0, 0.
Class-sourced argument that Rmax/(1-gamma) upper-bounds Q*, appealing to the previously derived geometric-series bound on the discounted return.

Arithmetic demonstration that the Even-Dar and Mansour initialization is astronomically large: with alpha_i = 0.1 held fixed, the product of reciprocal learning rates equals 10^T, exponential in the number of decision steps.
proofs_skipped: Proof of the gap-dependent logarithmic regret bound sum_a log T / Delta_a for UCB. It is stated as a result and contrasted with the previous lecture's gap-free bound, but never derived.

The relationship between the gap-dependent bound and the gap-independent bound (e.g. how splitting the arms on whether Delta_a exceeds a threshold converts one into an O(sqrt(K T log T)) statement). Asserted as 'related' with no argument.
Proof that greedy and fixed-epsilon greedy suffer linear regret. Referred back to L11 and used freely, but not reproduced.
Proof that a decayed epsilon schedule attains logarithmic regret, and the explicit form of the schedule (which involves the minimum gap). Only the existence of such a schedule is asserted.

Proof that sufficiently optimistic initialization gives sublinear regret in bandits, and any quantitative characterization of how optimistic 'sufficiently' is. Explicitly flagged as 'subtle' and left open.

A formal treatment of the lower-confidence-bound failure: the verbal two-arm argument never specifies the probability of lock-in, never handles the case where the lower bound of the good arm is initially higher, and gives no explicit instance with a proved linear lower bound.
Derivation of Beta-Bernoulli conjugacy, including the Gamma-function normalizing constant that is written on the board but never used or justified.
The general claim that conjugacy (and exponential families in particular) is exactly what makes closed-form Bayesian updating possible. Stated as folklore; no characterization theorem, no proof.

Proof that Thompson sampling implements probability matching. The identity P(a is optimal | h) = E_{theta | h}[ 1{a = argmax_a' Q_theta(a')} ] is written down and asserted to be 'what Thompson sampling is computing', but the equality of the induced action distribution with the probability-matching distribution is never proved.

Proof of the Bayesian regret bound for Thompson sampling. Explicitly deferred: the lecturer says she will not do the proof and will supply pointers instead. This is the single most conspicuous deferral in the lecture.
Proof that Thompson sampling attains the Lai-Robbins lower bound (the Kaufmann/Agrawal-Goyal line of results). Asserted only.
Statement and proof of the Lai-Robbins lower bound itself, including its KL-divergence form. Named but never written down.

The claim that frequentist analyses of Thompson sampling generically route through optimism/UCB-style arguments, and that making Thompson sampling frequentist-robust requires adding optimism. Given as an impression, not a result.
Proof (or even a precise statement) that PAC guarantees follow from optimism or from Thompson sampling in bandits. Asserted as a general pattern.
The definition and any bound from PAC-Bayes. The framework is named as combining Bayesian and frequentist guarantees; no theorem, no bound form, no citation detail.

The promised explanation of WHY PAC is the more natural framework for MDPs than regret, while regret dominates for bandits. Explicitly deferred ('we'll see one of the reasons for that probably later, or feel free to ask me about it').

Proof of the Even-Dar and Mansour (2002) PAC result for greedy Q-learning, and the precise learning-rate schedule alpha_i (polynomial vs linear decay) it requires. Only the initialization formula and its magnitude are discussed.

Proof and even the rate of the Jin et al. (NeurIPS 2018) model-free result. No regret expression is stated, no horizon/state/action dependence is given, and the size of the remaining gap to the known lower bound is described only as 'not tight yet'.
Proof that 'optimistic until confident' (R-max / E^3 style) model-based algorithms are PAC. Attributed to 2002 work and asserted.

The simulation lemma and the sample-complexity threshold m: how many samples per state-action pair are required for the MLE reward and transition estimates to be within a given accuracy, and how model error propagates through planning into value error. This is the mathematical core of every model-based PAC proof and is entirely absent.

Derivation of the MBIE-EB bonus constant beta from Hoeffding plus a union bound, and an explanation of why the union bound counts 2|S||A|m terms. The formula is written on the board and immediately used without justification.

Proof of the optimism lemma for MBIE-EB: that the Q-function computed from the MLE model plus bonus is, with probability at least 1-delta, an upper bound on Q* uniformly over state-action pairs. This is the property that makes the bonus work and it is never stated.

Proof that MBIE-EB is PAC (Strehl and Littman), and the explicit form of the polynomial sample-complexity expression. The expression is displayed on a slide and physically circled, but its terms are never read out or explained beyond 'polynomial in states and actions, inversely dependent on epsilon'.

Proof that greedy exploration in an MDP can require exponentially many suboptimal steps, i.e. the combination-lock / long-chain counterexample. Explicitly deferred to the following lecture ('we might talk about that on Wednesday').

Justification that reward-bonus methods achieve guarantees comparable to explicit confidence-set methods (MBIE-EB vs MBIE). Supported only by the remark that they do 'pretty much as well' empirically.

Analysis of why deterministic algorithms such as UCB degrade under delayed feedback while stochastic ones such as Thompson sampling do not. Argued by anecdote about batching patients; no model of delay, no bound.

Posterior consistency for the Beta-Bernoulli updates: the claim that a Beta posterior 'collapses toward the true value' if an arm is pulled forever, and hence that a bad prior can be outweighed. No rate, no concentration statement.
Any formal notion of robustness to a misspecified prior, despite the topic being raised twice by students. Answered qualitatively ('you can be misled for a while').

Validity of the value-iteration step inside MBIE-EB: that adding the state-action-dependent bonus preserves the contraction property of the Bellman operator and that the iteration converges to the optimistic Q-function.
Justification for the initialization Qmax for unvisited state-action pairs as a well-defined substitute for a bonus that is formally infinite when N(s,a)=0.
algorithms: UCB1 for stochastic bandits: maintain the empirical mean Qhat_t(a) and the pull count N_t(a); each round play argmax_a [ Qhat_t(a) + sqrt(2 ln t / N_t(a)) ], breaking ties at random. Every arm is pulled once at the start to make the counts nonzero.

Epsilon-greedy (fixed and decayed): with probability 1-epsilon play the empirical argmax, otherwise play uniformly at random over all arms, giving each non-greedy arm probability epsilon/|A|. Included as the baseline whose exploration is unstrategic.
Lower-confidence-bound (pessimistic) selection: play argmax_a [ Qhat_t(a) - bonus_t(a) ]. Presented as an instructive failure mode rather than a usable algorithm.
Optimistic initialization for bandits: seed each arm with one fictitious pull of very large reward and thereafter act greedily on the running empirical mean including that fictitious sample.
Beta-Bernoulli Bayesian updating: keep (alpha_i, beta_i) per arm starting at (1,1); on reward 1 increment alpha_i, on reward 0 increment beta_i. The posterior mean is alpha_i/(alpha_i+beta_i).
Probability matching: sample a_t from P(a = argmax_a' Q(a') | h_t). Specified as a target behaviour with no direct implementation.

Thompson sampling (posterior sampling): for each round, draw theta_i ~ p(theta_i | h_t) independently for every arm, set Q(a_i) to the mean of the reward distribution implied by theta_i (for Bernoulli this is theta_i itself, for Gaussian the mean parameter), play argmax_i Q(a_i), observe r, update the posterior of the played arm by Bayes' rule.

Optimistic-initialization tabular control: set Q_0(s,a) = Rmax/(1-gamma) for all (s,a), then run Monte Carlo control, Q-learning or SARSA with greedy action selection, relying on the optimistic values alone for exploration.
Even-Dar and Mansour PAC Q-learning: Q-learning with a prescribed learning-rate schedule alpha_i and the far larger initialization Rmax/((1-gamma) * product_i alpha_i), acting greedily throughout.

Jin et al. model-free Q-learning with UCB exploration: Q-learning with a UCB-style bonus added to the target and a specific (Hoeffding-type) learning-rate schedule, giving sublinear regret without ever building a model.

Optimistic-until-confident model-based RL (R-max style): treat the reward of every state-action pair as Rmax/(1-gamma) until that pair has been visited enough times for its MLE parameters to be provably close to the truth, then switch that pair over to its empirical estimate and replan.

MBIE (model-based interval estimation): build confidence sets around both the empirical transition distribution and the empirical reward for each state-action pair, and plan optimistically within those sets.

MBIE-EB (model-based interval estimation with exploration bonus), given in full: initialize N(s,a)=0, N(s,a,s')=0, Rc(s,a)=0, Q(s,a)=1/(1-gamma) with rewards in [0,1]; set beta from epsilon, delta, m, |S|, |A| and gamma. Each step: play argmax_a Q(s,a) with random tie-breaking, observe r and s', increment N(s,a), N(s,a,s') and Rc(s,a) += r. Form rhat(s,a) = Rc(s,a)/N(s,a) and Phat(s'|s,a) = N(s,a,s')/N(s,a) (unvisited pairs may be treated as uniform). Solve by value iteration the MDP with reward rhat(s,a) + beta/sqrt(N(s,a)), and override Q(s,a) = Qmax wherever N(s,a) = 0. Repeat.
notation_introduced: Q(a): the true expected reward of arm a; Qhat(a) or the 'empirical estimate': the running sample average of observed rewards from a
a*: the optimal arm, argmax_a Q(a)
Delta_a = Q(a*) - Q(a): the gap of arm a
t: the total number of arm pulls so far across all arms; N_t(a): the number of pulls of arm a specifically
UCB_t(a) = Qhat_t(a) + sqrt(2 ln t / N_t(a)): the upper confidence bound used throughout the worked example
'Problem-dependent bound': a regret bound whose constants involve instance quantities (here the gaps) that the algorithm itself does not know
phi_i: the unknown parameter(s) governing arm i's reward distribution; p(phi_i) the prior, p(phi_i | r) the posterior
theta_i: the Bernoulli parameter of arm i, which is simultaneously that arm's mean reward
Beta(alpha, beta): the prior/posterior over a Bernoulli parameter, with density proportional to theta^(alpha-1) (1-theta)^(beta-1) times a ratio of Gamma functions; Beta(1,1) is uniform
alpha = (number of observed rewards equal to 1) + 1 and beta = (number of observed rewards equal to 0) + 1, when starting from Beta(1,1)
h or h_t: the history of arms pulled and rewards observed so far
Bayesian regret: the frequentist regret additionally averaged over parameters drawn from the prior
PAC(epsilon, delta): choose an epsilon-optimal action with probability at least 1-delta on all but a polynomial number of time steps
Rmax: the largest reward achievable in any state-action pair; Qmax = Rmax/(1-gamma), which equals 1/(1-gamma) when rewards lie in [0,1]
N(s,a), N(s,a,s'), Rc(s,a): visit counts for a state-action pair, for a state-action-successor triple, and the accumulated reward sum for a state-action pair
rhat(s,a) = Rc(s,a)/N(s,a) and Phat(s'|s,a) = N(s,a,s')/N(s,a): the maximum-likelihood reward and transition models
beta (in MBIE-EB): the scaling constant of the exploration bonus, of the form (1/(1-gamma)) * sqrt( (1/2) ln( 2 |S| |A| m / delta ) ); the bonus added to the reward is beta / sqrt(N(s,a))
m: an input parameter of MBIE-EB, the per-state-action sample threshold entering both beta and the sample-complexity bound
N (in the PAC-for-RL statement): the mistake budget, polynomial in |S|, |A|, 1/(1-gamma), 1/epsilon and 1/delta
notation_hazards: The auto-captions consistently drop square-root symbols. 'UCB of a3 is gonna be equal to 2 log 3 divided by 1' must read sqrt(2 ln 3 / 1), and the general rule 'empirical average plus the square root of 2 log t' must read Qhat + sqrt(2 ln t / N_t(a)) -- the count belongs inside the radical, not outside.

The Even-Dar and Mansour initialization is stated as 'Rmax divided by 1-gamma TIMES the product of those learning rates'. That is mathematically backwards: multiplying by learning rates below 1 would make the value smaller, not larger. It must be Rmax/((1-gamma) * product of alpha_i), equivalently Rmax/(1-gamma) times the product of the RECIPROCAL learning rates -- as confirmed immediately afterwards when she computes (1/0.1)^T = 10^T.
In the same result, 't is the number of samples you need to learn optimal Q' overloads t, which everywhere else in the lecture is the bandit round counter. Read it as a separate horizon symbol T.

The MBIE-EB bonus constant is dictated as 'one over one minus gamma, two log the number of states, number of actions, two times m, divided by delta', which is missing both the square root and the one-half factor. The intended constant is (1/(1-gamma)) * sqrt( (1/2) ln( 2|S||A|m / delta ) ).

'beta' is badly overloaded: it is the second shape parameter of the Beta distribution in the first half of the lecture and the exploration-bonus scaling constant of MBIE-EB in the second half. These are unrelated quantities.
The epsilon-greedy probability of the bad arm is transcribed as '0.03' and then as '0323'; the intended value is epsilon/|A| = 0.1/3 = 0.0333.
Referring to the Thompson sampling trace, 'we're going to select theta as 0.6' should be 'we select the ARM whose sampled theta was 0.6' (arm 3). Actions are selected, parameters are sampled.

The Beta update is transcribed as 'if we observe a 1 we update the first parameter, ALSO we're gonna update the second parameter'; the intended word is 'otherwise' -- exactly one of alpha or beta increments per observation.
'rc of s, a = 0 for all s' should be 'for all s and all a'.

Q(a) is used for the TRUE mean of an arm, with the estimate called 'the empirical estimate' and written with a hat. Sutton and Barto reserve q_*(a) for the true value and Q_t(a) for the estimate, so the roles of the unadorned Q are swapped relative to the textbook.
Sutton and Barto write the UCB bonus as c * sqrt(ln t / N_t(a)) with c a tunable constant; this lecture hard-codes c via sqrt(2 ln t / N_t(a)), matching Auer et al. rather than the textbook.
Thompson sampling is dated to 'roughly the 1920s' and probability matching to 'around 1929'; Thompson's paper is 1933. The dates are approximate throughout.

In the PAC worked example, arm 2 (mean 0.9) is called 'within 0.05' of arm 1 (mean 0.95), which is a boundary case -- it is within epsilon only for epsilon >= 0.05, not for strict inequality with epsilon = 0.05.
The MDP PAC statement lists the mistake budget as polynomial in 'gamma', but the dependence is really on the effective horizon 1/(1-gamma), which blows up as gamma approaches 1.

The lecture uses discounted infinite-horizon notation (gamma, Rmax/(1-gamma)) throughout the MDP section, whereas the Jin et al. result it cites is for the finite-horizon episodic setting parameterized by H. The two are silently mixed.

animation_candidates.what: The 3-arm broken-toe instance under UCB, animated round by round: three bars for the empirical means with error whiskers of length sqrt(2 ln t / N_t(a)), the selected arm highlighted, and the whisker lengths visibly re-scaling every round because t changed for all arms while N changed for only one.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture's most surprising claim -- that a2 is selected next whether a1's last draw was 0 or 1 -- is entirely about a denominator moving, which is invisible in prose but obvious the instant the whiskers are drawn side by side. Static text forces the reader to recompute two square roots by hand.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Bar-and-whisker chart with a per-round step control; whisker lengths recomputed each frame, the argmax bar flashing, a running regret counter beneath.

animation_candidates.what: UCB versus LCB run side by side on the same two-arm instance, with the two confidence intervals shown as vertical bars and the true means marked as dashed lines; on the LCB side, the suboptimal arm's interval collapses onto its own true mean while the optimal arm's interval sits frozen forever.
animation_candidates.why: The linear-regret argument for pessimism is inherently about what does NOT happen over time -- an interval that never shrinks because the arm is never sampled. A frozen bar next to a collapsing one makes the confirmation-bias lock-in visceral, whereas the transcript's verbal version took the lecturer two tries and a student prompt.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Split-screen two-panel interval plot with synchronized round counter and two divergent cumulative-regret curves below (logarithmic vs linear).

animation_candidates.what: Beta posterior morph: the density smoothly deforming Beta(1,1) -> Beta(1,2) -> Beta(2,1) -> Beta(3,1) -> Beta(4,1), with each round showing a dart dropped from the curve onto the theta axis, three such curves side by side for the three arms, and the largest dart determining the action.
animation_candidates.why: Thompson sampling is literally 'sample a dart from a shape that keeps changing shape'. Animating the shape change and the dart together fuses the two halves of the algorithm that text has to present sequentially, and it makes obvious why arm 2, whose curve never moves, keeps losing the dart contest without ever being ruled out.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Three stacked density plots on a shared [0,1] axis, one animated sample dart per curve per round, with the winning dart highlighted and the corresponding curve then deforming.

animation_candidates.what: A race between UCB and Thompson sampling on the identical broken-toe instance: intervals on the left, posteriors on the right, and two cumulative-regret staircases at the bottom that visibly separate when UCB alternates a1/a2 while Thompson locks onto a1.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture's punchline comparison -- 'UCB was splitting its time between a1 and a2, in this case we still haven't taken a2 at all' -- is a claim about two trajectories, and trajectories are what animation is for. It also sets up the honest caveat that Thompson's fast commitment is only good here because a1 really is best.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two-column synchronized run with a shared random-seed banner and paired regret staircases; a second seed replayed to show Thompson committing to a2 by luck.

animation_candidates.what: A term-level morph of the probability-matching identity: P(a = argmax_a' Q(a') | h) rewritten as an expectation over theta ~ p(theta|h) of the indicator that a is the argmax, then that expectation replaced by a single Monte Carlo draw, revealing the Thompson sampling pseudocode underneath.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture asserts that Thompson sampling implements probability matching without proving it, and this is precisely the field flagged as a proof gap. A three-step formula morph is the shortest honest route from 'intractable-looking probability' to 'draw one sample and take the argmax', and it turns an unproved assertion into something the viewer can see.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Term-level formula morph in three beats, each beat annotated with what changed, ending with the four-line algorithm box.

animation_candidates.what: A grid-world value sweep for MBIE-EB: every cell coloured by max_a [ rhat(s,a) + beta/sqrt(N(s,a)) ], swept over training time, with the agent's path drawn on top and an unvisited corner glowing bright until the agent finally reaches it.
animation_candidates.why: The intuition that a decaying square-root bonus 'pulls the planner toward under-sampled corners' is asserted in one sentence but is a spatial, temporal phenomenon. Watching the optimistic glow retreat from visited regions and drag the trajectory into the dark corner is the entire argument for why bonuses give PAC guarantees while greedy does not.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Grid-world heatmap with a time slider, agent trajectory overlay, and a companion panel showing the bonus term beta/sqrt(N) decaying as 1/sqrt(N).

animation_candidates.what: A log-scale comparison of the two optimistic initializations: a modest bar at Rmax/(1-gamma) next to a bar at Rmax/((1-gamma) * 0.1^T) growing off the top of the frame as T is scrubbed from 1 to 50.
animation_candidates.why: The lecture's rhetorical point -- 'this is way, way, way larger' and 'incredibly optimistic' -- is a claim about orders of magnitude that no amount of prose conveys. Scrubbing T and watching one bar stay put while the other exits the screen is the fastest way to make 'sufficient for PAC but useless in practice' land.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two bars on a log axis with a scrubbable T, annotated with the crossover into absurdity (10^T tokens of optimism).

animation_candidates.what: Two runs with identical cumulative regret but different mistake profiles -- one making many sub-epsilon errors, one making a few large ones -- shown as a per-step error timeline with an epsilon threshold line, a shared regret total, and a PAC mistake counter that only increments above the line.
animation_candidates.why: The distinction between regret and PAC is the lecture's cleanest conceptual contribution and is defined purely by what a summary statistic hides. Showing two timelines that sum to the same number but trip the counter a very different number of times makes the case in one frame; the transcript needs a paragraph about headaches versus severe side effects.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two stacked per-step error timelines with a horizontal epsilon line, a shared cumulative-regret readout, and two divergent mistake counters.

code_experiment_candidates: Implement UCB1, fixed epsilon-greedy (0.1), decayed epsilon-greedy, greedy, and Thompson sampling on the lecture's Bernoulli(0.95, 0.9, 0.1) instance; plot mean cumulative regret over 10k rounds across 200 seeds with confidence bands, and verify empirically the linear/logarithmic separation.

Reproduce the lecture's exact traces: force UCB's first pulls to yield 1,1,0 and check the algorithm produces a1,a2,a3,a1,a2 with per-round regrets 0, 0.05, 0.85, 0, 0.05; separately force Thompson's first posterior draws to 0.3/0.5/0.6 then 0.7/0.5/0.3 and check the arm sequence a3,a1,a1,a1 and regrets 0.85, 0, 0, 0.

Sweep the gap: hold arm 1 at 0.95 and vary arm 2 over {0.94, 0.9, 0.7, 0.5}, then fit the empirical UCB regret against the predicted sum of log T / Delta_a to test whether the gap-dependent constant actually shows up in simulation.

Implement a lower-confidence-bound agent and estimate, over many seeds, the probability that it locks onto the suboptimal arm and the resulting slope of its regret curve; construct the two-arm instance from the lecture that maximizes this failure probability.

Prior misspecification study for Thompson sampling: run Beta(1,1) against Beta(5,1) (over-optimistic), Beta(1,5) (pessimistic), and Beta(20,20) (over-confident and wrong) on the same instance; measure regret and rounds-until-commitment to quantify the 'you can be misled for a while' claim.

Delayed-feedback experiment: buffer rewards for k rounds before revealing them, and compare UCB against Thompson sampling for k in {1, 10, 100}, reproducing the qualitative Chapelle-and-Li finding that a deterministic rule wastes a delayed batch on one arm while a stochastic rule diversifies it.

Optimistic-initialization threshold search for bandits: sweep the fictitious initial reward over several orders of magnitude and locate empirically the point at which regret turns sublinear, giving a concrete answer to the 'how optimistic is sufficiently optimistic' question the lecture leaves open.

Implement MBIE-EB in full on RiverSwim or a long chain MDP -- counts, MLE model, beta/sqrt(N(s,a)) bonus, value iteration, Qmax override for unvisited pairs -- and compare against epsilon-greedy Q-learning, optimistically-initialized Q-learning, and an R-max-style optimistic-until-confident agent.

Sweep beta in MBIE-EB from the theoretically prescribed (1/(1-gamma)) sqrt(0.5 ln(2|S||A|m/delta)) down by one and two orders of magnitude, and measure how far below the theory-mandated value the empirically best bonus sits -- a concrete demonstration of the theory/practice gap the lecture keeps gesturing at.

Instrument a PAC mistake counter: at every step log V*(s) - Q*(s, a_t) using the known optimal solution of the toy MDP, count the steps where it exceeds epsilon, and plot that count against the theoretical polynomial for greedy, epsilon-greedy, optimistic init, and MBIE-EB.

Implement the Even-Dar and Mansour initialization for small T and watch the algorithm's behaviour, then show numerically that for realistic T the initialization overflows floating point -- making concrete why a sufficient theoretical condition can be operationally meaningless.

Implement Jin-et-al-style Q-learning with a UCB-Hoeffding bonus in a finite-horizon tabular MDP and compare its regret curve against the model-based MBIE-EB baseline, testing the lecture's claim that model-free can now compete but is not yet tight.
dated_or_superseded: The Jin et al. result is presented as breaking news ('just came out in NeurIPS about two months ago') with a remark that its regret bounds are 'not tight yet'. That gap has since been closed: subsequent model-free work (notably the UCB-Advantage line, Zhang et al. 2020 and successors) achieves minimax-optimal regret for tabular episodic RL up to logarithmic factors, so the open question the lecture flags is now settled.

The claim that 'almost all of the work that's been going on has been in the model-based setting' and that model-based methods 'have the best bounds right now' is out of date.
