Model-based minimax optimality was already established around the same period (Azar et al.), and later work removed the burn-in requirements; in tabular RL the model-free/model-based statistical gap is now essentially closed and the interesting distinction is computational and memory-related, not statistical.

The assertion that frequentist analyses of Thompson sampling 'end up converting to upper confidence bounds' understates what is now available. Direct frequentist analyses of Thompson sampling (Agrawal and Goyal, and successors) give near-optimal problem-dependent regret bounds without routing through an optimism argument, and the Russo-Van Roy information-ratio technique gives Bayesian bounds via an entirely different and much more general route -- the same technique that produced information-directed sampling.

PAC-Bayes is name-dropped as speculative future work for combining Bayesian and frequentist guarantees in bandits. It has since become a substantial and well-developed literature, including PAC-Bayesian bandit and RL analyses, and is no longer an open gesture.

Count-based exploration bonuses of the beta/sqrt(N(s,a)) form are presented as the technique that will extend naturally to deep RL. The subsequent decade tempered this considerably: pseudo-count and curiosity-based bonuses gave benchmark-specific gains that often failed to transfer, and much of the deep-RL exploration literature from that era has been substantially deflated by later reproduction efforts. The bonus is still the right tabular story but should not be presented as the settled recipe under function approximation.

Chapelle and Li's news-recommendation study remains the canonical empirical argument for Thompson sampling, but it now reads as a historical result rather than current practice; production contextual bandits use linear/neural Thompson sampling with off-policy evaluation machinery, and the UCB-vs-Thompson debate is regarded as settled in favour of 'both work, tuning and delay structure decide'.

The lecture's framing that exploration in sequential decision making is fundamentally about count-based uncertainty in a tabular state space does not survive contact with modern LLM-agent settings, where exploration is effectively performed by sampling temperature, prompt diversity, and search over program-like action spaces rather than by any N(s,a) statistic.

relevance_to_user_research.why: This is the most directly applicable of the CS234 bandit lectures to the user's work, but only to one half of it. The half it serves well is the H=1 query-level routing case that AEP addresses. The reward there is binary (the workflow's terminal answer is correct or not), which is exactly Bernoulli, so a per-(query-cluster, fidelity) Beta(alpha, beta) posterior with Thompson sampling is a legitimate, near-zero-cost online router that the paper could either adopt or use as the baseline AEP must beat -- and reviewers will ask why it was not tried. Three specific transfers stand out. First, the delayed-feedback argument is squarely in the user's operating regime: terminal accuracy is only observable after the whole DAG executes, and vLLM batching means many queries are in flight at once, which is precisely the setting where Brunskill argues deterministic UCB wastes a batch on one arm while stochastic Thompson sampling keeps it diverse. Second, PAC is a better evaluation frame for their claim than regret: they care about how many queries get catastrophically mis-routed to the weak model, not about an averaged regret curve, and cumulative regret provably cannot distinguish a few disasters from many trivial slips. Stating a result as 'on all but N queries the assigned fidelity is within epsilon of the best assignment' is a cleaner ACL/NAACL claim than a regret plot. Third, optimistic initialization is a directly usable cold-start trick for their stated goal: initialize every node's 'the weak model suffices here' estimate optimistically so the searched workflow actually attempts Qwen-7B at every node before conceding to Qwen-72B -- the 'pretend everything is awesome until proven otherwise' pattern is exactly the inductive bias that maximizes weak-model coverage. The reason this is useful rather than critical is that the node-level fidelity assignment problem itself, which is the actual thesis, is not tabular and not primarily an exploration problem. Their state (query embedding, DAG position, partial execution trace, remaining budget) is high-dimensional and continuous, so N(s,a) counts and the beta/sqrt(N) bonus do not literally apply; the lecture explicitly defers function approximation to the next session, which is where the real content for them lives. Their setting is also plausibly offline: they can roll out a fixed dataset of (query, fidelity assignment, accuracy, token cost) tuples on the Phoenix A100s and fit a policy in batch, in which case online exploration is not the bottleneck and credit assignment across DAG nodes plus generalization across queries is. Finally the lecture says nothing about budget constraints, so the lambda-times-token-cost term and the remaining-budget component of their state have no counterpart here -- constrained MDPs are simply absent. Read this lecture for the Thompson sampling machinery, the delayed-feedback argument, and the PAC framing; do not expect it to address the node-level problem directly.

lecture_title: L13 - Fast Reinforcement Learning III (PAC-MDP analysis, Bayesian RL, and exploration with generalization)
one_paragraph_summary: This is the closing lecture of the fast-learning block, and it is the most proof-heavy hour in the course. It does three things. First, it sharpens the PAC-MDP criterion and contrasts it carefully with regret: regret judges you against the state distribution you would have reached had you acted optimally from the very first step, whereas PAC judges you only against the best action available in whatever state your own algorithm has landed you in — so PAC is the more forgiving, "make the best of where you are" criterion, and the two coincide more closely in episodic settings where you reset to a fixed start state. Second, it lays out a three-part sufficient-condition template for proving an algorithm PAC — optimism, accuracy against a hybrid analysis MDP, and bounded learning complexity — and then actually carries out on the board the one piece it can fit in the time: a full induction proof that MBIE-EB's reward bonus beta/sqrt(n) is large enough to make the computed Q optimistic. The proof composes a Hoeffding deviation bound on Bellman targets built from the true V*, a union bound over all |S||A|m estimator updates (which is why the algorithm artificially discards data past m samples per state-action pair), and induction over value-iteration sweeps from an optimistic initialization of 1/(1-gamma). Accuracy and bounded learning complexity are only sketched: accuracy via a knownness threshold plus the simulation lemma and two artificially constructed hybrid MDPs, and bounded learning complexity via a pigeonhole "either your escape probability is small and you are already near-optimal, or it is large and you burn through your finite budget of m counts per pair" dichotomy. Third, it pivots away from tabular theory: posterior sampling for MDPs (Dirichlet priors over multinomial transitions, Beta over Bernoulli rewards, sample a whole MDP and solve it), and then an honest survey of exploration under function approximation — counts do not generalize, so pseudo-count density models, hash-based counts, and learned embeddings stand in; MBIE-EB was chosen precisely because a reward bonus drops straight into a model-free Q-learning update; and uncertainty over Q* can be approximated by bootstrapped DQN ensembles or, more effectively and far more cheaply, Bayesian linear regression on a frozen deep embedding. Brunskill is candid that the theory here lags badly behind the empirics.
prerequisites: MDP fundamentals: Bellman optimality operator, value iteration, discounting, V* and Q*
Model-based RL: maximum-likelihood empirical transition and reward models built from counts
MBIE-EB from the previous lecture (L12), including its bonus form and the role of beta
Multi-armed bandits: regret, optimism under uncertainty / UCB, Thompson sampling
Bayesian basics: priors, posteriors, conjugacy, Beta-Bernoulli, multinomial distributions
Hoeffding's inequality and the union bound; comfort reading high-probability statements
Q-learning, DQN, target networks, replay buffers, and value function approximation
Asymptotic notation and the idea of polynomial sample complexity

concepts.name: Course logistics: midterm distribution, curve policy, and the two-stage quiz
concepts.one_line: Midterm mean (~71%) matched last year's (~69%), no formal curve is applied and roughly 42% earned an A last year; regrades close Friday; the upcoming ~5%-of-grade quiz is multiple choice, taken first individually (~45 min) then again in a randomly assigned group as a scratch-off, with the group portion able only to raise, never lower, your score.

concepts.name: Why fast learning matters
concepts.one_line: The regime of interest is where each data point is expensive or consequential — healthcare, education, customer-facing recommendation — so sample efficiency, not just asymptotic optimality, is the design target.

concepts.name: Two settings, two evaluation frameworks
concepts.one_line: Bandits and MDPs are the two settings; regret and PAC are the two formal yardsticks, with optimism-under-uncertainty and Thompson sampling the two dominant algorithmic strategies for achieving either.

concepts.name: Sample complexity vs computational complexity
concepts.one_line: The whole block analyses how much data an algorithm needs, not how much computation; she notes these frameworks can generally be extended to also demand polynomial computation per step, but that extension is not developed.

concepts.name: PAC (probably approximately correct) RL algorithm
concepts.one_line: Given inputs epsilon and delta, an algorithm is PAC if on all but N time steps it takes an action whose value is within epsilon of the best available in the current state, with probability at least 1-delta, where N is polynomial in |S|, |A|, 1/(1-gamma), 1/epsilon and 1/delta.

concepts.name: Looseness about constants
concepts.one_line: Throughout the lecture constants are deliberately suppressed — 1-delta may really be 1-2delta, and unnamed C1, C2 may multiply epsilon — because these bounds are about orders of magnitude in |S| and |A|, not tight constants.

concepts.name: Regret in an MDP
concepts.one_line: Regret measures the shortfall of your realised rewards against what you would have collected had you acted optimally from the very first step, so you are penalised not only for suboptimal actions but for the entire downstream state distribution those actions locked you into.

concepts.name: The coloring-contest metaphor for regret
concepts.one_line: A whimsical branching life-story — win the childhood coloring contest, reach Harvard, reach the Supreme Court, versus miss it and end up somewhere else entirely — used to make vivid that regret compares you to an irrecoverable optimal trajectory rather than to local decision quality.

concepts.name: PAC vs regret: which state distribution you are judged against
concepts.one_line: Regret holds you to the optimal policy's state distribution forever, while PAC holds you only to near-optimality within the state distribution your own algorithm actually induces — so PAC is 'making the most of the circumstances you got yourself into' and regret is the harsher criterion in continual online learning.

concepts.name: Episodic MDPs collapse the PAC/regret gap
concepts.one_line: When the MDP resets after H steps, PAC guarantees are stated with respect to the fixed start state (V*(s0) versus the value of what you actually do from s0), which is exactly what regret measures, so the two criteria converge; the gap is a phenomenon of non-resetting continual learning.

concepts.name: MBIE-EB as construction of an optimistic MDP
concepts.one_line: MBIE-EB builds maximum-likelihood empirical models R-hat and T-hat from counts, then defines a fictitious MDP M-tilde whose transitions are T-hat and whose reward is R-tilde(s,a) = R-hat(s,a) + beta/sqrt(n(s,a)), and plans optimally in that fictitious MDP.

concepts.name: Why MBIE-EB is the algorithm chosen for analysis
concepts.one_line: Among PAC-MDP algorithms it is the reward-bonus family that transfers cleanly to the model-free and deep settings, since a scalar bonus can simply be added to a Q-learning target, so it is worth analysing this one in detail.

concepts.name: Sufficient conditions for PAC: the three-part template
concepts.one_line: An algorithm satisfying (1) optimism, (2) accuracy with respect to a hybrid analysis MDP, and (3) bounded learning complexity is PAC; these are sufficient, not necessary, and are adapted from a general PAC-analysis paper that does not itself treat MBIE-EB.

concepts.name: Condition 1: optimism
concepts.one_line: The value the algorithm computes for the state-action pair it is about to take must, at every time step and with high probability, be at least the true optimal value for that pair minus epsilon.

concepts.name: Condition 2: accuracy
concepts.one_line: The value the algorithm computes must be within epsilon of the value of the policy it is actually executing, evaluated in a constructed hybrid MDP that is part optimistic model and part true model — this is what stops the algorithm from being trivially optimistic forever by never updating.

concepts.name: Why accuracy is needed at all
concepts.one_line: Optimism alone is trivially satisfiable by initialising all values enormously high and never learning; the accuracy condition forces the algorithm to actually incorporate data so that genuinely bad state-action pairs stop looking attractive.

concepts.name: Condition 3: bounded learning complexity
concepts.one_line: Both the total number of Q-value update sweeps and the total number of visits to state-action pairs classified as 'unknown' must be bounded by a function of epsilon and delta — the algorithm may not update or explore indefinitely.

concepts.name: Resulting sample complexity bound
concepts.one_line: If all three conditions hold, the algorithm is order-epsilon optimal on all but N steps where N is order (learning-complexity bound) divided by epsilon(1-gamma)^2, times logarithmic factors, and the learning-complexity bound itself carries the |S|, |A|, 1/epsilon and 1/delta dependence.

concepts.name: Epsilons in conditions 1-3 are the same epsilon
concepts.one_line: In answer to a student question, the epsilon in optimism, accuracy and the final guarantee is a single shared parameter (constants in front of it may differ), so an algorithm designer must satisfy all three at the same accuracy level.

concepts.name: MBIE-EB bonus and beta restated
concepts.one_line: The optimistic backup is Q-tilde(s,a) = R-hat(s,a) + beta/sqrt(n(s,a)) + gamma sum over s' of T-hat(s'|s,a) max over a' of Q-tilde(s',a'), with beta = (1/(1-gamma)) sqrt((1/2) log(2|S||A|m/delta)).

concepts.name: The m-sample data cap
concepts.one_line: Only the first m observations of each state-action pair are used to build R-hat and T-hat; all subsequent data for that pair is discarded, so each pair's estimator is updated at most m times.

concepts.name: Why the data cap exists, and why it is intellectually unsatisfying
concepts.one_line: Capping updates at m makes the total number of estimator events |S||A|m, which is finite and hence union-boundable; Brunskill flags that this violates Tom Mitchell's framing of machine learning as algorithms that keep improving with more data, notes practitioners use all the data anyway, and mentions later work with Tor Lattimore removing the restriction by replacing union bounds with sharper concentration.

concepts.name: Union bound
concepts.one_line: A device for guaranteeing that many individually high-probability events all hold simultaneously, by summing their failure probabilities — here across all state-action pairs and all m updates each.

concepts.name: Bellman-target samples X_i
concepts.one_line: For a fixed (s,a), define X_i = r_i + gamma V*(s_i') using the i-th observed reward and next state together with the true optimal value function; by construction E[X_i] = Q*(s,a), and V* need not be known since this object exists only inside the analysis.

concepts.name: Non-IID data in MDPs
concepts.one_line: Data collected in an MDP is not IID overall because which pairs get sampled depends on the algorithm's own history, but conditioned on visiting a particular (s,a) the reward and next state are IID by the Markov property — enough to apply Hoeffding, with martingale concentration as the technically careful alternative.

concepts.name: Hoeffding bound on the Bellman-target average
concepts.one_line: P(Q*(s,a) - (1/n) sum of X_i >= beta/sqrt(n(s,a))) <= exp(-2 beta^2 (1-gamma)^2), which at the chosen beta equals exactly delta/(2|S||A|m).

concepts.name: One-step deviation inequality after the union bound
concepts.one_line: With probability at least 1-delta, simultaneously for all t, s and a: R-hat(s,a) + gamma sum over s' of T-hat(s'|s,a) V*(s') - Q*(s,a) >= -beta/sqrt(n(s,a)) — i.e. one empirical Bellman backup applied to the true V* undershoots Q* by at most the bonus.

concepts.name: Proof that MBIE-EB is optimistic
concepts.one_line: By induction over value-iteration sweeps: base case Q-tilde_0(s,a) = 1/(1-gamma) >= Q*(s,a); assuming Q-tilde_i >= Q*, the next sweep gives Q-tilde_{i+1} = R-hat + gamma sum T-hat V-tilde_i + beta/sqrt(n) >= R-hat + gamma sum T-hat V* + beta/sqrt(n) >= (Q* - beta/sqrt(n)) + beta/sqrt(n) = Q*, where the last step is the deviation inequality rearranged.

concepts.name: Known state-action pairs
concepts.one_line: A pair is 'known' once it has been visited enough times that R-hat(s,a) and T-hat(.|s,a) are provably close to the true R(s,a) and T(.|s,a); the threshold is the line-in-the-sand that separates the exploited region from the region still needing exploration.

concepts.name: Simulation lemma
concepts.one_line: If an empirical model's transitions and rewards are close to the true ones, then the value functions computed in the two models are close — predictive error in the model propagates into a controlled amount of control error in the policy.

concepts.name: Hybrid analysis MDP M'
concepts.one_line: M' agrees with the true MDP's dynamics and rewards on all known state-action pairs and with the optimistic model M-tilde on all unknown ones; it does not exist physically and is purely a bridge in the inequality chain.

concepts.name: Hybrid analysis MDP M-hat'
concepts.one_line: M-hat' agrees with the empirical model M-hat on known pairs and with the optimistic model M-tilde elsewhere; note M-hat and M-tilde share the identical transition model T-hat and differ only by the reward bonus.

concepts.name: Pigeonhole argument for bounded learning complexity
concepts.one_line: Split experience into windows and ask the probability of reaching an unknown pair within the window: if that probability is small you are provably near-optimal on the known set, and if it is large you are rapidly consuming counts, but each pair only needs m counts before becoming known, so the high-probability case can recur at most on the order of |S||A|m times.

concepts.name: Explore-or-exploit dichotomy
concepts.one_line: At every step you are either acting near-optimally in a region you have good models for, or you are visiting something unknown and therefore gaining information you are guaranteed to need only m times per pair — so the number of genuinely bad decisions is finite.

concepts.name: Bayesian bandits recap and probability matching
concepts.one_line: Maintain a posterior over each arm's reward (Beta for Bernoulli rewards, with alpha and beta as counts of successes and failures), sample from it, and act greedily on the sample — this selects each arm with exactly the probability it is optimal, and empirically exploits faster than UCB.

concepts.name: Dirichlet prior over tabular transitions
concepts.one_line: In a tabular MDP each T(.|s,a) is a multinomial over next states, whose conjugate prior is a Dirichlet parameterised by a vector of pseudo-counts, one entry per possible next state — the natural multi-outcome generalisation of the Beta.

concepts.name: Thompson sampling / posterior sampling for MDPs (PSRL)
concepts.one_line: Place a prior over the dynamics and reward model of every state-action pair, sample a complete MDP from the posterior, solve it exactly for Q*, act greedily with respect to that Q* while collecting data, then update the posterior and repeat — far more computation per step than bandit Thompson sampling but often excellent empirically.

concepts.name: Attribution for posterior sampling work
concepts.one_line: Credited to Ben Van Roy's group at Stanford and his students Dan Russo (NYU) and Ian Osband (DeepMind), who often call the method posterior sampling rather than Thompson sampling.

concepts.name: Why polynomial-in-|S| bounds break under generalization
concepts.one_line: A sample-complexity bound polynomial in the size of the state space is vacuous when the state space is infinite or is the space of raw pixels, since it permits an infinite number of mistakes.

concepts.name: The theory gap for exploration with function approximation
concepts.one_line: Since off-policy control with function approximation lacks even asymptotic convergence guarantees, finite-sample exploration guarantees in that setting are largely absent; this is stated as an open, actively researched area rather than a solved one.

concepts.name: Counts do not generalize
concepts.one_line: Raw n(s,a) and n(s,a,s') counts are useless in pixel-scale state spaces because every observation is unique, so the count would remain one forever; what is needed is an uncertainty measure that shares credit across similar nearby states.

concepts.name: Candidate substitutes for counts
concepts.one_line: Density models over visited states, hash functions that bucket states and count bucket occupancy (with the hash function itself updated over time), and learned embeddings or state aggregations — noting that the right compression depends on which decisions you need to make and is therefore inherently non-stationary.

concepts.name: Why deep model-based RL underperforms
concepts.one_line: Model errors compound over a planning rollout, and a representation trained to minimise predictive loss is not necessarily the representation that supports good planning — illustrated by an early David Silver demo whose visually beautiful learned model was useless for planning.

concepts.name: Exploration bonus inside a model-free Q update
concepts.one_line: Add a bonus term for the visited state-action pair directly into the Q-learning or DQN update target, which is the model-free translation of MBIE-EB's optimistic reward and requires only that you can compute some uncertainty scalar per (s,a).

concepts.name: Bonus staleness in replay buffers
concepts.one_line: Bonuses are typically computed at the moment of visit, but MBIE-EB would recompute them as counts grow, so when a transition is later resampled from the replay buffer its stored bonus is stale and arguably should be refreshed.

concepts.name: Montezuma's Revenge as evidence for strategic exploration
concepts.one_line: A standard epsilon-greedy DQN had reached only about two rooms after 50 million frames, while the same agent augmented with a density-model exploration bonus (Bellemare's group) explored dramatically more of the game — the headline empirical case for principled exploration.

concepts.name: Thompson sampling over representations
concepts.one_line: Rather than sampling only model parameters, sample over state aggregations too — dynamically collapsing a large state space and treating the aggregation itself as a random object with a posterior; works but does not scale to the deep setting.

concepts.name: The difficulty of a posterior over Q*
concepts.one_line: Model-free Bayesian exploration requires a posterior over optimal value functions rather than over models, and it is not clear how to write such a posterior down even in the tabular case — an admitted open problem.

concepts.name: Bootstrapped DQN
concepts.one_line: Train an ensemble of Q-heads on bootstrap resamples of the replay data and act optimistically with respect to the ensemble, approximating a posterior over Q*; gives a real but, in her assessment, modest performance gain.

concepts.name: Bayesian linear regression on a fixed deep embedding
concepts.one_line: Freeze the deep network's penultimate representation and fit a Bayesian linear model on top — a very small amount of principled uncertainty machinery bolted onto a deep net, which is simple to implement and yields substantial gains in many cases.

concepts.name: Closing summary of what to retain
concepts.one_line: Understand why the exploration-exploitation tension is specific to RL, be able to state PAC and regret precisely, and be able to classify the algorithms covered against those criteria — noting explicitly that optimism-under-uncertainty methods serve both PAC and regret.

theorems_stated: Definition of a PAC RL algorithm: for inputs epsilon, delta, on all but N steps the algorithm's chosen action is within epsilon of optimal for the current state with probability at least 1-delta, with N polynomial in |S|, |A|, 1/(1-gamma), 1/epsilon, 1/delta.
Sufficient-conditions theorem: optimism + accuracy (against a hybrid MDP) + bounded learning complexity together imply the algorithm is PAC.

Sample complexity form: under those three conditions the algorithm is order-epsilon optimal on all but N = O~( zeta(epsilon,delta) / (epsilon (1-gamma)^2) ) steps up to log factors, where zeta is the learning-complexity bound.
Hoeffding-type deviation bound for Bellman targets: P( Q*(s,a) - (1/n) sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i >= beta/sqrt(n(s,a)) ) <= exp(-2 beta^2 (1-gamma)^2), where X_i = r_i + gamma V*(s_i').

Calibration of beta: with beta = (1/(1-gamma)) sqrt((1/2) log(2|S||A|m/delta)), the above tail probability equals exactly delta/(2|S||A|m), so a union bound over all |S||A|m estimator updates yields a delta/2 total failure probability.
Uniform one-step lemma: with high probability, for all t, s, a simultaneously, R-hat(s,a) + gamma sum_{s'} T-hat(s'|s,a) V*(s') - Q*(s,a) >= -beta/sqrt(n(s,a)).
Optimism of MBIE-EB: with that beta and optimistic initialization Q-tilde_0 = 1/(1-gamma), every value-iteration iterate satisfies Q-tilde_i(s,a) >= Q*(s,a) for all (s,a), with high probability.

Simulation lemma: if the empirical transition and reward models are close to the true ones, the value functions (and hence policies) computed from them are close to the true value functions — predictive error bounds control error.
Corollary of the simulation lemma: if every state-action pair is known, the value of the empirically-optimal policy evaluated in the empirical model is within a bound of its value in the true model.
MBIE-EB is a PAC-MDP algorithm.
Beta is the conjugate prior for Bernoulli rewards; Dirichlet is the conjugate prior for a multinomial transition distribution over next states.
Posterior sampling for MDPs implements probability matching (it selects each action with the probability that action is optimal under the posterior).
In episodic MDPs, PAC and regret guarantees come closer together because both are stated relative to a fixed start state.
Optimism-under-uncertainty algorithms yield guarantees under both the PAC and the regret criteria.
proofs_given: Full induction proof that MBIE-EB satisfies the optimism condition. Structure: (i) define X_i = r_i + gamma V*(s_i') as the i-th Bellman target for a fixed (s,a) and observe E[X_i] = Q*(s,a); (ii) apply Hoeffding to bound the probability that the empirical average of the X_i falls more than beta/sqrt(n) below Q*(s,a) by exp(-2 beta^2 (1-gamma)^2); (iii) substitute the specific beta so that this tail equals delta/(2|S||A|m), then union bound over all |S||A|m estimator updates to get a statement holding uniformly over t, s, a; (iv) rearrange to the one-step lemma R-hat + gamma sum T-hat V* >= Q* - beta/sqrt(n); (v) induct over value-iteration sweeps with base case Q-tilde_0 = 1/(1-gamma) >= Q*, using the inductive hypothesis to replace V-tilde_i by V*, then applying the one-step lemma so that the -beta/sqrt(n) from the lemma cancels the +beta/sqrt(n) bonus, giving Q-tilde_{i+1} >= Q*.
Verification that plugging beta = (1/(1-gamma)) sqrt((1/2) log(2|S||A|m/delta)) into exp(-2 beta^2 (1-gamma)^2) yields delta/(2|S||A|m) — done explicitly on the board.

Identification that (1/n(s,a)) sum_i X_i is algebraically the same empirical Bellman backup that MBIE-EB performs, except with the true V* in place of the algorithm's optimistic V-tilde — the observation that makes the induction go through.
proofs_skipped: The main sufficient-conditions theorem itself (optimism + accuracy + bounded learning complexity implies PAC) is asserted and attributed to a paper shown on a slide, with the explicit caveat that the cited paper does not analyse MBIE-EB and so 'things would have to be a little bit different'. No proof, and the modifications needed for MBIE-EB are never stated.

The derivation of the sample-complexity expression N = O~( zeta / (epsilon (1-gamma)^2) ) — where the 1/(epsilon(1-gamma)^2) factor comes from, and how zeta acquires its |S|, |A|, 1/epsilon, 1/delta dependence, is never shown.

The accuracy condition for MBIE-EB is never verified. She says explicitly 'I won't go through all of it in detail' and 'I'm very happy to talk about it offline'. The chain of inequalities relating V-tilde (computed), V^{pi_t}_{M'} (hybrid), V^{pi_t}_{M} (true) and V*(M) is set up conceptually but never carried out.

The simulation lemma is stated qualitatively only. No quantitative version is given: no explicit bound of the form ||V_M - V_M-hat||_inf <= f(epsilon_R, epsilon_T, gamma), and the characteristic 1/(1-gamma)^2 amplification is never derived. She notes students 'saw a little bit of this on the midterm' and moves on.

The knownness threshold m is never specified. It is repeatedly called 'some constant that we have not specified yet'. The relation m = poly(|S|, |A|, 1/epsilon, 1/delta, 1/(1-gamma)) that would make the whole argument close is never given.
The precise definition of 'close' for known pairs — the L1 or total-variation accuracy required of T-hat, and the accuracy required of R-hat, as a function of the target epsilon — is left implicit.

How the two hybrid MDPs M' and M-hat' are actually used: they are defined, but the sequence of add-and-subtract inequalities that uses them to bound the true value of the executed policy is described only as 'a series of inequalities' and never written.

Bounded learning complexity for MBIE-EB is only given as pigeonhole intuition. The formal explore-or-exploit lemma — that if the escape probability to unknown pairs over a horizon is below some threshold then the executed policy is epsilon-optimal in the true MDP — is asserted, not proved.
The bound on the total number of Q-value update sweeps is asserted to be 'very closely related' to the number of unknown-pair visits, but the actual counting argument is not given.
The choice of window length T over which the escape probability is measured, and how T relates to the effective horizon 1/(1-gamma) or to epsilon, is never specified.

Hoeffding is applied to data that is admittedly not IID (the visitation sequence depends on the algorithm's own history). She flags this as 'some technical details' and mentions martingale-based inequalities as the correct tool, but the martingale argument is not carried out.

The claim that the value-iteration fixed point (not merely each finite iterate) inherits optimism — i.e. taking the limit of the induction and invoking contraction of the optimistic Bellman operator — is never argued.

The base case Q-tilde_0 = 1/(1-gamma) >= Q* silently assumes rewards bounded in [0,1]; the reward-range assumption is never stated, nor is the corresponding range assumption on X_i that Hoeffding requires.

The claim that the m-sample data cap can be removed by 'using smarter things than union bounds' (joint work with Tor Lattimore and a student) is asserted with no sketch of the mechanism (time-uniform / mixture-martingale concentration).
The claim that in episodic MDPs PAC and regret guarantees become closer is given as an informal answer to a student question, with no formal reduction between the two criteria.

The claim that posterior sampling for MDPs implements probability matching is asserted by analogy with the bandit case; no argument is given that sampling a whole MDP and acting greedily yields action-selection probabilities equal to optimality probabilities.
No regret or PAC bound of any kind is stated or proved for Thompson sampling / PSRL in MDPs — only the algorithm and empirical praise.
Conjugacy of Beta-Bernoulli and Dirichlet-multinomial is asserted, never derived.
The claim that optimism-under-uncertainty algorithms give guarantees under both PAC and regret is asserted in the summary with no supporting argument.

The claim that model errors compound during planning (offered as the reason deep model-based RL underperforms) is anecdotal — no error-propagation bound over a rollout horizon is given, even though the simulation lemma discussed earlier is exactly the tool that would formalise it.

No guarantee whatsoever is offered for pseudo-count / density-model bonuses or hash-based count bonuses; their relation to the beta/sqrt(n) bonus that the optimism proof actually requires is never made precise.
The claim that bootstrapped DQN approximates posterior sampling over Q* is asserted; the bootstrap-as-posterior-approximation argument is not given.
The claim that Bayesian linear regression on a frozen embedding yields useful uncertainty is purely empirical; no analysis of when a fixed-representation linear posterior is calibrated is offered.
She explicitly states that a posterior over Q* is not known how to write down even in the tabular setting — an acknowledged open problem, flagged rather than resolved.
algorithms: MBIE-EB (Model-Based Interval Estimation with Exploration Bonus): maintain counts n(s,a) and n(s,a,s'); build MLE models R-hat and T-hat using only the first m samples per pair; solve, by value iteration to convergence, the fictitious MDP with transitions T-hat and rewards R-hat(s,a) + beta/sqrt(n(s,a)) where beta = (1/(1-gamma)) sqrt((1/2) log(2|S||A|m/delta)); act greedily with respect to the resulting Q-tilde.

Optimistic value iteration on the constructed MDP M-tilde: repeated application of Q-tilde_{i+1}(s,a) = R-hat(s,a) + beta/sqrt(n(s,a)) + gamma sum_{s'} T-hat(s'|s,a) max_{a'} Q-tilde_i(s',a'), initialised at Q-tilde_0 = 1/(1-gamma).

Known/unknown classification: label each (s,a) 'known' once its count crosses m so that R-hat and T-hat are provably close to R and T; use this partition both to define the hybrid analysis MDPs and to drive the explore-or-exploit dichotomy.
Thompson sampling for Bernoulli bandits (recap): maintain Beta(alpha_a, beta_a) per arm, sample a mean from each posterior, pull the argmax, update the corresponding alpha or beta.

Posterior Sampling for RL / Thompson sampling for MDPs (PSRL): place a Dirichlet prior on T(.|s,a) and a Beta (or other conjugate) prior on R(s,a) for every state-action pair; each iteration, draw a complete MDP from the joint posterior, solve it exactly for Q*, act greedily under that Q*, then update the posteriors with observed transitions and rewards.

Model-free exploration-bonus Q-learning / DQN: augment the Q-learning regression target (or the update itself) with a per-(s,a) bonus term reflecting uncertainty about future reward, the direct model-free analogue of MBIE-EB's optimistic reward.

Density-model pseudo-count bonuses (Bellemare et al.): fit a density model over observed states, convert its probability assignments into a pseudo-count, and derive an exploration bonus from that pseudo-count.
Hash-based count bonuses: hash high-dimensional states into discrete buckets, maintain counts over buckets, derive bonuses from bucket counts, and refine the hash function over time.

Thompson sampling over representations: treat the state aggregation itself as a random variable, sample a candidate aggregation together with model parameters from the joint posterior, and plan in the collapsed state space.

Bootstrapped DQN (Osband et al.): train K Q-function heads on bootstrap resamples of the replay data, giving an ensemble that stands in for a posterior over Q*, and act optimistically (or by sampling a head per episode) with respect to the ensemble.

Neural-linear / Bayesian last layer: freeze a deep network's penultimate embedding, fit Bayesian linear regression from that embedding to Q-values, and use the resulting posterior variance for Thompson sampling or optimistic action selection.
notation_introduced: epsilon: target optimality gap supplied as an input to a PAC algorithm
delta: allowed failure probability supplied as an input to a PAC algorithm
N: sample complexity — the number of time steps on which the algorithm is permitted to be worse than epsilon-optimal
zeta(epsilon, delta): the learning-complexity bound from condition 3, appearing in the numerator of N (she calls it 'sample complexity' informally)
C1, C2: deliberately unspecified constants used to signal that the bounds are stated up to constant factors
n(s,a): number of times state-action pair (s,a) has been visited
m: per-pair cap on the number of samples used to build the empirical model; also the number of times each pair's estimator may be updated
R-hat(s,a), T-hat(s'|s,a): maximum-likelihood empirical reward and transition models from counts
beta: bonus scale, beta = (1/(1-gamma)) sqrt((1/2) log(2|S||A|m/delta))
R-tilde(s,a) = R-hat(s,a) + beta/sqrt(n(s,a)): the optimistic reward (also written R-hat-prime)
Q-tilde, V-tilde: the optimistic action-value and value functions computed by MBIE-EB; Q-tilde_i denotes the i-th value-iteration iterate and V-tilde_i(s) = max_a Q-tilde_i(s,a)
M: the true MDP
M-hat: the purely empirical MDP with transitions T-hat and rewards R-hat
M-tilde: the optimistic MDP with transitions T-hat and rewards R-hat + bonus (same dynamics as M-hat, different reward)
K: the set of known state-action pairs
M-prime: hybrid MDP equal to the true (R, T) on pairs in K and to M-tilde elsewhere
M-hat-prime: hybrid MDP equal to the empirical (R-hat, T-hat) on pairs in K and to M-tilde elsewhere
X_i = r_i + gamma V*(s_i'): the i-th sampled Bellman target for a fixed (s,a), built from the true V*, with E[X_i] = Q*(s,a)
pi_t: the policy the algorithm is actually executing at time step t
V_t / Q_t: the value the algorithm computes at time t (used in the statements of the optimism and accuracy conditions)
Beta(alpha, beta): conjugate prior for Bernoulli rewards, with alpha counting observed 1s and beta counting observed 0s
Dirichlet(alpha_1, ..., alpha_{|S|}): conjugate prior for the multinomial transition distribution, with one pseudo-count entry per possible next state
notation_hazards: The PAC definition as written on the board conflates Q and V. She writes something like 'Q*(s_t, a_t) >= V*(s_t) - epsilon' and calls the left side 'the true optimal Q value of that action', which is impossible as stated (Q*(s,a) <= V*(s) always, with equality only for optimal actions). What is meant is the value of the algorithm's current policy or of the action it actually takes: V^{A_t}(s_t) >= V*(s_t) - epsilon, the standard Kakade-style definition. Notes must repair this.
The optimism condition is written with a 'V_t' on the left but indexed by both s_t and a_t; the object is a Q-value. V and Q are used interchangeably throughout the conditions.
Auto-caption renders V* as 'B star' repeatedly (and Q-tilde/Q-hat get swapped in places). Any transcript-derived formula containing 'B star' should read V*.
The sample complexity bound is spoken as 'divided by epsilon times 1 minus gamma squared'. The correct reading is epsilon * (1-gamma)^2 — the whole quantity (1-gamma) is squared, not (1 - gamma^2).

The Hoeffding exponent is spoken as 'exponential minus 2 beta squared, 1 minus gamma squared', i.e. exp(-2 beta^2 (1-gamma)^2). This is correct but only because the X_i are bounded in a range of width 1/(1-gamma) (assuming rewards in [0,1]) and the n from the deviation beta/sqrt(n) cancels against the n in Hoeffding's exponent. The reward-range assumption is never stated aloud and must be supplied.

beta is spoken as '1 over 1 minus gamma, square root of one half log 2 S, A, M divided by delta'. The intended expression is beta = (1/(1-gamma)) * sqrt( (1/2) * log( 2|S||A|m / delta ) ), with the 1/(1-gamma) outside the square root and the entire 2|S||A|m/delta inside the log. The capital 'M' in the caption is the sample cap m, not an MDP.

M-hat and M-tilde are near-homophones and the caption swaps them; a student asks about exactly this. The disambiguation is: M-hat = empirical model only; M-tilde = empirical model plus reward bonus. Crucially the two share the identical transition model T-hat and differ solely in the reward.

She says 'PAC can give much smaller regret' and immediately self-corrects. PAC and regret are different criteria measuring different things and their numeric values are not directly comparable; the intended point is that PAC's optimality gaps are measured locally and are therefore typically smaller than regret's globally-referenced gaps.

'MBIE' and 'MBIE-EB' are used interchangeably. Only MBIE-EB (the exploration-bonus variant with the additive beta/sqrt(n) term) is what the optimism proof actually analyses; plain MBIE uses confidence sets over the model instead.

The accuracy condition compares the algorithm's computed value against V^{pi_t} in the hybrid MDP M', not against V* and not against the true MDP. Getting this wrong collapses the whole point of introducing the hybrid MDPs.

In the induction, 'Q_i+1' and 'Q-tilde_i+1' both appear for the same object, and the index i runs over value-iteration sweeps, not over environment time steps — the same letter is used elsewhere in the lecture to index samples X_i of a state-action pair. Two distinct indices share the symbol i.

The 'total number of Q updates' in condition 3 means the number of times the algorithm re-runs optimistic value iteration (triggered by a model change), not the number of individual Bellman backups inside one value-iteration run.

Sutton and Barto do not cover PAC-MDP analysis, hybrid analysis MDPs, or the knownness construction at all; there is no S&B convention to reconcile against here, and readers coming from S&B will find the M', M-hat', K machinery entirely new.

animation_candidates.what: The regret-versus-PAC comparison, dramatised on the branching 'coloring contest' life-story tree
animation_candidates.why: This is the conceptual crux of the first third of the lecture and it is inherently about two different comparison brackets attached to two different trajectories through a tree — exactly the thing static text handles badly and a moving bracket handles well. Watching the regret bracket stay pinned to the root's optimal branch while the PAC bracket detaches and slides down to whatever node you currently occupy makes the distinction unforgettable in about fifteen seconds.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Branching state tree; two overlaid comparison brackets in different colours; animate one rollout, then sweep the PAC bracket node-by-node down the realised path while the regret bracket stays anchored to the optimal path from the root

animation_candidates.what: The optimism induction, with the +beta/sqrt(n) and -beta/sqrt(n) terms visibly annihilating
animation_candidates.why: The whole proof turns on a single cancellation that is easy to lose in a line of algebra. Rendering Q-tilde_{i+1} as a stacked bar and animating two substitutions in sequence — first swapping V-tilde_i for V* (inductive hypothesis, bar shrinks), then applying the one-step lemma (bar becomes Q* minus a red block) — and then having the red block slide into the green bonus block and both vanish, converts a three-line derivation into a physical event.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Term-level formula morph over stacked bars: Q-tilde_{i+1} decomposed into R-hat, gamma-T-hat-V-tilde_i, and bonus, with each substitution animated and the two beta/sqrt(n) blocks colliding and cancelling

animation_candidates.what: Confidence intervals collapsing at rate beta/sqrt(n), with the knownness threshold m drawn as a literal line in the sand
animation_candidates.why: Brunskill uses the phrase 'drawing a line in the sand' for the known/unknown boundary, and the entire bounded-learning-complexity argument depends on every pair eventually crossing it. Showing a grid of state-action cells, each with an error bar shrinking as its count ticks up and the cell flipping from red to green at m, makes the finiteness of the exploration budget visually obvious in a way the pigeonhole prose does not.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Grid-world of (s,a) cells, each with a shrinking confidence interval around Q-hat and a count meter; cells flip colour on crossing m; a global counter shows visits remaining out of |S||A|m

animation_candidates.what: The four MDPs — M, M-hat, M-tilde, M', M-hat' — as colour-coded state-action tables
animation_candidates.why: This is the single most confusing five minutes of the lecture and the part she explicitly declines to work through. A student asked mid-lecture just to disambiguate M-hat from M-tilde. A visual that lays out one table per MDP, cell-coloured by provenance (true / empirical / optimistic) and animates each hybrid literally borrowing rows from its two parents according to the known set K, resolves in one frame what several minutes of speech leaves murky.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Side-by-side state-action tables with per-cell provenance colouring; animate K growing and watch M' and M-hat' repaint cell-by-cell from optimistic to true/empirical

animation_candidates.what: The explore-or-exploit dichotomy as a rollout that either stays in the green region or punches into a red cell
animation_candidates.why: The pigeonhole argument is a case split, and case splits animate beautifully: run the same policy twice, once where every sampled trajectory stays inside the known set (annotate: near-optimal, no mistake charged) and once where it escapes into an unknown cell (annotate: mistake charged, but a count is consumed and the cell moves toward green). Repeating this until the budget exhausts shows why the mistake count must be finite.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Grid-world value sweep with two parallel rollouts, a shrinking |S||A|m budget bar, and per-episode annotations of which branch of the dichotomy fired

animation_candidates.what: Posterior sampling for MDPs: Dirichlet posteriors concentrating while sampled MDPs and their optimal policies converge
animation_candidates.why: PSRL is described in words but its distinctive feature — that a single draw commits you to a coherent whole-MDP hypothesis for an entire episode, which is what produces deep, temporally-extended exploration rather than dithering — is only visible when you watch the sampled models cluster over time. Contrasting a PSRL rollout against an epsilon-greedy rollout on the same chain shows the mechanism, not just the outcome.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Left panel: Dirichlet simplex per state-action with sampled points concentrating over episodes. Right panel: the greedy policy induced by each sampled MDP, drawn as arrows on a chain, stabilising as the posterior sharpens

animation_candidates.what: Simulation-lemma error propagation through the horizon
animation_candidates.why: She states that predictive error propagates into control error and calls it 'a really cool idea', then skips the quantitative version — leaving the characteristic 1/(1-gamma)^2 amplification invisible. Animating a small perturbation to T and watching value error compound backup by backup, with the discount factor's geometric series accumulating on screen, supplies exactly the intuition the skipped proof would have given.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Small chain MDP, model perturbation injected at one edge, then a backward value sweep with the error magnitude annotated per step and a running geometric-series tally converging to the bound

animation_candidates.what: Montezuma's Revenge room coverage, epsilon-greedy versus pseudo-count bonus, over 50M frames
animation_candidates.why: This is the lecture's one hard empirical result and its punchline for why any of the theory matters. A frame-counter driving a room map that fills in — two rooms and then stalling for the baseline, versus steady expansion for the bonus agent — is far more persuasive than the sentence 'it did much, much better'.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Room-connectivity map filling in over a scrubbing frame counter, two agents side by side

code_experiment_candidates: Implement MBIE-EB on RiverSwim (the canonical hard-exploration chain) and compare cumulative reward against epsilon-greedy, optimistic initialization, and a random policy. This is the reference implementation everything else in the lecture hangs off.

Directly falsify or confirm the optimism condition: run MBIE-EB, and after each optimistic value-iteration convergence check whether Q-tilde(s,a) >= Q*(s,a) holds for every pair (Q* computed exactly, since the MDP is known to the experimenter). Sweep beta downward and plot the fraction of violated pairs — this shows the proof's beta is sufficient but conservative, and finds the empirical breaking point.

Verify the Hoeffding calibration numerically: fix one (s,a), draw n samples of X_i = r_i + gamma V*(s_i'), and plot the empirical tail P(Q*(s,a) - mean(X) >= beta/sqrt(n)) against the theoretical exp(-2 beta^2 (1-gamma)^2). Reveals how much slack the bound carries.

Ablate the m-sample data cap — the intellectually unsatisfying device Brunskill flags explicitly. Run MBIE-EB that discards data past m samples per pair versus one that uses all data forever, and compare regret. Expect the theoretically-unsupported version to win, which is exactly her point.
Sweep m and plot the number of epsilon-mistake steps against it, looking for the predicted |S||A|m scaling. This makes the pigeonhole bound empirical.

Test the simulation lemma numerically: perturb T by a controlled total-variation distance alpha, compute ||V^pi_M - V^pi_{M'}||_inf exactly, and regress against alpha * gamma / (1-gamma)^2 to recover the amplification exponent the lecture skipped.

Implement PSRL with Dirichlet priors over transitions and Beta priors over Bernoulli rewards on the same chain MDP; compare regret curves against MBIE-EB and epsilon-greedy, and visualise posterior concentration. Also measure wall-clock per step to make concrete her remark that PSRL is far more computationally intensive than bandit Thompson sampling.

Isolate deep exploration: run PSRL and epsilon-greedy on Osband's 'deep sea' / N-chain, where epsilon-greedy requires time exponential in N and posterior sampling does not. Sweep N and plot episodes-to-solve on a log axis.

Build a hash-based count bonus on a small pixel gridworld and sweep hash granularity (from too-coarse, where distinct states collide and exploration stalls, to too-fine, where every state is unique and every count is one). Demonstrates the compression tradeoff she raises in response to a student question.

Implement a bootstrapped-DQN-style ensemble of Q-heads on a tabular or small-feature chain MDP and compare against a single head with epsilon-greedy; measure both performance and whether the ensemble spread actually tracks true value error (i.e. is the bootstrap posterior calibrated?).

Implement neural-linear: freeze a small network's penultimate layer, fit Bayesian linear regression on top, and use the posterior variance for Thompson sampling. Compare against the ensemble on the same task, measuring both performance and parameter/compute cost — this is the lecture's claim that a very small amount of uncertainty machinery buys most of the gain.

Replay-buffer bonus staleness experiment: compare storing the bonus at insertion time against recomputing it from current counts at sampling time, on a task with heavy replay reuse. Quantifies the subtlety she flags but does not resolve.
dated_or_superseded: The Strehl/Littman-era PAC-MDP bounds presented here are far from tight. For tabular episodic MDPs the minimax-optimal regret question was subsequently settled — UCBVI, EULER and successors achieve O~(sqrt(H S A T)) matching the lower bound — and modern analyses use Bernstein-style, variance-aware bonuses rather than the Hoeffding-style beta/sqrt(n) analysed here. Notes should present the beta/sqrt(n) proof as pedagogically canonical but quantitatively superseded.

The device of freezing each state-action estimator after m samples, purely so a union bound over |S||A|m events closes, is obsolete. Time-uniform concentration (law-of-iterated-logarithm bounds, mixture martingales, self-normalised bounds) lets modern proofs use all the data forever. Brunskill herself foreshadows this in the lecture as then-recent work with Tor Lattimore; it is now standard practice, not a novelty.

Her statement that there is 'relatively little theory' for exploration with function approximation was accurate in 2019 but is now the most dated claim in the lecture. Linear MDPs (LSVI-UCB), Eluder dimension, Bellman rank, bilinear classes and low-rank MDP theory subsequently produced a substantial body of provably sample-efficient exploration results under structural assumptions. The honest 2026 patch is that the gap has narrowed sharply under structure while remaining wide for general nonlinear function approximation.

Montezuma's Revenge is presented as an open hard-exploration frontier. It was effectively solved shortly after this lecture by Go-Explore, and by RND, Never Give Up and Agent57, which also cleared the broader Atari-57 hard-exploration set. The DQN-versus-pseudo-count comparison shown is a 2016-era result and should be labelled as historically motivating rather than current.

Her verdict that bootstrapped DQN 'is not incredibly effective' and 'gives you some performance gain' predates randomised prior functions (BootDQN+prior), which materially improved the method's ability to represent uncertainty in genuinely unvisited regions where a plain bootstrap collapses.

Bayesian linear regression on a frozen deep embedding is now a named, systematically benchmarked baseline ('neural-linear'), studied in the deep Bayesian bandits literature. Her framing of it as an informal trick that surprisingly works should be updated to reference the benchmark results, including its known failure mode when the frozen representation is stale relative to the current policy.

Posterior sampling for MDPs is presented with strong empirical praise but no theory. Regret analyses for PSRL now exist (Bayesian regret bounds from Osband and Van Roy, frequentist analyses from Agrawal and Jia), so the theoretical vacuum implied here has been partly filled.

Her assertion that model-free and policy-search methods dominate model-based deep RL 'in part because model errors accumulate' was already softening as she said it (she hedges 'it's starting to change recently'). It has since reversed substantially: MuZero, Dreamer-family latent world models, and modern MBPO-style hybrids are competitive or superior on many benchmarks, and learning models in latent rather than observation space directly addresses the David Silver anecdote she tells.

The teaser for the next lecture frames fast adaptation as meta-learning in the MAML sense. The dominant mechanism for rapid task adaptation in 2026 is in-context learning by large pretrained models, which reframes rather than refutes the meta-learning agenda but changes which algorithms a modern reader would reach for.

relevance_to_user_research.why: Genuinely useful but not critical, and useful for two specific transplants rather than for its main content. The transplantable parts: (1) The PAC-versus-regret distinction is the right framing device for how the node-level fidelity paper should state its guarantee. Their setting is offline-trained, evaluated on held-out queries, so the honest claim is PAC-flavoured ('after N labelled workflow executions, the assigner is within epsilon of the best achievable accuracy-cost tradeoff on the query distribution it induces'), not regret-flavoured. Brunskill's point that PAC judges you relative to the state distribution your own policy induces is precisely the caveat that matters when a cheap-model choice at node 1 changes the partial trace that node 3 conditions on — the assigner should not be blamed against a trace it never produces. (2) Bayesian linear regression on a frozen deep embedding (the last ten minutes) is the single most directly usable idea in the lecture. A Bayesian linear head on frozen Qwen2.5-7B embeddings of (query features, node position, partial trace) gives a calibrated per-node uncertainty at essentially zero marginal cost over the forward pass they are already paying, and 'escalate to Qwen2.5-72B where posterior variance over predicted node quality is high' is a defensible, cheap, implementable fidelity rule with a stated lineage. Bootstrapped-ensemble alternatives are strictly worse for them since they multiply inference cost, which is the exact resource they are trying to conserve. A third, weaker connection: the simulation lemma's 'predictive error propagates to control error' is conceptually the core question of node-level fidelity assignment — how does a weak model's degradation at an early node compound through the DAG into terminal accuracy loss — but the lecture states it without any quantitative form, so it is suggestive framing rather than a usable tool. What does not transfer, and this is most of the hour: the entire PAC-MDP proof apparatus (optimism induction, knownness thresholds, hybrid analysis MDPs, pigeonhole counting) is built for tabular, infinite-horizon, online continual learning where the bottleneck is covering an unknown state space. Their bottleneck is the opposite — the DAG structure is known and short (a handful of operators), the fidelity action set is tiny, and the hard part is generalising across queries, not exhausting state-space coverage. The beta/sqrt(n) bonus has no meaningful analogue when every query is unique. PSRL is worth one paragraph as a baseline for exploring fidelity assignments during workflow search (the per-node success probabilities are genuinely low-dimensional and Beta-conjugate, so it is cheap here in a way it is not in general RL), but it will not be the paper's method. Net: read for the last fifteen minutes and the PAC/regret framing; skim the proof, which is beautiful and will not appear in an ACL submission.

lecture_title: Batch (Offline) Reinforcement Learning and Safe Policy Improvement
one_paragraph_summary: This lecture builds the machinery for making decisions from a fixed, already-collected dataset of trajectories, with statistical guarantees attached before anything is deployed. Brunskill frames the goal as "safe policy improvement": produce an algorithm A mapping a dataset D to a policy such that P(V^{A(D)} >= V^{pi_b}) >= 1 - delta, where pi_b is the logging (behavior) policy. She decomposes this into three layers. First, off-policy policy evaluation: because the trajectory distribution under an evaluation policy pi_e differs from that under pi_b, reweight each logged trajectory by the ratio of its probabilities under the two policies; the initial-state, transition and reward factors cancel, leaving a pure product of action-probability ratios. The resulting importance-sampling estimator is unbiased and consistent, needs no dynamics or reward model, and — crucially — does not require the Markov assumption, since the environment factors cancel whether they depend on the last state or the whole history. Its validity requires coverage: pi_b(a|s) > 0 wherever pi_e(a|s) > 0. She then walks the variance-reduction ladder: per-decision IS (truncate each reward's weight product at the time that reward was earned, since the future cannot affect past rewards), weighted IS (self-normalize; biased but strongly consistent and much lower variance), control variates (X - Y + E[Y] preserves the mean and shrinks variance when 2Cov(X,Y) > Var(Y)), doubly robust (use a fitted Q as the control variate; robust to error in either the model or the behavior-policy estimate), weighted doubly robust, and MAGIC, which chooses the model/IS blend by directly minimizing an estimate of MSE — using the IS confidence interval to certify a *lower bound* on the model's bias. Gridworld results show roughly order-of-magnitude data savings per rung of the ladder. Second, high-confidence OPE: naively combining IS with Hoeffding is disastrous, because Hoeffding's range parameter is the largest possible weighted return, and weight products grow exponentially in the horizon — on mountain car with 100k trajectories the bound is about -5 million when the true value is 0.19 and all returns lie in [0,1]. Phil Thomas's fix is to discard the extreme upper tail of the weighted returns: this can only depress the estimate, so the resulting bound stays valid while becoming informative (0.145 against a true 0.19), with the truncation threshold tuned on a held-out split. Third, safe policy improvement: search over candidate policies, compute lower confidence bounds, and deploy only when a candidate's lower bound clears the incumbent — otherwise the algorithm is allowed, and expected, to refuse. Applications discussed are digital marketing with Adobe, a diabetes/insulin simulator, and intelligent tutoring; the closing survey lists long horizons, IS "unfairness" across candidate policies, unknown behavior policies, non-stationarity, and transfer as open problems.
prerequisites: MDP formalism: states, actions, transition and reward models, policies, discounting
Return G_t and value V^pi as an expectation over trajectories
Monte Carlo policy evaluation and why on-policy averaging of returns is unbiased
The on-policy / off-policy distinction, and why Q-learning is off-policy
Why bootstrapping introduces bias (Q-learning vs Monte Carlo), and the bias-variance tradeoff
Policy gradients, in particular the baseline trick and the 'future cannot affect past rewards' argument used in REINFORCE variance reduction
Hoeffding's inequality and concentration bounds, as introduced in the exploration/bandit lectures
Basic probability: change of measure, expectation of a ratio, variance and covariance algebra
Imitation learning's state-action distribution matching idea (referenced as an analogy)

concepts.name: Course admin: two-part quiz, projects, poster session
concepts.one_line: Upcoming quiz is split into an individual portion followed by a group portion in two assigned rooms, covers the whole course (meta-RL lightly), is multiple choice, and last year's quiz is recommended as forced-recall practice; assignments are done so effort should shift to projects, with the poster session on the last day of finals.

concepts.name: Motivating example: which order of tutoring activities for a new student?
concepts.one_line: Group A does a fractions-addition problem then cross-multiplication and averages 95 on an exam; group B does the same two activities in the reverse order and averages 92; deciding what to give a new student surfaces the need for sample sizes, variance, distributional shape, and who was actually in each group.

concepts.name: Censored / counterfactual data
concepts.one_line: Logged data reveals the outcome only for the action that was actually taken, so the counterfactual outcome under the alternative ordering for the same students is permanently unobservable — this is the fundamental obstacle in batch RL.

concepts.name: Need for generalization across states and actions
concepts.one_line: Even a two-action tutoring problem has a combinatorial space of activity orderings and a state space as large as one's model of a student, so one cannot run an experiment per policy and must generalize across states, actions, or both.

concepts.name: Batch (offline) reinforcement learning
concepts.one_line: The setting where a dataset D of trajectories has already been collected by someone else under a behavior policy pi_b, and the learner must produce a better policy without any further interaction — distinct from online off-policy algorithms like Q-learning that still choose their own data.

concepts.name: Application domains
concepts.one_line: Batch RL is the operative regime in healthcare (sequences of treatments maximizing quality-adjusted life years), education, equipment maintenance scheduling, digital marketing, and the counterfactual questions asked in economics, statistics and epidemiology.

concepts.name: Safety as high-confidence performance, not safe exploration
concepts.one_line: In this lecture 'safe' means being able to state a confidence bound on expected performance before deployment, as opposed to safe exploration (avoiding online mistakes) or risk sensitivity (caring about the return distribution rather than its mean).

concepts.name: Notation for batch RL
concepts.one_line: pi is a policy, tau or H or h_j a trajectory, D the logged dataset, pi_b the behavior policy that generated D, pi_e the evaluation (target) policy, and A(D) the possibly stochastic algorithm mapping data to a deployed policy.

concepts.name: When is the behavior policy known?
concepts.one_line: pi_b is known when decisions were made by logged software (ad serving, an RL or supervised agent) or by a codified protocol (a maintenance plan followed to the letter, an explicit clinical guideline), and unknown when humans such as doctors generated the data — humans neither randomize nor record if-then rules.

concepts.name: Safe policy improvement objective
concepts.one_line: The design goal is an algorithm satisfying P(V^{A(D)} >= V^{pi_b}) >= 1 - delta, with the option of demanding V^{pi_b} + Delta instead, since changing a real protocol carries fixed overhead and requires being not merely better but meaningfully better.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo estimation of the behavior policy's value
concepts.one_line: Because D was generated on-policy with respect to pi_b, V^{pi_b} is estimated without any reweighting by averaging the observed returns over the n logged episodes.

concepts.name: Three-stage pipeline for safe batch RL
concepts.one_line: Stage 1 is off-policy policy evaluation (estimate V^{pi_e} from D), stage 2 is high-confidence OPE (put a valid confidence bound on that estimate), stage 3 is safe policy improvement (argmax over candidate policies of a lower confidence bound, with the option to decline).

concepts.name: Algorithms that know their own limitations
concepts.one_line: A safe-improvement algorithm must be able to answer 'no policy I can certify is better' when the data is too thin — with one student per arm, honest refusal is the correct output, which matters for human-in-the-loop deployment.

concepts.name: Why not just run Q-learning on the batch?
concepts.one_line: Q-learning is off-policy but it both samples and bootstraps, so its estimate can be systematically biased at finite sample sizes; the lecture instead wants an unbiased estimator whose confidence intervals are easier to justify.

concepts.name: Distribution mismatch over trajectories
concepts.one_line: Different policies induce different distributions over full trajectories (state, action, reward, next state, ...), and if two policies induced identical trajectory distributions they would trivially have identical values — so the entire difficulty is the mismatch itself, not that the policies differ.

concepts.name: Importance sampling for a generic distribution mismatch
concepts.one_line: E_q[f(x)] = integral q(x) f(x) dx = integral p(x) [q(x)/p(x)] f(x) dx, estimated by (1/n) sum_i [q(x_i)/p(x_i)] f(x_i) with x_i drawn from p — a pure reweighting of the samples one actually has.

concepts.name: Trajectory probability factorization
concepts.one_line: P(h_j | pi) = P(s_0) times the product over t of pi(a_t|s_t) P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) P(r_t|s_t,a_t), where only the policy factor depends on which policy is being considered.

concepts.name: Cancellation of dynamics and reward models in the IS ratio
concepts.one_line: Forming P(h_j|pi_e)/P(h_j|pi_b) makes the initial-state distribution, transition model and reward model cancel term by term, leaving only the product of action-probability ratios pi_e(a_t|s_t)/pi_b(a_t|s_t).

concepts.name: Ordinary importance-sampling OPE estimator
concepts.one_line: V-hat^{pi_e} = (1/n) sum over trajectories j of [product over t of pi_e(a_jt|s_jt)/pi_b(a_jt|s_jt)] times G_j, the return of trajectory j.

concepts.name: IS does not require the Markov assumption
concepts.one_line: Because the environment's dynamics and reward model are the same under both policies whether they depend on the last state or on the entire history, they cancel regardless, so the IS estimator is valid in non-Markov settings — important since recorded patient or student features are rarely Markov.

concepts.name: Upweight/downweight intuition
concepts.one_line: Each logged trajectory's return is scaled up if the evaluation policy would have produced that trajectory more often than the behavior policy did, and scaled down otherwise, so that averaging the reweighted returns recovers the expectation under pi_e.

concepts.name: Coverage / support assumption
concepts.one_line: IS is valid only if pi_b(a|s) > 0 for every (s,a) with pi_e(a|s) > 0; pi_b may be zero wherever pi_e is also zero, and pi_b cannot be zero on anything actually observed, but it can be tiny.

concepts.name: Coverage as a ball of evaluable policies
concepts.one_line: In practice the behavior policy defines a neighborhood of policies one can evaluate — a random behavior policy on Montezuma's Revenge never reaches most states, so almost no interesting evaluation policy is covered without an enormous dataset.

concepts.name: IS is unbiased and consistent
concepts.one_line: Under coverage, the ordinary IS estimator has expectation exactly V^{pi_e} and converges to V^{pi_e} as the number of trajectories grows without bound; the lecture credits Precup (2000) with introducing this to RL.

concepts.name: Per-decision importance sampling
concepts.one_line: Rather than multiplying the whole discounted return by the full-trajectory weight, weight each reward r_t only by the product of ratios up to time t, since actions taken after t cannot have influenced r_t; still unbiased, strictly lower variance, and still Markov-free.

concepts.name: Weighted (self-normalized) importance sampling
concepts.one_line: Normalize by the sum of the importance weights rather than by n, which effectively confines the effective weights to [0,1]; the estimator becomes biased but is strongly consistent and empirically far lower-variance, especially at small n.

concepts.name: Importance weights grow exponentially in the horizon
concepts.one_line: If per-step behavior probabilities are small, the product of L ratios can be astronomically large — the lecture states a proof exists that weight magnitude generally grows exponentially with horizon length.

concepts.name: When is it acceptable to reintroduce bias?
concepts.one_line: Unbiasedness makes confidence intervals easy to construct, so it is preferred when bounds are the goal; when raw accuracy is the goal one should optimize MSE directly, and biased-but-consistent is a reasonable middle ground, unlike Q-learning with function approximation where even asymptotic behavior is unguaranteed.

concepts.name: Control variates
concepts.one_line: For random variables X and Y, mu-hat = X - Y + E[Y] has the same expectation as X, and its variance Var(X) + Var(Y) - 2Cov(X,Y) is smaller than Var(X) exactly when 2Cov(X,Y) exceeds Var(Y) — so a correlated Y buys variance reduction for free.

concepts.name: Doubly robust off-policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: Take X to be the IS estimator and Y a control variate built from an estimated Q function (from a fitted MDP model, or from Q-learning on the batch), yielding an estimator that remains reliable if either the model is good or the behavior-policy estimate is good.

concepts.name: Provenance of doubly robust estimators
concepts.one_line: Long-standing in statistics, imported into the machine-learning contextual-bandit literature around 2011 by Dudik and coauthors, and extended to sequential RL (including weighted variants) by Thomas and Brunskill, ICML 2016.

concepts.name: Gridworld empirical comparison of OPE estimators
concepts.one_line: On a roughly 4x4 or 5x5 gridworld, MSE versus dataset size on log-log axes shows model-based OPE flat at an asymptotic bias floor, ordinary IS decreasing, per-decision IS shifted down, doubly robust down again, and weighted variants best; to reach MSE = 1 per-decision IS needs about 2000 episodes, doubly robust under 200, and weighted doubly robust roughly 5.

concepts.name: MSE as a data-efficiency statement
concepts.one_line: The right way to read the MSE curves is horizontally rather than vertically: a better estimator means an order of magnitude fewer episodes to reach a target accuracy, which is what matters when only a few hundred patients have the condition of interest.

concepts.name: MAGIC: directly minimizing estimated MSE
concepts.one_line: Since MSE decomposes into squared bias plus variance, blend model-based and importance-sampling estimates by explicitly estimating both terms and minimizing their sum, rather than picking a rung on the bias-variance ladder by hand.

concepts.name: Lower-bounding the model's bias from an IS confidence interval
concepts.one_line: If IS gives a valid interval of, say, 5 plus or minus 2 and the model-based estimate is 8, then the true value lies in [3,7] and the model's bias is at least 1 — an optimistic but computable lower bound on bias that MAGIC uses as its bias surrogate.

concepts.name: Deferred: better weightings and non-stationarity
concepts.one_line: Improved weighting schemes beyond weighted IS exist and are skipped, as is the practically important problem of detecting non-stationary dynamics in logged data — e.g. a dietary guideline change mid-dataset alters patient dynamics.

concepts.name: High-confidence off-policy policy evaluation
concepts.one_line: Beyond a point estimate of V^{pi_e}, produce a lower bound that holds with probability at least 1 - delta, using the same concentration machinery that supplied optimistic upper bounds in the exploration lectures but pointed downward.

concepts.name: Hoeffding applied to IS returns is vacuous
concepts.one_line: On mountain car with 100,000 trajectories and a true evaluation-policy value of 0.19, IS plus Hoeffding certifies only that the value exceeds about -5 million, which is true but useless given that all returns lie in [0,1].

concepts.name: Why the Hoeffding bound explodes
concepts.one_line: Hoeffding's width scales with the range b of the quantity being averaged, and here that quantity is the weighted return, so b is the maximum of G times the weight product; with a per-step behavior probability near 0.1 and trajectories of length about 200, b can be of order 10^200.

concepts.name: Truncating the upper tail of weighted returns
concepts.one_line: Discarding the extreme upper tail of the weighted returns can only lower the estimated mean, so the resulting bound can only be conservative — an underestimate is safe for deployment decisions, costing at most a missed opportunity rather than a harmful rollout.

concepts.name: Tuning the truncation threshold on a data split
concepts.one_line: Use roughly 20 percent of the data to select the truncation level defining the conservative confidence interval, then compute the lower bound on the remainder.

concepts.name: Mountain car result with the truncated bound
concepts.one_line: With the same 100,000 trajectories, the truncated-return bound certifies the evaluation policy is worth at least 0.145 against a true 0.19 — tight enough to justify replacing a behavior policy worth 0.05 — whereas Chernoff-Hoeffding and the other classical inequalities except Anderson's remain vacuous.

concepts.name: t-test based confidence bounds
concepts.one_line: An alternative to distribution-free concentration inequalities is a Student t-test on the weighted returns, which is only approximately valid but is frequently much tighter in practice.

concepts.name: Safe policy improvement by data splitting
concepts.one_line: Spend part of the data searching over candidate policies and computing lower bounds, then use held-out data to verify the chosen candidate's lower bound clears the behavior policy's value before deploying — otherwise decline to deploy.

concepts.name: Deployed applications
concepts.one_line: The framework was applied to digital marketing with collaborators at Adobe, where the bounds were tight enough to certify a genuinely higher-revenue policy, and to insulin regulation on a diabetes simulator.

concepts.name: Open problems in batch RL
concepts.one_line: Remaining challenges include long horizons, the 'unfairness' that different candidate policies carry different estimator variance depending on how well they match pi_b, unknown behavior policies, combining these estimators with deep networks, and transfer or fine-tuning of evaluation models across related datasets.

concepts.name: Stated learning objectives
concepts.one_line: Students should be able to define and apply importance sampling, name its limitations, list alternatives, motivate safe RL applications, and state precisely what kind of guarantee these methods deliver.

theorems_stated: If two policies induce identical distributions over trajectories, they have identical value, regardless of whether the policies themselves differ.
The trajectory likelihood ratio P(h|pi_e)/P(h|pi_b) equals the product over timesteps of pi_e(a_t|s_t)/pi_b(a_t|s_t): the initial-state distribution, transition model and reward model cancel exactly.
The cancellation, and hence the validity of the IS estimator, does not require the Markov property; it holds for arbitrarily history-dependent dynamics and reward distributions.
Under the coverage condition, the ordinary importance-sampling OPE estimator is unbiased for V^{pi_e}.
Under the coverage condition, the ordinary importance-sampling OPE estimator is consistent: as n tends to infinity the estimate converges to V^{pi_e}.
Coverage/support condition: pi_b(a|s) > 0 is required for every state-action pair with pi_e(a|s) > 0; pairs where both are zero cause no problem.
Per-decision importance sampling remains unbiased while having variance no greater than ordinary importance sampling, because a reward at time t is independent of the action ratios after time t.
The magnitude of importance-sampling weights generally grows exponentially with the horizon (asserted as a proved result of Thomas and Brunskill).
Weighted importance sampling is biased but strongly consistent under conditions such as finite horizon, a single behavior policy, and bounded rewards (attributed to Thomas and Brunskill, ICML 2016).
