Deliberately violate coverage - set pi_b(a|s) = 0 for an action pi_e takes with positive probability - and observe that every IS variant silently returns a confidently wrong number; then add an effective-sample-size diagnostic (1 / sum of squared normalized weights) that detects the failure before it propagates.

Replace the true pi_b with one estimated by behavior cloning from the same logs and compare MSE of every estimator, testing the counterintuitive claim that the estimated propensities can outperform the true ones.

Run the full safe policy improvement loop end to end: search a parameterized policy class on split 1, certify on split 2, deploy or abstain, and over many independent datasets measure the empirical probability of returning a policy that is actually worse than pi_b (should not exceed delta). Then repeat while certifying on the SAME split used for search to demonstrate how badly the guarantee breaks.

Directly relevant to the user's own work: treat logged agentic-workflow executions as trajectories, with the per-node fidelity choice as the action and terminal accuracy minus lambda times token cost as the return, then use PDIS and WDR to estimate the value of a candidate node-level fidelity policy purely offline, and validate the OPE estimate against a small online rollout on the actual cluster.
dated_or_superseded: The OPE toolkit here stops at MAGIC (2016). Marginalized importance sampling / stationary-distribution correction methods (DualDICE 2019, GenDICE and GradientDICE 2020) estimate a state-visitation density ratio instead of a product of per-step ratios, which is precisely the fix for the exponential-in-horizon curse that dominates the second half of this lecture and that she flags as an open problem at the end.

Offline RL exploded as a field immediately after this lecture. Conservative and pessimistic value learning (BCQ 2019, CQL 2020, IQL 2021), behavior-constrained policy optimization (BRAC, TD3+BC), and model-based offline RL (MOPO, MOReL 2020) are now the standard practical approaches. IS-plus-confidence-bound certification is one branch among several rather than the default, and in 2026 pessimism baked into value estimation is far more common than post hoc concentration bounds.

The theoretical framing of coverage has moved on. The all-states-all-actions condition pi_b(a|s) > 0 wherever pi_e(a|s) > 0 has been replaced by single-policy concentrability and pessimism-based analyses (Rashidinejad et al. 2021, Xie et al. 2021, Jin et al. 2021), which require coverage only of the comparator policy and yield bounds that degrade gracefully rather than becoming invalid.

The bespoke Gridworld benchmark has been superseded by standardized suites: D4RL (2020) for offline RL and the Deep OPE / DOPE benchmarks for off-policy evaluation specifically, which is where any modern reproduction of these MSE comparisons should live.

Sequence-model formulations of offline RL - Decision Transformer and Trajectory Transformer (2021) and their successors - reframe batch RL as return-conditioned sequence modelling and sidestep importance weighting entirely. Completely absent here, and now a major branch.

Unknown-behavior-policy OPE, flagged as ongoing lab work, is now routine: estimate propensities by behavior cloning, then clip or self-normalize. The Peter Stone result she alludes to (estimated propensities beating true ones) is the well-understood variance-reduction phenomenon from the causal-inference literature (Hirano, Imbens and Ridder 2003) and should be presented as established rather than as a curiosity.

The specific concentration machinery has largely fallen out of practical use. Anderson's inequality and the tail-truncated bound are rarely deployed in 2026; empirical Bernstein bounds and studentized/BCa bootstrap intervals dominate because they adapt to the empirical variance rather than the worst-case range.

Non-stationarity detection, mentioned as their in-progress work, has since matured into a literature on distribution shift detection and time-varying OPE (Chandak et al. 2020-2021 on non-stationary policy evaluation and optimization).

For LLM-agent work in particular, these estimators are alive but relabelled: offline evaluation of prompting, routing and tool-use policies uses exactly IPS and doubly robust estimators, and the RLHF/DPO family is offline policy optimization under a KL constraint to a behavior policy - structurally the same 'stay near pi_b so the estimate stays valid' idea, arrived at from a different direction.

relevance_to_user_research.why: This is the one lecture in CS234 whose machinery can go into the user's paper more or less directly, for four concrete reasons. (1) Their node-level fidelity assignment is a finite-horizon MDP with H equal to the DAG depth, and every candidate fidelity policy they want to compare costs real A100 hours and tokens to evaluate online. Off-policy evaluation from logged workflow executions is exactly the tool that lets them score many candidate policies without re-running each one, and their horizon (roughly 3-10 nodes) is short enough that the exponential importance-weight blowup which ruins the mountain-car example is genuinely manageable for them - the regime where IS actually works is their regime, not the lecture's cautionary one. Per-decision IS plus doubly robust is the right estimator family here. (2) Their earlier AEP query-level routing is literally the H=1 case, where trajectory IS degenerates to the standard inverse-propensity-score estimator and DR degenerates to Dudik, Langford and Li's contextual-bandit doubly robust estimator - the exact reference this lecture cites. So the lecture supplies a single formalism that subsumes both their old and new problem settings, which is a genuinely useful framing for the paper's related-work and method sections. (3) The coverage/support condition is a hard, actionable constraint on their data collection, not an abstraction. If AFlow's search logs always assigned the strong model to a given operator type, they have zero support for evaluating any policy that assigns the weak model there, and every IS estimator will return a confidently wrong number with no error raised. This argues concretely for injecting deliberate randomization (epsilon-stochastic fidelity assignment) during log collection and for reporting an effective-sample-size diagnostic - a cheap change that materially strengthens the work. (4) The safe policy improvement framing maps onto a stronger and more honest empirical claim than the usual accuracy table: 'our learned fidelity policy beats the all-strong-model baseline with 95% confidence on held-out queries, at X% of the token cost', with an explicit abstention when the data does not support the claim. ARR reviewers reward that kind of certified comparison. Two honest caveats. First, the lecture assumes pi_b is known and stochastic; if their logs came from a deterministic heuristic they will need the estimated-propensity or model-based route instead, which the lecture defers. Second, the elaborate tail-truncation concentration machinery in the second half is over-engineered for a horizon of 5, so they should take the DR/WDR estimators and the coverage discipline seriously and reach for a studentized bootstrap rather than Anderson's inequality for the confidence intervals.

lecture_title: L16 - Monte Carlo Tree Search (and model-based RL / course wrap-up)
one_paragraph_summary: This is the final lecture of the course and it does two things: it rehabilitates model-based RL as a first-class tool, then builds Monte Carlo Tree Search on top of it as the decision-time planning method behind AlphaGo. The model-based half argues that once you fit an approximate transition/reward model you own a simulator, and a simulator lets you do anything — dynamic programming, Q-learning on synthetic rollouts, policy search — plus zero-shot transfer when only the reward changes. It pays for this with two stacked approximation errors (model error and planning error) that compound in the same way behavior-cloning error compounds under distribution shift. The AB example is re-used to draw the sharp line: batch TD converges to the value of the maximum-likelihood (certainty-equivalence) MDP because it assumes Markov, while batch Monte Carlo converges to the minimum-MSE fit to the observed returns because it does not. The planning half then walks a ladder of decision-time algorithms of increasing sophistication: full forward search over an expectimax tree (correct, but leaves grow like (|S||A|)^H and it wastefully refuses to merge identical states); simulation-based search, which samples single trajectories from the model and runs model-free RL on them; simple Monte Carlo search, which rolls out each candidate first action under a fixed policy and takes the argmax — exactly one step of policy improvement; and finally MCTS, which grows a partial, deliberately asymmetric tree using a statistics-driven tree policy inside the tree and a cheap (often random) rollout policy beyond its frontier, backing up plain averages of returns. UCT instantiates the tree policy by treating every tree node as its own independent bandit and adding a UCB-style optimism bonus. The lecture closes with an honest critique of that choice — optimism is the right idea when bad actions actually hurt you, but in planning you suffer nothing for simulating a bad action, so the correct objective is information gain about the root argmax, not cumulative regret — and with Go-specific material: sparse win/loss reward, minimax instead of expectation at opponent nodes, and self-play as both a bootstrapping trick for sparse reward and an automatic curriculum.
prerequisites: MDP formalism: states, actions, transition and reward models, discounting, finite vs infinite horizon
Bellman expectation and Bellman optimality equations; value iteration and policy iteration
Monte Carlo and TD(0) policy evaluation, including their batch/infinite-replay behaviour on a fixed dataset
The policy improvement theorem (used implicitly to justify simple Monte Carlo search)
Q-learning, replay buffers, and the distinction between model-free and model-based methods
Multi-armed bandits, UCB1, Hoeffding-style confidence intervals, and cumulative regret
Optimism under uncertainty as an exploration principle, including count-based bonuses in MDPs
Imitation learning / behavior cloning and its compounding distribution-shift error (invoked as an analogy)
Basic supervised learning: regression, density estimation, maximum likelihood, function-approximation vs estimation error

concepts.name: Course logistics and wrap-up admin
concepts.one_line: Final lecture housekeeping: project write-up and poster deadlines with no late days, quiz grades being returned, no office hours during finals week, pointers to follow-on RL courses (Kochenderfer, Van Roy, Brunskill's advanced seminar), and ten minutes reserved for course evaluations.

concepts.name: Why MCTS: AlphaGo as motivation
concepts.one_line: Beating human professionals at Go arrived far sooner than the field expected, and MCTS was one of the load-bearing components; it is also the natural entry point into model-based RL, which the course has otherwise underplayed because deep model learning had not yet produced comparable wins.

concepts.name: Model-based reinforcement learning
concepts.one_line: Rather than learning a value function or policy directly from data, fit an approximate transition model and/or reward model from experience and then plan with it; planning here means any method that maps a known model to a decision, not just dynamic programming.

concepts.name: A learned model is a simulator
concepts.one_line: Once you have a model you can generate unlimited synthetic experience, so any model-free algorithm (Q-learning, policy search, Monte Carlo) becomes a planning algorithm applied to fake data; the whole approach is only as good as the simulator.

concepts.name: Reward known, dynamics unknown
concepts.one_line: In many deployed systems the reward is a design choice you already know (engagement, purchases, task success), so the hard learning problem is almost always the dynamics model of the environment or user, not the reward.

concepts.name: The model-based RL loop
concepts.one_line: Collect (s,a,r,s') tuples from the real world, fit a model, plan with that model, emit the next action, execute it, and repeat — crucially the planner only has to output the next action, not a complete value function or global policy, which is the loophole MCTS exploits.

concepts.name: Compounding approximation error
concepts.one_line: Model-based RL stacks two errors — an approximate model and then approximate planning inside it — and following the resulting policy can drive you into regions where the model was never trained, exactly the escalating-error failure mode of behavior cloning under distribution shift.

concepts.name: Zero-shot transfer under reward change
concepts.one_line: A dynamics model is reward-agnostic, so if the goal changes (a different exit, a different +1) you re-plan against the same learned dynamics and get a new policy with no additional environment interaction.

concepts.name: Model learning as supervised learning
concepts.one_line: Fitting a model is a regression problem for the (usually scalar) reward plus a conditional density estimation problem for the (stochastic) next state, both conditioned on (s,a) under the Markov assumption; the default objective here is maximum likelihood, though non-MLE losses have proved useful elsewhere.

concepts.name: Tabular MLE model = counting
concepts.one_line: In the discrete case the maximum-likelihood model is just normalized transition counts, P-hat(s'|s,a) = N(s,a,s')/N(s,a), with R-hat(s,a) the empirical mean of rewards observed for that state-action pair.

concepts.name: The AB example
concepts.one_line: Eight episodes of a two-state Markov reward process: one episode goes A with reward 0 then B with reward 0, and the remaining episodes start in B yielding reward 1 six times and 0 twice, so the empirical value of B is 0.75 while A was observed exactly once with return 0.

concepts.name: Batch TD converges to the certainty-equivalence model
concepts.one_line: Running tabular TD(0) to convergence by replaying a fixed dataset indefinitely produces exactly the value function you would get by building the maximum-likelihood MDP from that data and solving it, giving V(A)=0.75 here because TD bootstraps through B and assumes the Markov property.

concepts.name: Batch Monte Carlo converges to the minimum-MSE fit
concepts.one_line: Batch Monte Carlo instead minimizes squared error against the observed returns and makes no Markov assumption, so it reports V(A)=0 (the single return ever seen from A) and V(B)=0.75, disagreeing with TD precisely because it refuses to chain evidence across states.

concepts.name: Sample-based planning from a learned model
concepts.one_line: Draw synthetic transitions from the fitted model and run model-free learning on them; the Markov structure lets you splice together state-action pairs that never co-occurred in the real data (e.g. A to B to reward 1), which is precisely how Monte Carlo on simulated data recovers the TD answer on real data.

concepts.name: Confirmation bias from refitting on your own samples
concepts.one_line: Feeding model-generated transitions back into model estimation as if they were real observations inflates confidence without adding information, since the samples carry only what the model already believed.

concepts.name: Quantifying confidence in a learned model
concepts.one_line: Hoeffding-style intervals over per-(s,a) reward and transition estimates give you a handle on how much to trust simulated data, and those intervals can be propagated into planning as bonuses in exactly the way the exploration lectures did.

concepts.name: Function-approximation error vs estimation error
concepts.one_line: Conditioning a model on the full history is trivially Markov but starves each estimate of data, while a compact Markov state gives plenty of data per parameter at the price of possible misspecification — every model class choice is a position on this tradeoff.

concepts.name: Bad model, possibly still good policy
concepts.one_line: Planning only needs the correct ordering of Q(s,a1) versus Q(s,a2), so a badly calibrated model can still induce an optimal policy; in general, though, a wrong model yields a suboptimal one.

concepts.name: Falling back to model-free RL does not fix everything
concepts.one_line: If the model is wrong because the world is non-Markov or the parametric class is misspecified, running Q-learning on the real data instead does not rescue you, because Q-learning assumes Markov too; likewise, reasoning about model uncertainty only addresses sampling error, never misspecification.

concepts.name: Predictive accuracy is not decision quality
concepts.one_line: Under limited data or limited model capacity, the model with the best likelihood can be worse for control, because capacity gets spent on high-variance nuisance features (the steam, the sunset) rather than the one feature that determines the right action (the water temperature) — a phenomenon the lecturer hit in intelligent tutoring systems.

concepts.name: Forward search
concepts.one_line: Given a model, plan from the current state only, by enumerating the branching tree of actions and possible next states out to depth H and backing values up to the root, ignoring the rest of the state space entirely.

concepts.name: Expectimax tree and its backup rule
concepts.one_line: Alternate two backup operations up the tree — a max over children at action nodes and an expectation weighted by P(s'|s,a) at chance nodes — which is exactly the Bellman optimality backup unrolled into a tree, with the model supplying both the transition probabilities and the rewards.

concepts.name: Expectimax is dynamic programming done wastefully
concepts.one_line: The tree recomputes the value of the same underlying state independently at every position it appears, refusing to alias transpositions, which is exactly why it is asymptotically worse than DP over the state space.

concepts.name: Minimax variant for two-player games
concepts.one_line: In an adversarial game the opponent's nodes take a min rather than an expectation over the same tree structure, so the Go version of everything in this lecture is minimax-shaped while the single-agent version is expectimax-shaped.

concepts.name: Simulation-based search
concepts.one_line: Instead of enumerating all futures, sample single complete trajectories from the model starting at the current state under some simulation policy, then apply Monte Carlo or TD learning to those simulated episodes.

concepts.name: Simple Monte Carlo search as one step of policy improvement
concepts.one_line: From the real current state, for each candidate first action run many rollouts under a fixed simulation policy pi to estimate Q^pi(s_t,a), then act greedily with respect to those estimates — a single policy-improvement step whose quality is capped by the quality of pi.

concepts.name: Expectimax complexity and the Go horizon
concepts.one_line: The forward-search tree has on the order of (|S||A|)^H leaves, so with a Go-like horizon of roughly 50 to 200 plies it is hopeless for anything but a trivial state space — this is the computational pressure that motivates MCTS.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo Tree Search
concepts.one_line: Grow a partial, deliberately lopsided approximation to the expectimax tree by repeating simulations from the root until a compute budget expires, expanding one node per simulation and concentrating effort on branches that currently look good; in the limit of infinite simulations the full tree is recovered.

concepts.name: Tree policy vs rollout (default) policy
concepts.one_line: Inside the already-expanded tree, actions are chosen by a statistics-driven tree policy that adapts as counts accumulate; beyond the tree frontier, where no statistics exist, a fixed cheap default policy (random in the vanilla version) plays out to termination.

concepts.name: Averaging returns as the node backup
concepts.one_line: MCTS stores at each node-action pair the plain average of the returns of all simulations passing through it — not a max and not an explicit expectation — and relies on the tree policy skewing the sampling distribution toward good actions so that these averages drift toward Q*.

concepts.name: Decision-time planning loop
concepts.one_line: All the tree building happens inside the agent's head before a single real action: plan, emit one action, observe the real s' and r, typically discard the tree, optionally refit the model on the new data, and start over from the new root.

concepts.name: UCT: upper confidence trees
concepts.one_line: Instantiate the tree policy by treating each tree node as its own independent bandit and selecting argmax over a of Q-hat(node,a) plus an optimism bonus that grows with the node's total visit count and shrinks with the count for that action, i.e. UCB1 applied recursively.

concepts.name: Nodes are distinct; it is a tree, not a graph
concepts.one_line: The same (s,a) reached via different paths gets separate statistics with no count sharing, even though the simulator is Markov, because merging transpositions into a graph complicates the implementation considerably.

concepts.name: Go as an RL problem
concepts.one_line: Go has fully known rules and reward — so this is planning, not learning, in the model sense — but a combinatorially enormous finite-horizon search space on a 19x19 board, with the simplest reward being a single sparse win/loss bit at the end and the value function therefore being the probability of winning from the current position.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo evaluation of a Go position
concepts.one_line: Fix a policy, play it out repeatedly against a (normally assumed stationary) opponent from the current board, and estimate the position's value as the empirical win fraction — two wins out of four rollouts gives 0.5.

concepts.name: MCTS in Go, iteration by iteration
concepts.one_line: First simulation picks an untried action at random and plays it out to a terminal win/loss; the second tries the other untried action; once all actions at a node have been tried, subsequent visits select by UCT, and the tree deepens preferentially along whichever branch is winning, with action-ordering heuristics buying large early savings.

concepts.name: Self-play
concepts.one_line: Playing the current agent against a slightly older copy of itself both solves the sparse-reward problem (a grandmaster opponent produces no signal for a very long time, whereas two weak players still generate wins and losses) and supplies an automatic curriculum that ratchets difficulty in step with skill; local optima are possible but any exploitable weakness should be findable with enough planning.

concepts.name: Why MCTS is attractive in practice
concepts.one_line: It is a highly selective best-first search — far more sample-efficient than full expectimax and strictly stronger than a single policy-improvement step — and it is both anytime (more compute simply means more rollouts) and easy to parallelize, which matters when the deadline may be one minute or eight hours.

concepts.name: Optimism is the wrong objective for planning
concepts.one_line: Optimism under uncertainty is justified in bandits because you actually pay for bad pulls, but in simulation you pay nothing for exploring a bad action — the only thing that matters is resolving the argmax at the root, so when one action already has a higher mean but overlapping uncertainty, sampling the *other* action separates the intervals faster; UCT will never do this, making it efficient but not optimal for search.

concepts.name: What makes RL distinctive (course wrap-up)
concepts.one_line: The closing synthesis: RL differs from supervised learning because the agent's own actions determine which (censored, non-i.i.d.) data it sees, and from planning because it must gather that data; the hardest practical skill is deciding how to formulate a problem as an MDP at all, and exploration-exploitation is the one challenge unique to the setting.

theorems_stated: Batch/infinite-replay tabular TD(0) on a fixed dataset converges to the value function of the certainty-equivalence MDP — the maximum-likelihood model estimated from that data, solved exactly.

Batch Monte Carlo policy evaluation on a fixed dataset converges to the value estimates minimizing mean squared error against the observed returns, and makes no Markov assumption; these estimates generally differ from the certainty-equivalence solution.
On the AB dataset the two disagree concretely: V(B)=0.75 under both, but V(A)=0.75 under batch TD and V(A)=0 under batch Monte Carlo.
The maximum-likelihood tabular model is the normalized empirical count P-hat(s'|s,a)=N(s,a,s')/N(s,a) with R-hat(s,a) the empirical mean reward.

The expectimax backup — max over actions at action layers, P(s'|s,a)-weighted expectation at state layers — is exactly the Bellman optimality operator unrolled over a depth-H tree, and computes the optimal value function of the model at the root.
A forward-search / expectimax tree has size on the order of (|S||A|)^H, i.e. it grows exponentially in the planning horizon.
Simple Monte Carlo search (estimate Q^pi(s_t,a) by rollouts for each a, then act greedily) implements exactly one step of policy improvement over the simulation policy pi.
MCTS recovers the complete expectimax tree, and hence the exact model-optimal action, in the limit of infinitely many simulations.
MCTS backups converge toward the true Q values even though they are plain averages, because the tree policy makes the action-sampling distribution concentrate on good actions over time.
With a fixed dynamics model and a changed reward function, an optimal policy for the new reward can be recomputed with zero additional environment interaction (zero-shot transfer).
Choosing an action requires only the ordering of Q(s,a1) versus Q(s,a2), so an inaccurate model can still induce the optimal policy.
Conditioning on the full observation history always satisfies the Markov property, but at the cost of vanishing data per estimated transition, especially as the horizon grows.
proofs_given: Numerical verification of the AB example rather than proof: V(B)=6/8=0.75 from six observed returns of 1 and two of 0, and V(A)=0+V(B)=0.75 under the TD/certainty-equivalence view (undiscounted) versus V(A)=0 under Monte Carlo, since A was visited exactly once with return 0.

Board derivation of the expectimax backup at a chance node: V(a) = P(s1|s0,a1)V(s1) + P(s2|s0,a1)V(s2), explicitly identified with the next-state expectation inside a Bellman backup, and the corresponding max at an action node.

Informal but complete argument that Monte Carlo run on data simulated from the certainty-equivalence model reproduces the batch-TD answer on the real data, by showing that the model can chain A-to-B with B-to-reward-1 into trajectories never observed in reality.
proofs_skipped: The batch TD = certainty-equivalence theorem is only recalled as a fact from an earlier lecture; no derivation of why the TD fixed point on replayed finite data equals the value function of the MLE MDP is given.

The batch Monte Carlo = minimum-MSE result is asserted with no derivation, and the follow-up claim (a student question) that a different loss or regularizer would move the Monte Carlo limit somewhere else is answered purely by intuition, with no characterization of which losses give which fixed points.
No consistency or rate result for the tabular MLE model: nothing on how fast P-hat concentrates, nor on when certainty-equivalence planning converges to the true optimal policy.

The central simulation-lemma-style result is entirely absent: how a model error epsilon in P-hat and R-hat translates into value error of the planned policy, and how that error amplifies with horizon (the usual epsilon*H^2 or epsilon/(1-gamma)^2 factors). 'Compounding errors' is stated qualitatively only. This is the single biggest gap for the academic notes.

The imitation-learning compounding-error result is invoked as an analogy without being stated: no O(epsilon*H^2) behavior-cloning regret bound, no DAgger guarantee, no formal statement of the distribution-shift argument being transferred to model-based RL.

Propagating model uncertainty into planning as optimism bonuses is asserted to work 'as in the exploration lectures', with no PAC-MDP or regret statement, no bonus construction, and no proof that the induced planning problem is optimistic.
The Hoeffding-interval construction for reward-model confidence is named but never instantiated (no failure probability, no union bound over state-action pairs, no dependence on N(s,a)).

The claim that a model with higher predictive likelihood can be strictly worse for decision-making under restricted capacity or data is supported only by the tea-kettle anecdote; no formal statement, no constructed counterexample MDP, and no reference to decision-aware / value-equivalent model learning results.

The claim that a wrong model can still yield an optimal policy is left without conditions: no action-gap argument, no statement of how small the model error must be relative to the Q-value margin for the argmax to be preserved.

The tree-size bound (|S||A|)^H is asserted without a counting argument, and the complementary fact — that merging identical states turns the same computation into O(|S||A|H) dynamic programming — is only gestured at as 'not as efficient as DP'.

The identification of the expectimax backup with the Bellman optimality operator is asserted by analogy on the board rather than proved, and no contraction/optimality argument for depth-H truncated search (nor the effect of truncating at horizon H) is given.

The policy improvement theorem underlying 'simple Monte Carlo search is one step of policy improvement' is never restated or proved, and — more importantly — nothing is said about approximate policy improvement: with finitely many rollouts you only have noisy Q^pi estimates, and no condition is given under which the greedy step still improves on pi.

No convergence analysis of UCT whatsoever: the Kocsis-Szepesvari result that UCT's failure probability at the root decays and that its value estimates converge to the minimax/expectimax value is not stated, let alone proved. 'In the limit you will fill in the entire tree' is the only guarantee offered.
The UCB1 regret bound itself is only referred back to ('same thing as what we've done before'); the bonus term is not even written down explicitly in this lecture.

The justification that averaging returns at a node converges to Q* is hand-waved as 'the sampling distribution converges'. The genuine technical obstacle — that returns at an interior node are NOT i.i.d. draws from a stationary bandit, because the subtree policy below it keeps improving — is acknowledged as 'a little weird' but never analyzed. This non-stationarity is exactly what makes UCT's analysis hard and belongs in the notes.

No analysis of the tree-versus-graph choice: not sharing statistics across transpositions of the same state is dismissed on implementation grounds, with no statement of the statistical efficiency lost or of when transposition tables are sound.

The critique of optimism for planning is delivered as a picture, not a theorem: no formal distinction between cumulative regret and simple regret / best-arm identification, no sample-complexity statement for identifying the root argmax, and no alternative algorithm (successive rejects, sequential halving, LUCB) named or analyzed. The lecture explicitly says 'it's not clear bandits at each node is optimal' and stops there.

Self-play claims — that it escapes sparse reward, supplies a curriculum, and converges toward strong play — are entirely informal. No game-theoretic statement (fictitious play, Nash convergence, exploitability), and the local-optimum concern raised by a student is answered with 'if there's something you could exploit, enough planning should find it' with no supporting argument.

The anytime and parallelizability properties of MCTS are asserted with no characterization of the anytime error curve (how root action quality improves with simulation count) and no discussion of the loss from parallel/virtual-loss variants.
The comparative claim that MCTS is 'way more sample efficient than expectimax' and 'much better than one step of policy improvement' is given no bound in either direction.
The function-approximation-error versus estimation-error tradeoff for history-conditioned models is described qualitatively; no bias-variance decomposition or sample-complexity statement is offered.
The claim that reusing model-generated samples to refit the model produces overconfidence ('confirmation bias') is intuitive only — no statement of how the variance estimate is corrupted.
algorithms: Tabular maximum-likelihood model estimation: P-hat(s'|s,a) = N(s,a,s')/N(s,a), R-hat(s,a) = mean of observed rewards at (s,a); then solve the resulting MDP exactly (certainty-equivalence planning).

The generic model-based RL loop: real experience -> fit reward/transition model -> plan (DP, Q-learning, policy search, or search) -> emit next action -> execute -> repeat, with the planner required only to produce the next action.

Sample-based planning (Dyna-style): draw synthetic (s,a,r,s') transitions from the fitted model and run any model-free learner (Monte Carlo or TD) over the simulated stream, optionally replaying it many times.

Forward search / expectimax tree search: expand all actions and all next states from the current state to depth H (or termination), then back up with max at action nodes and P(s'|s,a)-weighted expectation at state nodes. Two-player variant substitutes min at the opponent's nodes (minimax).

Simulation-based search: from the current real state, sample single complete trajectories from the model under a simulation policy until termination or horizon H, then apply Monte Carlo or TD learning to those simulated episodes.

Simple Monte Carlo search (the rollout algorithm): for each action a available at s_t, run K rollouts of (a, then simulation policy pi) through the model, average the returns to estimate Q^pi(s_t,a), and take argmax — one policy-improvement step.

Monte Carlo Tree Search: repeat until the compute budget expires — (1) descend the existing tree from the root using the tree policy; (2) expand a new node at the frontier; (3) play out to termination or horizon H with the cheap default/rollout policy; (4) back up the return by updating the running average and visit count at every node on the path. Then act at the root, discard or reuse the tree, observe the real transition, optionally refit the model, and re-plan.

UCT tree policy: at each in-tree node treat the action choice as an independent bandit and select argmax_a [ Q-hat(node,a) + c*sqrt(ln N(node) / N(node,a)) ], forcing every untried action to be tried once first; action-ordering heuristics for which untried action to try first were historically a large practical win.
Monte Carlo position evaluation in Go: play the current policy out from the board against a stationary opponent many times and take the empirical win fraction as V(s).
Self-play training: use the agent's own recent policy as the opponent, so that reward signal exists from the very first games and opponent strength tracks learner strength as an automatic curriculum.
notation_introduced: P-hat(s'|s,a) and R-hat(s,a): the learned/estimated transition and reward models, assumed Markov and conditionally independent given (s,a)
N(s,a), N(s,a,s'): visit counts used both for tabular MLE model estimation and for tree-node statistics in UCT
certainty-equivalence model: the MLE MDP built from a finite dataset, treated as if it were the true world
H: planning horizon / rollout depth / depth at which the search tree is truncated (roughly 50-200 for Go)
(|S||A|)^H: order of the number of leaves in a depth-H expectimax tree
Q^pi(s_t, a): value of taking a at s_t then following the simulation policy pi thereafter — the quantity estimated by simple Monte Carlo search
Q-hat(node, a): the running average of simulated returns passing through a specific tree node and action; deliberately per-node, not per-state
tree policy vs rollout (default) policy: the two distinct action-selection rules used inside and beyond the expanded tree
expectimax tree (max over actions, expectation over next states) vs minimax tree (max for you, min for the opponent)
V(A), V(B): the two state values in the AB example (0.75/0.75 for batch TD, 0/0.75 for batch Monte Carlo)
UCT bonus: c*sqrt(ln N(node)/N(node,a)) — the UCB1 exploration term reused as the tree policy
notation_hazards: The captions consistently render 'expectimax' as 'expecting max' or truncate it to 'expecti-'; every such occurrence means expectimax.

The UCT exploration bonus is never written down. The transcript garbles it into 'a discount factor that often looks like the number of times you've been in that particular node' — the intended object is the UCB1 term c*sqrt(ln N(s)/N(s,a)), which grows with the parent's total visits and shrinks with that action's own count. It is not a discount factor.

Tree size is spoken as 'S times A to the H', which is ambiguous. For a tree alternating action layers and state layers to depth H the leaf count is on the order of (|S||A|)^H, and that is what the Go horizon argument requires; read it that way, not as |S|*|A|^H.

The AB example counts are misstated mid-sentence ('six times we got a reward of 1, and then we got started in state B and got a reward of 0'), and only reconciled later when she says six 1s and two 0s. The correct Sutton and Barto batch is 8 episodes: A-then-B with reward 0 once, then B with reward 1 six times and B with reward 0 once; B is visited 8 times total giving V(B)=6/8=0.75.
She writes 'the reward here is equal to whichever of those was bigger' when performing a max at an action node; she means the *value* (or Q) at that node, not a reward.
She writes V(s,a1) > V(s,a2) when discussing which action to prefer; that object is Q(s,a), not V(s).
The AB example is undiscounted (gamma=1) and this is stated only in passing ('in this case there's no discounting'); V(A)=0+V(B) depends on it.
The example is repeatedly called an MDP but she corrects herself that with a single action it is really a Markov reward process — policy evaluation, not control.

Caption garbles worth silently fixing: 'prior metric estimates' means 'parametric estimates'; 'sensored data' in the wrap-up means 'censored data'; 'improvisional network' means something like 'provisional/neural network'; 'SCPD' is Stanford Center for Professional Development (admin only).

Terminology drift versus Sutton and Barto: what this lecture calls 'simple Monte Carlo search' S&B call rollout algorithms; what it calls 'simulation-based search' S&B group under decision-time planning; S&B's 'sample models' vs 'distribution models' distinction is used implicitly here but never named.

She says the reward of the bandit at a tree node is 'the full rollout from that node' — i.e. the return, not a one-step reward — and explicitly contrasts this with TD-style bootstrapping. Vanilla MCTS as taught here is pure Monte Carlo backup, no bootstrapping.

'In the limit you will fill in the entire expectimax tree' is a statement about MCTS's asymptotic completeness, not a claim that it does so efficiently; she immediately notes this never happens in practice.

animation_candidates.what: Batch TD versus batch Monte Carlo on the same eight AB episodes, converging to V(A)=0.75 and V(A)=0 respectively
animation_candidates.why: The whole point is that two consistent estimators disagree on identical data because one assumes Markov and one does not. Static text states the numbers; animation can show the eight episode strips, then show TD's update literally routing evidence from B's returns back through the A->B edge while Monte Carlo's update touches only the single A trajectory. The disagreement becomes mechanical rather than asserted.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Eight episode strips on the left; two synchronized backup diagrams on the right, with arrows lighting up on each replay pass and the two value counters diverging

animation_candidates.what: Expectimax tree explosion versus MCTS's asymmetric partial tree at an identical simulation budget
animation_candidates.why: The (|S||A|)^H bound and the phrase 'highly selective best-first search' are the two claims the lecture leans on hardest, and both are fundamentally geometric. Side-by-side growth under a shared budget counter makes the sample-efficiency argument visible in a way no equation does.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Split screen: left tree fans out uniformly and greys out when the budget runs out at shallow depth; right tree grows a thin deep spine down the promising branch, with node radius scaled by visit count

animation_candidates.what: One full MCTS iteration in four phases — selection, expansion, rollout, backup — with N and Q updating on every node of the path
animation_candidates.why: MCTS is a loop of four distinct operations on shared mutable state, and the transcript's step-by-step Go walkthrough is verbally sequential for a reason. Learners routinely conflate the tree policy with the rollout policy; animating the moment the traversal crosses the tree frontier and switches policy fixes that confusion permanently.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Single tree, four coloured phases in sequence, with a visible frontier line where the policy switches from UCT to random, and counters ticking up along the backup path

animation_candidates.what: The UCT bonus term decaying as visit counts accumulate, and the selected action flipping
animation_candidates.why: The lecture never writes the bonus down at all, so this is where the animation does real repair work. Watching Q-hat + c*sqrt(ln N / N(a)) for three actions, seeing the bonus collapse at different rates, and seeing the argmax switch two or three times before settling, makes optimism-under-uncertainty concrete instead of a slogan.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Three stacked bars per action decomposed into exploitation term and bonus term, animating over simulation count, with the selection marker jumping between them

animation_candidates.what: Optimism versus value of information: why sampling the apparently worse arm can resolve the argmax faster
animation_candidates.why: This is the lecture's most original point and it is delivered as a hand-drawn sketch in about ninety seconds. It is also the point most likely to be misremembered as 'UCT is wrong'. An animation that runs both sampling strategies against the same two uncertain values and shows which one separates the intervals first delivers the argument honestly and in seconds.
animation_candidates.visual_form: Two horizontal confidence intervals over Q(a1) and Q(a2) side by side; two parallel runs, one always sampling a1 (intervals barely move relative to each other) and one sampling a2 (its interval collapses and the ordering becomes certain), with a sample counter

animation_candidates.why: 'Compounding errors' is the lecture's hand-wave and the single largest proof gap. Showing two trajectories drifting apart, with the per-step gap accumulating into a horizon-scaled value gap, motivates the simulation lemma before any algebra appears.

code_experiment_candidates: Reproduce the AB example end to end: build the 8-episode batch, run tabular batch TD(0) to convergence and batch first-visit Monte Carlo to convergence, and verify V(A)=0.75 vs 0 and V(B)=0.75 in both.

Build the certainty-equivalence MDP from the same batch by counting, solve it with value iteration, and confirm it matches the batch-TD fixed point exactly — the lecture's stated equivalence, checked numerically.

Sweep dataset size on a small random MDP: certainty-equivalence planning versus Q-learning on the same trajectories, plotting policy value against number of real transitions, to expose the sample-efficiency advantage of the model-based route.

Empirical simulation lemma: inject controlled bias/noise into a learned transition model and plot the value loss of the planned policy against model error and against horizon H, recovering the missing epsilon*H^2 scaling that the lecture only gestures at.
Implement expectimax and MCTS on the same small domain (tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, or a chain MDP) and plot decision quality versus nodes expanded, directly measuring the (|S||A|)^H wall.

UCT exploration-constant sweep: measure root simple regret, deepest node depth, and tree asymmetry as a function of c, including c=0 (pure greedy, collapses) and very large c (uniform, degenerates to flat search).
Simple Monte Carlo search versus MCTS at an identical rollout budget, and additionally versus MCTS with a strong rollout policy, quantifying 'strictly better than one step of policy improvement'.
MCTS anytime curve: root action quality plotted against number of simulations, to characterize the anytime property the lecture asserts without describing.

Directly test the lecture's own critique: at the root of a small tree, compare UCB/UCT against a best-arm-identification allocation (sequential halving or successive rejects) under a fixed simulation budget, measuring simple regret rather than cumulative regret. This is the most valuable experiment on the list because it turns a ninety-second hand-drawn objection into a measured result.
Non-stationarity probe: log the sequence of returns backed up through one interior MCTS node and test it for stationarity, exhibiting why the per-node bandit assumption is not literally satisfied.

Transposition sharing: run MCTS as a tree versus as a DAG with merged transpositions on a domain with many identical states, measuring the statistical efficiency the lecture waves off as an implementation detail.

Decision-aware versus likelihood-trained model: construct a small MDP where one feature determines the optimal action and many high-variance nuisance features dominate the likelihood, fit a capacity-limited model by MLE, and show it achieves better held-out likelihood but worse control than a model trained on a decision-relevant objective — the tea-kettle claim, made falsifiable.
Confirmation-bias demonstration: refit the model on its own generated samples across several rounds and track the collapse of the (nominal) confidence intervals against the unchanged true error.
dated_or_superseded: The framing that model-based deep RL 'hasn't seen as much success' is a 2019 statement and no longer holds. The Dreamer line (v1-v3), PlaNet, TD-MPC/TD-MPC2, and MuZero's learned latent dynamics have all since demonstrated strong model-based deep RL, including on domains the lecture implies are out of reach.

The MCTS presented here is the pre-AlphaZero form: a random or heuristic rollout policy providing the leaf estimate. AlphaZero (2017) replaced rollouts entirely with a learned value network and replaced the UCT bonus with a policy-prior-weighted PUCT term; MuZero (2019/2020) further removed the requirement of a known simulator by learning a latent dynamics model, so the lecture's clean division between 'known rules' Go and 'unknown model' RL has dissolved.

The lecture's own critique — that optimism is the wrong objective for search because you do not suffer for simulated mistakes — was subsequently addressed head on by Gumbel MuZero / policy-improvement-based search (Danihelka et al., 2022), which replaces UCT root selection with sequential halving and reframes search as a guaranteed policy-improvement operator. Modern notes should present the critique alongside its resolution rather than as an open puzzle.

'Bayesian deep neural networks are hard to train' is accurate for 2019 but the field largely routed around the problem: deep ensembles (PETS-style probabilistic ensembles), bootstrapped/randomized value functions, and quantile/distributional models are now the standard practical uncertainty estimators in model-based RL.
Treating transposition merging as an implementation nuisance is dated; transposition tables and DAG-structured search are routine in modern engines.

The largest 2026 gap for this particular reader: MCTS has migrated wholesale into LLM inference-time search — tree-of-thought, MCTS-guided decoding, reward-model-guided and process-reward-guided rollouts, AlphaProof-style formal search, and MCTS over agentic workflow graphs (AFlow itself). None of that literature existed at lecture time, and it is the bridge from this lecture to current work.

Self-play is presented purely through two-player board games. Its 2020s descendants — self-play for LLM alignment, self-improvement loops, synthetic-data flywheels, and adversarial/debate setups — are absent, as are the known failure modes (mode collapse, model collapse from training on generated data), which sharpen the lecture's own unresolved 'confirmation bias' and local-optima worries.

relevance_to_user_research.why: Not critical, but genuinely more relevant than most of this course, for four concrete reasons. (1) MCTS is the literal search backbone of AFlow, which the user reproduced end to end — AFlow searches workflow space with MCTS, so this lecture is the algorithmic foundation of a paper they already own, and the tree-policy/rollout-policy split, the averaging backup, the per-node bandit treatment, and the anytime budget property are exactly the knobs in that search. (2) The lecture's most explicitly stated design principle maps directly onto node-level fidelity assignment: the planner does not need a full value function or a global policy, only the next action at the current state. Fidelity assignment per node in a DAG under a remaining-budget state is exactly decision-time planning — plan, commit one node's fidelity, observe the partial trace, re-plan — rather than learning a global policy over workflows. (3) The closing critique is the single most actionable idea in the lecture for this user. When searching offline over fidelity assignments under a compute budget, the objective is simple regret (find the best configuration) not cumulative regret (avoid paying for bad probes), because probing a bad assignment during search costs only compute, not deployed accuracy. UCB/UCT is therefore the wrong allocation rule at the root, and best-arm-identification methods (sequential halving, successive rejects, and in the modern literature Gumbel-MuZero-style root selection) are the right ones. That is a defensible, citable methodological improvement over an AFlow-style UCT search and is directly publishable-adjacent. (4) The 'higher predictive accuracy can mean worse decisions' point translates cleanly: a query-difficulty predictor trained to predict task accuracy is not the same object as a predictor trained to make the weak-versus-strong fidelity decision, and the lecture supplies the intuition (though no theory) for training decision-aware. Against relevance: the two-player Go material, minimax backups, and self-play are irrelevant here; the AB example is review; and the lecture offers no bound or guarantee the user could cite, since every result they might want — UCT convergence, simple versus cumulative regret, the simulation lemma — is asserted without proof.
